News.title: How do you pronounce Storm Boelo and what does it mean?
News.content:
Next

STORM Boelo has triggered two amber warnings and several yellow warnings as it hits the UK with wind and rain.

A roaring 170mph transatlantic jet stream has forced weather chiefs to issue severe Amber “danger to life” warnings for parts of the country.



Millions of Brits face a weekend washout with ferocious 80mph gales threatening to rip down power lines and uproot trees.

Named Storm Boelo, it comes directly after 2026/2027’s first, Storm Austen.



How do you pronounce Boelo?

The storm’s pronunciation was officially confirmed by the Met Office, because it is so rare – and is said using two syllables – “Boo-loh”

What does it mean?

Boelo is a very rare, traditional regional name meaning “brave” or “strong” – a traditional male first name with roots to the Netherlands.

The name was submitted to the Dutch National Weather Service (KNMI) by a man from the Netherlands.

His family had proudly passed the name through generations, even when it nearly became extinct.



The UK Met Office and the KNMI team up every year to name the storms.

Because Boelo is the second storm of the Brits’ 2026/2027 season, it took the Dutch entry on the alphabetical list.

When will the storm hit?

The storm will begin to hit Britain this afternoon, and has already arrived in the outer bands of the UK.

Yellow warnings were given at midday across Scotland, Northern Ireland, Northern England and Wales.

Wind speeds are ramping up, and huge torrents of rainfall are already spreading across the country.



The storm will be at its peak tonight, with a severe amber “danger to life” wind warning set for 9PM tonight.

This warning follows destructive 70 to 80mph gales which will batter the coast and high grounds this evening.

The destructive weather will continue through the weekend, and the amber warning will remain in place for 24 hours.

What is the name of the next storm?

The next storm will be called “Storm Chloe” – following the alphabetical list co-created by the UK Met Office and KNMI.

Chloe will be the third name given to storms in the season of 2026/2027.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

Forecasters are already tracking another deep area of low pressure right behind Boelo, meaning Storm Chloe could be with Brits as early as Tuesday.

News.title: Early release prisoners ‘handed tents’ as probation service ‘runs out of housing & puts freed lags onto streets’
News.content:
Next

EARLY release prisoners are being “handed tents” after the probation service “ran out of housing”, according to reports.

One probation office has given 100 tents to homeless lags leaving prison over the past year, but its supplies have reportedly run dry – forcing freed convicts onto the streets.



Probation officers are reportedly requesting tents from charities to distribute to lags, as nearly one in six convicts are left homeless upon release, The Telegraph reports.

Prisoners are supposed to be found suitable accommodation before the release, yet a probation source claimed this system was “a mess”, and they could not even find hostels to take the prisoners.



The release system allows prisoners to be freed as little as a third of the way into their sentences to ease prison over-crowding.

The first set of 1,350 crooks were released from October 1, 2026, over the space of two weeks.



Data from Nacro, a charity supporting ex-prisoners, show that two-thirds of people who leave prison homeless reoffend within a year.

Andy Burnham‘s grand plan also has prison bosses reporting a high likelihood of lags being released by mistake.



Probation officers have reportedly been left struggling to find homes for ex-prisoners after the Prime Minister announced the restarting of the scheme.

A probation officer said they usually have a year to find a prisoner housing, but the early releases have minimised house-hunting for convicts to a mere couple of weeks.

A whistle-blower told The Telegraph: “The process takes about a month and a half, then you suddenly get an update saying they will be out next week and need a probation hostel.

“In my computer I have 30 cases who are expected to come out in the next three years, then a load of them were suddenly shunted forward to October-December 2026.

“Now I’ve passed the point where I can make the relevant referrals for them, so everything is coming to a head at once.



They added: “I’ve had to say to someone, ‘I’ve got a tent, go and live in a park for a bit.’ You can tell them to go to the council, but they can’t help either because there’s a housing crisis.”

The housing shortage has meant that the number of released prisoners sleeping rough has more than doubled since 2022-23.

15.9 per cent of prisoners released are left homeless, causing fears they will reoffend.



Earlier this month, police forces admitted that many who had been freed returned to prison within the hour or day.

Labour is refusing to put a number on how many prisoners are being sent back.

It was also revealed today by The Telegraph that nearly half of the prison places freed by the early release scheme were already filled within 10 days.

Ten per cent of the first 700 released have already gone back to jail.

Data revealed by The Telegraph shows 420 people were recalled in the week the system started.



Nick Timothy, the shadow justice secretary: “Labour’s shambolic early release scheme is putting thousands of criminals back on to the streets, and their chaotic lack of planning means many released prisoners are now sleeping in tents.

“Angela Rayner promised to get all rough sleepers off the streets by Christmas, but early release will make the problem even worse.”

“We know rough sleeping makes reoffending more likely, so this once again shows that Labour’s early release crisis is putting public safety at risk.”

Zia Yusuf, Reform UK’s prisons spokesman, said: “Labour is releasing prisoners early and continues to allow foreign nationals to clog up our housing.

“The two together create this farce. Reform will deport all foreigners in our jails and end early release for good.”



Over the next 10 months, a grand total of 4,500 prisoners are planned to be freed under Labour’s scheme – including those who have served more than 12 years in jail.

Prisoners who are allowed to be released include violent offenders, domestic abusers, and burglars.

Demand for tents had increased in the 18 months, according to a whistle-blower, ever since the introduction of Labour’s early release scheme.

They said: “We used to have like 100 in a room and people would come in and say, ‘You don’t have anywhere to stay, here’s a homeless kit with a tent and water bottle.’

“Over the last 18 months or so there’s been frustration that we don’t have enough housing kits to give out, because while it is awful, the alternative is to sleep on a street corner.”



A Government spokesperson told The Sun: “It is not Government policy to provide tents to people being released from prison who are at risk of being homeless.

“Tents are not, and should never be, an acceptable housing solution.

“The Prime Minister has made it clear that the Government is committed to ending rough sleeping.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

“Backed by record investment in probation services, we’re helping those leaving prison to secure accommodation and move into work, as we work to halve prison leaver homelessness by the end of this Parliament, reduce reoffending, and keep the public safe.

“We’re also investing £47m in grassroots homelessness charities and community organisations, helping vulnerable people off the streets and into settled accommodation, alongside a national drive to end rough sleeping.”

News.title: How Chris Martin’s great-grandfather invented daylight saving: Coldplay star’s link to clocks changing
News.content:
Next

CHRIS Martin is known for singing about time through his band’s hit 2002 song, Clocks.

But the Coldplay frontman’s family has a long historical connection to timepieces.



The singer is actually the great-great-grandson of William Willett, the British builder who first campaigned for changing the clocks, and what would become known as British Summer Time.

Who was William Willett?

Willett was born in Farnham, Surrey, in August 1856, and worked for his father’s building firm, Willett Building Services.



The company built houses in parts of London and the south of England, including Chelsea and Hove, East Sussex.

While Willett made his living from building, his legacy remains the system of daylight saving now used in many countries.



How did he come up with daylight saving?

Willett conceived the idea during an early morning horse ride in Kent in the early 1900s.

As he rode, he noticed that many houses still had their blinds drawn, even though the sun was already up.

This struck the builder as a waste of daylight, and in 1907, he published a pamphlet at his own expense called The Waste of Daylight to encourage people to change their habits.

In the pamphlet, Willett wrote: “For nearly half the year the sun shines for several hours each day, while we are asleep, and is rapidly nearing the horizon when we reach home after the work of the day is over.”



His plan proposed setting clocks forward by 80 minutes in four steps of 20 minutes on Sundays in April, and then reversing them in September.

He argued this would save the country £2.5million in fuel and lighting costs, while giving people more evening light for outdoor recreation.

Did he live to see his idea become law?

Willett campaigned for his proposal, gaining support from figures including Winston Churchill.

A daylight saving bill was first introduced to the House of Commons in 1908, but the idea faced opposition from farmers and other groups.

Parliament rejected the bill, and Willett did not live to see the system introduced. He died of influenza in March 1915, aged 58.



But his clock changing ideas lived on, spurred by the economic pressures of the First World War.

Countries found themselves needing to conserve coal and electricity, and Germany was the first to introduce daylight saving in April 1916.

Britain followed just a month later by passing the Summer Time Act on May 17.

Is he really Chris Martin’s ancestor?

Yes, William Willett really is Coldplay frontman Chris Martin‘s great-great-grandfather.

Nearly 90 years after Willett died, Martin and Coldplay achieved fame with the single Clocks, which became one of their most successful tracks.



It was included as part of the band’s second studio album, 2002’s A Rush of Blood to the Head, which also included the track Daylight.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Martin has not explicitly said that the songs were written about his ancestor, and it could all just be a coincidence, though the link remains a point of interest for fans.

Today, Willett is commemorated with a blue plaque on his former home in Chislehurst, Kent, and a memorial sundial in Petts Wood that is permanently set to British Summer Time.

News.title: Death-defying Brit solo kayaking ‘world’s deadliest waterway’ in croc-infested jungle reveals most gruesome threat
News.content:
Next

A DEATH-DEFYING Brit is facing off with deadly crocodiles and Ebola as he braves one of the world’s most dangerous waterways in an inflatable kayak.

Extreme adventurer and TikTok phenomenon Ash Dykes is over halfway-through his daring 700-mile journey through the Congo River Basin and has already encountered a series of terrifying obstacles.



The 35-year-old from Wales has faced countless challenges navigating the densest and most dangerous jungle known to man since his mission began on October 3.

Detailing the intense struggles of navigating such a daunting and dangerous task, Ash told The Sun he and his team have run out of fresh water, are battling extreme heat, and are being eaten alive by flies and mosquitoes while navigating murky croc and hippo-infested waters.



He said: “It’s kind of like picking your poison.

“Be outside with the mozzies which carry malaria and dengue fever, and the blood-sucking tsetse flies which can cause river blindness and sickness or be inside the tent sweating through the night.

read more in World News THE ENEMY UNDERFOOT Inside the eerie 2ft high tunnels where Viet Cong guerrillas hid



“Dehydration is a real problem as our water filter broke.”

The Congo Basin has a notorious reputation of being a deadly waterway deep in sub-Saharan Africa.

In 2010, South African adventurer Hendrik Coetzee was killed in a horror crocodile attack as he attempted to become the first person to navigate the basin.

It is also the deepest waterway in the world at 720ft and runs through the Congo Rainforest – the second-largest tropical rainforest on Earth.



Ash, already a five-time World Record holder for a number of daring expeditions, has been planning the adventure for months but has spoken with dozens of people who have called it an “impossible mission”.

He has gained more than seven million followers across all his social media platforms in the last year alone but says he knows some people want to see him fail.

The brave Brit said: “You’ve got the 10 to 20 per cent of people that are just watching us in the hope that one of us dies via attack by hippo or crocodile.



“But if we’re not being attacked by snakes, silverbacks, crocodiles, or hippos, they say it’s boring.”

Directly responding to critics, Ash said: “My message to that is I’m an experienced explorer. I’m a five-time world first record holder. I’ve achieved far greater more difficult expeditions before.

“Don’t mistake the due diligence and preparation that I put into the mission as this being a boring place.

“It’s very dangerous. I’m just able to mitigate those risks by speaking to the locals.”

Despite his confidence, Ash did admit: “Seeing a hippo or a croc, if it’s too close, could potentially be the end of one of us.”



Another major potential issue is Ebola.

The Democratic Republic of the Congo is currently fighting a significant outbreak of the Bundibugyo virus strain of the deadly disease.

At least 4,600 people have died in the DRC during the current Ebola outbreak.



While Ash won’t go directly through the DRC he will traverse through Uganda which has 20 confirmed Ebola cases and Central Africa Republic and the Republic of the Congo.

As well as the physical struggles, Ash and his team are also battling long days with poor communication to the outside world.

On Wednesday his team shared a worrying statement saying they hadn’t heard from Ash for over 16 hours.

The team said the rare silence from Ash was “concerning”.

The influencer, who has a loving fiancée at home, routinely sparks fears with his loved ones over his safety.



Ash continued: “They’re very proud but they’re also very concerned. I need to keep them a little more up to date.

“They were really concerned with the fact I hadn’t touched base and I was just paddling through the night and my girlfriend was quite distraught which was heartbreaking to see.

“She thought something had happened.”

All of these major issues have resulted in the basin having severe Level 4 “Do Not Travel” advisories placed on the surrounding areas.

Since he was a young boy, the 35-year-old has always dreamt of leading a life of extreme action and adventure.



He has crossed Mongolia’s Gobi Desert unsupported and alone – dragging his own supplies.

Ash also walked for five days while riddled with malaria in Madagascar.

Doctors warned him if he had arrived just a few hours later, he would have gone into a coma.



In Dykes’ most recent mission, he completed a world first by being part of the first team to travel the Coppename River in the Surinamese Amazon from source to sea on foot and by kayak.

He explained: “I’ve always wanted to be this guy, you know, like an action man.

“Drop me from a helicopter, drop me in the water, I’ll scuba dive, I can fight, drop me in the jungle or the desert, I love it.

“The Congo Basin I’ve put off for many years now because it’s a scary place.

“At night, some of the sounds that I’ve heard have been quite haunting. The other night I heard a big deep vibrational growling noise and I didn’t know what it was.



“We had a forest elephant close to camp which sounded like a leopard.

“This is the ultimate bucket list and childhood dream that I’ve put off for many years and now I’m getting it done.”

The 1,425ft expedition down the Sangha River into the Congo Basin is the first of six missions titled “Project Six,” where Ash will visit six of the hardest places to reach on Earth.

He said: “I have already lost 5kg and I’m only halfway through and I’ve got the toughest section to come.

“I will probably be around 60kg when I return. I’ve got to do my best to put on as much weight as possible and make sure I check for parasites.



“The next location will be 30 to 40 degrees fahrenheit colder than where I am now; I’m going to have to adapt fast.”

The Congo Basin is riddled with folklore and enchanting myths about what lies at the bottom of the deep river.

Dykes said: “You have the ‘Mami Watta,’ which is the mermaid and the myth around that and ‘Mokele-Mbembe,’ which is like the Loch Ness monster of the Congo Basin.

“I’m not really superstitious but it’s nice that they still have those legends and myths.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

The extreme athlete is planning to reward himself with a well-deserved fizzy drink when he reaches the finish line in Mossaka, Uganda.



He said: “I could imagine craving something really cold, really fizzy, like either a Coke or a Sprite.”

News.title: Met admits force DID send letter to Meg about ‘child sex abuse’ claims against dad – but didn’t share it with other cops
News.content:
Next

THE Met Police has confirmed it DID send a letter to Meghan making “disturbing” allegations about her dad – but didn’t share it with other forces.

Scotland Yard has referred itself to the police watchdog over the letter, which allegedly detailed accusations against Thomas Markle Snr – as first revealed in a world exclusive investigation by The Sun.



We broke the story this week that that the Duchess’ estranged father, 82, is being probed by cops over a vast hoard of alleged child abuse images.

Meghan later revealed she was aware of previous allegations after being sent a “troubling and disturbing” letter by the Met.



The force originally said they were carrying out an internal inquiry to confirm the royal protection unit passed on a letter to the Duchess.

And now, in a bombshell statement, the Met Police has finally confirmed the information was passed onto the Sussexes.

The force admitted they did not share details of the letter with other law enforcement agencies.

Meghan previously told The Sun in a statement she had been assured that these claims were being investigated.



Markle Snr has vehemently denied possessing child sex images after The Sun’s world exclusive investigation.

A Met Police spokesperson today said: “Following a thorough review of Met Police systems and records, we have confirmed that in January 2019, we received a letter containing a number of claims about alleged offending outside the United Kingdom.

“It was sent to the MPS Protection Command to raise concerns in relation to the security of the Duchess of Sussex.

“The letter was reviewed and a decision was made that it should be passed to the office of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex for their awareness.

“The details of the allegations in the letter were not shared with other law enforcement agencies.



“The MPS is reviewing the handling of this matter in 2019 and considering whether a referral to the IOPC is necessary to review our approach.”

Meghan told The Sun she was advised not to speak out so as not to risk jeopardising a legal case.

And sources close to the Duchess say she was left frustrated for eight years by “not being able to speak openly”.

They say Meghan had trusted that “the appropriate authorities would do their job”.

And she was said to be horrified after we revealed “hundreds, if not thousands of child sex images” from her father’s devices had been seized by Filipino authorities.



Thomas Snr is being investigated over a huge stash of child sex images after being reported to police by his own son.

He is alleged to have kept the sickening hoard at his home in the Philippines, where Thomas Jnr claims he found it.

Thomas Jnr, Meghan’s half-brother, reported their father to detectives in the Philippines after allegedly finding the material at his home in the city of Cebu.

Markle Snr had been forced to leave the house in May and return to the US after suffering a stroke and a blood clot which led to the amputation of his left leg.

But he is alleged to have abandoned the enormous stash of vile content packed into storage boxes.



Thomas Jnr, 60, told police he unearthed the horrific pictures and videos mixed up with innocent family mementos.

He also contacted FBI investigators in the US who are also set to launch their own probe.

But Markle Snr said his accuser was ­peddling “sick lies” and even claimed the huge haul had somehow been planted among abandoned belongings.

But Thomas Jnr — who packed four boxes of horrifying images into his car boot to take to cops — insisted: “It’s incredible that he is still in denial.

“I’m sure the huge piles of ­evidence I’ve taken to the police today will reveal the truth once the police experts examine it.”

The Sun has seen the letter ­written by someone close to Thomas Markle Snr who cannot be revealed for privacy reasons.

In her statement Meghan described the reason she “kept her distance” since learning of the ­allegations was to “protect” her two children Archie, seven, and five-year-old Lilibet.

News.title: Ebola kills ANOTHER victim in Kenya as woman, 65, becomes country’s second fatal case deadly disease’s outbreak
News.content:
DEADLY VIRUS Ebola kills ANOTHER victim in Kenya as woman, 65, becomes country’s second fatal case deadly disease’s outbreak







Next

EBOLA has killed another victim in Kenya, marking the country’s second ever fatal case of the deadly disease.

A 65-year-old woman, a close relative of the first victim, has died after developing symptoms while quarantining.



It comes after a 40-year-old Kenyan man died in Nairobi late on Monday after travelling from the Democratic Republic of Congo, where the virus has already killed more than 4,000 people.

The latest Kenyan victim started showing symptoms 10 days ago and was treated at an infectious disease unit in Nairobi.



Medics did everything they could to save her, but she died Friday evening, Kenya’s health ministry said.

Seven Ebola patients are still receiving treatment at two isolation facilities, the health ministry said, but no new infections have been reported.

It said all the cases were within “one cluster, with no evidence of community spread”.

The man who died on October 5 was Kenya’s first-ever recorded case of Ebola and has sparked an urgent hunt for dozens of people who may have come into contact with him.

Authorities identified some 135 contacts and locked down 118 of those.

Eight of them tested positive while in quarantine.



They included the latest victim, four health workers and three close family members.

Contacts who have not yet shown symptoms are set to be released today.

Kenyan border points have been placed on high alert amid fears the highly contagious killer could spread further.

Despite the dramatic escalation, authorities urged terrified Kenyans “not to panic, as all systems are in place to mitigate the spread of the disease”.

It comes as the outbreak rips through eastern DR Congo at alarming speed, with health workers battling what one expert described as a viral “megafire”.



France has also recorded a case during the current outbreak.

Nigeria had its first ever Ebola patient, but the country has not confirmed how they contracted the disease.

The case was the wife of a Swiss diplomat, who tested positive for the virus when returning to Abuja from Uganda.

She did not visit DR Congo and is believed to have contracted the virus whilst travelling to Uganda, according to Switzerland‘s Federal Department of Foreign Affairs.

Her husband has not shown any symptoms and is isolating, Swiss authorities added.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

The Africa CDC said Nigeria and Kenya’s first patients had travelled through Entebbe International Airport, Uganda on October 3.

Nigerian health minister Muhammad Pate said on Friday that his country’s case “appears to be closely related” to the first case in Kenya in terms of the nature of their infection.

News.title: Gun maniac shot up wake for gang war suspect at Edinburgh pub weeks after death in horror crash while fleeing from cops
News.content:
Next

A MANIAC gunman fired shots at a boozer as mourners attended the wake of a gang war suspect who died in a horror bike crash.

Shots were fired at The Robin’s Nest pub in Edinburgh as friends and loved-ones of Paul MacAulay, 40, gathered to mourn his loss.



Cops are probing the horror incident that left one person injured while others fled in terror as shots rang out last night.

It comes just weeks after MacAulay died while fleeing from cops who ordered him to stop when he was spotted on a high-powered motorcycle.





MacAulay – who is linked to the mob headed up by caged kingpin Mark Richardson – was one of the 82 people arrested as part of Operation Portaledge – Police Scotland’s crackdown on the gang war that’s been raging since March last year.

A witness, who asked not to be named, said: “I heard loud bangs and it was a blur from that point. People were running for their lives.

SCOTTISH NEWS ICE TO SEE YOU Jamie 'Iceman' Stevenson pictured mingling with other gangsters at funeral



“I was told this morning it was linked to the Tamo Junto crew who have been involved in the gang war.

“Some of Paul McAulay’s close friends stayed away from the funeral because they were worried that something might happen.

“Everyone linked to Mark Richardson has been looking over their shoulders since the trouble started last March.

“People are constantly paranoid and are trying to distance themselves from Richardson’s crew so that they aren’t brought into any of it.”

Cops, firearms teams, and ambulance crews descended on the boozer at around 9:15pm last night.



An image shared with the Scottish Sun appears to show a bullet hole from inside the boozer.

A source added: “People were saying a final farewell to McAulay and had gone to The Robin’s Best for his wake.

“Enemies of Mark Richardson’s crew got wind of it and they’ve decided to go and cause a bit of carnage.

“It was terrifying. People were running in all directions when they heard the sound of a gun going off. Someone could easily have been killed. It’s utter madness.”

Forensic officers were also seen scouring the area with torches and collecting items in evidence bags after the incident.



One person suffered an injury which was treated at the scene.

Officers sealed off the area around the boozer and locked down Gilmerton Road.

Motorists are unable to access the area between Moredunvale Road and Mount Vernon Road, while Lothian Buses have diverted services onto Old Dalkeith Road.



A concerned parent and neighbour said: “We had just put our boy to bed when we heard a few pops. It was like, ‘Pop, pop,pop.’

“I thought it was distant fireworks. But now we’ve heard it was a shooting incident. It’s a bit concerning if it was gun related.

“We live near here and we’re more concerned about our children. We’ve been to the pub a few times and it’s always been fine.



“But when members of the public are being put at risk because of some crime and gang related incidents it’s just not on.”

Another neighbour said: “We heard about three bangs. It sounded almost like clapping. We thought it might have been the wind knocking over some signs from the building works.

“But when we woke up this morning there were cordons up and the police were here. We’ve only just found out what happened.

“The police were looking for evidence outside the pub and they put numbers on the ground outside the pub, trying to work out what happened and where the shots came from.

“It’s a popular pub and you see all sorts of things happen, like the occasional brawl. But never anything like this.



“Some time ago they had put bouncers at the door and things improved. But stuff like this makes you worry what could happen.”

Officers were unable to trace the gunman at the scene, and have now launched a probe into the incident.

Detective Inspector Dougal Begg said: “I understand that this will be concerning for the community, but I would like to reassure them that extensive enquiries remain ongoing to establish the full circumstances of this incident.

“At this stage we are treating the incident as targeted but any actions like this are extremely reckless and put the safety of the public at risk.”

“I am appealing to anyone who has any information, or saw something suspicious in the area, to come forward and speak with officers.



“We would also be keen to speak with anyone who has dashcam or private CCTV footage from the area which captures anything of note.

“A police presence will be in the area as our enquiries progress and anyone with concerns or information is encouraged to approach our officers.”

We told last month of claims MacAulay was on a gang war revenge mission at the time he crashed and died in the capital.

He had been hunting for rivals of jailed druglord Richardson’s crew when he fled from cops on a motorcycle – and struck a car.

The career criminal suffered fatal injuries in the collision in Leith, Edinburgh, and died at the scene.



MacAulay – who’d been put behind bars in 2017 over an earlier high-speed bid to get away from cops – roared off on a high-powered Yamaha YZF R6 when officers ordered him to pull over.He died nearby just a minute later.

Floral tributes were laid last week near the spot where MacAulay died.

It’s understood cops were about to launch a pursuit of him before he hit a motor a short distance away, near The Finch bar.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

The car driver was not injured but was later arrested in connection with a road traffic offence.

A Crown Office spokesman said of the tragedy: “An investigation is ongoing.”

News.title: Stunning ‘floating cloud’ skyscraper planned for top European holiday destination in surreal transformation
News.content:
Next

A STUNNING skyscraper, resembling a “floating” cloud, could be built in a top European holiday hotspot.

The unique building would function as a mixed-use venue, featuring apartments, offices and even a hotel.

Tirana, Albania‘s capital, has become the proposed destination for the Danish architectural studio BIG’s latest ambitious project.



Plans reveal that the cloud-like building, named Tirana Fountain Plaza, would “float” above Rinia Park – the city’s central green space.



To give the floating effect, the building would be covered in layers of white discs, with the actual skyscraper balanced on top of tall, raised columns with fluted edges.

Plans further reveal that the interior of the Tirana Fountain Plaza would be filled with apartments, offices, cultural spaces and water features – all while maintaining the garden greenery.

Below, brand-new planted gardens, plazas and water features hope to give the park a makeover while keeping the space largely open.



Albania has become one of Europe’s fastest-growing holiday destinations, offering jetsetters the chance to enjoy stunning coastlines at a low cost.

A visit to Tirana offers travellers a taste of Albania’s culture, Cold War history and vibrant nightlife.

Founded by Bjarke Ingels, the architectural company BIG won a competition to design Tirana’s newest project, which aims to improve the natural landscape and design of Rinia Park.

The skyscraper’s renders hint it would be based at the edge of the park on Rruga Sami Frashëri – the location of both the Taiwan Center restaurant plaza and the Taiwan Pool water feature in front.



By designing the Tirana Fountain Plaza, the park will have more open space while keeping its residential, commercial and cultural purpose.

The architects are also working on a bow-tie shaped National Theatre of Albania in Tirana as well.

BIG said: “Awarded first place in the international competition for Tirana Fountain Plaza, BIG’s proposal expands the landscape of Rinia Park beneath and around a new mixed-use development in the heart of Tirana.



“The project transforms a privately operated site into a new cultural and mixed-use destination, introducing gardens, plazas, water features, and gathering spaces that connect the park to the Lana River while preserving the historic fountain.

“Selected from a shortlist including Cobe, Barozzi Veiga, l’AUC, and JDSA, the design brings architecture, landscape, and water management together as a single civic experience.”

News.title: Met Police says letter with claims about Meghan's father not shared with other law enforcement
News.content:
A letter making a "number of claims" relating to the Duchess of Sussex's father was received by the Metropolitan Police in 2019, Scotland Yard has confirmed.

The Met said it passed the information to the office of the Duke and Duchess but did not share it with other law enforcement agencies.

It was reported on Friday that images of child sexual abuse allegedly belonging to Thomas Markle, 82, had been found in his former home in the Philippines. Markle, who is based in the US, denies possessing any such images.

Meghan then released a statement saying she was informed about "disturbing allegations" about her estranged father in 2018.

The claims were first carried by The Sun newspaper, which later said that the letter made direct allegations of child sex abuse against Markle.

In a statement, Scotland Yard said: "Following a thorough review of Met Police systems and records, we have confirmed that in January 2019, we received a letter containing a number of claims about alleged offending outside the United Kingdom.

"It was sent to the MPS Protection Command to raise concerns in relation to the security of the Duchess of Sussex.

"The letter was reviewed and a decision was made that it should be passed to the office of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex for their awareness. The details of the allegations in the letter were not shared with other law enforcement agencies.

"The MPS is reviewing the handling of this matter in 2019 and considering whether a referral to the IOPC is necessary to review our approach."

Markle moved to the Philippines last year after he had a series of strokes.

He is reportedly now living in a Florida rehabilitation centre learning to walk again after having a leg amputated in 2025.

In a statement released by Meghan on Friday she said that when she received the information of the claims against her father she was "given assurance that these were being investigated".

Meghan said she hoped it could be understood why she had kept her distance from her father and did "not allow him to have contact with our children".

News.title: Plan for Northern Olympics to get £7m in Healey's Budget
News.content:
The report will look in closer detail at how hosting the games could work.

It will consider the kinds of venues and transport links required, how different cities could share the games, how communities could benefit.

Crucially it will also examine how much it could cost as well as assess the chances of a bid succeeding. The Conservative-Lib Dem coalition government said in 2013 it estimated hosting in London had cost Â£8.9bn.

A report in 2013 by the UK Trade and Investment, which has since been replaced by the Department for International Trade, said it had sparked a Â£9.9bn boost to the economy through new contracts, sales and foreign investments.

But the estimated amount was queried by some, including the Federation of Small Businesses and the National Institute of Economic and Social Research (NIESR).

The new feasability study for the Northern Games will be done by government, UK Sport, the Northern Mayors and include the British Olympic and Paralympic associations.

Healey said: "Olympic legacy lasts way beyond the celebration of sport over the summer. The North hosting an event as big as this would be truly unforgettable.

"Britain's experience of London 2012 is proof we can host the world. I'm picking up the pace on our work to potentially bid for these prestigious games. It will lift communities, create opportunities and give the UK a huge boost."

News of the funding for the study was welcomed by the British Olympic Association, ParalympicsGB and UK Sport.

"We welcome the government's continued support for exploring the potential of a future bid for the Olympic and Paralympic Games in the UK in the 2040s," they said in a joint statement.

"Building on the success and legacy of London 2012, we look forward to working in partnership to explore this exciting opportunity and the benefits it could deliver for the nation, and for the global Olympic and Paralympic movements."

News.title: Between quick wins and big dreams lies Burnham's biggest test
News.content:
But the widespread suggestion that you'll be able to blink and miss the Budget has got some hackles up in the Treasury. A budget, by its very nature, can never be a small event - it sets billions upon billions of taxes and spending decisions.

And there are likely to be extra taxes on banks, vows to sweep away some business regulation, particularly for small business, more powers passing to local leaders under the guise of devolution and more action on energy bills which are heading back up again.

John Healey has made it clear publicly and to staff, that he wants to encourage people with the guts and drive to start a business. One source said: "If you are taking on John's mantra about talking up Britain then you can't say, 'Nothing to see here'."

Whatever else the chancellor brings to Parliament in his red box, do not expect him to arrive with all the solutions to the country's very well-documented problems, whether that's getting the economy growing more convincingly, sorting out gaps in defence cash, welfare, social care, or new ways to pay off the country's groaning debts more quickly.

One former minister suggests even if Healey and Burnham had stumbled upon all the answers in a few months, it's just not possible to fix everything at the same time because of the constraints on the economy.

They wondered: "Is he going to invest in growth? Is he going to put everything he has into the challenges people will face this winter? Is he going to throw it at defence? There is just not enough to tackle all these problems simultaneously - ministers are going to be exposed to the cold light of day."

Burnham and Healey have to find a way of maintaining the balance in an unusually happy Labour Party.

MPs talk of ministers and Burnham himself being more visible and approachable in Parliament, knocking around with colleagues in the evening, fewer "golden slips" doled out when ministers were excused from voting alongside colleagues so they could get on with their important jobs.

One minister told me they'd had to tell their private office not to arrange for them to be "slipped" , from going to the Commons in the evening to see backbenchers.

It's paying off in the mood among MPs. One told me: "You're not feeling like the only way you can ever have a chat with a minister is by arranging an appointment for three months down the line â the soft touches really matter."

News.title: Infantino tells BBC Sport he is backed by 'vast majority' of world football
News.content:
During the interview he reflected on having been "fully endorsed" by the Asian Football Confederation - following a U-turn by its president Sheikh Salman - and having the backing of "all African countries".

But only last week, he apologised to the Fifa Council over the "communication and consultation" regarding FFE.

He was told by Council members in that meeting that he was not "fit to be Fifa president" if he did not give them the documents they have asked for, including the rationale for FFE.

Yet, when pressed on when he would be providing the requested papers, he did not give a clear answer, saying they had to follow a "legal process" and that they were "working on it".

"We'll answer of course all the questions that are asked as far as the process allows, as far as we can," he said.

Speaking from the first Under-15 World Cup in Azerbaijan, he said he and the Fifa administration were doing "as best we can" but admitted they have done "some things which are maybe less good".

He also said that they need to have dialogue "more often" with Uefa, in an effort to repair their strained relationship.

Asked by the BBC if he was fit to be Fifa president, and whether he had considered standing down, he laughed, before saying: "Well you know I was elected by 211 member associations from all over the world.

"I think what is important is that in an organisation like Fifa, there can be different views, different points of view.

"But if we are serious about democracy, about the democratic process, about believing that everyone has the same vote and the same voice all over the world, that football belongs to everyone, if we are serious about that, then we need, to respect as well the views of the vast, vast majority.

"I'm just coming back off Tokyo where the Asian Football Confederation has fully endorsed me. I was in Cape Verde where all [Confederation of] African [Football] countries have endorsed me. I'm speaking to all associations everywhere in the world."

He continued: "There are different points of view it's not always easy to bring them all under one roof but we need to respect and I do respect all opinions all views and then it will be up to the Fifa member associations to decide who they want as a president and how they want Fifa to be run."

The deadline for candidates to confirm they are standing against Infantino for the election in March is 18 November - although none have yet filed and he could stand unopposed.

News.title: Strictly's new presenters - after mixed reviews have they found their feet?
News.content:
Strictly Come Dancing's new hosting trio received a very mixed reception when the latest series began a month ago. Ratings have dipped and the jury's still out, but critics say they are slowly getting into the groove.

Changing the hosting team on the BBC's flagship Saturday night entertainment show was never likely to be a waltz in the park.

And going from two presenters to three, and giving them slightly different roles, upset the show's rhythm even more.

Tess Daly and Claudia Winkleman were always going to be a hard act to follow.

Into their sparkly shoes have stepped the safe and smooth Emma Willis; the flamboyant former professional dancer Johannes Radebe; and cheeky comedian Josh Widdicombe, a wildcard who was not hitherto associated with either the dance world or prime-time TV.

Willis and Widdicombe have been paired on the live shows, where he is tasked with injecting humour into the moments before and after each dance - with mixed results, say critics.

Radebe, meanwhile, has taken over from Winkleman upstairs on the mezzanine, bringing his warmth and dance expertise to the celebrity interviews following each routine.

News.title: Are California voters about to impose 'world's first' tax on billionaires?
News.content:
But the vote is also offering regular residents a voice on an issue that has roiled politics for decades.

"I believe this is the first billionaire tax - meaning a wealth tax that is targeting a very extreme percentile of the wealth distribution," says Francesco Trebbi, a public policy professor at the University of California, Berkeley. He noted the measure's historic nature and how it could help even out California's wealth gap.

The state has the largest economy in the country and boasts the fourth largest global economy, bigger than India and the UK. And it is home to one of the highest concentrations of billionaires in the world. But it also has the largest share of homeless people in the nation and one of the highest wealth gaps.

Those who back the measure have argued it helps ensure that the ultra-wealthy are contributing their fair share and will help backfill gaps in the state's budget. The move aims to raise $100bn (Â£75bn) to make up for federal funding cuts to the state's health-care system.

Suzanne Jimenez, chief of staff for Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, which helped lead the charge for the initiative, says the measure is a "short-term solution" for massive federal funding cuts coming to California as a result of US President Donald Trump's sweeping tax and spending bill.

"If we do nothing, we're going to see a collapse of our healthcare system, while we figure out a longer-term solution to fund our healthcare," she tells the BBC.

News.title: Before you crank up the thermostat, try these tips to keep you and your home warmer for longer
News.content:
With the clocks going back this weekend, the nights will be drawing in.

So if you have a thicker duvet, now is the time to bring it out. Some supermarkets sell winter duvets for under Â£20 - look for 10.5 tog or higher.

But there's something to be said for a craftily placed blanket, too. When it gets cold, Rebecca, 44, from Hertfordshire, sleeps with a blanket underneath her mattress, which she says stops draughts. "This was passed to me by my nan, she swore by it," she says. Others swear by placing a blanket above the mattress but under the bedsheet.

You can heat your bed before getting in with a hot water bottle, but make sure you check the expiry date. A guide by NHS Scotland, external says to let the water from the kettle cool for a few minutes before filling, only fill it two-thirds full, squeeze air out of the top before putting the stopper on, and don't hold it directly against your skin.

Using an electric blanket - to heat your bed before you get in or to wrap around yourself on the sofa - is "one of the cheapest ways" to stay warm, says Emily Seymour, energy editor at consumer organisation Which?. Testing by Which?, external shows it typically costs between 2p and 8p an hour to run an electric blanket at its highest setting. The London Fire Brigade, external says to unplug your blanket before you get into bed unless it has a thermostat control, not to use a hot water bottle at the same time, and replace it every 10 years.

News.title: The artist dropping her debut album after a billion streams
News.content:
Jazzy is rooted in the Dublin club scene, starting her career as part of a group called Powerful Creative Minds in the city.

But as more and more clubs close, the DJ says there are fewer opportunities for artists to cut their teeth offline.

"When I first started going out, there was a lot more going on," she says.

"There was a lot more nightclubs to go to and it's very different when we look at it now, which is sad.

"There's definitely a home for dance music on the internet of course but club culture is very important and I think that's something that we need to keep going for sure."

Latest figures from the Night Time Industries Association, external suggest about 12 venues are closing across the UK every month, with almost 30% of the night time economy lost since the coronavirus pandemic.

"I hope to God that it doesn't disappear, the club scene altogether," says Jazzy, who describes a similar issue in Ireland.

"We all need to try and put a hand in to keep it going."

Jazzy's taking her new album on tour across the UK from next month, but first she has her biggest gig yet: Dublin's 3Arena in front of a home crowd.

Even after a Coachella set and supporting Calvin Harris, she describes this as the "biggest milestone of my career to date".

While she says fans can mostly expect her brand of uplifting records on the album, she says it's also more personal than her usual work.

She highlights one track in particular, Invisible, as a change from her more upbeat releases. It deals with a bad experience she had in the music industry, describing it as "like my first ever diss track".

"I hope [fans] learn a little bit more about me, because that was one of my goals with the album - to open up a little bit about experiences in life as well.

"So there's a little message from me in each song."

News.title: UK to invest £100m in 'world first' AI Biosecurity Lab
News.content:
The UK says it will establish a national AI Biosecurity Lab (AIBL) to help strengthen its defences against emerging biological threats.

As part of Wednesday's Budget, the government will commit Â£100m to establishing the new, "world first" institute with the support of leading AI firms.

The chancellor will also pledge millions of pounds in spending across a range of initiatives aimed at shoring up the UK's ability to respond to evolving cyber, biological and AI-enabled threats.

"AI will transform daily life: every firm, community, hospital, school, and every aspect of our economy can benefit," John Healey said.

"I understand and share the concerns of working people, so I am setting out a distinctively British approach to AI.

"One that doesn't leave workers behind and defends our national interest, while ensuring the benefits of AI-enabled growth are felt right across the country."

The full details about the role and remit of the new lab are yet to emerge.

But the AI Minister Kanishka Narayan said it would be a "major new global institution" that brings together "world-leading scientific expertise" to ensure the UK can safeguard its citizens and goals as AI develops.

"That means staying ahead of emerging threats, from cyber attacks to biological risks, while building more of the critical technology our security depends on," he said.

"By backing British science, advanced chips and our own AI companies, we can strengthen our national security, rebuild Britain's industrial strength and create good, skilled jobs across the country."

The AI Biosecurity Lab's creation will also be supported by leading AI developers, with OpenAI and Anthropic providing Â£200m worth of AI model credits that can be spent on the use of their models.

News.title: Tory activist in 'contract killing broker' claim had worked for party HQ
News.content:
A former Tory activist who appeared to offer to "broker" the hiring of contract killers in an undercover film report previously worked for Conservative headquarters.

Jack Ross was contracted to do social media work for the party until earlier this year, the BBC has been told.

It comes after Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch referred to them as "shocking allegations", adding that she did not "believe that person is a member anymore".

A Conservative spokesman said Ross's party membership had "been suspended with immediate effect pending an investigation". It has reported that Ross said his words were not meant to be taken seriously.

Ross was paid to provide social media advice to the party for a brief period, the BBC has been told. He was never an employee or Conservative Campaign Headquarters pass holder.

However, he met Badenoch on several occasions as part of his role as chief executive of Turning Point UK, an offshoot of a right-wing American organisation.

Ross has also met several other right-wing politicians including the former Prime Minister Boris Johnson and Nigel Farage, the Reform UK leader.

In undercover filming broadcast this week by Al Jazeera, Ross appears to offer to "broker" the services of contract killers.

The Al Jazeera report said its undercover journalist approached Ross in 2022 with a fictitious situation of a family business at risk of being taken over by a criminal gang.

Ross is alleged to have asked the undercover reporter what was needed from him, and listed violent options that could be bought including stabbing, shooting and killing.

Al Jazeera said Ross denied the finding "completely" and claimed everything he said to the reporter was not meant seriously.

Turning Point UK has been approached for comment.

News.title: How does the UK state pension compare with other countries?
News.content:
Getting older is something few of us want to think about. Yet how we fund our later years, and how much we'll get, has been a hot topic.

The triple lock formula - state pensions increasing by the greatest of 2.5%, earnings growth, or inflation - means those benefits have risen far faster than the earnings of workers since its introduction in 2011.

But as housing costs have also been rising fast, pensioner poverty has actually increased slightly in the last decade.

Nevertheless, even if you take those costs into consideration, pensioners are less likely to be in relative poverty - that is, having to get by on less than 60% of the income of the typical household - than families with children or working-age people.

News.title: The convicted £33m tax fraudster evading justice and living it up in Dubai
News.content:
In the early part of the millennium, Arif Patel appeared to be a businessman very much on the up.

His company, Faisaltex, headquartered in his home city of Preston, was known for manufacturing textiles, such as socks and nighties, which it supplied to retailers.

Patel was a fixture in the Sunday Times Rich List with his wealth in 2006 estimated to be Â£105m. He was also investing heavily in property across the city and beyond.

In 2007, his teenage son bought a minority stake in Preston North End Football Club. There was even a plan to build a Â£100m, 19-storey tower block - complete with botanical gardens and restaurant - in the centre of the city.

Behind the facade, though, something very different was going on.

In the early 2000s, organised crime groups had turned to large-scale attacks on the tax system through what became known as carousel fraud.

Chains of fake business transactions are created as a way of stealing VAT repayments from HMRC.

Goods move between different companies, into and out of the country, to generate false tax refunds.

The same shipments of goods are often moved around repeatedly, hence the name carousel fraud.

This type of fraud was costing taxpayers billions of pounds a year and experts like Stone were at the vanguard of the fightback.

This is how Patel's textiles empire appeared on his radar.

"When we started to look at them we did notice some very strange shipments of goods - a container load of hats to Switzerland seemed odd because they were actually Swiss hats," he said.

News.title: GP says she was forced out of job after raising concerns about gender treatment
News.content:
Although Doyle at first denied to the tribunal he knew Hall before this, it emerged during the tribunal that he had previously had a number of mentoring meetings with the GP.

The GMC investigation was not taken forward. However, the NHS launched an investigation into Redvers, bringing in an external investigator.

The tribunal heard she was called to what she described as a "brutal" four-hour interrogation.

"It was oppressive, very upsetting. I didn't feel I had the chance at all to explain what had happened," she said. "I broke down at one point".

She said she was off sick for several months as a result and received treatment for trauma.

Other colleagues who were interviewed as part of the investigation into Redvers also complained about the process and the NHS upheld most of their complaints.

The investigation concluded the CEO and trust should apologise to Redvers.

It also warned that Redvers' treatment would have a "broader negative impact" on the willingness of staff to raise concerns.

In 2023, a year after the grievance outcome, when a trans campaigner suggested in an NHS meeting that she was transphobic, Redvers told the tribunal she felt the NHS did not do enough to support her. She felt she had no choice but to leave her job as a safeguarding GP.

"I just felt there's no way I could carry on working in this organisation," she told the BBC.

At about that time, a group of parents, school governors and social workers began raising concerns about WellBn and Hall.

The co-founder of campaign group PSHE Brighton, Rachel Cashman, said: "It is a travesty that Sarah Redvers was punished for doing her job safeguarding and expecting the best standards of care for gender distressed children."

Redvers is now waiting for the outcome of her employment tribunal. She may not get the judgment for several months.

She described what has happened as "personally and professionally difficult" and said the NHS "needs to remember that patients come first" and it should "listen to staff who raise legitimate concerns."

In a statement NHS Surrey and Sussex said: "We engaged professionally and supportively with the Employment Tribunal. We recognise that some employment processes should have been handled differently and have apologised whilst Dr Redvers was employed with us, before, and during the hearings. We await the findings of the tribunal to make any further comment."

NHS England said: "When concerns about prescribing practices by an individual GP were escalated to NHS England national directors in 2023, they met directly with an affected family and asked regional professional standards leads to undertake formal investigations.

"Wider concerns were subsequently identified, and the WellBN practice was asked to stop providing a specialised prescribing service. Further new information led to NHS England and NHS Sussex initiating an independent patient safety investigation in 2025."

Dr Sam Hall and WellBN have been contacted for comment.

In response to the investigation report in June, WellBN said it recognised "the seriousness and sensitivity of the matters raised" and that its priority remained providing "compassionate, safe and effective care for all patients".

News.title: Burnham suggests stocking up on tinned food and bottled water
News.content:
The prime minister has advised people to stock up on tinned food and bottled water in order to be prepared for emergencies.

With storms battering the UK, and in the wake of online disruption caused by a major security flaw, Andy Burnham said "unexpected events seem to be becoming more and more common".

The government has drawn up recommendations for households to have three days' worth of bottled water and tinned food to deal with a crisis such as a war, an online attack or a natural disaster.

Burnham added: "It's not about panicking... It's about just taking sensible measures to have enough in the house to tide you over should there be a difficult situation."

At Labour's conference last month, Housing Secretary Angela Rayner joked that her emergency box, external would include a bottle of wine.

She said she'd include: "Mascara, concealer, I don't know, a bottle of Sauvignon Blanc, a tin of baked beans because you've gotta have some baked beans, and I like a good tin of custard as well so I think that'll keep me going for a while."

Asked whether he agreed with her, Burnham told BBC Radio 5 Live's Matt Chorley: "Well, I'm not sure a bottle of wine is your best first port of call if you're in a slightly crisis situation, but it probably helps when you've done the hard work.

"But I'll stick to the basics I think - I do like my beans, so I have plenty of those in the cupboard, and soup.

"I think those are the kind of things that I would recommend people to have, as well as Twiglets, I'm not sure I can get by for too long without those."

Last month, the National Audit Office (NAO) warned Britain's food supply chain is at risk given the growing threat of cyber-attacks and the climate crisis and said the Department for Food, the Environment and Rural Affairs (Defra) had not done enough in recent years to improve supply chain resilience.

The chief executive of the Cold Chain Federation, which represents firms transporting temperature-controlled foods, also told the BBC the UK is being targeted by Russian cyber-hackers who "know that there are pinch points in the food supply system".

Speaking at a wildfire resilience summit in Liverpool, Burnham denied the government had failed to properly prepare, saying: "No, we're having the conversation with people about being better prepared because we're living in a world where unexpected events seem to be becoming more and more common.

"Obviously, weather events, and we're in a situation today where the UK is facing storms and obviously, we feel for the people without power in Cornwall right now.

"It is just having those supplies in the house to get you through those moments. So we are having that conversation about resilience."

News.title: Trump says Burnham 'getting it done' after Jackdaw decision
News.content:
Burnham announced the decision to approve the drilling of the Jackdaw gas field earlier this week.

Jackdaw is situated 150 miles (241km) east of Aberdeen and is operated by Adura, a joint venture between Shell and Norwegian state energy firm Equinor.

Ministers said the first gas could be produced by the end of this month, helping heat millions of homes, and also announced the creation of a new energy wealth fund.

Environmental campaigners say the decision would hamper efforts to tackle climate change and make "no meaningful difference" to UK energy security.

Based on official forecasts for the amount of gas the UK will need over the next decade, that suggests Jackdaw has the potential to meet around 1.6% of total projected national gas demand between 2026 and 2036.

Operators say it could be connected to the Great British gas network within weeks and could produce gas for the next 11 years.

Trump responded to the decision on Friday, but appeared to confuse oil and gas.

He said: "They're opening up the North Sea oil. I've been after them to do that for two years."

Trump added: "Andy is getting it done, and I guess it's against the liberal principle, but he knows what's right. It's going to make UK a very wealthy country."

In a discussion on Friday, Burnham and Trump spoke about the decision to approve Jackdaw.

The two leaders "agreed on the significant benefits this will bring to the UK, boosting the economy and supporting jobs for British workers", a statement from Number 10 read.

It added that Trump and Burnham "welcomed the continued collaboration between UK and US companies, especially on nuclear power".

Earlier this week, on Wednesday, Trump said the decision was "great news for the wealth and prosperity" of the UK.

Writing on his Truth Social platform, Trump urged the UK to go "full blast" and called the North Sea "one of the greatest and most prosperous areas of oil in the world".

A decision is yet to be taken on whether production can begin at Rosebank, the UK's largest known untapped oil field, which is located off the coast of Shetland in the North Atlantic.

News.title: Celebrity Traitors left on a knife edge after a trip to the field of screams
News.content:
Spoiler warning: This article reveals details from episode eight of The Celebrity Traitors, series two.

Original Celebrity Traitor Maya Jama, latest recruit King Kenny and now even the reluctant James Acaster - hooray! - have developed a real appetite for murder this week.

And going into Friday's episode we knew that their collective cruel intention was to see that one of three faithfuls, Miranda Hart, Romesh Ranganathan or Sebastian "Bash" Croft, did not make it to breakfast.

When it became clear that the murdered Miranda had danced her last dance in the castle - leaving only 10 of the initial 21 players - the pressure began to mount and speculation was rife as to whodunnit and why?

The self-declared Miss Marple wannabe had been stitched up, of course. "Miranda is a good detective," noted James A in a flashback to the turret talk from the night before.

"I don't know who I'm becoming," responded Maya - who has taken to treachery like a duck to water - "but I feel it in my loins, and Miranda is the only one that makes sense."

Miranda, who had been in her element sleuthing away on the show, did not take the news of her untimely death at all well, throwing her murder note to the ground. "No! Absolutely not," she cried.

"Oh bottoms!"

"I'm so cross with myself, I was wholly focusing on my Joanne issue," she added, with reference to her theory about Joanne McNally being a traitor. One that even Miranda herself had - unwisely - "debunked" at the roundtable.

Ending on a more positive note, the comedian, who has had health issues in recent years, reflected: "Ultimately, in my little personal story, this has been quite extraordinary that I've been able to get back and do the thing that I love professionally and do the things that I love personally.

"Like wandering around a Scottish island and being in nature and laughing and connecting. There were times that I didn't think that would be possible again".

News.title: Trump merchandise stores are shutting down across the country. ‘He has peaked’
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Rob Cortis has faith in President Donald Trump - and in the MAGA-themed store he owns in Michigan.

“There’s still the chance that Trump always pulls rabbits out of his hat,” he said. “Is he gonna run in 2028?”

Cortis runs the Trump Unity Bridge Shop in the Detroit suburb of Livonia. And, unlike the several Trump-themed stores shutting their doors across the country, he has no plans to close. “It's always busier during the elections, and then it slows down in between,” he told The Independent. “It’s getting very busy now during the election again.”

Trump merchandise accounts for about 80 percent of the store’s sales, Cortis said, with hats remaining a strong seller. “MAGA hats are still moving pretty good…ICE hats are selling,” he said.

But other retailers are not so optimistic and find themselves confronting a challenging political reality: the president is an unpopular lame duck with no reelection campaign on the horizon to fuel sales.

open image in gallery Over the past year, at least four Trump stores nationwide have shut their doors, including locations in Pennsylvania and Tennessee, according to NPR ( AFP/Getty )

Roughly 20 stores nationwide sell Trump merchandise, according to Ron Solomon, who heads the online retailer MAGA Mall. But over the past year, at least four stores nationwide have shut closed up shop, including locations in Pennsylvania and Tennessee, according to NPR.

“He's no longer a viable business model for entrepreneurs because he has peaked,” Wes Alker, a Trump supporter who frequented the Pennsylvania store, told the outlet.

The closures come amid a broader sales slump for MAGA merchandise. Retailers selling hats, T-shirts and other items bearing the president’s likeness and slogans have seen sales fall sharply, The Wall Street Journal reported last month. Some blamed economic conditions, with inflation driving up prices even for official Trump merchandise.

Trump’s approval rating has fallen to record lows in recent months amid voter frustration over the cost of living and the ongoing Iran war, which has no clear end in sight.

On January 5, the Trump Store in Bensalem, Pennsylvania, announced it was shuttering its brick-and-mortar operations after six years in business. “Come in tomorrow until January 31st for store-wide savings,” the store said in a Facebook post.

open image in gallery ‘The store has kind of run its course,” the owner of a Trump store in Pennsylvania said. ‘You know, it's been six years and the elections are over. Trump's not gonna be in another election, even though he'll be part of it’ ( Getty Images )

open image in gallery This summer, a Trump superstore outside Knoxville, Tennessee, closed after some of the president’s policies, including DOGE’s spending cuts, hurt business ( Google Maps )

Owner Mike Domanico told CBS News that he opted to shut it down because he’s semi-retired and focusing on other business ventures.

“The store has kind of run its course,” he said. “You know, it's been six years and the elections are over. Trump's not gonna be in another election, even though he'll be part of it.”

David Russell, who frequented the store, added: “Most of the stuff they sell was to promote Trump. He's already in this last term. You can't do much more for him than he's already gotten.”

A Trump superstore outside Knoxville, Tennessee, also closed this summer. Owner Bill Hays told NPR that some of the president’s policies, including DOGE’s spending cuts, had hurt business. He also noted that some customers were choosing to have their purchases bagged rather than putting on their new Trump apparel in the store.

“People were not wearing their colors, so to speak, like they did before the [2024] election," Hays said, noting that sales had fallen to $20,000 a month from a high of $200,000.

“After the inauguration, I think a lot of people felt that their job was done,” he said.

News.content:
