News.title: Who is supporting Gianni Infantino and how many votes will secure re-election as Fifa president?
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Gianni Infantino is facing a battle to cling onto his Fifa presidency heading into next year’s election after his botched bid to sell off stakes in the World Cup to private investors resulted in a significant loss in support.

England and Wales have been among the football associations to join European governing body Uefa in leading the charge for Infantino’s removal from power, formally withdrawing their endorsement of the Swiss-Italian for re-election in March 2027.

But as the dust has settled on his privatisation ploy, Infantino’s bid for a third term has strengthened. His allies have surfaced, with the likes of Mexico and Argentina joining Caf, the African football governing body, in reaffirming support for the under-fire president, and now the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) has reversed its position and backed Infantino with AFC president Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa underlining that there is “a true understanding between us”.

Infantino has now laughed in response to a question over whether he had considered resigning as president, declaring he retains the support of the “vast, vast majority” of world football.

Infantino needs 106 votes from the 211 member associations to be re-elected as president. Here is every country and confederation to have expressed their opposition or support for Infantino:

Who is opposing Infantino?

Uefa (55 members) 🇪🇺

Uefa, the governing body for Europe, has staunchly opposed Infantino’s leadership. They threatened a boycott of Fifa competitions before Infantino’s eventual climbdown but has continued to assert that his position is untenable, even taking legal action against the Swiss-Italian.

The body points to how there have not been “assurances” that attempts like the privatisation of the World Cup “to disfigure the game in this way will never be made again”.

Uefa general secretary Theodore Theodoridis has written to his Fifa counterpart Mattias Grafstrom setting out a series of questions on behalf of European members of the Fifa Council, demanding documents covering a series of Infantino controversies. Fifa has until 2 November to answer these questions.

Concacaf (41 members) 🌎

Concacaf, the Confederation for North America and the Caribbean, came out in opposition of Infantino after being left stunned at the lack of consultation during the Fifa sell-off plan, which they went on to reject.

After the plan was aborted, the confederation said: “This recent unilateral and egregious act of poor governance and leadership follows a pattern of missteps and similar behaviour. A comprehensive reckoning with this presidency is imperative.”

Concacaf president Victor Montagliani was initially seen as a front-runner to challenge Infantino in next March’s election but he now looks set to pursue another term as Concacaf chief.

England 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿

The English FA is one of many European member associations to send a letter to Fifa withdrawing its support for Infantino’s re-election in 2027.

Infantino’s apology letter changed nothing for the FA, who was “deeply concerned about the lack of process and governance” surrounding his sell-off scheme.

open image in gallery FA chief executive Mark Bullingham (left) next to Gianni Infantino ( PA )

Wales 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁷󠁬󠁳󠁿

The Football Association of Wales was one of the first to send its letter withdrawing support for Infantino.

“The ‌recent failures in good governance, processes, ‌leadership, values, stakeholder management, communications and sound judgment ​have led us to a position ‌where Mr Infantino has lost the confidence of the FAW to ‌remain at the helm of world football,” a statement read. “Failing to put the best interests of football first is a failure we cannot accept.”

Scotland 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁳󠁣󠁴󠁿

The SFA’s chief executive Ian Maxwell told the BBC that the governing body’s position has “been clear” since Uefa’s collective statement.

He said: “We have aligned ourselves with the Uefa position and 55 nations are stronger than one voice. Their statement since then has talked about a lack of confidence in the Fifa leadership and the Scottish FA agree completely with that decision. The SFA will not be voting for Gianni Infantino come the re-election in early 2027.”

Republic of Ireland 🇮🇪

The Football Association of Ireland (FAI) has followed in withdrawing its support for Infantino while backing Uefa’s stance.

"Following an FAI board meeting, the decision was taken to rescind the letter of support that the Association supplied earlier this year," it confirmed. "It has since written to Fifa to explain its reasoning. The Association is grateful for the support that Fifa provides to Irish football, but recent events have raised significant concerns regarding governance, transparency and the lack of meaningful consultation.”

Italy 🇮🇹

The Italian Football Federation (FIGC) initially delayed taking official action but it has now withdrawn its support for Infantino's candidacy in the next Fifa presidential election scheduled.

"This decision is intended to clearly and transparently express the FIGC's position - in full agreement with Uefa and its president Aleksander Ceferin - regarding the recent initiatives promoted by the FIFA president concerning the governance and development of international competitions," FIGC said in a statement.

Finland 🇫🇮

Finland kickstarted the process of formal withdrawals, with it being revealed that the Scandinavian member association was the first to send a letter officially withdrawing support for Infantino.

Serbia 🇷🇸

The Football Association of Serbia then sent a similar letter to Fifa.

“We would like to remind you that we provided our support to Mr Infantino in writing on 25 May of this year, but after carefully considering the events that have seriously damaged the image and reputation of both Fifa and its president in the past period, this is the only logical and rational course of action,” a statement read.

Sweden 🇸🇪

Sweden’s federation (SvFF) followed suit: "At an extraordinary board meeting on Monday, SvFF has chosen not to support Fifa President Gianni Infantino ​in the upcoming re-election.

"This is after a long-term assessment of the development within Fifa and the organization's leadership. The decision is based on recurring shortcomings in governance, transparency and management, which means that trust in Gianni Infantino's leadership no longer exists."

open image in gallery Infantino has officially lost the endorsement of numerous Uefa nations ( PA )

Croatia 🇭🇷

As did the Croatian Football Federation (HNS): "The Croatian Football Federation has informed Fifa of its decision to withdraw the support previously expressed for Mr Gianni Infantino's candidature for another term as Fifa president.

"This decision followed a thorough reassessment within the federation in light of recent developments surrounding the Fifa World Cup 2026 and discussions within our governing bodies. We consider our position to be clearly communicated to Fifa and have no further comment to add at this time."

Albania 🇦🇱

The Albanian Football Federation also took the same stance, aligning with Uefa.

“The Albanian Football Association has sent an official letter to Fifa Secretary General Mattias Grafström, informing him that it has withdrawn its support for Mr Gianni Infantino’s candidacy for another four-year term as Fifa President,” the statement confirmed.

Greece 🇬🇷

The Greek Football Association has backed Uefa’s push for a change in Fifa’s leadership, similarly withdrawing support to underscore a united European front in opposition to Infantino.

"The Greek FA (EPO) has taken a clear position against a candidacy of Gianni Infantino," EPO presdient Makis Gagatsis told reporters. "We saw things happen at the World Cup that are not acceptable to football public opinion. Then... came a programme to sell World Cup rights and we are clearly against it, so we withdrew our support of the Fifa president."

Germany 🇩🇪

The German federation (DFB) already opted against endorsing Infantino earlier in the year so has not had to send a letter withdrawing support to take an opposing stance.

“The DFB has not signed a letter of support for the re-election of Gianni Infantino," the governing body stated in July. "Further steps will be discussed in the DFB presidential board."

Former Germany national team director Oliver Bierhoff further reiterated the nation’s loss of trust in Infantino: "We have to take care of football. It is already commercial but it is a property for all of football. The world views may be different but in the last weeks and months a lot happened so that we have no trust any more that it will be going in the right direction."

Denmark 🇩🇰

Denmark are in a similar position to Germany, having not endorsed Infantino’s re-election bid prior to the scheme’s reveal.

There is also a precedent for their opposition to Infantino, with federation president Jesper Moller not supporting his re-election efforts back in 2022: “There is only one candidate ... but Denmark will not be supporting the current president.”

Norway 🇳🇴

The Norwegian Football Federation (NFF) have been one of the most vocal bodies to call for Infantino’s resignation.

NFF president Lise Klaveness told the Guardian: “We decided that there is no trust in Infantino now. We have been worried consistently and there has been one more step in worrying direction every year, every part of the year. The trust is now gone for us, there is no way back for Infantino.

“We’re left in a very polarised cooperation globally and, I would say, chaos. So we will ask him to resign immediately so that the global football community can look ahead and cooperate going into the future.”

open image in gallery Lise Klaveness has called on Infantino to resign ( Reuters )

Netherlands 🇳🇱

The Royal Dutch Football Association (KNVB) is among the many to have confirmed it has lost confidence in Infantino’s leadership.

“The way this process has unfolded has resulted in a fundamental loss of confidence in the leadership of Fifa President Gianni Infantino. The KNVB no longer has confidence in his leadership,” a statement read.

Romania 🇷🇴

The Romanian Football Federation (FRF) was among the countries to resolutely reject the sell-off proposal, calling it “a dangerous initiative to turn football into a private asset”.

As a result, the FRF will withhold support for Infantino’s re-election for the time being, with a statement reading: “FRF is suspending the discussion regarding the support of Fifa President Gianni Infantino for a new term, until further clarifications.”

Northern Ireland ☘️

The Northern Irish football association (IFA) has expressed “concerns” over Infantino’s leadership.

"We take our responsibilities as a member association of both Uefa and Fifa seriously," said an IFA spokesperson. "We support the current Uefa position on the matter and will continue to engage constructively on issues relating to football governance. We are of course aware of the recent developments and wider concerns within the football community. We are considering these matters carefully and will continue to engage through the appropriate governance structures and channels.”

Jordan 🇯🇴

Jordan were the first non-Uefa member association to publicly oppose Infantino after federation president Prince Ali bin Hussein levelled accusations of blackmail against Fifa.

Prince Ali alleged the organisation offered assistance with the kingdom's issues in exchange for his endorsement, following Infantino's withdrawal from a World Cup stake sale proposal. Among the problems cited was the association's eight-month wait for prize money, due since December for reaching the Arab Cup final in Qatar.

After taking to X to reveal the outstanding payments, the Jordan Football Association received the prize money two days later - but Prince Ali has not changed his stance over not endorsing Infantino: “It does not change my clear position concerning the leadership of Fifa: my FA and I will not endorse president Infantino, nor will we vote for him.”

New Zealand 🇳🇿

New Zealand have broken rank with Oceania’s confederation by withdrawing their support for Infantino.

"After careful consideration, NZF has formed the view that decisions and actions within Fifa have contributed to a breakdown in trust and increased division within international football, and that an independent review is required to restore confidence and trust,” a statement read.

Who is supporting Infantino?

Confederation of African Football (54 members) 🌍

Caf, the governing body for African football, was the first confederation to unanimously back Infantino.

“We are committed to continue working together with Fifa, its member associations, other football confederations and stakeholders to safeguard and adhere to governance, due process, and transparency global best practises and to contribute to the development and growth of football worldwide,” Caf president Patrice Motsepe said.

Motsepe later added that the position of embattled president Infantino can only be decided by Fifa elections.

Asian Football Confederation (47 members) 🌏

The Asian Football Confederation (AFC) has endorsed Infantino in an apparent turnaround in its stance from two months ago when it criticised the head of football’s world governing body for a breach of trust.

AFC president Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa, speaking at the body’s extraordinary congress meeting in Tokyo on Friday, embraced Infantino with a large hug in front of the membership as he delivered his endorsement.

“We affirm our full commitment to supporting you and your leadership as you seek a new mandate as the Fifa president.” Sheikh Salman said. “You’ve visited a lot of countries in Asia. I’ve spoken to a lot of members within this continent. I know your feeling and I think your commitment is clear as well.”

Argentina 🇦🇷

Argentina became the first member from South America to voice its support for Infantino, on the same day that confederation Conmebol - which had previously only expressed backing of Infantino - expressed concern over Fifa’s procedures.

"Of our highest consideration, on behalf of the Argentine Football Association (AFA), and its Executive Committee, we address you, dear President, and through your worthy intermediary the Fifa board, to express our support for the management carried out during the last 10 years, which had as its main axes the development of football throughout the world and institutional solidity based on a clear governance model, stable and transparent,” a statement read.

open image in gallery Argentina president Javier Milei (left) behind Infantino at the "Board of Peace" hosted by US president Donald Trump ( AFP/Getty )

Paraguay 🇵🇾

Paraguay also followed suit as Infantino’s Conmebol support base surfaced.

Their federation published a letter of support addressed to Infantino, writing that it "reaffirms its commitment to continue working alongside Fifa”.

Mexico 🇲🇽

Mexico joined Argentina from the Americas, breaking rank from the United States, Canada and the rest of Concacaf that had condemned Infantino’s plan and aligned itself against his leadership.

The Mexican Football Federation (FMF) stated: "The FMF will neither recognise nor approve any process convened outside of that institutional framework, and it joins the call made... by President Infantino to collectively continue developing football for the benefit of the 211 member associations."

Grenada 🇬🇩

Grenada’s federation (GFA) has also broken away from the Concacaf block and reaffirmed its support for Infantino.

“The GFA reaffirms its support for Fifa President Gianni Infantino and expresses its sincere appreciation for his continued support for football development in Grenada and across the Caribbean over his period of service in office and for the years to come,” a statement read.

Saint Kitts and Nevis 🇰🇳

Like Grenada, the Saint Kitts and Nevis Football Association (SKNFA) has welcomed Infantino’s decision to scrap the plan, called for respect of Fifa’s institutional processes and backed the president to continue.

It said: “The SKNFA concluded by reaffirming its support for Infantino’s leadership and vision, and said it looks forward to supporting him as he completes his current constitutional mandate and continues efforts to advance football development across Fifa’s 211 Member Associations.”

Qatar 🇶🇦

Qatar was the first football association to publicly back Infantino, even though they later welcomed the decision to scrap the plan.

"While the proposal had merit, we applaud the wisdom behind prioritising unity among member associations. The Qatar Football Association fully supports President Infantino's efforts to continue growing and strengthening the game globally,” a statement read.

open image in gallery Qatar's FA has backed Infantino to continue as president ( Getty )

Sri Lanka 🇱🇰

Like Qatar, Sri Lanka welcomed the decision to scrap the investment plan and has since reaffirmed its support for Infantino.

"One of President Infantino's defining leadership qualities has always been his willingness to listen to the views and concerns of Member Associations. This decision is a clear reflection of his inclusive leadership style, built on dialogue, mutual respect, and a genuine commitment to serving the global football community," its statement read.

Kuwait 🇰🇼

Like others, Kuwait welcomed the decision to halt the plans but Sheikh Ahmed Yusuf Al-Sabah, the president of the Kuwait Football Association, affirmed his support for Infantino.

A statement read: “He concluded by affirming the Kuwait Football Association's confidence in the leadership of Fifa President Gianni Infantino, and its support for efforts aimed at developing the game and enhancing its opportunities for growth in a way that serves all national associations and achieves the shared interests of global football.”

Lebanon 🇱🇧

Lebanon, who granted Infantino citizenship last year, have backed the Swiss-Italian, with FA president Hashim Haidar all but echoing the same sentiments as Kuwait.

“Haidar reaffirms the Lebanese Football Association’s support for Fifa President Gianni Infantino and his confidence in the decisions he makes in the best interests of global football, as well as in his efforts and initiatives aimed at developing the game,” he said, while also asserting that Infantino’s proposal “could be re-examined ... in a away that serves the greater good of the sport and preserves its unity”.

Indonesia 🇮🇩

The president of the Indonesian FA supported Infantino’s sell-off plan and has now backed him for another term.

Hailing Fifa as a “strategic partner that is truly present” in its football development, Erick Thohir said: “This is proof of President Infantino’s vision that football development must not be centered on a single region; it must proceed worldwide.”

Philippines 🇵🇭

Philippines have also backed Infantino and called for co-operation among confederations.

"We stand behind President Gianni Infantino's leadership, and trust that continued dialogue among all confederations and member associations will keep the global game moving forward together,” the Philippines confirmed.

Mongolia 🇲🇳

Joining the Philippines, the Mongolian Football Federation has put out a statement in support of Infantino.

Bhutan 🇧🇹

The Bhutan Football Federation has published a letter that extends its “sincere appreciation” to Infantino for scrapping the plans, hailing him for demonstrating “true leadership” by “prioritising consensus over commerce”.

“We stand united with Fifa and President Infantino in their ongoing efforts to serve the global football community,” wrote federation president Dasho Ugen Tsechup.

Morocco 🇲🇦

The location of Infantino’s initial crisis meeting back in the summer, Morocco have stuck by the Swiss-Italian as one of his most loyal allies.

“What has been achieved in recent years through Fifa’s development programmes, particularly in Africa, represents an important accomplishment that must be preserved, to the benefit of all member associations,” said the Royal Moroccan Football Federation’s president Fouzi Lekjaa.

open image in gallery Infantino held his crisis meeting in Rabat, Morocco ( AP )

Egypt 🇪🇬

Similar to their north African counterpart, Egypt have maintained their endorsement of Infantino.

"The Egyptian Football Association reiterates its full trust in President Gianni Infantino's leadership and its continuous support for any initiatives that benefit Fifa member associations and the future of world football,” a statement read.

Mauritania 🇲🇷

Ahmed Yahya, the country's representative on the Fifa Council, was one of a number of African football leaders to say he was backing Infantino early on, pledging his support before Caf took its stance.

Niger 🇳🇪

Same as above, with Hamidou Djibrilla from Niger coming out quickly in support of Infantino.

Sudan 🇸🇩

Sudan’s federation joined five other Arab nations - Qatar, Lebanon, Morocco, Egypt and Mauritania - in writing a joint statement backing Infantino.

"Recognising the important role of Arab football in bringing people together and strengthening co-operation among football associations across the Arab world, we ... express our full support for Mr Gianni Infantino, president of Fifa, and reaffirm our confidence in his leadership and continued commitment to the development of football worldwide," the statement read.

"We deeply appreciate Mr Infantino’s sustained efforts to advance football globally, expand opportunities across all regions and strengthen the game’s role in bringing people and communities together. We look forward to continuing our close cooperation with him towards a stronger and more prosperous future for world ‌football, expanding opportunities and further enhancing Arab football’s contribution to ​the global game."

DR Congo 🇨🇩

DR Congo's federation (Fecofa) president Veron Mosengo-Omba, who was only elected in May, spoke out in “full support” of Infantino. The two studied at university in Switzerland together.

Fecofa said it had "greatly benefited" from Fifa's programmes, citing investment in development and infrastructure.

Nigeria 🇳🇬

The Nigeria Football Federation (NFF) has largely aligned itself towards a supportive stance for Infantino's leadership, with former NFF president and deputy chairman of Fifa's Men's National Teams Competitions Committee, Amaju Pinnick, backing his initial sell-off plan.

Comoros 🇰🇲

The president of the Comoros Football Federation, Said Ali Athouman, also backed Infantino’s scheme due to the financial benefits to smaller nations.

"Our problem is how to obtain money,” he said. “Right now, we have no sponsors. So how do we compete? The richest nations can train players, have infrastructure and equipment, and it's no coincidence that they then achieve results. Most European countries don't have ​these problems.”

open image in gallery A number of African nations have fallen in line with the stance of Caf president Patrice Motsepe ( Getty )

Malawi 🇲🇼

Fleetwood Haiya, Malawi's football chief, echoed the same concerns in his support for Infantino.

He told BBC Sport: "Our government is not able to make sure that they have medical supplies in hospitals and at the same time to look at football. Malawi needs money."

Uganda 🇺🇬

The Ugandan federation are said to have echoed Malawi’s sentiments, with football officials from the federation telling BBC Sport that Fifa investment has transformed their game both on and off the pitch.

Gambia 🇬🇲

Lamin Kaba Bajo told BBC Sport that his federation not just stood by Infantino, but would do "everything within our means" to get him re-elected.

"That's my personal opinion as president of the federation, and a good number of African memberships also stand on that line. He is here to stay,” he said.

Djibouti 🇩🇯

The Djiboutian Football Federation has similarly welcomed the decision to withdraw the sell-off proposal, with president Souleiman Hassan Waberi saying the climbdown “demonstrates a firm commitment to preserving the unity, solidarity and cohesion that define the football family”.

He said in a statement: “I reaffirm my full support for Fifa President Mr Gianni Infantino and for all initiatives aimed at promoting the sustainable, transparent and inclusive development of football around the world.”

South Africa 🇿🇦

While not an official statement from the federation, South Africa’s Minister of Sports, Arts and Culture of South Africa, Gayton McKenzie, posted on X saying that Infantino had been "very good to African football".

"Africa should be cautious in joining the public lynching of Infantino,” he warned. “He has been very good to African football. We can debate his ideas but let's not forget who has been a friend to us. Many of those calling for his head want the old status quo back too."

Who is yet to take a stance?

The Oceania Football Confederation (OFC), with its 11 member associations, stopped short from pulling its support for Infantino in their statement after welcoming the scrapping of the sell-off plan, very much staying on the fence as it called for a “review”.

A statement read: "The OFC recognises the progress achieved over the last decade in advancing football development in Oceania under Fifa's leadership and encourages Fifa to use the review as an opportunity to identify and implement any changes that may be necessary."

Meanwhile, South American governing body Conmebol, with its 10 member associations, expressed “concern about the repeated unilateral actions taken” and welcomed the decision to withdraw the plans, affirming it will “not support any action” that “ignores or deviates” from the “democratic procedures that represent the 211 Fifa member associations”.

However, as a long-time ally of Infantino, it did endorse him to get elected for a third term earlier in the summer, with Conmebol eager for his 64-team World Cup plans to go through for the 2030 edition. They have not explicitly confirmed this stance since the scandal, though.

open image in gallery Conmebol has not explicitly endorsed Infantino since the scandal but is expected to back the Fifa president ( Getty )

State of play

As things stand, Infantino has 105 member associations backing him for re-election, while 95 members are outwardly confirmed to be opposing him. This is taking into account the endorsements of confederations, which are being considered as a blanket vote from all members under that governing body unless a member has broken rank.

For example, Jordan’s opposition to Infantino means he is not included in the other 47 AFC member associations supporting Infantino, per the confederation’s endorsement, while the likes of Mexico, Grenada, and St Kitts and Nevis are all separate from the other 38 Concacaf members in opposition.

This suggests that Infantino is teetering on securing re-election, theoretically needing just one more vote. However, each nation has a vote for itself and some could go against their confederation’s stance to turn the tide against the Swiss-Italian come March’s election.

News.title: Infantino says he's supported by 'vast, vast majority' of soccer ahead of FIFA elections
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

FIFA’s embattled president Gianni Infantino said he has the backing of the “vast, vast majority” of soccer, despite his failed plan to sell stakes in the World Cup.

Infantino is seeking re-election next year as the head of soccer’s world governing body in the face of attempts to force him to stand down in the wake of the divisive plan.

He infuriated soccer leaders in Europe, North America and Asia over the proposal to sell profits in the World Cup through a commercial subsidiary.

But in an interview released Saturday with the BBC at the Under-15 World Cup in Azerbaijan, Infantino brushed off doubts about him being able to continue as president.

“Well you know I was elected by 211 member associations from all over the world," Infantino said. "I think what is important is that in an organization like FIFA, there can be different views, different points of view.

“But if we are serious about democracy, about the democratic process, about believing that everyone has the same vote and the same voice all over the world, that football belongs to everyone, if we are serious about that, then we need, to respect as well the views of the vast, vast majority.”

Infantino is standing for a final term in office in March. The deadline for potential candidates to come forward to stand against him is Nov. 18.

His latest comments came after he apologized to FIFA’s ruling council last week for “mistakes” in his secretive investment plan for the World Cup.

Despite his apology, European delegates said they left the meeting disappointed about what they saw as a lack of clarity.

On Friday, the Asian Football Confederation endorsed Infantino for another term as FIFA president in an apparent turnaround in its stance from two months ago when it criticized him for a breach of trust.

The Metropolitan Police is “reviewing its handling” of allegations made to the force about the Duchess of Sussex’s father Thomas Markle.

Authorities in the Philippines are investigating allegations that Meghan’s estranged father kept child sex abuse images at his former home. He denies the accusations, calling them a “bunch of lies”.

On Friday, the Duchess said she was made aware of “disturbing allegations” about her father in 2018. She said she was shown a letter sent to Scotland Yard eight years ago making “troubling” allegations against him and she was assured that these were being investigated.

The Met on Saturday confirmed it received a letter in 2019 about a “number of claims” relating to Mr Markle, but admitted it did not pass details of the allegations to other law enforcement authorities.

It said it was now looking into whether it needed to refer itself to the police watchdog over its conduct.

In a statement, Scotland Yard said: “Following a thorough review of Met Police systems and records, we have confirmed that in January 2019, we received a letter containing a number of claims about alleged offending outside the United Kingdom. It was sent to the MPS Protection Command to raise concerns in relation to the security of the Duchess of Sussex.

open image in gallery Meghan became estranged from her father in 2018 ( Instagram )

“The letter was reviewed and a decision was made that it should be passed to the office of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex for their awareness. The details of the allegations in the letter were not shared with other law enforcement agencies.

“The MPS is reviewing the handling of this matter in 2019 and considering whether a referral to the IOPC is necessary to review our approach.”

Meghan’s half-brother Thomas Jr told The Sun that he had found “hundreds” of child sex images on computers and a cellphone, which were left behind at his father’s home on Cebu when he moved from the Philippines earlier this year.

Mr Markle Sr was forced to return to the US from Cebu after suffering a stroke and a blood clot, which led to the amputation of his left leg and he is reportedly now living in a rehab centre in Florida, where he is learning to walk again.

Meghan “reached out” to him in the aftermath of the operation, a spokesperson for the duchess said, and she was also said to have tried to do so previously.

She became estranged from her former TV lighting director father in the run-up to her 2018 wedding to Prince Harry after he was caught staging paparazzi photographs.

Mr Markle Jnr said he submitted a police statement in the Philippines, telling the newspaper he was “horrified” by what he found, which gave him “no option” but to report his father.

“I won’t speak to my father ever again unless I’m called to give evidence against him”, he said.

open image in gallery Authorities in the Philippines are investigating allegations that Thomas Markle kept child sex abuse images at his former home ( ITV/GMB )

He is said to have reported his discovery to the FBI Hotline and to the state police in Pennsylvania, as well as the US-based National Centre for Exploited and Missing Children in July.

Nicholas Ty, undersecretary for the Philippines Department of Justice, confirmed an investigation was underway.

He told ITV News: “Our Anti-Trafficking and Online Sexual Abuse and Exploitation of Children taskforce in Cebu is currently investigating the matter.”

Mr Markle Sr has denied the accusations and said he believed his son was “trying to destroy” him.

He said: “I’m shocked, I’m hurt and I’m very upset that my son is making these accusations against me. I could never do what I’m being accused of. It’s the worst thing anyone could accuse me of.

“This is bulls***. It’s just a bunch of lies. It’s sick. I have no idea why Tom is trying to destroy me with these lies.”

Authorities in the Philippines are investigating allegations that the Duchess of Sussex’s father Thomas Markle kept child sex abuse images at his former home.

Meghan’s half-brother Thomas Jr told The Sun that he had found “hundreds” of child sex images on computers and a cellphone, which were left behind at his father’s home on Cebu when he moved from the Philippines earlier this year.

Mr Markle Jnr said he submitted a police statement in the country, telling the newspaper he was “horrified” by what he found, which gave him “no option” but to report his father. “I won’t speak to my father ever again unless I’m called to give evidence against him”, he said.

He is said to have reported his discovery to the FBI Hotline and to the state police in Pennsylvania, as well as the US-based National Centre for Exploited and Missing Children in July.

Now, Nicholas Ty, undersecretary for the Philippines Department of Justice, confirmed an investigation was under way. He told ITV News: “Our Anti-Trafficking and Online Sexual Abuse and Exploitation of Children taskforce in Cebu is currently investigating the matter.”

open image in gallery Thomas Markle Sr, the father of the Duchess of Sussex, is accused of having kept child sex abuse images ( ITV/GMB )

Mr Markle Sr has denied the accusations and said he believed his son was “trying to destroy” him.

He said: “I’m shocked, I’m hurt and I’m very upset that my son is making these accusations against me. I could never do what I’m being accused of. It’s the worst thing anyone could accuse me of.

“This is bulls***. It’s just a bunch of lies. It’s sick. I have no idea why Tom is trying to destroy me with these lies.”

Mr Markle Sr was forced to return to the US from Cebu after suffering a stroke and a blood clot, which led to the amputation of his left leg and he is reportedly now living in a rehab centre in Florida, where he is learning to walk again.

Meghan “reached out” to him in the aftermath of the operation, a spokesperson for the duchess said, and Meghan was also said to have tried to do so previously.

The duchess became estranged from her former TV lighting director father in the run-up to her 2018 wedding to Prince Harry after he was caught staging paparazzi photographs.

On Friday, Meghan said she was made aware of “disturbing allegations” about her father in the same year.

Referencing her brother’s claims, she said in a statement: “I am deeply distressed at the news that has come to light in the last 24 hours, and my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed.

“In 2018, a letter was sent to the Metropolitan Police and Royalty and Specialist Protection. That letter was subsequently shared with me.

“It made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father and I was given assurances that these were being investigated.

open image in gallery Meghan Markle and father Thomas Markle Sr ( Instagram )

“I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications’ distortion over the years, any distance from my father and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children, was for one reason: to protect them.

“I trusted that the authorities were doing the same for other families.

“Although the breadth of what has now been uncovered is more sickening than one could ever imagine, my sincerest hope is that justice will be fully served and that the priority remains the safety and protection of innocent children.”

Mr Markle Sr did not attend Meghan’s wedding, leaving the King to accompany her down the aisle and meaning the only member of her family present was her mother, Doria Ragland.

The Duchess was the only child of Mr Markle’s marriage to Ms Ragland, though he has two children – Samantha and Thomas Jr – from an earlier marriage.

It is understood the Metropolitan Police is not currently and has not previously investigated Mr Markle Sr.

The force said it is making internal inquiries regarding officers from the Met’s Royalty and Specialist Protection Command being involved in the passing on of a letter.

A spokesperson said: “We are aware of media reports that officers from the Met’s Royalty and Specialist Protection Command were involved in the passing on of a letter in 2018.

“We are undertaking inquiries internally in an effort to confirm this.”

News.title: Gianni Infantino laughs in the face of critics and claims ‘vast majority’ support him
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Gianni Infantino laughed in response to a question over whether he had considered resigning as Fifa president as he declared he retains the support of the “vast, vast majority” of world football.

Infantino came under significant pressure this summer following the collapse of his proposals to sell off commercial stakes in the World Cup to private investors under the Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) plan.

Fifa president Gianni Infantino could stand for re-election unopposed next March ( Reuters )

After facing calls to resign from Uefa over the proposals, Infantino is planning to stand for re-election in March, while he has also outlined plans for reform within Fifa and last week apologised to members of the Fifa Council.

Infantino’s hopes of re-election received a significant boost this week when the Asian Football Confederation (AFC), which had previously supported Uefa’s stance, declared its “full commitment” to supporting him.

The AFC’s apparent U-turn, means Infantino will likely to have enough votes to win an election – while candidates seeking to oppose him have until next month to declare they are standing and no has one currently done so.

Asked by the BBC if he had ever considered standing down following the collapse of the FFE plans, Infantino laughed and said: “Well you know I was elected by 211 member associations from all over the world.

“I think what is important is that in an organisation like Fifa, there can be different views, different points of view.

“But if we are serious about democracy, about the democratic process, about believing that everyone has the same vote and the same voice all over the world, that football belongs to everyone, if we are serious about that, then we need to respect as well the views of the vast, vast majority.

“I'm just coming back off Tokyo where the Asian Football Confederation has fully endorsed me. I was in Cape Verde where all [Confederation of] African [Football] countries have endorsed me. I'm speaking to all associations everywhere in the world.”

Uefa were joined by Concacaf, the Confederation of North, Central America and Caribbean Association Football, and the AFC in signing an open letter accusing Infantino of breaking trust through “deception” over the FFE plans.

Uefa are also preparing to bring a legal challenge against Infantino in the United States and Infantino conceded that further “dialogue” was needed with European football’s governing body, which has remained committed to opposing the Fifa president.

Infantino also told reporters: “I always said as far as I’m concerned, I’m always there with my arms open, with my mind open, with my heart open to discuss with everyone, to engage with everyone, to see what can be done better for everyone.

“We need to recognise that there are processes, there are democratic processes, and you cannot always make everyone happy everywhere. Unfortunately, I would love to, and I’m trying my best to do that. We try all at Fifa.

“If there are different points of view and different opinions, then we just have to be able to discuss them, to engage, to understand each other, where we are coming from, and maybe sometimes that’s a little bit what is missing, the dialogue, the discussion, the culture of debate, the culture of disagreeing as well.

“There is nothing bad in disagreeing, we see it every day in so many countries in the world. It’s OK to disagree. It’s OK to have different points of view, but then we need to be able to move on.”

Infantino was speaking in Baku, Azerbaijan on the opening day of Fifa’s Under-15 World Cup. The tournament features teams from 189 member associations, including Russia – marking their first appearance in a Fifa competition since their invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

News.title: Sacha Baron Cohen says Trump possesses 'elements of brilliance'
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Sacha Baron Cohen believes that Donald Trump possesses "elements of brilliance", arguing that critics have routinely "underestimated" the US president.

The 55-year-old actor sat down with the politician in character as Ali G for Da Ali G Show in 2003, and maintains that the public failed to judge him accurately.

Speaking on the Happy Sad Confused podcast, Baron Cohen said: "I mean, how has he survived a second term? People underestimated him.

"We were too easy to dismiss him as a nincompoop. There are elements of brilliance to him, otherwise.

"And that explains his appeal with the fact that he's there for a second term, the fact that he's transforming this country. I won't say positively or negatively."

open image in gallery Sacha Baron Cohen, as Ali G, interviewed Donald Trump in 2003

Recalling their TV interview, Baron Cohen said that Trump was initially impressed by director James Bobin, before his mood "immediately" changed upon discovering he would be speaking with Ali G.

"I actually met a woman who was in the car with him after that interview, and he was apparently furious," the comedian recalled.

"He actually went out publicly a couple of times to criticise me. And in the end, we used all those clips and used them to advertise another show that I did."

The Borat actor, who brings back his persona for the feature film Ali G: Who Iz I?, previously called Trump "amusing" and said there was "a huge amount of comedy in the way he speaks".

Expanding on the Pivot podcast, he said: "He's intentionally being funny.

"And if you have a look on the far right, they use comedy and sarcasm as an engaging way to dismiss criticisms."

open image in gallery Sacha Baron Cohen returns as Ali G for the film 'Ali G: Who Iz I?' ( AP )

The Bruno star recently outlined why he chose to revive Ali G.

He told Time magazine: "The fact that Ali G is outdated and problematic is the very reason I resurrected him.

"The world he’s returned to is, in many ways, worse than the one he left 20 years ago. All the prejudices my characters are designed to expose haven’t just lingered - they’ve metastasised. They’re fuelled by the greatest propaganda machine in history - social media - and now by its monstrous child, AI."

Baron Cohen added that prejudice has "gone mainstream" in the years since Ali G's height.

"Back when I first created Borat, it took a few minutes – or a few drinks – to get people to reveal the racism that often simmered below the surface," he stated.

"Now, those views have gone mainstream - whether it’s fans hurling slurs and abuse at Black players during the World Cup or hundreds of white nationalists marching through Washington, D.C., on July 4."

News.title: England hammer France to keep Rugby League World Cup hopes alive
News.content:
With Samoa beating Papua New Guinea 64-6 earlier on Saturday, England’s task was put into stark and imposing focus. The Pacific Islanders have a points difference of plus-132. Courtesy of this mauling, England’s is plus-64. So they must see off Papua New Guinea by a big number next Friday and then pray that Tonga defeat Samoa two days later. That is their only route through.

In truth, that is as much as McDermott could hope after their initial shortcomings, as they seek to avoid missing out on the last four for the first time in the World Cup’s 72-year history.

It should be remembered that this was only McDermott’s second game in charge and, even allowing for the poor opposition, they were dramatically improved. It is incredible to think that England took 22 minutes to break the deadlock, when the ever-excellent Dom Young burst through. From there, they averaged a try every four or so minutes, with France looking increasingly forlorn and fatigued.

News.title: How an aid initiative maimed thousands of children in war-torn Africa
News.content:
Tormented by pain from severe internal burns, Amza Kebbie is one of thousands of children in Sierra Leone damaged for life by an aid intervention which went horribly wrong.

It has been five days since the four-year-old boy drank caustic soda, one of the two main ingredients for making soap, after mistaking it for drinking water. The highly corrosive liquid, also known as sodium hydroxide, has stripped the lining of his oesophagus and part of his stomach, causing life changing damage.

He’s now in intensive care, clinging precariously to life. An intravenous drip provides fluids and there’s a nasal cannula that enables him to breathe. Medics and relatives look over him around the clock.

If he can gather enough strength (which the nurses say is by no means guaranteed) the dangerously sick child will undergo a gastrostomy, an operation that will see a tube directly inserted into his stomach so that he can be fed long term.

Amza drank caustic soda while being looked after by a neighbour who was making soap at home Credit : The Telegraph/SImon Townsley

He can no longer swallow properly and may never be able to do so again, say his doctors.

This is not an isolated tragedy. Across Sierra Leone, there are thousands of children like Amza, and their number is growing every year.

At the Goderich Surgical Centre in the capital Freetown, around 200 children are admitted annually with caustic soda poisoning. Many more are thought to die in remote regions where emergency medical treatment is unavailable.

Behind the calamity is a humanitarian initiative that has spectacularly backfired. It’s a prime example of the law of unintended consequences; of a seemingly sensible and undoubtedly well meaning public health intervention doing more harm than good.

Fatmata Kamara accidentally drank caustic soda at her grandmother’s house in 2014 and has had a feeding tube ever since Credit : SImon Townsley

The story starts in the aftermath of Sierra Leone’s vicious civil war, which ran between 1991 and 2002.

Fought between the government and the Revolutionary United Front – backed by Liberian warlord Charles Taylor – the war claimed an estimated 50,000 to 70,000 lives, displaced 2.5 million people and left the country brutalised and in ruins.

In its aftermath, international aid agencies and NGOs desperately sought ways to revive the country and alighted on DIY soap making as a way of killing two birds with one stone.

Siblings Aminata Fofana and Salieu Bangura help out with the family soap-making business Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

Organisations including UNHCR, UNICEF and World Vision thought the practice would both improve sanitation in the country’s disease-ridden shanty towns and provide home-bound women with the means to earn a sustainable income.

It seemed like an obvious “win-win”, and schemes to help women set up in the soap making business rapidly proliferated.

An annual report by the International Federation of the Red Cross, published in May 2002, promoted a micro-finance scheme to fund small-scale soapmaking.

Saieu Bangura, 13, with a tub of soap flakes Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

In 2005, the Centre for War Affected Women in Sierra Leone’s Kono district, backed by the UNHCR, listed soap making as one of the main training courses for war widows and female amputees.

And at about the same time, the Freetown-based Safer Future Youth Development Programme, supported by UNICEF and the charity War Child, provided “a tool kit for soap production” at its training workshops.

As recently as 2020, Action Aid ran a promotional article on its Sierra Leone website showing how soap making had enabled women to become financially independent of their husbands.

The article ran under the headline: “With Soap Making Skills – I'm Empowered!”

Mabinty Bangura is taken to theatre for an endoscopy Credit : Simon Townsley

It is for good reason that the ancient Greek physician Hippocrates urged doctors “first, do no harm”.

To follow the rule literally is not possible as all health interventions entail some risk but it's a reminder never to underestimate the capacity of a new intervention to backfire.

There are plenty of examples from history to choose from.

During the British Raj in India, the government offered a cash bounty for every dead cobra as a way of reducing the danger of venomous snakes.

The surgical team examine the internal damage via an endoscopy Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

But rather than leading to a decline in snake numbers, the plan resulted in entrepreneurial individuals breeding cobras just so they could kill them and then claim the reward.

Once officials realised what was happening and the scheme was stopped, thousands of the then worthless cobras were released into the wild, greatly increasing the risk of snakebite.

In the late 1950s, the Chinese Communist regime introduced an equally calamitous public health campaign involving sparrows.

They issued a directive ordering the birds to be destroyed because they were thought to spread disease and destroy crops.

A child’s gastrostomy scar with a feeding tube in place Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

What those behind the idea failed to consider was that sparrows are natural predators. As their numbers declined, the locust population exploded, decimating agriculture and contributing to the Great Chinese Famine in which millions died.

So what went wrong in Sierra Leone? What did those behind the soap making scheme fail to foresee?

Experts say the initiative simply failed to consider the danger inherent in encouraging people to use toxic chemicals in their homes.

The brightly coloured buckets in which caustic soda is made, and then mixed with oil and scent to make soap, are the same buckets used across the country to fetch and hold drinking water. And just like drinking water, the lethal solution is cool, clear and inviting.

Just a drop is enough to cause the most horrific burns. So when a thirsty young child like Amza runs in from play and mistakenly scoops up a cup of it to quench their thirst they will lose their oesophagus, if not their lives.

Giuseppe Meucci, chief surgeon at the Goderich Surgical Centre Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

Giuseppe Meucci, chief surgeon at the 56-bed Goderich hospital in Freetown where four year old Amza is being cared for, has been treating patients burned by sodium hydroxide nearly every day since arriving in Freetown in 2019.

Three quarters of patients seen by the hospital’s specialist programme for oesophageal burns, set up in response to the crisis and run by the Italian medical charity Emergency, are under five.

“It’s a struggle in this country,” says Dr Meucci. “Almost every family knows someone who has suffered because of this problem. But they just keep coming.”

Hospital director Jasna Sundic Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“In most countries you remove the source of danger for the child, but here that doesn’t seem to happen,” he says.

“It’s one of the main health problems of this country. Soda is there with malaria, malnutrition and typhoid complications. It’s one of the reasons why so many children die before they reach five years old.”

Hospital director Jasna Sundic agrees.

“This is a very severe issue but one which is very preventable,” she tells the Telegraph. “[But] however much we do here, we have not been able to decrease the overall number of soda patients being admitted.

“We cannot stop mothers who have no other source of income except making soap.”

Ibrahim Kerah is fed by his father Mohamed Credit : SImon Townsley

In a handful of rare cases, burns victims are sent abroad for complex oesophageal reconstruction surgery but this is not an option for the vast majority of children injured in Sierra Leone.

More than 60 per cent require surgery, but for these children, like Amza, a feeding tube that bypasses the oesophagus is the only option.

The hospital has many of these gastrostomy patients.

Critically underweight Mabinty Bangura Credit : The Telegraph/SImon Townsley

In a ward dedicated to soda burns, four-year-old Ibrahim Kerah is being fed through his stomach tube by his father Mohamed.

They travelled together on the back of a motorbike taxi for nearly 10 hours to get here for his third check-up appointment.

The Telegraph watches as Mohamed carefully prepares his son’s meal, adding spinach leaves to the porridge-like mix which is fed into a syringe at the end of the tube.

At an adjoining bed two-year-old Mabinty Bangura is critically underweight after ingesting soda about six months ago. Nurses have put her on a high protein drip so she can regain enough strength to undergo the same bypass surgery.

In the courtyard outside, mothers whose children have just had a gastrostomy are being taught how to prepare the liquid food.

Ibrahim and his father Mohamed endured a 10-hour motorbike journey to attend his hospital check-up Credit : The Telegraph/SImon Townsley

Isatu Alie, 24, has been living with a stomach tube for 12 years, and now works for Emergency as a patient ambassador.

She is eight months pregnant with her second child and proud to have overcome her injury and the stigma of having to feed through a tube.

“I remember what happened so well,” she says. “I had just got back from school. I took my cup and dunked it into the water bucket. My aunt made soap and, on that day, I didn’t ask about the liquid in the bucket. The pain was incredible”.

More than a decade has passed since her surgery, and Isatu has adjusted well.

“I’m okay with it now. I feel like a normal human being; I’m blessed to be here,” she says.

“Now I speak to children and their parents who have just experienced the same thing and tell them not to lose hope.”

Pregnant Isatu Alie now works as a patient ambassador Credit : The Telegraph/SImon Townsley

A small proportion of the patients needing treatment following caustic soda burns are adults.

Among them is 21-year-old Junisa Bundeh, who is on a follow-up visit to check his stomach tube. He explains that he gulped down what he thought was a cup of water from a basin while eating at his grandmother’s house three months ago.

“It was so painful,” recalls Junisa. “I realised what it was straight away because it was so harsh. I tried to spit it all out but the liquid was already going down my throat.”

Mothers are taught how to prepare liquid food; Junisa Bundeh shows his feeding tube Credit : SImon Townsley

In the muddy lanes of Freetown’s Waterloo district there are makeshift soap making operations all over.

The coloured plastic buckets full of either soda or water are everywhere.

Against the backdrop of the rainy season’s persistent gloom, the containers symbolise a measure of cleanliness for families sheltering from torrential downpours under mouldy concrete awnings.

As the Telegraph watches Yabom Kapro, a village elder, making soap, the risks involved are immediately obvious.

Chief Yabom Kapro makes soap at her Waterloo town home, near Freetown Credit : The Telegraph/SImon Townsley

As she tips a purple bucket of caustic soda solution into a large basin and then adds palm oil from a plastic jerrycan, local children hover round the cluster of colourful containers.

Yabom uses a wooden paddle to stir the mixture into a creamy paste and then pours it into a mould held in place by an old motorcycle tyre.

Buckets containing caustic soda dissolving, top. Caustic soda crystals, below Credit : The Telegraph/SImon Townsley

Once set, the beige-coloured cake of soap is cut into blocks which are then grated on a wire mesh contraption to be sold at the local market.

“When you dilute the caustic soda, it is completely clear like water at first,” says another soap maker, 43-year-old Cilina Bangura.

“Afterwards a white scum forms on the top, but you cannot be watching all of the time, [even] with all of these children around.”

Cilina knows the risks but says she can't afford to stop making soap. It has, as the NGOs intended, become an economic lifeline for her and her family.

“I want my children to continue making soap when I stop working,” she says. “I took out a loan to buy everything I needed, and now it is the only way I can make a living.

“Of course, I know how dangerous soda is – it has burned my skin many times – but I don’t have another option.”

Home-made soap, in Waterloo Credit : The Telegraph/SImon Townsley

Maimunatu Sankoh, three, whose family lives in a nearby tin-roof shack, is sadly too well aware of that danger from her own bitter experience of soda poisoning.

As she feeds her daughter through a stomach tube, Maimunatu’s mum Iyesatu complains: “I have never seen any public information about soda.

“There are warnings on the packets but that is no use once the product is dissolved in water. They need to tell people to keep buckets out of the way.”

Iyesatu Kamara feeds her daughter Maimunatu Sankoh at their home Credit : SImon Townsley

Incidents of children consuming harmful chemicals are not confined to developing countries and were once common in the west.

In the US, the Poison Prevention Packaging Act was introduced in 1970, mandating childproof containers and the labelling of harmful household products.

The UK followed suit in 1975 with the introduction of child-resistant safety caps on containers of caustic soda and most other noxious household substances.

Despite the risks, Cilina says she can't afford to stop making soap Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

Such legislation is still a long way off in Sierra Leone and is anyway far too late for four-year-old Amza.

Under heavy sedation in the intensive care unit, his glazed eyes open only occasionally.

The only visible evidence of his injuries is some scarring on his lips, but the doctors say his throat, oesophagus and stomach have all been seared by several large gulps of soda.

The boy’s mother, Mamie Kebbie, 30, keeps a watchful vigil, stroking his listless head tenderly. She says he used to be a playful and vivacious child.

If they are taken to hospital quickly, children with soda burns are normally given an oesophageal dilation endoscopy – a procedure which aims to keep the oesophagus open – but for Amza this has not been possible.

Freetown, Sierra Leone Credit : Simon Townsley

“This is a very severe case,” explains nurse Annette Turay, who heads the hospital’s intensive care unit. “When he was brought in, about 10 hours after he had ingested the soda, we were unable to conduct an endoscopy because he already had respiratory problems.

“He has pneumonia and he cannot feed through his mouth. He cannot even swallow his own saliva.

Mamie Kebbie keeps a vigil at her son's bedside Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“It will be a week before he is strong enough for us to be able to operate. We will insert a gastric tube into his stomach. He will have to keep this as his main way of being fed for a long time, potentially forever.”

But nurse Turay has seen worse.

“I have seen so many children suffering a lot after ingesting soda, so many dying too.

“A few weeks ago, we had a child in the ward who died because his stomach was completely gone”.

The Telegraph contacted all the NGOs involved in the setting up of and promotion of soap making schemes in Sierra Leone that are mentioned in this story for comment.

Protect yourself and your family by learning more about Global Health Security

“In most countries you remove the source of danger for the child, but here that doesn’t seem to happen,” he says.

“It’s one of the main health problems of this country. Soda is there with malaria, malnutrition and typhoid complications. It’s one of the reasons why so many children die before they reach five years old.”

Hospital director Jasna Sundic agrees.

“This is a very severe issue but one which is very preventable,” she tells the Telegraph. “[But] however much we do here, we have not been able to decrease the overall number of soda patients being admitted.

“We cannot stop mothers who have no other source of income except making soap.”

Ibrahim Kerah is fed by his father Mohamed Credit : SImon Townsley

In a handful of rare cases, burns victims are sent abroad for complex oesophageal reconstruction surgery but this is not an option for the vast majority of children injured in Sierra Leone.

More than 60 per cent require surgery, but for these children, like Amza, a feeding tube that bypasses the oesophagus is the only option.

The hospital has many of these gastrostomy patients.

Critically underweight Mabinty Bangura Credit : The Telegraph/SImon Townsley

In a ward dedicated to soda burns, four-year-old Ibrahim Kerah is being fed through his stomach tube by his father Mohamed.

They travelled together on the back of a motorbike taxi for nearly 10 hours to get here for his third check-up appointment.

The Telegraph watches as Mohamed carefully prepares his son’s meal, adding spinach leaves to the porridge-like mix which is fed into a syringe at the end of the tube.

At an adjoining bed two-year-old Mabinty Bangura is critically underweight after ingesting soda about six months ago. Nurses have put her on a high protein drip so she can regain enough strength to undergo the same bypass surgery.

In the courtyard outside, mothers whose children have just had a gastrostomy are being taught how to prepare the liquid food.

Ibrahim and his father Mohamed endured a 10-hour motorbike journey to attend his hospital check-up Credit : The Telegraph/SImon Townsley

Isatu Alie, 24, has been living with a stomach tube for 12 years, and now works for Emergency as a patient ambassador.

She is eight months pregnant with her second child and proud to have overcome her injury and the stigma of having to feed through a tube.

“I remember what happened so well,” she says. “I had just got back from school. I took my cup and dunked it into the water bucket. My aunt made soap and, on that day, I didn’t ask about the liquid in the bucket. The pain was incredible”.

More than a decade has passed since her surgery, and Isatu has adjusted well.

“I’m okay with it now. I feel like a normal human being; I’m blessed to be here,” she says.

“Now I speak to children and their parents who have just experienced the same thing and tell them not to lose hope.”

Pregnant Isatu Alie now works as a patient ambassador Credit : The Telegraph/SImon Townsley

A small proportion of the patients needing treatment following caustic soda burns are adults.

Among them is 21-year-old Junisa Bundeh, who is on a follow-up visit to check his stomach tube. He explains that he gulped down what he thought was a cup of water from a basin while eating at his grandmother’s house three months ago.

“It was so painful,” recalls Junisa. “I realised what it was straight away because it was so harsh. I tried to spit it all out but the liquid was already going down my throat.”

Mothers are taught how to prepare liquid food; Junisa Bundeh shows his feeding tube Credit : SImon Townsley

In the muddy lanes of Freetown’s Waterloo district there are makeshift soap making operations all over.

The coloured plastic buckets full of either soda or water are everywhere.

Against the backdrop of the rainy season’s persistent gloom, the containers symbolise a measure of cleanliness for families sheltering from torrential downpours under mouldy concrete awnings.

As the Telegraph watches Yabom Kapro, a village elder, making soap, the risks involved are immediately obvious.

Chief Yabom Kapro makes soap at her Waterloo town home, near Freetown Credit : The Telegraph/SImon Townsley

As she tips a purple bucket of caustic soda solution into a large basin and then adds palm oil from a plastic jerrycan, local children hover round the cluster of colourful containers.

Yabom uses a wooden paddle to stir the mixture into a creamy paste and then pours it into a mould held in place by an old motorcycle tyre.

Buckets containing caustic soda dissolving, top. Caustic soda crystals, below Credit : The Telegraph/SImon Townsley

Once set, the beige-coloured cake of soap is cut into blocks which are then grated on a wire mesh contraption to be sold at the local market.

“When you dilute the caustic soda, it is completely clear like water at first,” says another soap maker, 43-year-old Cilina Bangura.

“Afterwards a white scum forms on the top, but you cannot be watching all of the time, [even] with all of these children around.”

Cilina knows the risks but says she can't afford to stop making soap. It has, as the NGOs intended, become an economic lifeline for her and her family.

“I want my children to continue making soap when I stop working,” she says. “I took out a loan to buy everything I needed, and now it is the only way I can make a living.

“Of course, I know how dangerous soda is – it has burned my skin many times – but I don’t have another option.”

Home-made soap, in Waterloo Credit : The Telegraph/SImon Townsley

Maimunatu Sankoh, three, whose family lives in a nearby tin-roof shack, is sadly too well aware of that danger from her own bitter experience of soda poisoning.

As she feeds her daughter through a stomach tube, Maimunatu’s mum Iyesatu complains: “I have never seen any public information about soda.

“There are warnings on the packets but that is no use once the product is dissolved in water. They need to tell people to keep buckets out of the way.”

Iyesatu Kamara feeds her daughter Maimunatu Sankoh at their home Credit : SImon Townsley

Incidents of children consuming harmful chemicals are not confined to developing countries and were once common in the west.

In the US, the Poison Prevention Packaging Act was introduced in 1970, mandating childproof containers and the labelling of harmful household products.

The UK followed suit in 1975 with the introduction of child-resistant safety caps on containers of caustic soda and most other noxious household substances.

Despite the risks, Cilina says she can't afford to stop making soap Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

Such legislation is still a long way off in Sierra Leone and is anyway far too late for four-year-old Amza.

Under heavy sedation in the intensive care unit, his glazed eyes open only occasionally.

The only visible evidence of his injuries is some scarring on his lips, but the doctors say his throat, oesophagus and stomach have all been seared by several large gulps of soda.

The boy’s mother, Mamie Kebbie, 30, keeps a watchful vigil, stroking his listless head tenderly. She says he used to be a playful and vivacious child.

If they are taken to hospital quickly, children with soda burns are normally given an oesophageal dilation endoscopy – a procedure which aims to keep the oesophagus open – but for Amza this has not been possible.

Freetown, Sierra Leone Credit : Simon Townsley

“This is a very severe case,” explains nurse Annette Turay, who heads the hospital’s intensive care unit. “When he was brought in, about 10 hours after he had ingested the soda, we were unable to conduct an endoscopy because he already had respiratory problems.

“He has pneumonia and he cannot feed through his mouth. He cannot even swallow his own saliva.

Mamie Kebbie keeps a vigil at her son's bedside Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“It will be a week before he is strong enough for us to be able to operate. We will insert a gastric tube into his stomach. He will have to keep this as his main way of being fed for a long time, potentially forever.”

But nurse Turay has seen worse.

“I have seen so many children suffering a lot after ingesting soda, so many dying too.

“A few weeks ago, we had a child in the ward who died because his stomach was completely gone”.

The Telegraph contacted all the NGOs involved in the setting up of and promotion of soap making schemes in Sierra Leone that are mentioned in this story for comment.

News.title: Carrick weighs up stripping Bruno Fernandes of Man Utd captaincy
News.content:
A defiant Michael Carrick refused to rule out stripping Bruno Fernandes of the captaincy as the Manchester United manager told his players to cut out their public sniping and start doing their talking on the pitch.

Carrick struck a bullish tone as he came out fighting and moved to reassert his authority after a tumultuous past fortnight that has left him battling to save his job ahead of Sunday’s must-win game against Bournemouth at Old Trafford.

The United manager began his press conference on Friday afternoon with a stirring five-and-a-half-minute monologue in which he issued an emotional call to arms to his players to demonstrate the values of hard work, sacrifice, humility and resilience that define the club.

Referencing Sir Matt Busby, Sir Alex Ferguson, Sir Bobby Charlton, Ryan Giggs and Wayne Rooney, Carrick warned there could be no “entitlement” culture in echoes of complaints from his predecessor Ruben Amorim.

United are actively considering their options in the event Carrick cannot quickly arrest a shocking start to the season that hit a new low with Wednesday’s 4-1 humiliation by Como. The likes of Julian Nagelsmann, Eddie Howe, Unai Emery, Fabian Hürzeler and Antonio Conte are in the frame.

But Carrick insisted he was “100 per cent” convinced he was the right man to take United forward and, while he claimed the dressing room was “not divided”, he has had to contend with first defender Lisandro Martínez and then Fernandes venting in public.

Martínez was fined and publicly apologised for an extraordinary tirade at Jason Wilcox, the director of football, and the Old Trafford board last week before Fernandes appeared to call out Carrick’s tactics in the wake of the Como debacle.

Carrick responded at the time to having his set-up and approach questioned by suggesting tactics count for little if players are unprepared to run.

Asked if he would consider taking the captaincy off Fernandes, Carrick said: “I’m just saying I’ll always – whatever the situation is – do what’s best for the club.”

News.title: Oil hits five-month high amid fears of fresh strikes on Iran
News.content:
The price of oil has hit a five-month high amid fears Donald Trump will ramp up strikes in the Middle East following the midterm elections.

Brent crude, the international benchmark, climbed as much as 2.8pc to more than $116 a barrel, pushing down stock markets in the US and Europe.

It followed a New York Times report that the US and Israel had drawn up plans for renewed strikes against Iran after the midterm elections.

Oil has climbed more than 4pc this week, increasing pressure on stock markets at the same time as fears grow about the valuations of AI companies.

European shares fell on Friday, with the FTSE 100 down as much as 0.8pc, the Cac 40 in Paris down 1pc and the Dax in Frankfurt down 1.1pc.

On Wall Street, the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell as much as 1pc, while the S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite fell at a slower pace than the previous day.

Traders were rattled on Thursday after Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s chief executive, warned that a “scarcity of capital” was hampering the rollout of the technology.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq in New York dropped by 2.6pc on Thursday while the S&P 500 fell 1.2pc on its worst day since July.

Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta was one of the worse hit in the sell-off, as its shares finished trading almost 7pc lower.

Overnight, the sell-off spread into Asian markets. Japan’s Nikkei 225 dropped by as much as 2.3pc and was down more than 4pc on the week.

The Kospi index in South Korea declined as much as 4.1pc on Friday but recovered to be marginally higher as markets closed.

The stock market turmoil led to a jump in safe haven assets like bonds.

The yield on 10-year US Treasury bonds, a benchmark for the cost of borrowing for governments around the world, fell by the largest amount since March 2023.

News.title: Europe’s record-breaking summer heat estimated to have killed 50,000 people
News.content:
More than 50,000 people are estimated to have died across Europe as a result of this summer’s record-breaking heatwaves, according to research.

In the UK alone, researchers estimate there were 4,354 excess deaths this summer.

The number of excess deaths across Europe is double the number recorded in 2025 and it is also far higher than the previous record of 29,000 deaths. This was recorded in 2022 when the continent also endured exceptionally high temperatures, with the mercury hitting 40 degrees celsius for the first time in the UK.

According to the Met Office the UK saw its hottest ever summer this year with five widespread heatwaves and 40 days where the temperature was above 30 degrees celsius. Mainland Europe experienced its third hottest summer, with temperatures particularly high in the south and west.

Researchers from Imperial College, London and the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine (LSHTM) looked at 854 urban areas in 30 countries across Europe. Using temperature records and modelling based on the relationship between heat and mortality they estimated the number of heat-related deaths that occurred between June and August.

They said findings from previous years’ excess heat mortality modelling matched official figures released later by national health authorities.

Because the study only looked at urban areas – making up 40 per cent of the population of the countries studied – researchers believe the number of deaths is likely to be an underestimate.

According to the study, published in Nature Health, southern and western Europe were hardest hit. Italy experienced the highest number of excess deaths (13,303), followed by France (7,268), Spain (6,824), Germany (6,340) then the UK.

There were an estimated 22,000 deaths among those aged 85 and over but researchers pointed out that an estimated 6,000 people under the age of 65 are also likely to have died as a result of the heat.

Around a third of the deaths took place in late June, when average temperatures across Europe were more than 5°C above what would be expected during this time of year. Researchers say in early summer people were less likely to have acclimatised to the sweltering weather. This period was marked by both extremely high humidity and unusually high night-time temperatures, making it difficult for people to cool down.

Researchers also estimated that more than two thirds of the total excess deaths were attributable to climate change. Across the continent as a whole Europe was an average 2.9°C higher than would have been expected. However, in some places temperatures were as much as 12°C higher.

Dr Clair Barnes, extreme weather and climate change researcher at Imperial College, said extreme heat was having a severe impact on public health.

“It is yet another reminder both of the imperative of rolling out targeted interventions to protect those who are most vulnerable to this increasingly extreme heat, and of the growing need to rapidly transition away from fossil fuels to slow the pace of change and limit future warming.”

Dr Pierre Masselot, assistant professor of statistics and epidemiology at LSHTM and one of the study’s authors, said “climate change is everybody’s problem”.

“It is not just hot regions that are suffering any more with some parts of Western and Northern Europe experiencing extreme heat and historically high health burden. And the whole population is affected, as shown by the significant death toll among younger age groups.

“It is becoming increasingly clear our cities are poorly adapted to rising heat, and it is critical we improve our efforts towards adaptation. This means cooling the cities through more green spaces and less pollution, and providing health care for affected populations.”
