Sports.title: Premier League news: Spurs’ nine injuries ‘normal’, says De Zerbi; ‘emotional control’ keeps Blues red-free
Sports.content:
1. ‘Big confidence’ in Tottenham’s injury team Roberto De Zerbi has insisted Tottenham’s medical staff bears no responsibility for the numerous selection issues he faces against Chelsea at Stamford Bridge on Saturday where his club will attempt to win for only the second time in 42 matches in all competitions. The head coach has been boosted by the return of Pedro Porro from injury while he reported that Andy Robertson, Omar Marmoush and Dominic Solanke were “good” in light of fitness concerns. De Zerbi had bad news elsewhere, however, saying Destiny Udogie was still out and Tosin Adarabioyo was a doubt. James Maddison did not train for three days after the home win over Coventry on Monday and may not be ready, while caution will remain the watchword with Dejan Kulusevski, who played his first minutes since May 2025 against Frank Lampard’s side. De Zerbi could be without nine players due to injury when the longer-term absentees are factored in, including Lucas Bergvall and Savio. Rodrigo Bentancur is suspended. Spurs appointed a new performance director last season in Dan Lewindon and he oversaw a clutch of new hires in the performance department in July. De Zerbi made the point that the club would make a “total report” on injuries at the end of the season but “so far we can’t say anything bad about the medical staff”. “I am convinced our medical staff this season is high level. I have big confidence because I know how they are working and they are good enough to believe in. We are suffering a normal situation in football.” De Zerbi went into detail on the cases of Porro, Bergvall and Robertson to reinforce his argument. “Pedro won the World Cup with Spain,” he said. “Maybe with the head or body he didn’t recover enough to start this season without a pre-season. He already suffered in the World Cup the muscular problem of the hamstring. He felt it in training and played anyway against Aston Villa [on 29 September] because he pushed to come back before the right time and he suffered another injury. What is the responsibility of the medical staff? “Bergvall turned his knee and felt pain in the first minute against Manchester United [on 10 October]. He finished the game and the day after he felt pain. What is the responsibility of the medical staff? Nothing. Robertson played four games in a row for Scotland [during the recent international window] and after that felt a small problem and did not play in Manchester. He played 65 minutes against Coventry and was fatigued. It’s normal fatigue for a player who played [so much].” On Spurs’s terrible record at Stamford Bridge, De Zerbi said: “What is the problem? We didn’t play in the past for Tottenham and I was not the Tottenham coach in the last seasons. We have already many problems and this is not a problem.” David Hytner

2. Alonso: ‘We keep calm, don’t lose our heads’ Xabi Alonso has said greater emotional control is behind the improvement of Chelsea’s disciplinary record, one that saw them picked up 11 red cards last season. Alonso focused on the problem after becoming manager last summer and has been rewarded with better behaviour from his new side. Chelsea, who can expect a feisty encounter when hosting Tottenham on Saturday evening, have not had a red card this season and showed intelligence when they won 2-0 at Everton last weekend. “For me it comes a lot with emotional control, with the control of the game,” Alonso said. “If you are focused on what you have to do, you are prepared for what’s going on. Normally you don’t make that many mistakes and don’t overreact to certain situations. “This is a fundamental part of the game, to have that emotional control. The momentum is coming – we keep calm, I don’t lose my head and I don’t get stupid yellow cards, make stupid penalties.” Alonso pointed to Chelsea signing more experienced players last summer. “I think it helps,” he said. “Absolutely. It helps for that composure that you need in certain moments. You have players that sometimes, even during the game, they take a step back to see this is happening and now we need to keep focused and calm.” Stamford Bridge is usually at its loudest when Spurs turn up at a ground where they have not won since 2018. Alonso expects an “electric” atmosphere but admitted that playing with control in the Premier League can be tough when crowds feed off duels and end-to-end football. “It is really difficult,” he said. View image in fullscreen Chelsea manager Xabi Alonso has played down the impact of his influence from the touchline: ‘I have from the touchline some kind of input but the real one is from the players.’ Photograph: Phil Noble/Reuters “To find a total dominance in a game when you are in full control and you have few problems like in other leagues, it’s difficult to find it in the Premier League unless you have become a top, top, top team. That’s why you can’t rest on your laurels when you are 2-0 up.” Alonso played down the impact of his influence from the touchline. “It is people on the pitch,” the Spaniard said. “I can say many things but sometimes I don’t reach [the players], I don’t control. I can do it in advance. I have from the touchline some kind of input but the real one is from the players. Normally the most experienced ones. It’s the ones that feel it.” Chelsea are without Emiliano Martínez after the goalkeeper broke his jaw against Everton. Mike Penders will start and Alonso sees similarities between the young Belgian and his compatriot Thibaut Courtois. “I spoke with Thibaut as well when he was in the World Cup, asking about Mike, and he even said that he could see resemblances with Mike,” Alonso said. Jacob Steinberg

3. Go easy on Ngumoha, says Iraola Andoni Iraola has insisted Rio Ngumoha must be allowed to make mistakes and not have his development stifled by “impossible” demands. The 18-year-old sparkled for Liverpool in their Champions League comeback against Villarreal on Tuesday while still adapting to playing on the right wing. It was only a fifth start under Iraola for Ngumoha, who last month became the third-youngest player to make his competitive debut for England, after Wayne Rooney and Jude Bellingham. The Liverpool head coach has described it is a “privilege” to coach the teenager but is wary of too many expectations being heaped on such a young talent. “I feel very lucky to have him but this is a moment when, because he has played well, we cannot straight away put expectations on him super high because it is not fair for him,” Iraola said. “He will still have to make mistakes, he will still have his moments where it is up and down, because this is a natural process that every player goes through. “We cannot straight away put demands on Rio that are impossible to beat. No, we have to help him in this process knowing that he will have good games and probably some games when it is not so good.” Iraola believes Ngumoha’s personality offers reassurance that he will not be unduly affected by the growing attention. The winger has two years remaining on the contract he signed on turning 17 but is expected to be rewarded with a new deal. “I haven’t felt that he’s very affected, positively or negatively, by all the things that are said about him,” Iraola added. “He’s very focused on the football side, on improving his performances and trying to get the things that we need from him. It’s not easy when you are 18 and everyone is talking about you but he knows that what matters is what is happening today in training and the things that he can add to his game. He’s very focused on that.” Liverpool will again be without the injured Dominik Szoboszlai when hosting in-form Brighton on Sunday and Victor Muñoz is doubtful with a knock sustained in last weekend’s win at Brentford. Andy Hunter View image in fullscreen The 18-year-old Rio Ngumoha sparkled for Liverpool in their Champions League comeback against Villarreal on Tuesday. Photograph: Adam Vaughan/EPA

4. Farke faces triple injury blow Daniel Farke has been dealt a blow before Sunday’s Premier League game at Sunderland after revealing Dominic Calvert-Lewin, Anton Stach and Noah Okafor are all injury doubts. Calvert-Lewin, whose fourth league goal of the season earned Leeds a 1-1 home draw against Manchester United last week, and midfielder Stach both sustained foot injuries in that match. Winger Okafor is struggling with a thigh strain and all three players are rated “major doubts” after missing out on team training this week. Farke confirmed Daniel James is in restraint after recovering from his recent injury, while Lukas Nmecha, Harry Wilson and Jean-Mattéo Bahoya will also be hoping to feature. Nmecha has made six league appearances off the bench this season and Farke added: “Overall you have to say for a back-up striker, Lukas has scored I think seven goals last season,” said Farke. “Of course, if he doesn’t play each and every minute due to the fact that Dominic was so outstanding, I think this is a really good record and I would have to say in the last game he looked sharp.” Press Association

5. Nothing has changed for us, says Arbeloa Alvaro Arbeloa maintains “nothing has changed” as his Fulham side look to build on a first Premier League win. The Spaniard – who took over as head coach at Craven Cottage in the summer – has come under scrutiny following a testing start to the campaign before easing some of the pressure with a 1-0 victory over Hull at Craven Cottage. Fulham come up against another promoted side at Coventry on Saturday and Arbeloa wants his players to continue to show the same focused mindset. “Nothing has changed for us,” Arbeloa said. “When we were not winning games, we believed that we were doing so many things well, and now we have the same targets, so we should come in and try to win a tough game. “Yes, now we have the reward that we were looking for, and now it is another week, another game, so we need to fight again for the win.” Arbeloa added: “When you are working and you are not winning, it is not easy, so everything is easier when you play well, in the way that you want and you win matches. That is the most important thing, and it is very important for your confidence, and I think we deserve it.” Press Association

Sports.title: Older, calmer, but still playing the hits: Mourinho and Madrid primed for clásico
Sports.content:
José Mourinho has done the por que?, the printout and the press conference no-show, and he’s been here only three months. The Real Madrid manager has played the classics without even playing a clásico. Not yet anyway, but it’s time: on Sunday night he returns to the stadium he first arrived at 30 transformative years ago as Bobby Robson’s talented young translator, and last visited in 2013 as the most famous manager in football.

The coach who once declared “today, tomorrow and always, Barcelona in my heart,” and claimed he would only ever go to Real Madrid to destroy them, has been entrusted with attempting to bring about the destruction of Barcelona. It is not the first time: if his return is about nostalgia, which it is, that’s wrapped up in their rivals too.

“The clásico is just another game in the championship but to say it’s a game like any other would be to lie, totally unreal,” Mourinho said on Wednesday, and he knows. As for Barcelona’s latest star, he’s looking forward to seeing Mourinho again. “I love the needle,” Lamine Yamal says. “The Mourinho-Guardiola era, I loved all that. That’s football. Sport is serious but I want a show and we have more fun.”

There are bigger things, sure; life beyond Barcelona. Madrid’s astonishing Champions League record since Mourinho was last here – following up the elusive decima, the 10th title which had evaded them for 12 years, with the 11th, 12th, 13th, 14th and 15th in 10 years – played out without Barcelona. There has not been a European clásico since the 2011 Champions League semi-final when the man Pep Guardiola had just called the puto amo, the fucking master, produced his por que speech, asking why Barcelona were favoured by the continent’s referees and accusing Uefa of fixing it for them.

Yet right now it doesn’t feel as if anything is bigger, this week’s Champions League matches framed around what they meant for the game that really matters, even with Barcelona going to Paris. The rivalry is always there; in Mourinho’s case it is at the heart of it. The day he got the Madrid job in 2010 was the day he won the Champions League with Inter but its genesis lay in the semi-final, when he had sprinted across the Camp Nou pitch, finger raised, celebrating. Madrid were relieved and grateful, spared the sight of Barcelona lifting the European Cup in their stadium and shown how to stop a team that appeared unbeatable. Mourinho, leaving the Santiago Bernabéu in Florentino Pérez’s car while his joyful players returned to Milan, was asked to repeat that with Madrid.

Pérez, who had presided over the galácticos’ failure and walked away, had returned in 2009 but won nothing. Instead, Barcelona dominated. They had the core of Spain’s World Cup 2010 winners: six starters in the final. Madrid needed a culture shift, to go to war, a manager to rule over the dressing room. “This year’s galáctico is José Mourinho,” the president said.

View image in fullscreen José Mourinho (left) with Bobby Robson and Ronaldo after Barcelona defeated Paris Saint-Germain in the Cup Winners’ Cup final in 1997. Photograph: Colorsport/Shutterstock

By the time Mourinho left, it had turned nasty, his enemies internal too. They had been, Mourinho later said, “three intense, almost violent years”. Yet Pérez had always felt drawn towards the only manager he has truly liked. Including when Mourinho was belligerent; especially when he was belligerent. Mourinho had, Pérez said, returned Madrid to their rightful place. After every subsequent success the president called to tell him he started this. And if Mourinho’s first clásico brought a 5-0 defeat, Barcelona going on to win the league and Champions League; if his final season had ended trophyless; and if Guardiola had won twice as many trophies, it was also true that of the four competitions Guardiola failed to win at Barcelona, three were taken from him by Mourinho.

Time has passed, things have changed, but the parallels are clear. Madrid have gone two years without a trophy. In the first of those, Barcelona won the league with two weeks to spare, completing a domestic treble. They had defeated Madrid four times, scoring 16 goals. Last season they wrapped it up with three weeks to spare via a clásico victory as incontestable as their superiority throughout a season when Madrid’s splits played out in public. Then Spain won the World Cup with eight Barcelona players in the squad. Madrid’s only representative, Marc Cucurella, joined the club after the tournament started.

If this was a crisis, it was time for Mourinho. A man whose flaws had been forgotten over time, nostalgia eclipsing all else. A man with the authority – a man afforded the authority – to impose on the dressing room. One with the personality to fight, go to war again. With just about everyone, and Barcelona especially. When you listened to Pérez’s extraordinary rant in May, the quiet part said out loud, all campaigning and conspiracy, politics and paranoia, it made sense.

When it comes to the still unresolved Negreira case, in which Barcelona paid the vice-president of the referees’ committee, José María Enríquez Negreira, more than €7m between 2001 and 2018, there is substance to Madrid’s complaints. Barcelona have denied corruption, saying Negreira worked as an adviser, but that case has become the centrepiece of Madrid’s discourse, unlike when the two clubs were still holding out in the Super League. It doesn’t help when the league president likens your TV channel to Joseph Goebbels’ propaganda.

Whether those complaints have validity now is a different question; whether the discourse of conspiracy does is another step again, even when decisions go against you. Every mistake – and decisions that are not even mistakes – is framed as a machiavellian plan, the insinuations constant – when they are not said outright.

When Mourinho arrived he said he was older, calmer, but here he is. In defeat, perhaps he was always likely to be. After losing to Betis, he asked por que? (Why? Because that’s the rule, the decision correct.) After losing to Atlético, he turned up with a printout. And then he didn’t turn up to the press conference after he had run on to the pitch to embrace Vinícius Júnior after the Brazilian scored against Villarreal only for the goal to be ruled out and Vinícius sent off for pulling Nathan Saliba’s hair. That led to a four-game suspension, the forward ruled out of the clásico.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

The reason for the no-show was that Mourinho didn’t want to risk saying something that would earn him a suspension for the clásico, the game. And he is happier now, if only for a little while, something shifting. When last Saturday Barcelona made it 11 wins from 11, averaging more than four goals a game, most agreed they would win the clásico and the title would be done: they were flying, led by Lamine Yamal, while Madrid, beaten twice, hadn’t taken off. Mourinho’s team had not been very good, familiar problems still there. In short, there was not much football.

The previous Wednesday Madrid had delivered another of their seemingly inexplicable comebacks, from 3-1 down at Roma, to win 4-3 in the final seven minutes, but was there really anything to build on? It turned out there was something of an explanation. In those minutes Arda Güler played, Yan Diomande played, Fede Valverde played at right-back, and Vinícius didn’t play.

It seemed so obvious to everyone, including the manager. So he did it again, and Madrid scored four against Sevilla – three of them glorious – last Sunday and four more against Leipzig on Wednesday, Diomande belting in a wonderful volley once Vinícius had gone off. The night before, Barcelona conceded four at the Parc des Princes.

Hansi Flick admitted he prioritised the clásico over PSG, leaving out Rodri and withdrawing Pedri and Raphinha early to keep them fresh for a game that could be decisive and tends to shape a season. But he has injury concerns at the back and warned his players that 15 goals conceded is too many. Mourinho couldn’t resist complaining that Madrid have a day less rest for the clásico – something perhaps mitigated, much like any analysis, by playing at home against Leipzig rather than away at Paris Saint-Germain – which got the excuse in early, more evidence of how “they” have it in for his side.

“We need to cut the gap and we can only do that by winning,” said the Real Madrid goalkeeper, Thibaut Courtois, of the six-point deficit. “We’re going with confidence.” Yet things do feel a little better now, defeat for Madrid not inevitable, a title still there to played for and something like a team taking shape. “I had to get to know them,” Mourinho said on Wednesday night. “I’ve only been here 105 days; it’s not long.”

Sports.title: Change captain? Play the kids? How to solve the problems at Manchester United
Sports.content:
Take captaincy from Fernandes, then try to sell him and Martínez

The big question as Bournemouth arrive for Sunday’s 2pm kick-off at Old Trafford is whether Michael Carrick will show his authority by stripping the captaincy from Bruno Fernandes and/or dropping Manchester United’s five-times player of the year. On Friday, Carrick refused to deny he may do so, but the bigger picture concerns whether cashing in on the Portuguese and his fellow mutineer, Lisandro Martínez, in the winter window would be prescient to initiate a new era. Fernandes and Martínez are out of contract in the close season (the club has an extra year’s option in both cases) and, judging by recent behaviour, intend to leave. So yielding, say, £40m and £25m respectively for them in January would allow investment as the rebuild begins. Even a few days on, Fernandes’s words in Como seem incredible: “It’s a decision from the staff to not press man-to-man and sometimes leave space behind and try to get the ball, wait for them, but sometimes when you give space to these teams they get confidence,” he said after Wednesday’s 4-1 humiliation. Fernandes’s open questioning of the tactics is a challenge to the head coach’s authority and we wait to see how/if Carrick will face it down. If Carrick acts and proves he is not a lame duck then even if he is removed a favour is done for his successor.

Ensure the players connect with the fans

Seven hundred United supporters made the trip to Lombardy and witnessed a horror show in incessant rain as their team folded against Cesc Fàbregas’s side. Yet, as always, the faithful will be there on Sunday desperate to cheer their men on against Bournemouth and beyond. Carrick constantly talks of how fans are the club’s lifeblood but do all of the players feel this? Performances such as that at Como will surely be averted if a base creed citing how fundamental supporters are to United is laid down to the squad by the manager.

Play with joy again

Sir Alex Ferguson’s flying wingers, Sir Matt Busby’s holy trinity of Best, Law, Charlton, the “attack, attack, attack” mentality: none of this is evident currently on the field; part of what Carrick admitted on Friday had been “lost”. What is needed is a return to this tradition, and this team are capable as was evident in the spirit of Carrick’s first game of his second tenure. Then, on 17 January 2026 at Old Trafford, he sent out an XI that went at Manchester City from the opening whistle, gave Pep Guardiola’s men zero time to breathe, and a rousing 2-0 victory sent all of a United stripe home jubilant. This, basically, was Carrick’s side last season, a proposition that played with a bounce that landed in third place. This term the smile has vanished and a prevailing sense of doom has settled over the club – precisely what Carrick had vanquished after the gloom of Ruben Amorim’s final days. Time to restore the cavalier edge.

United have suffered, in part, this term owing to Carrick’s drive to move to a more possession-based proposition. The problem is one of the key midfielders recruited to execute this, Youri Tielemans, does not have the legs for a central role, and so has been fielded at 10, while Kobbie Mainoo, who can run an engine room, is injured, and Fernandes’ penchant for running about, out of position, means gaps appear where a ball receiver should be.

Give the young players more of a chance

In Fernandes, Luke Shaw, Harry Maguire, Diogo Dalot, Marcus Rashford, Amad Diallo and Martínez there is a core of long-serving senior players who are not performing. To wake this cadre and freshen the mood from what feels a pervasive staleness, why not blood, more regularly, the younger players? The “play the kids instead” trope can be a cliche but it is a truism for a reason: youth has zero to lose, should run around with a smile and can brighten the darkest of times. Shea Lacey, a nippy wide man, Harry Amass, a promising left-back, and the Fletcher twins, Jack, a clever No 10, and Tyler, a defensive midfielder, are 19 and have 22 appearances between them. None could do worse than those senior players ahead of them.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Get the attack firing

In seven of their 11 games this season United have scored either a solitary goal or none, a shocking statistic that shows up how dysfunctional the attack is and, as part of the creative collective, the midfield too. United have only 10 goals in seven league outings and in three Champions League games have managed five – four of these against the minnows Sabah. At Como there was, again, zero pattern of play, control and a paucity of chances that has to be a serious concern. This has to change or a relegation fight could be United’s. A more off-the-cuff style, allied to an attacking outlook, would suit Matheus Cunha, Bryan Mbeumo and others and start menacing teams again as United did when beating City, Arsenal, Chelsea and Liverpool last year.

Sports.title: Enciso rescues point in storm for Ipswich to deny Nottingham Forest
Sports.content:
Amid a Suffolk squall, winds whipping, a constant drum of rain, an encounter full of half-chances, mistakes, the obligatory refereeing controversy and searching questions. Do Ipswich possess the stones to deal with the big league? Perhaps so. How long can Nottingham Forest’s dip sustain before their president, Evangelos Marinakis, takes his usual course of action. Perhaps not much longer.

Ipswich’s Gary O’Neil was the happier manager, Forest had created the cleaner opportunities, only for familiar failings to cost them. “We were never quite good enough with the ball to turn it into a football match,” said O’Neil. Further adding to Forest’s disappointment, Ipswich’s Issa Diop escaped what looked, on first glance, a red card for a last-man foul. A first-half exchange of goals, both owing much to defensive laxness, determined the result.

Ipswich’s aim is to establish themselves as Forest have in the Premier League. Though Forest and their manager cannot be presumptive of their statuses. “The result doesn’t reflect the performance but I don’t see another solution other than to keep going,” said Oliver Glasner. Forest have six points from eight matches, just a single win.

Glasner admitted he is still “waiting for this click” while saying: “I see great togetherness. The spirit I start to feel … I loved everything I saw today, just not the result.” A record of starting slow only to flourish at previous clubs offers partial protection, though Forest’s ownership is not like other clubs’. Wednesday was the anniversary of Sean Dyche’s appointment. That tenure lasted just 100 days.

Liam Delap’s presence in the Forest ranks, the striker barracked at every touch by home fans, served as a reminder of Ipswich’s failed mission two seasons ago. Unloved in Ipswich for decamping to Chelsea, Delap continues to be short of the confidence he showed back then.

Forest kicked off as lowest scorers in the division; no side had drawn a blank more often. Their drought did not take long to break but no flood followed. Neco Williams’s goal came via an overlap and then a looping cross from Daniel Muñoz. Williams glided in unmarked, his finish low and true beyond Christian Walton.

Another Forest goal appeared likely before home fans, previously exasperated, were lifted by Jaden Philogene forcing a save from Matz Sels and Julio Enciso dancing through red shirts to force another.

The equaliser came via a collective loss of concentration characteristic of Forest’s season so far, echoing defeat at Crystal Palace, and at home to Coventry. Jair Cunha gallivanted forward and, adrenaline coursing, lost possession. Dara O’Shea’s punted clearance was poorly dealt with by Nikola Milenkovic, an under-amped back-pass allowed Enciso to show admirable calm when others had surrendered theirs.

Forest’s failure to claim the rewards on offer from the first half told a familiar story. So too do repeated refereeing controversies, and howls of conspiracy among their supporters. How the officials, led by Thomas Bramall, the referee, did not view Diop’s clattering of James McAtee as a foul defied belief. Play was waved on. More understandable, if still highly debatable, was the verdict via video assistant that McAtee had conceded possession with a heavy touch as the collision came. “Leif [Davis] was there to cover,” said Diop, shown a yellow card. “I don’t think it’s a red.”

“I think they came to the right conclusion, a good process,” O’Neil said. As well he might. “It looks like the VAR was not from the East Midlands today,” said Glasner. “It felt like it was a red card.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Injustice fuelled Forest though did not make them any more clinical, the best of their second-half flurry of chances involved Murillo missing a free header from a corner. That asked for staying power from Ipswich. So far this season, they have not been the soft touch under O’Neil they became in Kieran McKenna’s survival attempt. “We had to show another side to get something,” said O’Neil. “We can play better but if we think we’re going to be dominant in every game … we’ll be fighting for scraps a lot of the time.”

Luck was definitely ridden. Callum Hudson-Odoi, as eight messy minutes of injury time were being added, received more than enough time and space to do far better than drag beyond the far post. The story of the night encapsulated for Forest. And of their season.

Sports.title: Arteta concerned over Saka’s durability as forward faces possible six-week absence
Sports.content:
Mikel Arteta has expressed concern over Bukayo Saka’s robustness after a series of injuries to the forward in the past year and as he awaits further news on how long he will be out for with a thigh issue.

Saka is set for an MRI scan after limping off in the 2-2 draw with Bayern Munich in the Champions League, with Arteta revealing the 25-year-old had “quite a lot of fluid in the area so it was difficult to understand the extent of the injury”. Saka will definitely miss Saturday’s game against Evertonand, it is understood, Arsenal fear it could be a grade-two tear that could potentially keep him out for up to six weeks.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Saka missed a large portion of last season due to hamstring, hip and achilles tendon injuries having also been sidelined by another hamstring issue in 2024-25. In total, he has had 11 different injuries since September 2023 and Arteta insisted that he has been trying to ease his workload as a result. “It’s certainly been different in the last year or so,” the Spaniard said when asked if Saka remains robust enough to start every match. “The demands that we are putting on every player are immense. The amount of games, the intensity of those matches, the international competitions, the times as well between games are getting narrower.

“Bukayo against Lille [in the Champions League last week] didn’t start the game because we knew what was happening. We have to play three times in less than six days. And especially when the games are so demanding, until the last minute you are there, you are chasing the game, you want to win. The necessity is to win every game, so we know that. So we are preparing the players for those scenarios and we do the best that we possibly can.”

Saka missed only three Premier League matches in three seasons between 2021 and 2024 and broke the Arsenal club record by playing in 83 consecutive top-flight games. He is already approaching 300 appearances for the club he joined as a seven-year-old and was rewarded with a lucrative new contract in February that made him one of the highest-paid players in the club’s history.

Asked whether he feared Saka could suffer from burnout having made his Arsenal debut three months after his 17th birthday, Arteta said: “I don’t have that feeling at all but something we have to be very mindful of is to create the right ecosystem around the player to fulfil his qualities. We really need to understand, whenever he comes back, how we are going to manage his load, what he is capable of to sustain having an impact in the team.”

Saka had only three weeks off after the World Cup but Arteta rejected suggestions that he should have been given more We want to pick on something, we will find it, but we won’t know whether it is for that or not. Maybe we needed to load those tendons more during those three weeks? Because if you don’t load the tendons, it becomes a problem. Who knows? I don’t know.”

Saka’s absence could hand an opportunity to Max Dowman on Saturday. The 16-year-old has played only nine minutes in the league this season and Arteta feels sure he is ready to make an impact after he became the youngest goalscorer in Premier League history, against David Moyes’s side in March.

“There is something inevitable to go back to that memory and the feeling of the moment. That’s with us, that’s going to stay in that stadium for a long, long time,” said Arteta. “He’s training and every time he’s got a moment to play, he’s showing that he’s a player that is going to impact the game. For sure he’s going to have minutes.”

Sports.title: Pascal Gross: the obsessive runner keeping Brighton ‘one step ahead’ after fast start
Sports.content:
Most footballers like to spend their summers unwinding after a long season but not Pascal Gross. Having been part of the Germany squad eliminated in the quarter-finals of Euro 2024, the midfielder entered – and won – a running race.

Gross completed the 8.4km course on Juist, in the East Frisian islands, in 31 minutes and 35 seconds. He is not known as someone who courts attention, and his victory by more than a minute came to light only when a video was posted on social media by a competitor.

Gross was moving from Brighton to Borussia Dortmund after seven years in the Premier League and reported to his boyhood club for pre-season training days later. Running is an obsession for Gross, as it is for his former teammate James Milner, who revealed last month he was training for a marathon after finally hanging up his boots, and that has shown since he returned for a second spell at the Amex in January for a bargain £1.2m.

“I think he’s looking in his free time now: ‘Where can I run a race?’ Because he will never stand still,” joked Brighton’s head coach, Fabian Hürzeler, after the 35-year-old scored the opening goal in a 3-0 victory over Arsenal last month. “ During the off-season he’s never the person who can lay on the beach for several hours and do nothing. He always needs to do something.”

Given that Gross has this season racked up an average distance of more than 11.5km per match and has covered the third-most ground of any player in the Premier League, it is no surprise Hürzeler has compared his compatriot to a good wine: “The older the wine gets, the better it gets.”

That analysis is borne out by the rest of his statistics this season as Brighton have emerged as challengers for Champions League qualification, at the very least, before Sunday’s game at Liverpool. Not only has Gross, the Premier League’s player of the month for September, contributed a combined seven goals and assists, he is in the top five for several other metrics such as big chances created (six), chances created from open play (14) and line-breaking passes leading to a goal (three). In a team that have scored the fourth-most goals (23) in Premier League history after seven games, Gross has been the standout performer.

View image in fullscreen Pascal Gross (in white) up against Jablonec's Matej Polidar in the Conference League. The match finished 0-0. Photograph: David W Cerny/Reuters

“Sometimes he’s just one step ahead than his opponent,” said Hürzeler, who is understood to have been instrumental in bringing back Gross. “He might not be the quickest player, but he can be the quickest in the head and sometimes being the quickest in the head is very helpful. No one expected that it would be this good. But it also shows that he still has this capacity in his body.”

At a club where experience is valued despite Hürzeler being the youngest permanent manager in the Premier League’s history, insiders describe Gross as the perfect role model for some of Brighton’s younger players. Charalampos Kostoulas has scored three goals in his past four league matches and the 19-year-old Greece striker is clearly thriving alongside the man who is approaching 300 appearances for the club. Diego Gómez, the dynamic Paraguayan who scored a goal-of-the-season contender against Crystal Palace that will go down in Brighton folklore, the homegrown talent Jack Hinshelwood and the midfield linchpin Yasin Ayari are others benefiting from his vast experience, as is Hürzeler.

Gross managed 75 Brighton goals and assists after joining from Ingolstadt in 2017 in the summer when Brighton were promoted. His departure for Dortmund, a year after his first Germany cap, was to fulfil a boyhood dream but there was always something drawing Gross – who wears a long-sleeve shirt owing to a grass allergy – back to the club where he is known as the Kaiser.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

“It was really difficult,” Gross said of his Brighton exit. “Only something really special got me out of here. There were a couple of other options [before returning], but Brighton was always the priority. I just stayed in touch with all the lads over the time away. Maybe you watch less of the games or you don’t stay in touch as much any more, it gets less and less. But it never really did.”

Gross retiring from international football after the World Cup has also been to Brighton’s benefit. His status as a club legend was augmented by delivering the free-kick that Palace’s Jaydee Canvot headed into his own net during the 5-0 humiliation on Sunday. That was the third game in a row in which Gross has provided an assist and he has an opportunity to become the oldest player to make it four since Chelsea’s Gianfranco Zola in December 2002.

The trip to Anfield continues a gruelling run of five away fixtures in a row. Brighton drew at the Czech club Jablonec on Thursday in the Conference League and after Sunday they go to Manchester City twice in four days – the first in the Carabao Cup – before heading to Spain to play Getafe. It will test Brighton’s mettle after their spectacular start. Hürzeler can count on Gross – who has started every game in all competitions – to last the course.

Sports.title: Bayern Munich insiders were worried about 'workaholic' Vincent Kompany weeks before Man City legend's training ground collapse, new report claims - as German giants confirm boss will be out for 'weeks'
Sports.content:
Bayern Munich insiders had expressed concern for Vincent Kompany weeks before their manager's collapse at the club's training ground, a new report has revealed.

The German giants confirmed on Saturday that Kompany, 40, will be out for weeks after he was rushed to hospital on Friday following his collapse while watching the second team training.

He had earlier taken training for the first team ahead of their Bundesliga clash against Freiburg on Sunday. The session was then abandoned, BILD said, with those present said to be 'deeply affected' by the incident.

The Man City legend has been suffering from a viral infection which is said to have caused problems with old scar tissue in his hip, leaving him in pain and with difficulties climbing stairs.

Kompany, who won four Premier League titles while captain at the Etihad Stadium, is understood to be in a stable condition.

According to BILD, several figures at the German giants had noted the 'workaholic' Belgian's lack of work-life balance, claiming he was getting too little sleep, eating irregularly, barely exercising, drinking excessive amounts of coffee, and taking on too much work.

Bayern Munich insiders were reportedly worried about Vincent Kompany before his collapse

Kompany is pictured with his wife Carla at Oktoberfest in Munich last month

Bayern Munich chief Max Eberl provided an updated on Saturday, confirming Kompany is stable, but his recovery may not be a swift one.

He said: 'The good news is: He's stable. I spoke with him last night, as well as with his wife.

'That was no pleasant moment for any of us; he collapsed on the pitch yesterday and will have to stay in the hospital for a few more days until everything has been checked and verified.

'This once again shows that health is the most important thing in life—not football.

'Therefore, the best wishes for a speedy recovery from all of us go out to him; we at FC Bayern stand together.

'The most important thing is that the cause is found and that he gets fit again. That he only comes back once he's fit.

'Vinnie will be given all the time he needs. We're not starting to build any timeframes.

'We need to figure out what it is, and then we'll discuss what recovery time means.

'We won't be talking about days, but weeks. We all understand that. And we have such a fantastic coaching staff, with Vinnie at its head.

'But the success is based on an outstanding team behind the scenes. There's absolutely no thought of changing anything.

'All the guys who are here are outstanding – and therefore we can all approach the next few weeks in the spirit of Vinnie, which everyone has within them.'

After Wednesday night's 2-2 draw against Arsenal in the Champions League, Kompany admitted that he hadn't listened to his body while battling his viral infection.

'As a coach, you always want to do everything. I caught a pretty nasty virus last week, and of course, I didn't listen to my body, and then at some point, my body just said: 'That's enough!''

Kompany is deeply embedded in the entire football operation at Bayern Munich, with the report adding that he has been the driving force behind the construction of new XXL privacy screens at the training ground to prevent outsiders from spying on sessions.

Assistant coach Aaron Danks will be standing in for Kompany for Sunday's game, but suspects it will be difficult to force his boss to take an extended break.

'It's really not easy to get Vincent to rest,' he said. 'That's a challenge – you know him as a person! He's a true leader and works hard. But he has a virus, and it's important that he rests.'

Kompany had been spectating the reserve taam with their new coach Dante, 43, before collapsing 20 minutes into the session.

It is understood that most players were back in the changing rooms when the incident occurred but those who witnessed it were shaken, and the reserve team's game against DJK Vilzing on Saturday has been called off.

Kompany's viral infection caused issues with his hip that left him struggling to stand for long periods of time and was thoroughly examined by team medical staff earlier in the week and was given a pill by one of the doctors early on in the game against Arsenal.

BILD claim insiders noted Kompany's lack of work-life balance leading up to the episode

Bayern said in a statement: 'Vincent Kompany had to seek medical treatment on Friday after collapsing during training for FC Bayern's amateurs.

'The first-team coach had been watching the second team's session. Kompany will undergo thorough examination in the hospital and remain in medical care. For the time being, his coaching staff will manage training and match operations.'

Bayern's sporting director, Max Eberl, added: 'The health of Vincent Kompany is our utmost priority. At FC Bayern, we will do everything to ensure he recovers quickly.

'Vinnie is receiving all necessary medical care and support, as well as all the time he needs. His coaching team, which we fully trust, will take over his duties. All of us at FC Bayern wish Vinnie a speedy recovery.'

Kompany's former club Manchester City were among those to send a message of support to the Belgian following the incident. City wrote on X: 'Everyone at Manchester City is wishing a speedy recovery to our former captain and Club legend, Vincent Kompany. Get well soon, Vinny.'

The Belgian was captain of Man City during some of their most successful years under Pep Guardiola but was regularly ruled out through injuries.

Kompany moved to Munich in 2024 and has won two Bundesliga titles with England captain Harry Kane as his star player in attack. He has three children with wife Carla, who he met in Manchester.

His viral infection was the talk of the build-up before Wednesday's Champions League match.

Kompany's assistant coach Aaron Danks said on Tuesday: 'It has affected his legs, yes. He has had pain in his legs.

'The most important thing for him now is to rest and I don't know if he will be ready tomorrow or in two or three days' time.

'Getting him to rest is hard. He's a leader. But it's a virus and it's really important that he rests.'

Bayern are top of Germany's Bundesliga after four wins and two draws in their opening six matches. They lie 14th in the Champions League's league phase after a win and two draws.

Sports.title: 'It's been seamless... I'm over the moon': JAMES PATER, Northampton's 19-year-old 'Slim Reaper' on his rapid rise into the first team, taking Jonny Wilkinson's advice and how he's trying to bulk up
Sports.content:
'It's been seamless... I'm over the moon': JAMES PATER, Northampton's 19-year-old 'Slim Reaper' on his rapid rise into the first team, taking Jonny Wilkinson's advice and how he's trying to bulk up

When James Pater was 15, his team-mates at Shelford RFC clubbed together to bid for a training session with Jonny Wilkinson in a charity auction. To their amazement, they won – and suddenly found themselves sharing a pitch with English rugby’s most famous man.

‘It was an auction prize at a big memorial match between the two local schools, Perse and The Leys,’ Pater tells Daily Mail Sport.

‘One of the dads drove us to Pennyhill Park in the Shelford minibus. We had breakfast in the hotel and then we went out on the pitch with him. I brought my kicking tee. It was funny because there were props and hookers and second rows doing a kicking session with Jonny Wilkinson.

‘He went through everyone individually and talked about how he deals with challenges. He was quite insightful on how to control your emotions and manage things that don’t go your way.

'Don’t dwell on it. Move onto the next thing. We have a similar mindset here at Northampton so it’s something I take into everyday life.’

James Pater, 19, has made an astonishingly quick rise into the Northampton first team and is now their go-to full-back

A 15-year-old Pater does some kicking under the watchful eye of Jonny Wilkinson (Source: Instagram/Jamespater_)

Pater has carried Wilkinson’s advice into his fledgling career. Now 19, the rangy 6ft 3in full-back is showing composure beyond his years, thrusting himself into contention for an England A call-up next week.

But rugby was not always his destiny. ‘I hadn’t played academy rugby at the time we met Jonny Wilkinson. I played football for Cambridge Academy until I was 15 or 16. We played Chelsea when I was like 12 years old but more often we played teams like Luton and Peterborough.

'I played central defensive midfield or centre back. I liked Sergio Busquets in that 4-3-3 formation at Barcelona – or the quick centre backs like (former PSG man) Presnel Kimpembe. I grew up wanting to be a footballer, 100 per cent, but GCSEs came along and I didn't really progress any further. That’s when I called it.’

Rugby was never far away. Throughout secondary school, Pater played for the Huntingdon Stags – the junior club that brought through George Furbank. He joined Shelford at Colts level and his rugby snowballed when he starred at Warwick Festival as a 16-year-old.

‘I was picked for Ireland IQ, which is for Irish-qualified English people,’ reveals Pater. ‘My mum’s from Letterkenny, County Donegal. She’s one of 10 so I’ve got 40 or 50 cousins. We’d go down to the beach with any kind of ball. We’d have enough of us to play our own match!

'I played for Ireland IQ against Ealing Trailfinders and a week later I got a call-up for England Under 18s. I started playing in the Under 18s Academy League for Northampton and that’s when rugby became something to really go after. Charlie Reed, the manager, said, “If you keep playing well then you could get offered a contract”.

‘We won the Academy League and then I made my PREM debut a few weeks after that against Gloucester, when I was still at school, which was pretty sick.

'I was doing my A Levels at the time. It was half-term, I was revising, and I got the message saying I might be travelling with the team. I came up and trained on the Thursday and it was announced that I was on the bench. It all happened so quickly.’

'We won the Academy League and then I made my PREM debut a few weeks after that against Gloucester, when I was still at school, which was pretty sick'

‘It’s been pretty seamless,' Pater says. 'I didn't feel like I was the next in line. I just got an opportunity at the start of the season and played well'

At the time, Pater was only on a part-time contract with Northampton. A highflyer at the Leys School, he secured the grades required for a three-year economics degree at the University of Bath.

‘I had my accommodation sorted and everything was ready to go. I would play BUCS University rugby there on Wednesdays and come back every few weeks to train as part of a uni deal.

‘That was the plan. I stayed with Northampton for pre-season and that summer I had conversations with Sam Vesty and Phil Dowson about staying on and doing this full time. It got to late August – a few weeks before uni started – and I decided to defer my first year at Bath. I put all my eggs in one basket and decided to go for it.’

Pater has not looked back. He had been earmarked as the club’s long-term successor to Furbank, who joined Harlequins during the summer. He opted not to move to Bath, instead enrolling with the Open University for an online course.

He scored a hat-trick in the opening game of the season and has been praised for his unflappable abilities as a ball-playing 15.

‘It’s been pretty seamless,' he says. 'I didn't feel like I was the next in line. I just got an opportunity at the start of the season and played well. My aim was actually to make more than half of the matchday 23s. I've been pretty over the moon with how it’s gone so far.

‘Furbs is an idol of mine. When I joined the academy, the players I liked to watch were the dual playmakers like Dan Carter and Beauden Barrett. I’d watch their YouTube highlights. Now I look at guys like Sascha Feinberg-Mngomezulu, Ruben Love and Will Jordan.

‘But when you’re with someone 24/7 in this environment, you learn so much quicker than watching online. Furbs taught me so much. When you're training against him, you learn so much, like what he does positionally.

Pater celebrates a try with his Northampton team-mates Tommy Freeman (left) and Fin Smith

Pater scores Northampton's fifth try during their remarkably high-scoring PREM match against Bath earlier this month

‘I want to be involved all the time. I want to get my hands to the ball. I don't want to miss moments and I want to have a triple threat: run, pass, kick. I don’t want to feel like I’m watching the game.

'I never have targets, but I always look at the stats sheets. Especially at Under 20s, I’d want to have the most carries and play 80 minutes every game.’

Pater has played his way into Test conversations. Furbank, Freddie Steward and Marcus Smith are England’s senior full-backs but, if he continues on the same trajectory, then Pater could be their longer-term successor.

Weighing 86kg, the willowy teenager is nicknamed ‘The Slim Reaper’ by his club-mates. On Northampton's pre-season tour to Sri Lanka, the senior players ribbed the youngster about bulking up for the demands of senior rugby.

‘That nickname actually came from Chunya Munga,’ laughs Pater. ‘He started calling me it because I’m tall and thin, but it’s also what they call Kevin Durant in the NBA. It's not a terrible nickname, to be fair.

'I’m trying to put a bit of weight on but it's hard when you're playing every weekend and running a lot. I’m just trying to put more on my plate at dinner time, speaking to the nutritionist.’

Still living in the club’s academy house, dinners are an unglamorous affair. ‘You hear about Tigers putting 20 people in an academy house with two kitchens but we just have three or four people. It’s quite civil.'

Pater touches down against Newcastle Red Bulls on the opening day of the season, when he grabbed a hat-trick

‘You’re brought up knowing that Leicester’s a big game,' Pater says about this weekend's opponents. 'That’s never lost on you in the academy'

Which means he might stay with his mates in the house even if the academy contract he's on should shortly be upgraded, what with him now being the club’s first-choice full-back. His ball-playing skills have fitted seamlessly into Northampton’s expansive attack and this weekend he will be taking on Leicester in the East Midlands derby.

‘You’re brought up knowing that Leicester’s a big game,' he says. 'That’s never lost on you in the academy. If you look at the scores, we used to put 70 points on them in the academy!

'We had Tim Rodber, our old forward, come in and talk to us this week about these being the best times of your life. He talked about what it means for yourself, the club, and the town.’

Pater, still carrying Wilkinson’s unflappable advice, will no doubt take it all in his long stride.

Sports.title: Defiant Michael Carrick's monologue was straight out of the Sir Alex Ferguson playbook but his powerful words will be empty unless he can drag Man United from the depths of despair, writes CHRIS WHEELER
Sports.content:
Defiant Michael Carrick's monologue was straight out of the Sir Alex Ferguson playbook but his powerful words will be empty unless he can drag Man United from the depths of despair, writes CHRIS WHEELER

Not since Sir Alex Ferguson’s opening monologues has a Manchester United manager begun his weekly press conference at Carrington without taking a question.

Louis van Gaal once turned up with a dossier of stats ready to refute Sam Allardyce’s claims that United were a long-ball team, and flounced off on another occasion at Christmas – telling us to ‘enjoy the wine and mince pies’ – after using his first answer to demand an apology for stories claiming his job was on the line.

Jose Mourinho had United’s European record over the previous eight years at his fingertips when he gave his ‘football heritage’ speech in the wake of a Champions League defeat to Sevilla in 2018, but at least he waited for the first question.

When Michael Carrick walked into the room at 1.30pm on Friday, it was clear he had something on his mind.

‘I’ll start today,’ said Carrick, taking his seat. ‘I just want to say a few things, really.’

Over the course of the next five minutes and 40 seconds, spanning nearly 1,000 words, Carrick faced the growing crisis at United head on.

Man United boss Michael Carrick began Friday's press conference with a lengthy monologue

Carrick is fighting for his job after United's poor start to the season and their 4-1 loss to Como

He spoke about the responsibility of being United’s head coach and the principles that have made this club great.

He conjured up the spirit of Ferguson, Sir Matt Busby and Sir Bobby Charlton. He mentioned United’s strength in the face of adversity, forged in the dark days after Munich.

He spoke of the humility and hard work epitomised by great United players like Ryan Giggs and Wayne Rooney.

No-one is bigger than the club and no-one is entitled to be there, said Carrick in what felt like a message to his captain Bruno Fernandes and Lisandro Martinez over their recent public criticism.

At times, he looked just as distracted as when he left us in Lombardy on Wednesday night, reeling from a 4-1 Champions League defeat to Como. He spoke hesitantly at times, emotionally at others.

This was a defiant and heartfelt speech from a man who is fighting to save his job, but more importantly to drag his club from the depths of despair and self-destruction as United stumble through their worst start to a season since 1986 with cracks beginning to appear from the boardroom to the dressing-room.

The Amazon documentary makers are certainly getting a lot of bang for their buck.

‘We haven't done well enough lately, I think that's pretty obvious to say,’ said Carrick, who has stood among the fans in the past as well as serving United as a player, coach, caretaker and head coach.

‘Wednesday was a bad night for a lot of reasons, and it was a bad night that hurt a lot. It obviously hurt me to see us play that way.

‘My responsibility is to get a team on the pitch that represents this football club and the supporters, and they can be proud of the identity that we show.

‘We have gone away from that just recently in certain games, which I'm totally fully aware of and definitely doing something about.’

Referencing the success he enjoyed last season after taking over in January, Carrick added: ‘Our supporters are of the utmost importance to me.

‘For them to feel like they felt for five months at the start of the year – for us to have that connection and that real vigour and intensity and enjoyment and passion that we all felt through that period – was something we need to get back to. And we will get back to it.

‘The foundation and values of this football club have been etched for many, many years. I totally understand and I get every single one of them.

‘It comes down to humility and being humble. It comes down to being hard-working and really proud to live up to those values.

‘There's a resilience about this football club that's been shown for a long, long time. Whether that's bouncing back from adversity, comebacks, late goals, there's a resilience that runs very, very deep.

‘I've seen it with my own eyes, I've felt it, I'm aware of some of the individuals and know them closely who have been a big part of that history.

‘Ryan Giggs, arguably one of the greatest to play for this football club, it was never about Ryan Giggs, it was about Manchester United.

‘Wayne Rooney was top goal scorer for this football club. His biggest thing was sacrificing for the team and what was good for Manchester United.

‘Sir Alex Ferguson, the best manager of all time, the greatest for me, and his main priority was Manchester United. Going back to Sir Matt, Sir Bobby, the resilience was beyond belief of what they showed and the way they rebuilt this football club.

‘Again, it was based on being humble, having humility and hard work. We can never lose that, and I won't let us lose that. It inspires me to live up to that and keep driving that.

‘So we need to show exactly what it means and respect this football club; respect what it takes to be here and respect what it takes to win.

‘It takes a lot of sacrifice. You've got to invest yourself in the football club and you've got to do a lot of things that maybe aren't so nice.

‘We've had it and we've lost our way a little bit, if I'm totally honest. We will get it back. I'm totally confident we'll get it back.’

Carrick's move was straight out of the playbook of his former United boss Sir Alex Ferguson

These were strong words from Carrick, but unless he and his players can back it up on the pitch, they will be empty words

Only then did Carrick take questions from reporters as he addressed his own future, concerns over a divided dressing-room and Fernandes’ position as captain following his criticism of the tactics in Como.

It was a ballsy move by a man who has his back to the wall and possibly felt he had nothing to lose by coming out fighting. Who knows, it might already be too late.

As long as the rot continues, questions will be asked about Carrick and whether he has the tools to turn this around.

After drawing at Leeds last weekend, he said it felt like a fresh start only to see his team capitulate in embarrassing fashion in Como.

Carrick spoke powerfully, no doubt about it. But unless he and his players can back it up on the pitch, his words will be empty.

Sports.title: Chelsea vs Tottenham combined XI according to the stats: In-form Cole Palmer and Joao Pedro make the cut, while a World Cup villain earns a surprise play - but which FOUR Spurs stars get the nod?
Sports.content:
The latest instalment of the Battle of the Bridge gets started tonight, with Tottenham travelling to London rivals Chelsea. Despite their mega-money spending in the summer, Spurs have endured a sluggish start to the Premier League campaign, with Roberto De Zerbi's side finally getting off the mark with a win against Coventry on Monday night. They will have to be at their best to stop Xabi Alonso's high-flying Blues, who earned a gritty 2-0 win at Everton last Saturday - an opponent they have notoriously struggled to get points from on the road. So, with a combined squad value of roughly £1.6billion, which 11 players make our combined XI ahead of Saturday night's grudge match? Stats gurus SofaScore have crunched the numbers and given their verdict. Tottenham and Chelsea will renew their rivalry on Saturday evening at Stamford Bridge GK: Antonin Kinsky Sofascore rating 6.49/10 Antonin Kinsky gets the nod in goal, even if he has had a difficult time at Tottenham. His debut in the Champions League away to Atletico Madrid last season saw him make two massive errors leading to goals which resulted in him being substituted after only 17 minutes. Since then, Kinsky has become Spurs’ No1, a position that has been solidified further after Guglielmo Vicario’s summer move to Juventus. Kinsky has only kept two clean sheets in all competitions this season for Tottenham, but Emi Martinez suffered a head injury at Everton and is absent, while it's too early to judge Mike Penders, so the Czech stopper gets the nod. RB: Wesley Fofana Sofascore rating: 6.92/10 One of two Chelsea representatives in the back four is Wesley Fofana, who has shown his versatility this season. Chelsea have conceded six goals in the three matches Fofana has started though, so his presence in this combined XI highlights how poor both teams have been defensively at the start of this campaign. Chelsea have conceded 13 goals in the Premier League overall, more than 13 other sides, and that is a record that Xabi Alonso will want to address as soon as possible. One of two Chelsea representatives in the back four is French defender Wesley Fofana CB: Jan Paul van Hecke Sofascore rating: 7.63/10 Jan Paul van Hecke, an international team-mate of Micky van de Ven, moved to north London from Brighton in the summer, and there is no doubt he is still trying to find his feet, although he has featured in all of Tottenham’s Premier League matches so far this season. He is also one of six Spurs players to have scored a goal – a reflection of where Tottenham are in terms of going forward, rather than Van Hecke’s finishing skills. CB: Micky van de Ven Sofascore rating 6.87/10 Alongside his fellow Dutchman is Van de Ven, even though Spurs have shipped 10 goals in the league. Van de Ven has been a regular feature for Tottenham this season, playing 466 minutes in the Premier League and, following Spurs' victory against Coventry on Monday, he should be in good spirits heading into this one. LB: Jorrel Hato Sofascore rating 6.73/10 Perhaps helped by injuries to Tottenham left-backs Andy Robertson and Destiny Udogie, Jorrel Hato takes this spot in the XI. Despite Chelsea's defensive deficiencies, Hato continues to improve and appears to be in Alonso's first-choice XI ahead of Pep Chavarria right now. CM: Cole Palmer Sofascore: 7.53/10 Following on from the disappointment of not making England’s World Cup squad, Cole Palmer has started this season impressively, so there will be no surprise he is in this XI. The Englishman seems to be thriving under new coach Xabi Alonso, playing over 600 minutes in the league. He will be looking to continue his fine form after an injury-plagued campaign in 2025-26 where he often looked short of confidence and match sharpness. So far this term, Palmer has scored two goals and added three assists. CM: Sandro Tonali Sofascore rating: 7.31/10 The final Spurs player to feature in this team is £100m summer signing Sandro Tonali. The Italian has grown into the campaign, even though Spurs’ Premier League position doesn’t indicate it. Tonali has featured seven times so far this season, registering one assist and he will be hoping that he can develop into a talisman for Roberto De Zerbi over the next few months. CM: Valentin Barco Sofascore rating 7.16/10 Valentin Barco signed for Chelsea in the summer from Strasbourg on a contract running all the way to 2033. Barco reached the World Cup final with Argentina, although his run-in with Jude Bellingham during and after the semi-final made him the bad boy in England’s eyes. Barco has featured in three Premier League matches, and twice in the EFL Cup - and it is his displays in that competition, including a goal and assist in the 6-3 win over Leeds - that have earned him a place in this side. LW: Morgan Rogers Sofascore rating: 7.48/10 It's no surprise that Rogers makes the team following his then-British-record £117m transfer from Aston Villa. Rogers, 24, has built upon what was a breakout couple of years at Villa Park, which included his first major tournament with England over the summer. Since scoring on his debut for Chelsea, things couldn’t have gone much better at his new club. Sitting on four goals already, Rogers is among the top scorers in the league. He will be looking to improve upon the 16 goal involvements he had last season as Chelsea aim to get back into Europe. RW: Pedro Neto Sofascore rating: 7.19/10 On the back of his match-winning brace against Everton last weekend, Neto rightfully gets in this team. He had a disappointing goal output last season, scoring just five times in the league, but Neto is another Chelsea star who is benefiting from Alonso’s style of play. The Portuguese international has three goals and one assist so far this season in just six starts. Pedro Neto's match-winning brace at Everton earns him a spot on the right wing in this team CF: Joao Pedro Sofascore rating; 7.54/10 Completing the Chelsea front three is their No 9 Joao Pedro. Like Palmer, the Brazilian had a point to prove this season after not being selected to represent his nation at the World Cup. Carlo Ancelotti surprisingly selected Neymar and Endrick over Pedro, who netted 15 goals in the Premier League last season despite the Blues enduring a turbulent campaign. He has started this league season well, with only Erling Haaland having scored more goals than his five so far. It is a no brainer to have him in this team, especially considering the issues at Tottenham in the attacking department.
