In basic public administration (Public Administration 101), the civil service is recognised strictly as a subset of the larger public service framework. It constitutes the permanent, tenured bureaucracy within ministries and operates under its own distinct civil service rules. By failing to grasp this foundational distinction, the editorial builds its thesis on a fundamentally flawed premise.

The public service spans a far wider scope than the core civil service, incorporating political appointees, commission heads, and leaders of extra-ministerial departments whose offices exist at the president’s pleasure. Federal parastatal chief executives operate as political appointees and public servants rather than career civil servants.

To equate a presidentially appointed director-general, governing under a specific statutory Act, with a career Level 8 civil servant in the Ministry of Works is either profound intellectual laziness or deliberate mischief. If we are to accept Punch’s distorted logic from its, then federal ministers—who are also presidential appointees—must similarly be barred from political engagement. Would Punch ever dare to publish an editorial claiming the Minister of Information cannot campaign for his own government? The absolute absurdity of that premise exposes the emptiness of their entire argument.

The foundation of this debate is not the opinion of Punch. It is Section 40 of the 1999 Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria, as amended, which the newspaper conveniently ignored. Section 40 guarantees every person, including public officers, the right to assemble freely and associate with other persons, including forming or belonging to any political party.

This right is not a privilege granted by any media organisation. It is constitutionally guaranteed. Any restriction on that right must be justifiable under Section 45—meaning that it must be reasonably justifiable in a democratic society in the interest of defence, public safety, public order, public morality, or public health. Where is the public danger in a director-general mobilising support for the president who appointed him? There is none.

Punch writes as if the Supreme Court has not spoken on this matter. It has, and authoritatively so. In INEC v. Balarabe Musa & 7 Ors (2003) 10 WRN 1, the apex court demolished the very argument Punch is now recycling.

Justice Emmanuel Ayoola (JSC) delivered a definitive blow to restrictions on civic freedoms, ruling that barring public and civil servants from political party membership is entirely indefensible in a democratic society. The apex court explicitly rejected the argument that public safety, order, morality, or health could justify such a ban, declaring that any attempt to weaponise Section 45(1)(a) to undermine the fundamental political rights guaranteed under Section 40 of the Constitution is fundamentally erroneous.

The Supreme Court explicitly branded it erroneous, yet the newspaper—in a blatant characterisation—upheld it as law. In his landmark concurring judgment, the former Chief Justice of Nigeria (CJN), Justice Mohammed Lawal Uwais, dismantled any ambiguity.

He declared that the provisions of Section 40 of the 1999 Constitution are absolute: every citizen, including civil servants and public office holders, possesses the fundamental right to assemble freely and associate with any political party, trade union, or association to protect their interests. Justice Uwais underscored that the constitution makes zero exceptions and enforces no restrictions on public officers. Where the highest law of the land refuses to draw lines, Punch has arbitrarily invented them.

Even the Head of Service circular, upon which Punch’s argument implicitly relies, was clarified by the Supreme Court judgment. After her office was inundated with requests for clarification on the apex court’s ruling, the Head of the Civil Service of the Federation issued a memo dated May 5, 2022, attempting to enforce the 2008 Public Service Rules regarding partisan politics.

That clarification is exactly what the newspaper missed. The Public Service Rules cannot override the constitution. Because the rules are merely subsidiary legislation, the constitution remains supreme. Where the PSR conflicts with Section 40 (as interpreted by the Supreme Court), it becomes void to the extent of that inconsistency. This is the core principle of constitutional supremacy under Section 1(3)—something paper should well know.

We are arguing for legal precision, not anarchy. The law draws a sharp line between the right to belong to a political party and the act of partisan mobilisation on official duty. This distinction is anchored in explicit terms of appointment, strict codes of conduct, and enabling statutes. It cannot be erased by a blanket editorial lumping everyone into a single category.

A chief executive retains every lawful right to be a committed member, supporter, and mobilizer for the All Progressives Congress (APC), provided these activities are conducted within legal boundaries and outside official functions. The law does not demand political neutrality; it demands structural integrity.

What it strictly forbids is the weaponisation of the office—specifically, the diversion of public funds, the exploitation of official hours, and the use of coercive power to compromise subordinates. By issuing a sweeping, lazy ban, Punch completely bypassed this crucial legal nuance, mistaking legitimate association for institutional abuse.

This editorial is a masterclass in legal illiteracy and political alarmism. It is a transparent attempt to intimidate appointees legitimately driving the re-election campaign of President Bola Ahmed Tinubu. Let there be no mistake: momentum is firmly on our side, and the opposition is visibly feeling the heat.

Recent media commentary has drifted into fiction, yet our resolve remains unshaken. We will continue to consolidate our gains and sustain the momentum of our strategic political engagement. Moving forward, our actions will remain strictly within the law, guided exclusively by our official mandates and the constitution—not by outside noise.

The law is settled and the Supreme Court has cleared the air. All Nigerian workers, whether civil or public servants, possess the constitutional right to participate in politics. No media editorial can rewrite the constitution. The Punch is simply late to class.

* Otunba Ajiboye is Chairman, Media & Publicity Committee of FORCEPA, and Executive Secretary/CEO, National Institute for Cultural Orientation (NICO)

World.title: Wahala App, NIIA Forge Alliance to Deploy AI for Security Intelligence, Business Risk Management
World.content:
Nigerian technology company, Wahala App Ltd, has partnered with the General Leo Irabor Early Warning Systems Centre (GLIC) of the Nigerian Institute of International Affairs (NIIA) to deploy artificial intelligence (AI) and real-time data analytics for security intelligence, operational risk management and business continuity.

The partnership is expected to strengthen early warning capabilities by integrating citizen-generated incident reports with AI-powered analytics to identify emerging threats, monitor security trends and provide businesses, government institutions and other organisations with information to support timely decision-making.

In a statement issued in Lagos, the company said the collaboration would give the Centre access to its Wahala Network, a digital platform that aggregates incident reports from individuals, businesses and participating organisations to provide insights into security risks and potential operational disruptions. The initiative comes amid growing demand for technology-driven solutions to security challenges, particularly as businesses seek to minimise exposure to threats affecting logistics, supply chains, personnel and other critical operations.

According to the company, the platform’s analytical capabilities enable organisations to identify recurring incidents, detect previously overlooked vulnerabilities and assess the potential impact of security developments on their operations. It explained that AI-powered analysis could also establish connections between seemingly unrelated incidents, providing insights into wider security and socioeconomic risks affecting industries and communities.

The Co-Founder and Chief Executive Officer of Wahala App Ltd, Oriekaose Agholor, said the partnership represented an important step towards integrating citizen participation with institutional early warning systems and expanding the commercial application of real-time security intelligence.

“Safety is a shared responsibility, and timely information can help people make more informed decisions about their surroundings. Our partnership with GLIC is an important step towards connecting citizen participation with wider early warning efforts,” Agholor said.

He added that the company was seeking further partnerships with government agencies, corporate organisations and other institutions to expand the reach of its technology and improve access to actionable security information. Under the arrangement, businesses connected to the Wahala Network would be able to receive information on incidents that could affect their operations, including developments requiring adjustments to transportation routes, logistics planning and personnel safety measures.

The company said its technology could also support preventive risk management by identifying patterns of incidents that might otherwise develop into larger operational or security crises. Agholor noted that wider adoption of the platform could strengthen information sharing across sectors and help organisations respond more effectively to emerging risks.

“We invite Nigerians, businesses and institutions to join us in building a more informed and safety-conscious society,” he said.

Also speaking, Acting Head of the General Leo Irabor Early Warning Systems Centre, Dr Omotola Ilesanmi, said technology and reliable information were increasingly important to effective risk management and institutional preparedness.

“Effective early warning depends on the timely identification of risks and the availability of reliable information to support informed decision-making,” Ilesanmi said. “Technology and citizen participation can contribute to this process by strengthening awareness of emerging risks and supporting preparedness.”

Beyond institutional collaboration, Wahala App said it was expanding public engagement through its Ambassadors Against Wahala programme, which encourages responsible incident reporting and safety awareness across workplaces, educational institutions, religious organisations and communities. The company explained that its digital platform enables users to report incidents, receive location-relevant alerts and send emergency notifications to designated contacts, while its broader technology offerings provide organisations with data-driven insights for security planning and operational resilience.

It emphasised that the platform was intended to complement the responsibilities of government security agencies and emergency response institutions rather than replace existing security structures. Wahala App said the partnership formed part of its broader strategy to deepen collaboration with public institutions and private sector operators, expand the application of AI in risk intelligence and strengthen the role of technology in Nigeria’s security and business environment. The company, which specialises in real-time crisis awareness and management, operates a digital network connecting citizens, businesses and institutions through incident reporting, emergency alerts and AI-powered risk analysis.

World.title: Nigeria Shows Global Tech Giants Are Not Beyond Reach, Says Luminate CEO
World.content:
The Chief Executive Officer of Luminate, Melanie Hui, has praised Nigeria as a leading example of how African countries can shape the global artificial intelligence economy rather than simply consume it. She pointed to the country’s regulators, workers and innovators as proof that the continent is already setting its own terms.

Hui gave the keynote address at the Build 2026 Conference in Abuja on Wednesday. The audience included the Honourable Minister of Communication, Innovation and Digital Economy, heads of government parastatals, members of the diplomatic community and members of the Nigeria AI Collective. She said research Luminate commissioned this year on the continent’s AI landscape “found not only patterns of extraction and inequality. It found imagination and leadership.”

“Here, there are important reasons for optimism,” she said.

Hui cited the action Nigeria’s competition authority took against Meta over data exploitation and discriminatory practices. She said this showed that “global tech companies are not beyond the reach of national institutions.” She also praised app-based drivers in Nigeria for securing government recognition for Africa’s first e-hailing trade union.

She said innovators across Nigeria are “using locally built, practical technology to serve the underserved: from bringing reliable banking for rural communities to tackling massive crop losses.”

Her examples from elsewhere on the continent were litigation in Kenya establishing that global technology companies can be brought before Kenyan courts civil society coalitions in South Africa challenging bulk surveillance at the Constitutional Court AI-assisted learning materials in local languages helping children in Mali drones extending healthcare to remote islands in Uganda

“They are not merely enduring technology,” she said of Africa’s technologists, teachers, climate advocates, feminists, trade unions, youth movements and public interest lawyers. “They are shaping and reshaping it.”

“These examples matter because ownership is also about power: the power to negotiate, regulate, organise and secure remedy,” she added.

Hui’s speech was titled “Africa in the Global AI Order: Towards Equitable Ownership and Shared Prosperity.” She made clear that Luminate stands behind Africa’s ambition to be a full participant in the AI economy.

“My African friends tell me they will not be confined to the role of consumer, supplier of raw data, source of critical minerals or provider of low-paid labour in somebody else’s AI economy,” she said. “And Luminate will stand with them in securing a better digital age.”

She said equitable ownership “means moving beyond participation alone.” It means having “meaningful influence over the infrastructure, the institutions, the partnerships, the choices that will determine Africa’s digital future.”

She also said Africa’s young and growing population, along with its markets, languages and cultures, “will be enormously valuable to the development of future AI systems.”

Hui rejected the argument, made by some in the tech industry, that regulation holds innovation back. She offered a more hopeful view of how growth and fairness can go together.

“Those of us who promote tech justice must not lend credence to some in the tech industry who would paint regulation as a brake on progress. I disagree,” she said. “Safeguards are the allies of progress. Inclusion is the engine of meaningful scale. Sovereignty means being stronger together.”

“Prosperity is not shared automatically,” she added. “It is shared because workers have bargaining power. Because markets can compete. Because regulators and courts have resources and authority. Because people can seek remedy when they are harmed.”

To show what successful AI deployment needs, Hui described how India’s Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers’ Welfare used AI to predict the start of the monsoon for 40 million farmers. She credited African expert Rose Mutiso with the insight that AI “was the last piece of this breakthrough, not the first.”

World.title: Nigeria’s Judiciary and Its Corruption Malady
World.content:
By Mobolaji Sanusi

“An impartial judiciary is essential to the administration of justice and the preservation of liberty.”

— James Madison (1751-1836)

Democracy without a credible judiciary is an invitation to a Hobbesian state of nature, where life is brutish, nasty, poor, and short. Like all human creations, state institutions established by human reasoning are not infallible and are susceptible to sometimes avoidable foibles. But when such imperfections become abysmally alarming, every right-thinking citizen should be deeply perturbed.

That is the shameful state of the Bench in Nigeria today, which is continually acknowledged by very senior stakeholders in the legal profession and beyond. Conflict, which is an essential part of societal coexistence, is becoming increasingly difficult to resolve fairly through the instrumentality of the courts.

This must have informed the country’s uninspiring, dismal ranking of 120th out of 143 countries in the 2025 World Justice Project Rule of Law Index. Given the exposed entrenched corruption on the Bench and in the legal profession generally, coupled with unchecked political interference and inadequate funding, the rating might even be worse by the time the 2026 ranking is released.

Expectedly, the court is a reflection of the society we live in, and the depth of its rot raises a pertinent and fundamental question: Is there any facet of Nigerian life that is immune to the malady of corruption? Yours sincerely acknowledge that there are still honourable judges and other Nigerians who remain above board, but they are so few in number that their feeble voices of reason have been drowned by the tumultuous horde of corrupt plunderers of the public till.

From the days of yore till the present, stakeholders within the legal system and observers outside the noble profession have been concerned and have consistently spoken out against the rot in that increasingly desecrated, fast diminishing profession in the country. Yet, the abysmal state of affairs in the judiciary and legal profession is not improving, and it continues to trouble reputable persons in the polity.

It is therefore unsurprising that retired Justice Amina Adamu Augie has become the latest voice in that regard. She is in a better position to know the extent of endemic corruption in the legal profession as a former teacher of lawyers and a retired Justice of the nation’s apex court. She might not be completely insulated from the rot like other justices/judges and lawyers, but she has raised a justifiable alarm at the recently held 40th anniversary of the Nigerian Law School Class of 1986, where she decried high-level corruption within Nigeria’s judiciary and legal profession.

She declared that corruption in the legal profession, wherever it exists — “on the Bench, at the Bar, or in the Registry — poisons everything by turning the one place where a citizen should find impartiality into one more market stall.”

That damning description of the judiciary as a “market stall” should not be taken lightly, because of the significance of the judiciary and the legal profession towards resolving recurring societal disputes, both human and institutional.

Until now, some Justices of the apex court have curiously deployed their valedictory sessions to expose the rot in the judiciary and the legal profession as a whole. Justice Musa Dattijo Muhammad, who retired as the second most senior Justice of the Supreme Court and Deputy Chairperson of the National Judicial Council, some time earlier noted the “witheringly scornful and monstrously critical” public perception of the judiciary, stemming from “court officials and judges easily being bribed by litigants to obviate delays and/or obtain favourable judgments.”

Similarly, Justice Adefope-Okojie, JCA, at the point of her exit, asked what qualifies any person to bear the exalted title of ‘Honourable Justice’ if not to administer justice without fear or favour. She bemoaned the increasing degeneration of honourable traits in members of the Bench and the Bar.

Justice Ejembi Eko, at his valedictory from the Supreme Court in 2022, expressed concerns about the tepid handling of corruption issues on the Bench by the NJC when he said: “With deference to the NJC, the punishment usually falls short of public expectation… When the punishment for an outstandingly bad and outrageous conduct is far too lenient, it encourages impunity and/or a repeat by others of such errant or atrocious misconduct.”

So far, the effort of the NJC in this regard is work in progress.

Afam Osigwe, the immediate past Nigerian Bar Association President, also earlier this year, during the National Association of Seadogs-organised Ralph Obiora Lecture that held in Enugu State, corroborated the rapacious corruption ravaging especially the Bench when he said: “The judiciary, once revered as the last hope of the common man, is increasingly perceived as a marketplace where justice is auctioned to the highest bidder.”

Osigwe relied on a 2024 survey by the UNODC and the National Bureau of Statistics which revealed that approximately N721 billion in cash bribes was received by public officials in 2023, with judges named as top recipients. An ICPC survey also reportedly showed that N9.4 billion in bribes passed through the justice sector, with lawyers and litigants identified as primary bribe-givers between 2018 and 2020. This is alarmingly condemnable.

Even the revered quintessential jurist of our time, Justice Kayode Eso, who passed on in November 2012, observed the rot in his book The Judiciary: The Shield of Justice, thus: “Corruption in the judiciary is a major problem that needs to be addressed. It is a problem that has been affecting the integrity and effectiveness of the judicial system… We need to take urgent steps to address corruption in the judiciary.”

Again, the question arises: are the necessary steps being taken to address this problem when the judiciary unfortunately relies absolutely on the executive branch for its survival? It made for shameful optics when, not too long ago, the Chief Judge of the nation’s Federal High Court, Honourable Justice John Terhemba Tsoho, led fellow judges cap-in-hand to beg the FCT Minister, Nyesom Wike, for landed property and other perquisites.

In my Yoruba culture, there’s a saying that “Ti enu ba je, oju a ti” — He who pays the piper dictates the tune. Following from this, it can be inferred that it will be difficult for the Bench to say a complete NO to the demands of their benefactor called Wike or anyone in the executive arm whenever the need arises. Too bad!

No wonder it is widely believed that corruption in the judiciary will subsist for as long as we have a judiciary that “…must beg the executive for a courtroom roof, vehicles, judges’ entitlements and financial autonomy for the courts” — all of which should ordinarily be constitutional perquisites of office for Justices and Judges.

The 2027 general elections are fast approaching and ours is a country where no politician contesting for positions accedes to defeat at the polls. Election losers in our clime always approach the Election Petition Tribunal on the flimsiest of excuses to contest their loss. Do we rely on “compromisable or tainted judicial officers” to move our democracy forward? This question under the prevailing circumstance is better left unanswered. Too bad!

The country must get its act right if we truly desire a judiciary that is, in words and deeds, largely an impartial referee, not a player in the game. What we have now is largely a courtroom where the calm and neutral administration of the law yields to political interests and pecuniary inducements; a complete reflection of the times we all live in and shamelessly adore for parochial sentiments. On this note, l rest my case for this week.

Ipoola Omisore Relocates ‘Ile-Ife Greats’ To Lagos

“A room without books is like a body without a soul.”

– Marcus Tallius Cicero (January 3, 106 BC—December 7, 43 BC).

The date is October 30, 2026. On that day, Lagos will be agog with a momentous event meant to celebrate recorded reputable sons and daughters of the Yoruba cradle from the Source in Ile-Ife, Osun State.

The convener of the event is none other than the elder statesman, accomplished advertising professional, educationist, author, and two-term former member of the House of Assembly of the Centre of Excellence, Hon. Ahmed Ipoola Omisore, who authored the book titled: “Great Ifes in History,” which will be launched on that day.

The Royal Father of the Day is His Imperial Majesty, Oba Babatunde Enitan Ogunwusi, CFR, while the Principal Guest of Honour is His Excellency, Dr. Kadri Obafemi Hamzat—the incoming governor of Lagos state come May 29,2027, insha Allah. The Father-of-the-Day is Chief Oyekunle Alex-Duduyemi, while the book reviewer is the accomplished journalist, President Emeritus of the Nigerian Guild of Editors and Provost of the Nigerian Institute of Journalism, Mr. Gbenga Adefaye.

Definitely, next Friday promises to be an interesting day at the Lagos Airport Hotel, Ikeja, venue for this promising event by Honourable Omisore.

Trust me, yours sincerely will be present at the occasion to celebrate the day with invited guests…..Congratulations in advance Honourable Omisore…

World.title: Ebola: FG Tightens Surveillance, Screening, Infected Woman Identified as Swiss Diplomat’s Wife
World.content:
* Kenya Reports Second Death from the disease

* WHO says source of infection remains unknown, calls for regional vigilance

* Nigeria’s NCDC begins genomic sequencing

*Edo sets up emergency response committee

Onyebuchi Ezigbo in Abuja, Ayodeji Ake in Lagos and Felix Omoh-Asun in Benin City, with agency reports

The federal government yesterday tightened Ebola control measures across Nigeria, directing ministries, departments and agencies (MDAs), public health institutions and other stakeholders to strictly enforce screening, surveillance and other approved entry protocols as Switzerland confirmed that the woman who tested positive for the virus in Nigeria was the wife of a Swiss diplomat.

The directive by the Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare followed concerns raised by the Office of the National Security Adviser (ONSA) over reported breaches of government-approved Ebola Virus Disease (EVD) entry protocols at Nigeria’s designated points of entry.

The ministry’s directive was contained in circular PS/FMOH/08/VIII/48, dated October 22, 2026, and signed by the Permanent Secretary, Daju Kachollum S., on behalf of the Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Welfare, Prof. Muhammad Ali Pate.

This comes as Kenya’s Health Ministry yesterday announced a second Ebola death, adding that the 65-year-old woman had developed symptoms during quarantine and was a close relative of a ‌Kenyan man who died of Ebola earlier this month.

Also yesterday, Edo State Governor, Senator Monday Okpebholo, established a committee to coordinate the state’s emergency preparedness and response.

Swiss Ministry Confirms Diplomat’s Wife Tested Positive

Switzerland’s Foreign Ministry confirmed that the woman who tested positive for Ebola in Nigeria was the wife of a Swiss diplomat.

The 42-year-old Ugandan-born woman, who lives in Abuja, tested positive on October 20, becoming Nigeria’s first confirmed Ebola patient in more than a decade.

The couple had travelled to Uganda earlier in October. Her husband is currently in isolation but has not developed symptoms, according to the Swiss Foreign Ministry.

The ministry told the BBC that all 25 staff members at its embassy in Nigeria were in good health and did not need to isolate. The decision, taken in consultation with Nigeria’s Ministry of Health and the World Health Organisation (WHO), covered eight Swiss staff members and 17 local employees.

The embassy remains open and operational, with health and safety measures in place.

The woman had reportedly spent about a week at a private clinic in Abuja experiencing symptoms before her diagnosis. She returned to Nigeria on October 3 after spending about two and a half weeks in Uganda. She developed symptoms four days after arriving in Abuja and sought treatment at two private health facilities before testing positive on October 20.

WHO said the woman was receiving treatment in isolation and showing signs of improvement.

Although there were reports that she had travelled to eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DR Congo) for business, the WHO, Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) and Nigeria’s health ministry said they had not received verified information confirming that she visited the country. The Swiss government had also told Reuters that she did not travel to DR Congo, contradicting accounts from Uganda.

Health officials are investigating whether she may have crossed paths with a Kenyan man who died of Ebola after travelling through Uganda’s main airport on the same day. The Africa CDC said investigators were examining whether the two could have been exposed through shared equipment or other contact.

The agency’s Head of Emergency Preparedness and Response, Dr. Wessam Mankoula, described this as one of the possible scenarios but stressed that no link had been established.

The Kenyan man had travelled from DR Congo through Uganda before arriving in Nairobi on October 3. He subsequently died, becoming Kenya’s first recorded Ebola fatality. Kenya has since confirmed nine cases and traced 135 contacts, all of whom were placed in quarantine.

Ebola has infected nearly 10,000 people and killed more than 4,600 in Congo. The disease can cause fever, vomiting, diarrhoea and, in severe ⁠cases, internal and external bleeding. Only people with symptoms can transmit the virus. The rare Ebola species behind the current outbreak has no approved treatment or vaccine.

WHO said it was too early to determine where the woman in Nigeria contracted the virus.

“The source of exposure is still not known. The travel history of the patient is still being pieced together,” said Dr Patrick Otim, a WHO emergency response official.

He said investigators had struggled to obtain a complete account of her movements because opportunities to interview her were limited while she remained in hospital.

The Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) is conducting genomic sequencing to help establish whether her infection is linked to other cases. However, the woman has been confirmed to have the Bundibugyo species of Ebola, the same species responsible for the outbreak in DR Congo.

“The investigation is reconstructing the full travel and exposure history. Genomic sequencing is given a high priority,” said Dr Pavel Ursu, WHO’s representative in Nigeria.

Meanwhile, Nigerian authorities are tracing additional people who may have been exposed to the woman beyond the 44 contacts initially identified.

Kenya’s Director-General of Health, Dr Patrick Amoth, said all nine confirmed infections in his country were linked to the first patient, with no evidence of wider community transmission. He urged the public to remain vigilant without panicking, while warning that the country was not yet out of danger.

He added that the eight surviving patients remained in isolation and were responding well to treatment.

The developments have renewed concerns about the movement of infected people across international borders, particularly between DR Congo and neighbouring Uganda, where thousands of people cross daily for trade, work and family visits.

WHO’s Regional Director for Africa, Dr Mohamed Janabi, called for regional vigilance and urged countries to strengthen surveillance, investigate infections and protect frontline health workers.

Ebola is a serious viral disease transmitted through direct contact with the blood or other bodily fluids of an infected person, or contaminated objects. It does not spread through the air like influenza. Symptoms can include fever, severe weakness, vomiting and diarrhoea, and the disease can be fatal. People are not considered infectious before developing symptoms.

Health authorities say rapid contact tracing, isolation of suspected cases and early treatment are crucial to preventing further transmission.

FG Orders Strict Compliance with Ebola Protocols

In the circular, the Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare directed relevant institutions to ensure strict adherence to approved EVD screening, health declaration, surveillance and other applicable entry requirements at all designated points of entry into Nigeria.

According to a statement signed by the Assistant Director, Information and Public Relations, Ado Bako, the directive followed concerns communicated to the Coordinating Minister by ONSA over reported non-compliance with government-approved protocols.

The ministry emphasised the need for consistent, effective and non-discriminatory enforcement of the measures to mitigate potential cross-border transmission and protect public health and national security.

It also called for stronger coordination, communication and information-sharing among stakeholders to support effective surveillance, early detection and prompt responses to potential threats.

“All concerned institutions have been urged to promptly document and report any actual or attempted breach of approved protocols through established channels, provide necessary support to officials responsible for enforcement, and establish effective monitoring and accountability mechanisms to sustain compliance,” the statement said.

The ministry stressed that personnel responsible for enforcing the protocols should be allowed to perform their duties professionally and without undue interference.

It also directed the immediate and widespread dissemination of public advisories to relevant departments, units, field offices and personnel to ensure that they understood their responsibilities.

“All concerned MDAs are expected to accord the directive the highest priority, address identified lapses promptly and sustain compliance with approved EVD entry protocols in the collective interest of public health and national safety,” the statement added.

The directive comes amid efforts to contain the confirmed Ebola case in the Federal Capital Territory, with the government intensifying surveillance at airports, seaports and land borders.

Kenya Reports Second Death from Ebola

Kenya has recorded a second Ebola death, the health ministry said yesterday, adding that the 65-year-old woman had developed symptoms during quarantine and was a close relative of a ‌Kenyan man who died of Ebola earlier this month.

The outbreak, which started in the Democratic Republic of Congo, has now been reported in four countries across eastern, central andwestern Africa, giving it the widest geographic spread of any Ebola outbreak on the continent to date.

The Ebola victim who died yesterday, was a direct contact of the index patient, Reuters quoted the Kenyan ministry to have revealed.

“This loss brings the number of deaths to two among the nine confirmed cases. The remaining seven patients continue to receive care in the ‌two ⁠isolation facilities,” the ministry said, adding there was no evidence of community spread in the country.

Late on Monday, the US State Department advised Americans to reconsider travel to Kenya and raised its travel advisory level for the countrybecause of health risks.

Edo Sets Up Ebola Emergency Response Committee

Edo State Governor, Senator Monday Okpebholo, has established a committee on Ebola emergency preparedness and response.

The committee is chaired by the Deputy Governor, Dennis Idahosa, according to a statement issued yesterday by the Chief Press Secretary to the Governor, Dr Patrick Ebojele.

The committee is expected to coordinate the state’s preparedness and response to any Ebola threat.

Its members are drawn from the state ministries responsible for health, environment, livestock, local government, finance, and information and communication; the Edo State House of Assembly Committee on Health; the governor’s Special Adviser on Health; the State Emergency Management Agency; the Department of Port Health; and the National Orientation Agency.

Other members include personnel from the Department of State Services, Nigeria Immigration Service, Nigeria Police Force and Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps.

The committee also includes representatives of the University of Benin Teaching Hospital, Irrua Specialist Teaching Hospital, Edo State University Teaching Hospital, Federal Neuropsychiatric Hospital in Uselu, Edo Specialist Hospital, Central Hospital in Benin City and Stella Obasanjo Hospital.

Professional bodies represented include the Nigeria Medical Association, National Association of Nigeria Nurses and Midwives, and the Edo State chapter of the Association of Private Medical Practitioners of Nigeria.

Other members include a traditional ruler, a leader of the Christian Association of Nigeria in Edo State, the state’s Chief Imam and a market women’s leader.

Development partners and agencies represented on the committee include the WHO, UNICEF, Nigeria Red Cross Society, DataFi, National Primary Health Care Development Agency and Edo State Primary Health Care Development Agency.

The committee will operate through the Public Health Emergency Operations Centre, which has designated areas of responsibility covering coordination, epidemiology, surveillance, infection prevention and control, risk communication, logistics, laboratory services, case management, and safe and dignified burial. A centre manager will oversee operations.

The statement added that a stakeholders’ meeting would be scheduled for the committee.

World.title: State Police: 25 Assemblies Approve Amendment, Bill Crosses Constitutional Hurdle
World.content:
• Lagos, Ondo, Ebonyi, Kogi, Niger, Borno, Bauchi, Jigawa, Katsina, Kano, Sokoto yet to approve

Deji Elumoye in Abuja

The constitutional amendment seeking to establish State Police in Nigeria has crossed a major legislative hurdle, with 25 of the 36 State Houses of Assembly approving the 2026 Constitution (Sixth Alteration) Bill, surpassing the two-thirds threshold required for the amendment to proceed to the next stage.

However, 11 States —Lagos, Ondo, Ebonyi, Kogi, Niger, Borno, Bauchi, Jigawa, Katsina, Kano and Sokoto — have yet to approve the amendment.

With the required constitutional threshold secured, the amendment can now be returned to the National Assembly for transmission to President Bola Tinubu for assent.

Chief of Staff to the President and Chairman of the Presidential Working Group on the National Policing Bill, Hon. Femi Gbajabiamila, disclosed the development in a statement, commending the State Houses of Assembly for their decisive action on the reform.

He also expressed appreciation to the National Assembly for passing the amendment in both chambers.

The development came as the National Policing Bill and 29 consequential amendment bills were undergoing legislative drafting review and validation at the Federal Ministry of Justice.

Gbajabiamila explained that the approval by 25 state assemblies had provided the constitutional backing required for the proposed dual policing framework.

He stated: “The approval gives constitutional backing to the policing framework that the Working Group’s draft National Policing Bill, 2026 is designed to implement.

“The Working Group’s efforts remain on track. The draft Bills are currently undergoing legislative drafting review and validation at the Federal Ministry of Justice and are expected to be returned on or before Friday, 30th October 2026. Thereafter, the Group will give them final consideration before presenting them to Mr President.

“The Working Group urges all stakeholders to support a smooth transition to a dual policing system that makes Nigerians safer.”

The Presidency had on Tuesday disclosed that the draft National Policing Bill, 2026, was ready.

Gbajabiamila explained that the Working Group had completed the drafting stage of its assignment and formally submitted the proposed National Policing Bill, together with 29 consequential amendment bills, to the Federal Ministry of Justice for legislative drafting review and validation.

According to him, the submission was made to the Attorney-General of the Federation and Minister of Justice on Monday, October 19, 2026, in accordance with the Working Group’s work plan.

He said the ministry’s review would ensure that the proposed legislation conformed to established legislative drafting standards and conventions and did not conflict with existing laws.

The Ministry of Justice, he added, was expected to return the validated draft bills to the Working Group on or before October 30, 2026.

Thereafter, the Working Group would give the bills final consideration before presenting them to the President, thereby concluding its mandate.

Gbajabiamila stated: “The proposed National Policing Bill seeks to establish the constitutional and legislative framework for a dual policing structure, comprising a Federal Police Service and State Police Services.

“The Working Group remains committed to a rigorous and transparent process that will deliver a comprehensive legislative proposal for consideration by the President and subsequent transmission to the National Assembly.

“The work on preparing the National Policing Bill is proceeding alongside the ongoing consideration of the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria, 1999 (Sixth Alteration) Bill, 2026 by the States Houses of Assembly, which must be completed before the Bill is transmitted to the National Assembly.”

The Presidency had last Thursday indicated that the National Policing Bill would be transmitted to the National Assembly within two weeks.

Speaking with journalists after a steering committee meeting at the State House, Abuja, Gbajabiamila said the proposed legislation was nearing completion.

“The National Policing Bill is more or less ready for transmission to the National Assembly. We will probably have one more meeting after this to cross the t’s and dot the i’s and make sure every area is covered. So, we are 90 percent ready.

“The governors have one or two observations, and we should be ready in about a week or so,” he said.

Gbajabiamila described the proposed legislation as “the most consequential Bill of the administration so far,” explaining that it had undergone extensive deliberations since the Working Group’s steering committee commenced its meetings on August 3, 2026.

Responding to concerns that some states might delay approval of the Sixth Constitution Alteration Bill on state police, particularly when only about six states had reportedly approved the amendment, Gbajabiamila expressed confidence that the required support would be secured.

He maintained that there was a “national consensus” among Nigerians on the need for the constitutional amendment.

“I see no reason why anyone will want to have a rethink on it,” he said.

Those present at Thursday’s steering committee meeting, held at the conference hall of the Chief of Staff’s Office at the State House, Abuja, included the Chairman of the Nigeria Governors’ Forum and Governor of Kwara State, AbdulRahman AbdulRazaq; Ogun State Governor, Dapo Abiodun; Kaduna State Governor, Uba Sani; Inspector-General of Police, Tunji Disu; and the Attorney-General of the Federation and Minister of Justice, represented by the Solicitor-General and Permanent Secretary of the Federal Ministry of Justice, Mrs Beatrice Jedy-Agba.

Others included the Chairman of the Policy Advisory Committee, Justice Abdullahi Liman (retd.); Head of the Nigeria Police Reform Secretariat, Professor Olu Ogunsakin; Special Adviser to the President on National Assembly Matters (House of Representatives), Dr Lanre Smart; and Senior Special Assistant to the President on Planning and Research and Secretary of the Committee, Nnadubem Moghalu.

Also in attendance were a representative of the President of the Nigerian Bar Association and AIG Abraham Nabhon Thomas, who represented the National Security Adviser, among others.

President Tinubu had, on July 7, 2026, inaugurated the Presidential Working Group on the National Policing Bill to prepare the legal framework for the implementation of state police across the country.

The inauguration followed the National Assembly’s passage of the Constitution Alteration (State Police) Bill, 2026, which provides for a dual policing structure comprising a Federal Police Service and 36 State Police Services.

Tinubu had explained that although the constitutional amendment would establish the framework for state police, the National Policing Bill would provide the legal structure necessary for its implementation.

“The Constitution Amendment Bill establishes the framework for dual policing, but it does not operationalise it. That work is left to the National Policing Bill,” the President stated.

World.title: Oramah: Africa Must Break Economic Bondage, Build Its Own Industrial Power
World.content:
· Says political independence incomplete without economic freedom

· Urges investment in manufacturing, skills, technology

Nume Ekeghe

The immediate past President of the African Export-Import Bank (Afreximbank), Dr. Benedict Oramah, has urged African countries to intensify efforts to achieve economic independence through industrialisation, deeper intra-African trade, strategic deployment of capital and investment in human development.

Oramah, who spoke in an interview on the sidelines of the recently concluded International Monetary Fund (IMF)/World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok, Thailand, said the continent’s political independence would remain incomplete unless African countries developed the capacity to produce goods, create decent jobs and determine their economic future.

He called on governments, financial institutions, businesses and other stakeholders to see themselves as fighters for Africa’s economic freedom, warning that the continent must overcome the fragmentation and dependence that continue to constrain its development.

“Everybody in the banking business, including our governments and corporates, has to regard themselves as economic freedom fighters. We are combatants for economic freedom. Those in banking and financial services are engaged in financial guerrilla warfare,” he said.

According to him, political independence was only the beginning of Africa’s struggle, with the ultimate objective being economic self-determination.

“Political independence gives you the platform to achieve the ultimate independence, which is economic independence,” Oramah said, adding that the struggle must now be fought through ideas, industrial production, technology and human capital rather than weapons.

“The fight we are in now is not going to be fought in trenches, but on factory floors, in technology incubation centres and so on. It is not going to be fought with brute force. It will be fought with ideas. Capital is key, not bullets. That capital includes human capital,” he added.

Oramah, who recently completed his tenure at Afreximbank after two terms, said he had established Marob Strategies, a strategy and advisory firm, to continue contributing to Africa’s development by helping institutions formulate and implement strategies.

He explained that Africa’s challenge was not merely a shortage of ideas but the inability to execute them effectively and mobilise the resources required to achieve continental ambitions.

On regional integration, he lamented that Africa’s trade with external partners remained disproportionately high compared with trade among its own countries, despite the continent’s significant infrastructure assets and productive capacity.

He said existing infrastructure could support between $1 trillion and $1.4 trillion in African trade, yet intra-African trade accounted for only about $170 billion to $200 billion.

Oramah further urged African countries to develop their own artificial intelligence capabilities rather than remain mere users of technologies developed elsewhere.

World.title: Babalakin Hails Tinubu Over Resolution of 19-year MMA2 Dispute, Pledges Jobs for Nigerians
World.content:
Dike Onwuamaeze



The Chairman of Bi-Courtney Aviation Services Limited (BASL), Dr. Wale Babalakin, SAN, has commended President Bola Tinubu for facilitating the resolution of the longstanding dispute surrounding the Murtala Muhammed Airport Terminal Two (MMA2), describing the settlement as a victory for Nigeria.



Babalakin also pledged that Bi-Courtney would fulfil its obligations under the agreement and pursue projects expected to create quality employment opportunities for Nigerians.



He spoke at the signing ceremony of the settlement agreement involving the Federal Government, the Federal Airports Authority of Nigeria (FAAN), Bi-Courtney Limited and Stabilini Visinoni Limited, which resolved an impasse that had lasted more than 18 years.

The BASL chairman attributed the breakthrough to Tinubu’s intervention through the Minister of Aviation and Aerospace Development, Olorogun Festus Keyamo, SAN.



“This is not a win for us alone; it is a win for Nigerians,” Babalakin said, expressing appreciation to the President, the minister and Nigerians who had followed the dispute over the years.

He said the resolution sent a positive signal to investors that longstanding disputes between the government and private enterprises could be settled through dialogue and constructive engagement.



According to him, prolonged uncertainty over commercial agreements could discourage long-term investment, making the settlement an important step towards strengthening confidence in Nigeria’s investment environment.



The agreement is also expected to pave the way for the advancement of key development projects at MMA2, particularly the proposed hotel and conference centre, as well as the commencement of regional flight operations.



Babalakin said completing the hotel and conference centre would enhance the airport environment by providing accommodation and conference facilities for business travellers, corporate organisations and other airport users.



He added that the project could generate employment across construction, engineering, hospitality, facility management and related services.



The commencement of regional flight operations, alongside the planned expansion of the airport apron, would also create opportunities for skilled employment and commercial growth.

The settlement further addresses outstanding issues arising from the parties’ longstanding commercial relationship, including matters relating to the General Aviation Terminal (GAT), which remained under FAAN’s control and operation.



The agreement incorporates reciprocal concessions and revised obligations, providing a framework for the parties to move forward.

Babalakin acknowledged the responsibility to translate the settlement into tangible results, assuring stakeholders that Bi-Courtney would fulfil its obligations and work constructively with the relevant parties.



“We will not disappoint the President, the Ministry of Aviation and Aerospace Development, FAAN or Nigerians,” he said.

He reiterated his appreciation to Tinubu for facilitating the resolution, describing the agreement as an opportunity to renew cooperation, deliver infrastructure projects and realise the full potential of MMA2.

World.title: New sheriffs in town: Male and female orca pair terrorise whales off Cape coast
World.content:
A large male orca and a female appear to be targeting southern right whale calves. Image: Simon's Town Boat Company/ Facebook

Two orcas – a massive male accompanied by a female – have been creating havoc along the Cape coastline for the past fortnight.

The pair has been linked to multiple attacks on southern right whale calves, from the Eastern Cape all the way down to False Bay near Cape Town.

Their encounters with southern rights have stunned marine scientists, who are investigating what could mark a fascinating shift in the hunting behaviour of these apex predators.



For years, an orca pair, affectionately named Port and Starboard, have been regular visitors to Cape waters. Known for preying on great white sharks, the male pair are usually the ones blamed when something big goes down.

This new pair seems to be going after bigger prey.

The orca pair made an appearance in False Bay on Friday. Image: Dave Hurwitz

Orcas target southern right whale calves

According to the Simon’s Town Boat Company, the male and female pair’s coastal journey began off Kaysers Beach near East London.



There, they reportedly killed a southern right whale calf before remaining in the area for another two days.

After sightings at Kids Beach, the orcas reached Plettenberg Bay on the 14th of October, where the pair were filmed attempting to prey on another southern right whale calf.

The amateur drone footage captured the mother defending her youngster for four gruelling hours before the predators eventually gave up.



On 15 October, the pair were spotted off Knysna before continuing west towards Jongensfontein, near Still Bay.

Here, surf instructor Shannon Ainslie filmed an encounter which showed the orcas again attempting to isolate and attack a southern right whale calf.

Marine scientist Dr Simon Elwen, founding director of Sea Search, confirmed that the footage showed a hunting attempt.



“It was almost certainly a predation attempt,” Elwen told CapeTalk earlier this week. He added that southern right whales are excellent mothers, and good at defending their young.

Elwen also noted that orca attacks on large whales, like southern rights and humpbacks, have been rare in South Africa.

“Having three attacks in just over a month, basically, is a real game changer,” he said.



Researchers are still gathering information to confirm whether the same orcas are responsible. “Presumably they are,” Elwen added.

new pair spotted in False Bay

Following the Jongensfontein attack, the orca pair were clocked off Hermanus on Thursday morning, before making an appearance in False Bay on Friday.

The Simon’s Town Boat Company reported that researchers, including Dr. Elwen, joined a whale-watching trip to collect DNA samples and potentially attach a satellite tag.



“Our main concern though, was for a mother and calf southern right whale and sub-adult humpback whales that were in False Bay for the whole day yesterday,” the Company said.

“We certainly did not want to witness them being preyed upon.”

After eventually locating the orca pair, who had become “super interactive and surface active” with the boats, scientists were able to successfully collect biopsy samples and attach a satellite tag to the female orca.



The animals also “buzzed” three Cape fur seals during the encounter, causing the seals to leap from the water.

Whether the pair continues heading westwards along the coast should become clear in the next few days.

World.title: Kaizer Chiefs in tears after CAF Confederation Cup penalty heartbreak
World.content:
Kaizer Chiefs were knocked out of the 2026/27 CAF Confederation Cup after losing 3-2 on penalties to Red Arrows. Image: Kaizer Chiefs website

Kaizer Chiefs were knocked out of the 2026/27 CAF Confederation Cup after losing 3-2 on penalties to Red Arrows, despite winning Friday’s second-leg encounter 1-0 at the Moses Mabhida Stadium in Durban.

Amakhosi levelled the aggregate score at 1-1 through a second-half header from Bradley Cross, but missed opportunities in normal time proved costly as the Zambian side secured qualification for the group stage.

Kaizer Chiefs had entered the match needing to overturn a 1-0 first-leg defeat and started aggressively, determined to give themselves a chance of continuing their continental campaign.



However, Red Arrows defended resolutely in the opening half, frustrating the home side and limiting clear scoring opportunities.

Kaizer Chiefs struggle to break down Red Arrows

Pule Mmodi won a corner inside the opening minute as Kaizer Chiefs immediately looked to put their opponents under pressure.

Amakhosi pushed forward and attempted to stretch the Red Arrows defence, with Mmodi and Reeve Frosler providing width on either flank.

Thulani Mabaso forced a save in the 12th minute, but clear chances remained limited as the visitors crowded the edge of their penalty area.

Wandile Duba went down inside the box in the 36th minute, but his penalty appeal was waved away.

Shortly before half-time, Frosler delivered a cross towards Mmodi at the far post, but the winger’s header lacked the power to trouble the goalkeeper.



The teams went into the break with the score still goalless, leaving Kaizer Chiefs needing a stronger second-half performance.

Bradley Cross puts Amakhosi back in the tie

Kaizer Chiefs increased the pressure after the restart, with Faiz Abrahams firing over in the 47th minute before Mmodi almost sent Duba through on goal.

Mmodi then curled an effort wide as Amakhosi continued searching for the goal that would level the contest.

The breakthrough finally arrived in the 66th minute.

Substitute Mfundo Vilakazi delivered a dangerous free-kick into the penalty area, where Cross beat his marker and guided a header inside the far post.

The goal made it 1-0 on the night and levelled the aggregate score at 1-1, giving Kaizer Chiefs renewed hope of reaching the group stage.

Cross also made an important defensive clearance moments later, preventing Red Arrows from capitalising at the other end.

Missed chances haunt Kaizer Chiefs

The Soweto giants had several opportunities to find the goal that could have secured qualification without a shootout.

In the 79th minute, Vilakazi produced an excellent run down the right before setting up Mduduzi Shabalala, who fired over from inside the box.

Five minutes later, substitute Ethan Chislett sent Shabalala through on goal, but his effort went straight at the goalkeeper.

Asanale Velebayi also missed the target with a late opportunity as Kaizer Chiefs failed to find a decisive second goal.

With the aggregate score remaining level at 1-1, the tie went to penalties.

Red Arrows win the shootout

Kaizer Chiefs endured a painful end to their continental campaign during the penalty shootout.

Shabalala and Vilakazi converted their attempts, but Lebohang Maboe and Chislett both struck the crossbar, while Frosler’s penalty was saved.

Goalkeeper Bruce Bvuma gave Amakhosi hope by saving Red Arrows’ first spot-kick, but the Zambian side recovered to win the shootout 3-2.

Is the early exit a blessing in disguise for Kaizer Chiefs?

Let us know by clicking on the comment banner below …

World.title: HOW to check if you’re registered to vote on 4 November
World.content:
Are you registered to vote in local government elections on Wednesday 4 November 2026? With less than two weeks to go, now is the time to confirm you’re on the voters’ roll, and in the correct right ward you think you are.

CHECK IF YOU’RE REGISTERED TO VOTE

Go to elections.org.za and enter your 13-digit ID number.

A green banner reading ‘You are registered’ confirms your status and your ward. Your voting district and station will be listed underneath.

You can send your ID number to 32810 at R1 per SMS.

at R1 per SMS. Phone the IEC contact centre is on 0800 118 000 .

. Use the voting station finder by typing your address into maps.elections.org.za/vsfinder to see your local station and ward.

If you voted in 2021 or 2024 and haven’t moved, you should still be on the roll, but it’s worth checking.

ARE YOU REGISTERED TO VOTE IN CORRECT AREA?

The good news is Wednesday 4 November is a public holiday. Image: File

Here’s the catch, in local elections you must be registered to vote at the station where you ordinarily live. In 2024, some voters could cast a ballot elsewhere, but not this time. Your registration address decides your ward, and your ward decides which councillor candidates appear on your ballot.

And it’s too late to change now if you haven’t registered to vote in your area. The IEC voters’ roll closed on 7 August 2026. What this means in practice is:



Registered at an old address? Sorry for you. You will have to travel to your old voting station to vote.

Not on the roll at all? You cannot vote on 4 November at all.

at all. Hoping for a special vote? Applications closed on 12 October, and special votes are only for approved applicants, taking place on 2 and 3 November.

WHAT TO DO NEXT

Check your status and station, and whether you are indeed registered to vote, and where.

If your station is far from home, work out transport now.

Bring along your ID: Smart ID card, green barcoded ID book or temporary ID certificate all count.

Voting stations open at 7am and close at 9pm on 4 November, which is a public holiday.

But what do you think? Do you know if you’re registered to vote or not? Please share your thoughts in the comments section below …

World.title: Jake White makes winning start as new Fiji coach
World.content:
Fiji edged Japan in Tokyo on Saturday to give new coach Jake White a winning start in his reunion with Eddie Jones. Image: Fiji Village website

Fiji edged Japan 34-28 in Tokyo on Saturday to give new coach Jake White a winning start in his reunion with Eddie Jones, less than a year until the World Cup.

The 62-year-old White led his native South Africa to World Cup glory in 2007 and went on to coach teams in Australia, France and Japan before being handed the Fiji job this month.

White is reportedly being helped by fellow South Africans Gert Smal and Allister Coetzee.



READ | Sonny Bill Williams undergoes open-heart surgery

Roller-coaster game

Jake White’s new side came out on top against Jones’s Japan in a roller-coaster game in the rain.

The Australian Jones was White’s technical adviser for South Africa’s World Cup win.

Japan and Fiji each scored three first-half tries, before visiting substitute Ben Volavola made the difference with two penalties after the break.

The two sides had met in the Pacific Nations Cup final in Tokyo a month earlier, with Japan winning 20-15.

Saturday’s game served as a warm-up for Japan and Fiji’s trips to Europe next month for the Nations Championship.



Japan will play Wales, England and Scotland, while Fiji will take on France, Ireland and Italy.

The game was being played to mark the 100th anniversary of the Japan Rugby Football Union.

Perfect start

Japan, wearing special white commemorative shirts, made the perfect start when Naoto Saito scurried over the line for a fourth-minute try.

Fiji hit back just over five minutes later through Kitione Salawa, then took the lead when captain Tevita Ikanivere touched down after a counterattack.

Japan captain Warner Dearns rampaged over the line to even the scores, but Fiji regained the lead when Tuidraki Samusamuvodre pounced on a mistake in the Japan defence.

Upgraded to red

Fiji were temporarily reduced to 14 men when Motikai Murray was yellow-carded in the 35th minute and Japan took advantage immediately with a try from Faulua Makisi.

Murray’s yellow card was later upgraded to a red but Fiji regained their lead when Terio Tamani scored four minutes into the second half.

Japan hit back with another Dearns try but Volavola stayed cool to edge Fiji back ahead for good.

Jake White coached the Springboks in 54 Test, winning 36, losing 17 and drawing one, for a win-percentage of 66.7%.

Meanwhile, Coetzee coached the Springboks in 25 Tests, winning 11, losing 12 and drawing two, for a win-percentage of just 44%.

By Garrin Lambley © Agence France-Presse

World.title: Proteas suffer key injury blow ahead of Newlands Test decider
World.content:
The Proteas have named a 16-man squad for the third and final Test against Australia at Newlands in Cape Town. Image: Ellisroger (Flickr).

The Proteas have named a 16-man squad for the third and final Test against Australia, which gets underway on Tuesday, 27 October at Newlands in Cape Town.

Fast bowler Anrich Nortje has been ruled out of the Test due to a mild groin injury.

He sustained the injury while bowling during the first innings of the second Test in Gqeberha on Wednesday.



Subsequent scans on Thursday revealed the extent of the injury.

No replacement has been named for Nortje.

Proteas squad – 3rd Test against Australia

Temba Bavuma (captain), Marques Ackerman, David Bedingham, Corbin Bosch, Matthew Breetzke, Gerald Coetzee, Simon Harmer, Marco Jansen, Keshav Maharaj, Aiden Markram, Wiaan Mulder, Senuran Muthusamy, Dane Paterson, Kagiso Rabada, Ryan Rickelton, Kyle Verreynne
