World.title: Liberia’s Supreme Court Weighs Whether Parliament Defied Its Order in Expelling Outspoken Lawmaker
World.content:
MONROVIA, Liberia — Liberia’s Supreme Court on Thursday reserved judgment in a case that could determine whether the country’s House of Representatives defied a court order when it expelled one of its most outspoken members, Yekeh Kolubah, in April.

By Victoria G. Wesseh

The case turns on a narrow but consequential question: was the House leadership legally served with a Supreme Court order instructing it to halt proceedings against Kolubah before it voted to remove him? If it was, the vote may have been taken in breach of a binding judicial directive. If not, the House may have been free to act.



How the Dispute Began

Kolubah represented District 10 of Montserrado County, which includes the capital, Monrovia, and was long one of the Legislature’s most combative voices. The disciplinary case against him followed a controversial statement he made about the Makona River boundary dispute, one that many considered provocative, even offensive.

Kolubah was formally notified on April 9, 2026, to appear before the House Committee on Rules, Order and Administration on April 13. He and his lawyers walked out of a later committee hearing after it refused to grant them an additional five days and access to evidence.

His lawyers then asked the Supreme Court for a writ of prohibition, an order used to stop a body from exceeding its authority. Associate Justice Yussif D. Kaba granted the petition on April 16, summoning House leaders to a conference on April 20 and ordering them to stay all further proceedings pending its outcome. The directive was addressed to Speaker Richard Nagbe Koon, Deputy Speaker Thomas Fallah, the House Chief Clerk, the Sergeant-at-Arms and everyone acting under their authority.

The next day, the House went ahead. Kolubah was expelled by the full House on Friday, April 17, after a resolution was signed by 49 of the chamber’s 73 members, the two-thirds majority the Constitution requires. The resolution said he was removed for acts and utterances deemed unpatriotic and detrimental to the country’s sovereignty and territorial integrity.

The Service Dispute

The House says it was never properly served. Its lawyers cited Rule 26.5 of the House rules, which names the Sergeant-at-Arms as the only officer authorised to receive court orders on behalf of the House. Court records show the Supreme Court Marshal instead served the documents on a receptionist and a computer operator attached to the offices of the Speaker and the Chief Clerk.

That argument has already succeeded once. In May 2026, Justice Kaba dismissed Kolubah’s follow-up complaint, known as a bill of information, for improper service, reportedly finding that the House had not been properly served with the writ and stay order. Kolubah appealed to the full five-member bench, which heard arguments on Thursday.

Jonathan Massaquoi, who leads Kolubah’s legal team, told the justices that the validity of service should be judged by Liberia’s Civil Procedure Law, not by the House’s internal rules for handling correspondence.

He cited Section 3.38(9), which states: “Personal service upon a subdivision of the government subject to suit or upon a municipal corporation shall be made by reading and delivering the summons to the chief executive thereof.”

On that basis, the petitioners argued that delivering the order to the office of the Speaker, the House’s presiding officer, was sufficient. A court officer identified as Joshua B. delivered the document there, they said, and a receptionist acknowledged receipt and signed for a copy.

Whether the provision covers the House at all is an open question. It refers specifically to “a subdivision of the government subject to suit” or “a municipal corporation,” and the Court must decide whether a branch of the national Legislature falls into either category.

Did the House Defy the Court?

The justices must weigh the wording of the order, the Marshal’s report of service, the receptionist’s acknowledgment and the legal standing of the office that received it.

Even a clear answer on service may not end the dispute. If the Court upholds the dismissal, it will not necessarily have examined or endorsed the disciplinary proceedings; and a win for Kolubah on service would not automatically prove the expulsion unconstitutional.

Other questions hang over the vote itself. A Bomi County lawmaker has denied backing the expulsion, raising questions about whether the House reached the legally required majority. A media adviser to Speaker Koon also told FrontPage Africa the expulsion took place on April 22, not April 17, before abruptly ending the conversation. A later date could matter, because it would fall after the scheduled court conference.

The case has become a test of the balance between Liberia’s branches of government. Critics have likened it to the recent standoff over former Speaker Fonati Koffa, which tested the limits of legislative authority. Prominent lawyer Tiawan Saye Gongloe has said the Court’s options include voiding the expulsion, holding House leaders in contempt, or ordering Kolubah’s reinstatement pending a hearing that satisfies due process.

The Court did not say when it would rule.

World.title: Liberia: PLP Elevates Zarwolo to Two Top Posts as Party Eyes New Political Framework With Bility’s CMC
World.content:
MONROVIA, Liberia — The People’s Liberation Party (PLP) has appointed education policy expert Tonzeah N. Zarwolo to two senior leadership positions, a move that could position him to help shape the party’s policy direction as it explores political collaboration with Musa Hassan Bility’s Citizens Movement for Change (CMC).

Zarwolo, a former PLP National Youth Chairman, has been named National Vice Chairman for Political Affairs and Acting National Secretary General, according to two appointment letters dated October 22, 2026.

The appointments come as the PLP engages in discussions with Bility’s CMC about a possible political collaboration intended to offer an alternative to the country’s established political blocs, the Coalition for Democratic Change (CDC) and the ruling Unity Party (UP).

While neither appointment letter explicitly links Zarwolo’s elevation to the discussions, his combination of political, administrative and education policy experience could make him a significant figure in developing the principles and policy priorities of any proposed arrangement.

A Possible Role in Policy Development

Zarwolo’s professional background could be particularly relevant if the proposed collaboration moves beyond political consultations toward developing a formal policy document.

An education policy expert, he has worked on national education projects involving the United States Agency for International Development (USAID) and CODE Canada. He is also a university lecturer.

That experience could provide a foundation for contributing to discussions on education reform, public-sector performance, institutional accountability and national development priorities.

Zarwolo’s appointment as National Vice Chairman for Political Affairs could place him in a position to coordinate discussions on behalf of the PLP, while his role as Acting National Secretary General could give him a hand in documenting decisions and coordinating the party’s internal processes.

However, there is no confirmation in the appointment letters that he has been assigned to lead or draft a policy document for the proposed collaboration.

The Search for a Different Political Arrangement

The PLP’s reported discussions with Bility’s CMC come amid wider efforts by Liberian opposition parties to determine how they might cooperate ahead of the 2029 general and presidential elections.

In September, the CMC withdrew from a proposed opposition coalition process convened by former President George Weah, arguing that the draft arrangement did not adequately reflect its objectives. The party has emphasized the need for cooperation built around a clear reform agenda rather than political unity alone.

That position underscores a central question for any alternative political framework: whether participating parties can agree not only on political cooperation but also on a defined program for governing and addressing Liberia’s challenges.

For the PLP and CMC, a formal arrangement could require decisions on policy priorities, accountability mechanisms, internal decision-making, the roles of participating parties and how commitments would be communicated to the public.

Zarwolo’s policy background could be relevant to that process, particularly if the parties seek to develop proposals grounded in sectoral experience and implementable public policy rather than a general declaration of political unity.

Zarwolo Accepts Both Appointments

Zarwolo thanked the Political Leader, Tapple Doe, Bernard Blue Benson, National Chairman, David Woods Beyan Sr. National Vice Chair for Administration and the wider PLP membership for the confidence placed in him.

“I hereby formally accept these appointments and assure the Party of my unwavering commitment to discharging my responsibilities with diligence and loyalty,” he said.

He pledged to work with the party’s leadership and fellow partisans to advance its collective vision and strengthen its ideals.

World.title: Liberia: Commerce Minister Designate Plan Meets a Market That Isn’t Waiting
World.content:
MONROVIA — Stephen M. Yekeson Jr. told senators Wednesday that he wants to be “judged by what is delivered.” His confirmation statement gives the Senate one promise it can test within 100 days, and many more it cannot.

By Rodney D Sieh

Appearing before the Senate Committee on Commerce and Industry, the acting Commerce and Industry Minister set out a vision to have Liberia “produce more of what Liberia consumes” by 2029. He pledged to protect consumers, enforce Liberian-only business sectors and cut the cost of moving goods “between the ship and the shop.”



His firmest commitment: within 100 days, the ministry will publish weekly prices for rice, fuel and cement in all 15 counties. Beyond that, the statement leans on verbs such as “work with,” “engage” and “address,” with few numbers, dates or budgets attached. Set against the problems now pressing on traders and households, the distance between promise and mechanism is where the scrutiny belongs.

A stronger dollar that isn’t reaching the market

Yekeson’s most striking admission was that prices have kept rising “in spite of a stronger Liberian Dollar.” The Liberian dollar was Africa’s best-performing currency in September, closing the month at about L$172 to US$1.

Small traders in Monrovia say the gains are not passed on. They report that some wholesalers still price stock at about L$190 to the dollar while the market rate sits near L$170, a gap of nearly 12 percent.

On October 6, Yekeson announced a five-point plan under which the ministry would work with the Central Bank to require supermarkets, wholesalers and retailers to post the bank’s daily exchange rate. That measure does not appear in his Senate statement. Instead, he cites a “reengineered” Price Analysis Department and a better-resourced Inspectorate. Whether the posting rule is still coming, and when, is a question the committee should put to him.

Fuel: a review, but no formula

Fuel is where the Senate already has its own findings. A Senate probe found that diesel rose from L$840 to L$1,235 a gallon between October 2024 and September 2026, a 47 percent increase. Gasoline climbed from L$775 to L$985 over the same period. The probe also found that Bea Mountain paid nothing on 16.4 million gallons of diesel.

The senator leading that inquiry proposed that the Liberia Petroleum Refining Company (LPRC) publish its full pricing formula every week. Yekeson’s statement moves in that direction but stops short. He promises to review pricing with the LPRC, and says regulated prices should be “transparent, rule-based and regularly reviewed,” reflecting verified import costs, duties, transport and a reasonable margin.

He does not commit to publishing that formula. His weekly price list would show what motorists pay at the pump, not how the figure was reached. He also names the LPRC, a petroleum body, as his partner in reviewing rice and cement pricing, a pairing he did not explain.

Rice: a global squeeze is coming

The next test may arrive before his 100 days are up. World rice prices are up about 67 percent on the year and hit a 26-month high in early October.

At home, the price of the staple was last fixed in March. After an emergency meeting with six major importers, the ministry announced that a 25kg bag would stay at US$14.00 wholesale and US$14.50 retail.

With import costs climbing, importers are likely to push for an increase. Yekeson’s formula of verified costs plus a reasonable margin may justify one. His weekly price list will then put any rise in public view, county by county. The Senate should ask him now whether US$14.50 can hold, and on what basis it would change.

An Inspectorate that barely registers

Yekeson promises inspectors will pursue “hoarding, collusion, false invoicing and short measures.” The ministry’s own figures suggest little enforcement capacity today.

At a budget hearing last week, he reported that the ministry had collected about US$4.12 million by September 30. Of that, inspectorate fees and fines brought in roughly US$48,700, about 1 percent. He acknowledged those collections could improve.

The pledge is also not new. In 2024, his predecessor Amin Modad rolled out a rebranded Inspectorate Division to keep vendors from selling rice above the government ceiling. The committee should ask how many inspectors the ministry has, how many cases it opened this year, and what money comes with “resourcing” them.

Small business: right diagnosis, no deadlines

On Liberian enterprise, Yekeson’s diagnosis matches what traders report. He has said that women make up 75 percent of traders reporting financial constraints.

His answers are sensible but undated:

* Procurement set-aside. The law already reserves a quarter of qualifying public procurement for Liberian-owned small businesses. He promises to publish compliance “agency by agency,” but gives no date.

* Credit. A credit guarantee programme will come “only with the requisite approvals and clear fiscal safeguards,” a signal that no money is yet set aside.

* Late payment. He will “engage” concessionaires and “report progress,” with no target for how quickly government and companies must pay.

* Business registration. Service centres exist in seven counties, with nationwide expansion planned for 2027. His “every county” pledge carries no date.

* Liberians-only sectors. He will enforce the reservation of rice and cement retail, fuel stations and sand supply through ownership checks. He did not say how many such businesses are now foreign-owned.

The 2029 goal to “produce more of what Liberia consumes” has no baseline or target. He has also warned that a stronger currency can cut what farmers and processors earn, a tension his import-substitution plan does not address.

Questions of record

Yekeson told senators he will disclose all relevant interests, comply with the Code of Conduct and recuse himself where conflicts arise. He did not say whether he still holds shares or roles in South Atlantic Capital Group or Panchariya Group West Africa, where he previously served as CFO and president, respectively.

His appointment has also revived older questions. Smart News Liberia reported that his name appeared in a 2013 Liberia Anti-Corruption Commission asset verification that raised questions about deposits totaling more than US$300,000. His statement did not address it.

What the Senate should hold him to

Yekeson’s statement is the work of someone who knows the market’s pressure points. The question for senators is whether they will confirm the diagnosis or demand the mechanisms.

Five commitments would turn the speech into a record that can be checked:

1. Weekly county-level prices for rice, fuel and cement, published by the 100-day mark.

2. A date for the rule requiring traders to post the Central Bank’s daily exchange rate.

3. Publication of the full fuel pricing formula alongside pump prices.

4. An agency-by-agency report on the 25 percent procurement set-aside, with a deadline.

5. Full disclosure of his remaining business interests before confirmation.

He has offered quarterly reports to the committee. If confirmed, the first should show progress on each.

World.title: Liberia: Economist Samuel Jackson Appeals to Court for Permission to Travel Abroad Amid Health Concerns
World.content:
Jackson (center), who is seeking court permission to travel abroad for medical treatment, remains barred from leaving Liberia. He was seen being assisted by two men at the courthouse.

MONROVIA — Liberian economist and political commentator Samuel Jackson has appealed to Criminal Court “A” Judge Onesimus Barwon for permission to travel abroad for specialized medical treatment, citing concerns about his deteriorating health as he faces charges in connection with the death of his wife.

By Victoria Wesseh

Jackson was seen struggling to walk on the grounds of the Temple of Justice in Monrovia on Thursday, October 22, prompting renewed attention to his reported health condition.



The economist is seeking medical leave to obtain treatment outside Liberia but remains barred from leaving the country as his legal proceedings continue.

Jackson is facing charges in connection with the March 2026 death of his wife, Ntombi Khumalo Jackson, a South African attorney who was found dead in their Monrovia home.

Jackson told authorities that he discovered his wife semi-conscious in their bedroom after returning home from a television talk show engagement.

Khumalo Jackson, who was born in Gauteng, South Africa, was the founder of NK Attorneys. Her death attracted widespread public attention, particularly after images allegedly showing bruises and other injuries on her body circulated on social media.

Reports indicated that she suffered severe head injuries and required emergency brain surgery.

The circumstances surrounding her death have since become the subject of legal proceedings involving her husband.

Jackson’s request for permission to travel abroad for medical treatment now presents the court with a matter requiring consideration alongside the conditions imposed on him as the case proceeds.

The court’s decision on his request was not immediately available.

World.title: Liberia: War Victims, Survivors Protest at Court Office, Capitol as House Chairman Pledges to Put Court Bill Before Plenary Tuesday
World.content:
Some of the protesters at the war crimes court office. Credit: Anthony Stephens/New Narratives.

Hundreds of war victims, survivors and justice advocates protested at the war crimes court office and the Capitol Building, demanding approval of legislation to establish the long-awaited court.

A disagreement erupted at the Capitol after a lawmaker said a legislative committee had decided to exclude economic crimes from the proposed court. Protesters objected, prompting another lawmaker to assure them that both categories of crimes would be covered.

The House Committee Chairman pledged to bring the matter before plenary Tuesday, as the government’s timetable for establishing the courts faces uncertainty.

By Anthony Stephens, senior justice correspondent with New Narratives

Hundreds of victims and survivors of Liberia’s civil wars, joined by justice advocates, protested Thursday outside the government office overseeing the establishment of a war crimes court, temporarily disrupting operations, before moving to the Capitol Building, where a senior lawmaker pledged to place the long-delayed legislation before the House plenary on Tuesday.

The peaceful demonstrations drew people with disabilities, rural women, elderly victims and survivors, young people, and traditional and religious leaders. For hours, protesters gathered outside the Office for the Establishment of the War and Economic Crimes Court, holding placards demanding justice. One read: “REAL PEACE IS NOT THE SILENCE OF GUNS. REAL PEACE IS DISPENSING JUSTICE AND ENDING IMPUNITY. WE CALL ON THE EXECUTIVE AND LEGISLATURE TO GIVE THE PEOPLE JUSTICE & ACCOUNTABILITY NOW…”



“What’s going on wrong? We are suffering,” said Korpo Dennis, president of the Women in Peacebuilding Network, her voice cracking as she broke down in tears, burying her face in her lappa, a traditional cloth wrapped around her waist. Addressing Jallah Barbu, the office’s executive director, Dennis questioned why President Joseph Boakai had not raised the issue at the United Nations General Assembly, as she said he had promised. “He na come, we can hear nothing. We want answer today or else, we will sleep on this street.”

The protests underscored mounting frustration over Liberia’s failure to establish a court to prosecute atrocities committed during its civil wars, more than two decades after the fighting ended. Despite repeated government commitments and consultations, competing bills remain before lawmakers, leaving uncertain when those accused of wartime crimes will face prosecution.

Dennis’s organization was among the women’s peace groups widely credited with helping pressure Liberia’s warring factions to end the conflicts.

Barbu told protesters he remained confident that Boakai had not abandoned his commitment to establishing the court. Prevented from entering his office, along with other staff, he unsuccessfully attempted to reach House Speaker Richard Koon by telephone.

He then contacted James Verdier, the speaker’s chief of staff, who assured protesters that the legislation would be approved. Unsatisfied, the protesters moved to Capitol Hill to press lawmakers directly.

Kula Fofana, Boakai’s press secretary, did not respond to a request for comment on the protesters’ concerns.

“It has taken us too long,” said Jeremiah D. Cooper, a member of the Group of 77, an organization representing people with disabilities. “The same Liberian people who voted for you are the same Liberian people demanding that you pass certain documents in the interest of the country,” he added. “You people say you will not do it. Why?”

Jeremiah D. Cooper, one of the protesters.

But the gathering soon exposed a disagreement over whether the proposed court would prosecute both war crimes and economic crimes.

Prescilla A. Cooper, a Montserrado County representative and member of the House Committee on Claims and Petitions, told protesters that a joint legislative committee tasked with harmonizing the competing bills had agreed to proceed with legislation establishing a war crimes court, leaving economic crimes to be handled separately by the Liberia Anti-Corruption Commission.

The protesters rejected her account, insisting that economic crimes allegedly committed during Liberia’s civil wars must also fall within the proposed court’s jurisdiction.

Justice advocates have long argued that including economic crimes would allow the court to order convicted warlords and other perpetrators, including institutions found responsible, to pay restitution to victims and communities harmed by their actions.

Prince Toles, chairman of the House Committee on Claims and Petitions, sought to reassure the protesters, saying he shared their position that the legislation should establish a War and Economic Crimes Court.

“We signed it in 2024 (the joint resolution). We signed it 5G. But this one, we will give it 20G,” Toles said, referring to the Legislature’s earlier support for establishing the court. “If people did not rob the system, all of us would have lived better. I want to tell you that we are with you.”

“We will bring this matter before plenary,” Toles said. “But if they ask us to bring a paper signed by the different stakeholders, I will just propose that you draft something for us temporarily. Bring it here tomorrow (Friday), then I will put it on the floor on Tuesday.”

Plenary, the full membership of either legislative chamber, is its highest decision-making body. Toles’s pledge does not guarantee a vote or passage Tuesday.

House leaders subsequently invited protest organizers to a meeting.

“We feel a little bit relieved that it will work,” Peterson Sonyah, executive director of the Liberia Massacre Survivors Association, said by phone afterward. “We are impressed with the discussion. We are planning to be there on Tuesday.”

The protests came as Liberia approaches a deadline in its plans to establish the courts.

Under a 36-page roadmap submitted to Boakai in July 2025 , the court office projected that the National Anti-Corruption Court would be operational by November 2026, followed by the War and Economic Crimes Court in November 2027.

With neither court’s establishing legislation approved, the timetable faces uncertainty. The roadmap also envisaged completing trials by 2031, after which the war crimes court would transition to a residual mechanism.

Liberia is also preparing to assume the rotating presidency of the United Nations Security Council in December, a moment justice advocates say will draw international attention to the country’s unfinished accountability efforts.

A FrontPage Africa/New Narratives survey of 1,150 people across 11 counties found that 91 percent supported establishing the court, while 89 percent said they would not vote for lawmakers opposing it.

The survey was not scientifically sampled. Only 4 percent of respondents reported awareness of lawmakers’ consultations on the proposed court.

The legislative process has been complicated by six competing proposals.

They include a War Crimes Court bill from the Liberian National Bar Association ; a separate proposal from civil society organizations working with the Independent National Commission on Human Rights ; and two bills introduced by Senate President Pro Tempore Nyonblee Karnga-Lawrence and Senator Joseph Jallah , one proposing a War Crimes Court and another a Special Economic and Corruption Crimes Court.

The remaining two bills were prepared by the court office , proposing a War and Economic Crimes Court and a separate National Anti-Corruption Court. Boakai subsequently forwarded both proposals to the Legislature .

The senators’ proposals drew criticism from justice advocates , who warned that provisions concerning jurisdiction and appeals could weaken wartime accountability.

In June, more than 40 House members attended a two-day technical deliberation in Buchanan, Grand Bassa County , organized by the court office and its partners to examine the legislation.

Separately, the Senate Committee on Judiciary, Human Rights, Claims and Petitions began consultations on the competing bills , seeking to resolve differences over senior appointments, prosecutorial independence and appeals.

The committee also outlined plans to harmonize the proposals , with further consultations and hearings expected before the legislative session ended.

Neither chamber approved the legislation before lawmakers departed for their constituency break.

The Legislature was scheduled to return October 9, but a dispute over lawmakers’ benefits delayed the House’s reopening. Regular business resumed October 13.

For Sonyah and the other organizers, Tuesday will test the assurances they received. They intend to return to the Capitol to see whether the matter reaches plenary — and whether the proposed legislation retains both war crimes and economic crimes.

This story was a collaboration with New Narratives as part of the Investigating Liberia project. Funding was provided by the U.N. Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights and the European Union. The funders had no say in the story’s content.

World.title: FAZ hails Arrows CAF group stage qualification
World.content:
The Football Association of Zambia (FAZ) has hailed Red Arrows for qualifying to the group stage of the CAF Confederation Cup after eliminating Kaizer Chiefs.

Red Arrows won the first leg 1-0 in Ndola but lost 1-0 in the return leg in South Africa on Friday night before securing a 3-2 victory on penalties to advance.

FAZ President Keith Mweemba said the qualification is an important step for Zambian club football as the country seeks to regain its standing in continental competitions.

“On behalf of my executive and the entire football family, I wish to congratulate Red Arrows on this achievement. Qualifying for the group stage is a proud moment for the club and Zambian football,” Mweemba said.

He said Zambia needs to build on this progress to regain the two additional slots lost during the 2022/2023 season.

“Our ambition must be to see Zambian clubs competing consistently at this level and restoring the country’s representation to four slots,” Mweemba said.

Mweemba urged Red Arrows management and sponsors to provide necessary support for adequate preparations ahead of the group stage and assured the club of FAZ’s support.

World.title: Zambia At 62: Hichilema Honours Founding Heroes, Charts Path To Accelerated Growth
World.content:
Zambia celebrates 62 years of independence today, with President Hakainde Hichilema honouring the heroes who won the nation’s freedom and setting out a future built on accelerated growth under the Grow Zambia Agenda.

In his message on the eve of the anniversary, the Head of State paid tribute to the men and women who lifted the national flag on 24 October 1964, when Zambia secured what he called the sovereign right to define its own destiny.

“Tomorrow marks 62 years since our forefathers and mothers lifted our national flag, with pride and determination,” President Hichilema said.

He honoured Kenneth David Kaunda, Harry Mwaanga Nkumbula, Simon Mwansa Kapwepwe, Alexander Grey Zulu, Humphrey Mulemba, Nalumino Mundia, Mama Julia Chikamoneka and Mama Betty Chilombo Chilunga, among others, for their courage and sacrifice.

This year’s celebrations run under the theme “Zambia at 62: Our journey, our growth, our future.” Reflecting on that journey, Mr Hichilema said the nation has walked the path of peace, unity, stability and progress under its motto, One Zambia, One Nation, One People, building schools, hospitals, roads, airports and power stations.

“We have held elections and seen smooth transitions of leadership. Through every challenge, the spirit of One Zambia, One Nation, One People, has kept us united,” he said.

Turning to the nation’s growth, the President celebrated Zambians as a smart, hard-working people. He singled out the resilience of farmers, the hard work of miners, the creativity of youth, the courage of the armed forces, the resourcefulness of women and the tenacity of entrepreneurs.

Young people drew his warmest praise. He recalled that they fought for the nation’s independence and its democracy.

“Today, they are the backbone of our economy, our innovators and our leaders,” President Hichilema said.

His ultimate focus, he said, is the future. The Grow Zambia Agenda is designed to move the economy from stabilisation to accelerated growth.

“We want to produce more maize, more wheat and more copper,” the Head of State said. The country, he added, is generating more electricity, attracting more tourists and facilitating more exports, all while safeguarding the vulnerable and building strong institutions.

He also called on citizens to protect Zambia’s abundant natural resources and use them sustainably for present and future generations.

Unity ran through the entire message. “We are a family made up of unique cultures from all corners of our country, but united as one country. When we face challenges, we do not break. We come together,” Mr Hichilema said.

“We stood tall through every storm,” he added, urging Zambians to look to the future with confidence and to recommit themselves to hard and smart work, discipline, integrity and service.

He closed by calling on the nation to celebrate the 62nd anniversary with joy and unity, in peace and responsibly.

The anniversary also returns attention to a chapter of the national story that reaches well beyond Zambia’s borders, one President Hichilema addressed in separate remarks months ago.

At the time, speaking out against xenophobic attacks in South Africa, Mr Hichilema expressed concern that South Africans would turn against Zambians and others who had stood with them during the liberation struggle.

“We fought with South Africans. We put our lives on the chopping board,” he said then.

“Some of our military people died, civilians died, together with South Africans. Why should we separate ourselves now, now that you have the freedom?”

He described the question as homework that South Africans must mark, and mark properly.

The history behind those words is deep. Zambia is often described as the cradle of Southern African liberation movements, and the record behind that title is one of sanctuary offered, attacks endured and an economy placed under strain for the freedom of others.

When Kaunda became Zambia’s first President in 1964, much of Southern Africa remained under white minority rule. South Africa was under apartheid. Zimbabwe, then Rhodesia, was governed by a white minority regime, while Namibia remained under South African control.

Kaunda believed Zambia’s freedom was bound to that of its neighbours. Rather than settle into the comfort of its own independence, the young nation opened its doors to the movements fighting for theirs.

The African National Congress (ANC) established its main headquarters in exile in Lusaka under Oliver Tambo. From the capital, the movement directed its campaign against apartheid for years.

Zimbabwe’s two main liberation movements, ZAPU and ZANU, also operated from Zambian soil, both fighting to end white minority rule in Rhodesia. SWAPO, the movement fighting for Namibia’s independence from South African rule, found a base in the country too.

Zambia gave these movements refuge, political space and support. It paid heavily for that choice.

The governments they were fighting began launching military attacks inside Zambian territory. On 19 October 1978, Rhodesian forces launched Operation Gatling, an offensive aimed at Zimbabwean liberation camps at Chikumbi near Lusaka and at Mkushi.

Hundreds were killed in the raids, among them women and children. The exact death toll remains disputed to this day.

The assaults did not end there. In April 1979, Rhodesian commandos raided the Lusaka residence of Zimbabwean liberation leader Joshua Nkomo, bringing the war to the heart of the capital.

Zambia’s transport infrastructure also came under attack, disrupting trade and placing the economy under pressure. The timing could hardly have been worse for a landlocked state whose copper exports depended heavily on routes running through Rhodesia and South Africa, the very regimes its guests were fighting.

Kaunda held his course. He continued to support the liberation movements while pursuing diplomatic solutions to the conflicts pressing on Zambia’s borders.

Over the decades that followed, the region was transformed. Zimbabwe won its independence in 1980 and Namibia followed in 1990. In 1994, South Africa held its first democratic national elections, closing the chapter of apartheid that the ANC had fought from its Lusaka headquarters.

Zambia was one of several African countries that helped sustain those struggles. Its contribution, however, went well beyond political speeches. It provided sanctuary, resources and support even while absorbing military attacks and economic pressure.

That record gave weight to President Hichilema’s earlier challenge. When he spoke of Zambian lives placed on the chopping board, the history pointed to the camps at Chikumbi and Mkushi, a raided home in Lusaka and trade routes cut by hostile neighbours.

It also carries a warning for the present: to remain alert to people and outside influences seeking to divide Africans. Division was a tool used during colonial rule to weaken African societies, while cooperation across borders became one of the foundations of the struggle that eventually freed Zimbabwe, Namibia and South Africa.

Zambians celebrate Independence Day today with that legacy in full view. The freedom many Southern African nations now enjoy was built in part on the sanctuary Lusaka once gave.

Red Arrows have qualified for the group stage of the CAF Confederation Cup after beating South African giants Kaizer Chiefs on penalties.

World.title: Lavushimanda DEBS cites career guidance gap
World.content:
Lavushimanda District Education Board Secretary (DEBS) Beatus Nshenda has observed that most learners from rural schools end up choosing wrong careers because of lack of exposure to other professions.

Mr Nshenda says the limitation in career choices by most school leavers is because they chose to become like the people they interact within their localities.

He was speaking today when he addressed learners during the first career’s Day for Mununga Day Secondary School held at the school.

“Some of you don’t even know what you want to become when you complete school because you are not exposed to other professions,” he said.

And Mr Nshenda said Careers Day in schools is an important event that gives learners exposure to diverse professionals.

He says careers day also connects classroom learning to real world jobs and inspires learners to early career planning.

The DEBS further said the purpose of careers day is to help learners understand the different career opportunities so that they make proper choices in future and avoid ending up in wrong careers where they may be frustrated.

He added that education is the foundation of every opportunity one can get in life, adding that learners must put education first even if they may want to become farmers or entrepreneurs.

Mr Nshenda encouraged learners to take education seriously, set clear goals and choose careers according to their interest.

And Mununga Day Secondary School Head Boy Chipo Kunda said he is grateful to the school authorities for organising a careers’ day.

He said the event has given learners a clear picture of different professions.

“We are grateful for this day because we have learnt a lot from professionals from different departments,” he said.

Another grade 11 pupil, Kezia Wingabile said her dream of becoming a lawyer will be achieved as she has insight of what it takes to study law.

“Some of us will come back and show you that we have achieved what we learnt at this careers day,” she said.

And Evance Kolala, another grade 11 pupil said the careers day has opened his mind and made him understand what he will become in future.

“I want to be a police officer and I have learnt what it takes and what I should have in order to become one,” he said.

The Mununga Day Secondary school first ever careers day saw people from various government departments such as Agriculture, Health, Information, the judiciary, engineers from the local authority and others giving career talks to the learners.

Other people who spoke to the learners at the event were from the Tanzania Zambia Railway Authority (TAZARA) and the Tanzania, Zambia Mafuta (TAZAMA) as well as engineers.

World.title: Mukubesa calls for child-focused growth
World.content:
Ministry of Finance and National Planning Permanent Secretary for Budget and Economic Affairs Mwaka Mukubesa says Zambia’s Grow Zambia Agenda must translate economic growth into improved living conditions for vulnerable citizens, particularly children.

Mrs Mukubesa said economic growth would only be meaningful if its benefits reached all citizens and improved access to essential services such as education, healthcare and nutrition.

She was speaking today at Kabwata Orphanage and Transit Centre in Lusaka when she handed over donated foodstuffs, bedding and other essential supplies to support children at the institution ahead of Zambia’s 62nd Independence anniversary.

Mrs Mukubesa said the donation was in line with this year’s Independence theme, “Zambia @62 Our Journey, Our Growth, Our Future,” which calls for reflection on the country’s development journey and a renewed commitment to an inclusive and prosperous future.

She said the government’s Grow Zambia Agenda, which seeks to accelerate economic growth, unlock productive potential and create employment opportunities, should ensure that vulnerable groups are not left behind.

Mrs Mukubesa stressed that investing in children’s welfare, education, healthcare, nutrition and protection was essential to building the country’s human capital and securing its future prosperity.

“The children we nurture today are the citizens, innovators, entrepreneurs and leaders who will shape our country tomorrow,” she said.

She said the donated items were intended to provide practical assistance to the centre and improve the comfort and well-being of the children under its care.

Mrs Mukubesa added that, beyond material assistance, children needed access to quality education, adequate nutrition, healthcare and psychosocial support to enable them to develop their abilities and reach their full potential.

She said the Ministry remained committed to supporting responsible financial planning and the allocation of public resources towards policies and programmes that addressed the needs of vulnerable populations.

Mrs Mukubesa has urged Zambians to work together in building a prosperous nation where every child had an equal opportunity to learn, develop and contribute to national development, regardless of their circumstances.

Meanwhile, Ministry Director of Economic, Human Resource and Administration, Nalituba Mwale said every child deserved an opportunity to develop their potential and contribute meaningfully to the country’s future.

Mrs Mwale said independence is not only about celebrating the country’s freedom but also reflecting on the collective responsibility to ensure that every child had an opportunity to succeed.

She urged communities to work together to protect children, nurture their abilities and create a future where no child felt forgotten or left behind.

Mrs Mwale encouraged the children at the institution to remain hopeful, continue learning and pursue their dreams despite the challenges they might face.

She also commended caregivers for their dedication to supporting vulnerable children and urged them to continue with their work of providing care and guidance.

And Founder and Director of Kabwata Orphanage and Transit Centre, Angela Miyanda, has urged the Permanent Secretary to present issues affecting children at the institution that may require assistance.

Mrs Miyanda said the occasion was significant as the country prepares to celebrate its independence tomorrow.

Mrs Miyanda said Independence Day serves as a reminder of the importance of peace, noting that some of the children at the centre are refugees.

She said the presence of refugee children at the institution highlights the importance of appreciating the peace Zambia enjoys.

World.title: Veep welcomes President Hichilema’s Vice-Chairpersonship to COMESA
World.content:
Vice President Mutale Nalumango says President Hakainde Hichilema’s election to the Vice-Chairpersonship of the Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa (COMESA) will support the country’s vision for the grow Zambia agenda.

Mrs Nalumango says the Grow Zambia Agenda is an export-based programme, and COMESA provides an important platform for Zambia to advance its agenda, as trade requires working with other nations.

She added that COMESA also plays a role in advancing the African Continental Free Trade Area, Therefore, taking a leading role in the organisation is a positive development.

Speaking during the Vice President’s question time in Parliament, Mrs Nalumango noted that COMESA is an opportunity for Zambia to benefit from the vast market represented by member countries.

“His vision and recognition for his economic acumen should be appreciated. His leadership will help strengthen COMESA by bringing to the table the kind of leadership that is needed,” she noted.

Meanwhile, she further stated that providing land for COMESA is also very important because it will facilitate the development of infrastructure, indicating that under the Grow Zambia Agenda, this includes energy trading, interconnectivity and other infrastructure needed to support economic growth.

“We need leadership that can bring member states together and encourage them to work towards linking our regions through improved infrastructure,” she said.

And Mrs Nalumango says the maize export market is open, indicating that exports are already permitted within the existing arrangements.

She explained that arrangements are already in place for maize exports to countries such as Kenya and the Democratic Republic of the Congo, which have placed orders, while the government is considering Malawi as another market.

The Vice President has clarified that there is no load shedding in the country, but that the power interruptions being experienced in parts of Lusaka are due to ZESCO scheduled maintenance and other works.

Mrs Nalumango explained that the work being undertaken goes beyond routine maintenance, indicating that substantial investment and work are required to expand and improve the country’s electricity network.

“There are areas where people are experiencing interruptions to their electricity supply, but these interruptions are not necessarily the result of load shedding,” she said.

She highlighted Zambia’s long-term objective to achieve wider electricity coverage by around 2030 or 2031, saying that it requires considerable work on transmission lines and distribution networks, thereby resulting in temporary disruptions to electricity supply.

World.title: Lions club donates wheelchairs, supplies to UTH
World.content:
The Lions Club of Sunningdale has donated 10 wheelchairs, kitchenware and associated cleaning products at University Teaching Adult Hospital (UTH) Emergency Ward.

Speaking at the handover, UTH Senior Medical Superintendent, Charles Mbewe welcomed the Club’s gesture expressing that it will improve access to emergency care by providing mobility to patients that are unable to move.

Dr Mbewe said the donation demonstrates the vital role that service organisations play in supporting and complementing government efforts to enhance healthcare delivery.

“We are particularly encouraged by the Lions Club’s commitment to serving communities and supporting those in need,” he said.

Dr Mbewe further pledged to put the donations to good use by meeting the needs of patients who depend on the services offered at the emergency department.

Meanwhile, Lions Club President, Jonathan Maliki stated that the club responded to the needs of the hospital as it understands that a wheelchair can make a difference.

“From our visits we have observed a serious shortage of equipment and supplies and decided to extend this gesture,” he said.

Mr Maliki stated that the donation will make a difference because without enough functional wheelchairs, patient’s lives are endangered.

World.title: Government urges Local Leaders to Drive Grow Zambia Agenda
World.content:
Government has urged Mayors, Council Chairpersons and Councillors across the country to take an active role in spearheading development projects and advancing the Grow Zambia Agenda.

Cabinet Office Permanent Secretary for Special Duties, Wisdom Bwalya says civic leaders should prioritise development and avoid unnecessary conflicts that may hinder progress in their respective districts.

Mr Bwalya said this in Chongwe district when he officially closed a five-day training workshop for a cohort of newly elected civic leaders at Chalimbana Local Government Institute.

He also presented certificates to participants, who included Mayors, Council Chairpersons, Councillors and traditional leaders.

He emphasised that all leaders serving in councils, regardless of how they were appointed or elected, had a common responsibility of promoting development and should therefore be treated equally.

The PS urged the civic leaders to embrace one another and work collectively towards addressing the needs of the people in their respective communities.

He also acknowledged the important role traditional leaders play in resolving conflicts and supporting local development initiatives.

Meanwhile, Chalimbana Local Government Institute Principal James Paipi said the training was designed to equip the newly elected civic leaders with the knowledge and skills required to effectively discharge their responsibilities.

Mr Paipi said the training had brought together various categories of councillors, including those elected from wards, traditional leaders and representatives appointed through the mixed-member proportional representation system.

And Chongwe Mayor Frederick Saashi said the participants would apply the knowledge acquired during the training to improve the performance of their respective local authorities.

Mr Sashi described the training as an eye-opener that had enhanced the participants’ understanding of their civic responsibilities.

The Mayor assured that the participants would return to their respective districts with valuable knowledge to support effective service delivery and local development.
