World.title: Yogurt shop murders fuel family questions about accomplice as rage lingers over wrongfully accused
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Nearly 34 years after his 13-year-old sister died during the 1991 Austin, Texas, yogurt shop massacre, Shawn Ayers and his wife, Angie, have launched a national cold case effort while still seeking answers about the attack and whether an accomplice is out there.

Angie, along with Shawn, whose sister Amy was among four girls killed in the attack, have joined former prosecutors Mindy Montford and Anne Marie Schubert to establish the National Cold Case Center.

The decades-long search for answers in Amy’s case inspired the couple to help establish the nonprofit, which helps to fund unsolved homicide investigations, train investigators and support victims’ families.

FORENSIC GENEALOGY UNMASKS COLD CASE SUSPECT AS STRANGLER, SEXUAL PREDATOR DECADES LATER: OFFICIALS

"Due to what we've gone through and seen, not only from our own experience, but from listening to other families struggle throughout this process," Angie told Fox News Digital. "Years ago, we had wanted to start a nonprofit."

The Austin yogurt shop murders

Amy, Jennifer Harbison and Eliza Thomas, both 17, and Jennifer’s sister, Sarah Harbison, 15, died in the attack at the I Can’t Believe It’s Yogurt! shop on West Anderson Lane on Dec. 6, 1991.

On the night of the killings, Jennifer and Eliza were working the closing shift, while Sarah and Amy waited for them to finish so the four could head to a sleepover.

Shortly before midnight, authorities received a report of a fire at the shop. The blaze and water from the sprinklers altered the crime scene and diluted evidence, according to FBI files.

Inside, police discovered Sarah, Eliza and Jennifer stacked together in the shop’s storage room. They were stripped, gagged and bound with their own undergarments, and then shot in the back of the head with .22-caliber bullets.

Investigators found Amy in a separate area with a ligature around her neck and burns covering up to 30% of her body, according to court documents.

DNA FROM CHEWING GUM NAILS LONGTIME SEXUAL PREDATOR DECADES AFTER REIGN OF TERROR: REPORT

FBI records described two gunshot wounds: an initial .22-caliber shot that missed Amy’s brain and a second shot from a .380-caliber pistol through her cheek and jawline.

Investigators recovered a .380 cartridge casing in a floor drain. During the autopsy, officials recovered four .22-caliber bullets from the bodies.

Killer identified

The search for answers stretched across decades, combined with false confessions, arrests, convictions and appeals before DNA and ballistics evidence identified serial killer Robert Eugene Brashers in September 2025.

Brashers fatally shot himself during a January 1999 police standoff in Missouri, leaving the families no chance to confront him at a murder trial.

CALIFORNIA AUTHORITIES IDENTIFY FINAL UNKNOWN VICTIM OF ‘HAPPY FACE KILLER’ KEITH JESPERSON AFTER 34 YEARS

Authorities had previously connected him to other violent crimes, including killings in South Carolina and Missouri.

According to Austin police, Brashers used the same .380-caliber handgun in the yogurt shop murders to kill himself during the Missouri standoff.

For the Ayers family, identifying Brashers didn’t answer whether someone else participated in the yogurt shop killings. Angie questioned whether another perpetrator may have been involved, since two weapons were used during the attacks.

"I may be incorrect, but I don't think that I am," Angie told Fox News Digital. "There's never been an instance where he [Brashers] used both of those guns in his other cases."

DETECTIVES' TRUE CRIME PODCAST TAKES FRESH SHOT AT KILLER WHO VANISHED AFTER CAUGHT-ON-CAMERA MURDER

"There has been absolutely no definite answer on whether or not he was by himself, or had an accomplice.

"So, to us, we still don't have all the answers, and knowing that this case is still ongoing, I don't think anyone can say that they know exactly what happened because we can't ask."

Wrongful convictions

Years before identifying Brashers, Austin investigators focused on four local teens: Robert Springsteen, Michael Scott, Maurice Pierce and Forrest Welborn.

Austin police arrested all four in 1999. Springsteen and Scott confessed during police questioning but recanted before trial, saying investigators pressured them into giving false statements.

Travis County juries convicted Springsteen of capital murder in 2001 and Scott in 2002. Springsteen received a death sentence, while Scott received life in prison.

The Texas Court of Criminal Appeals overturned Springsteen’s conviction in 2006 and Scott’s in 2007.

DNA testing failed to match any of the men to the crime scene. A judge released Springsteen and Scott in June 2009, and prosecutors moved to dismiss the charges that October.

Pierce proclaimed innocence but implicated Welborn. In 1991, he wore a police wire and tried to coax Welborn into confessing. An Austin police officer reported that Welborn denied any involvement. Welborn later passed a polygraph test.

Welborn never went to trial. When two grand juries failed to indict him, authorities dropped the case against him in 2000.

By then, he had spent months behind bars.

"I’m still really upset and mad at them. If they didn’t confess to something they didn’t do, we wouldn’t be here right now doing this today," Welborn told Texas Monthly.

Austin police officers arrested Pierce in 1999 on capital murder charges. Prosecutors dismissed Pierce’s charges in 2003, citing insufficient evidence, after he spent more than three years in jail.

In 2010, an Austin police officer fatally shot Pierce in 2010 following a traffic stop. Pierce fled the scene on foot and stabbed an officer in the neck with a knife, prompting authorities to open fire.

Settlement

After investigators linked Brashers to the killings, Travis County Judge Dayna Blazey declared the four men innocent on Feb. 19, 2026. Months later, the Austin City Council approved a $35 million settlement covering the three surviving men and Pierce’s family.

Welborn initially rejected the city’s apology, saying that he lost an auto-repair business while incarcerated and endured years of public ostracism.

"Their apology is not accepted," he told Texas Monthly. "Their apology means nothing to me."

Welborn later said "it felt good" to have closure, although he wanted some of the detectives who worked the case "to go do some prison time."

None of the detectives have faced criminal charges in the case, Texas Monthly reported.

The Ayers couple said neither they nor the men or their relatives have contacted the other side.

"We haven't reached out and they have not reached out," Angie said.

Welborn could not immediately be reached for comment.

The Austin Police Department and Travis County District Attorney’s Office did not respond to requests for comment by publication.

Helping other families

Their experience seeking answers in Amy’s case, and hearing other families describe similar struggles, prompted Shawn and Angie to consider starting a nonprofit years ago.

FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X

"The frustrating part is being told no, but yet someone somewhere leaks the information and you're the last one to know when you should have been first and that is still happening today," Shawn told Fox News Digital, recalling his sister’s case.

Their partnership with Montford began in 2017, when they met with prosecutors about the yogurt shop killings. Montford, a Travis County assistant district attorney at the time, promised to stay with them.

"She made it a point to tell us that she was going to stick with us no matter what until the end," Angie said.

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS

Montford then connected with Schubert, a former California prosecutor who helped bring the Golden State Killer to justice. The Ayers couple met Schubert at a 2023 cold case conference in Marble Falls, Texas, where the idea for the nonprofit took shape.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FROM THE FOX TRUE CRIME HUB

Now, they want to help other families find that kind of support.

SEND US A TIP

"It is up and running now... to provide funding and training for law enforcement, to have tools that they need to investigate cold cases, to be able to collect and report accurate data on unsolved cases, and connect law enforcement agencies around the world, and to have peer to peer family support and communication," Angie added.

GOT A TIP?

"Right now, funding is a, for us is a big thing, so we can get the first cases up and running."

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

Shawn said they have spread awareness by attending cold case conferences in several states, including California, Florida, Missouri, and North Carolina.

GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL

For the couple, the work extends beyond families still waiting for answers. Solving those cases could also identify killers who remain free.

World.title: DOJ demands California counties help identify noncitizen voters
World.content:
The Department of Justice is warning local election officials in California to cooperate with the administration to identify noncitizens on a list of registered voters or face potential legal action, according to a letter obtained by NBC News.

The department sent letters Friday to 57 of California’s 58 counties in a move that signals an escalation in the Trump administration’s effort to prevent the state from counting ballots from voters the federal government identifies as likely noncitizens.

Los Angeles County received a similar letter last week.

NBC News obtained the letter sent to San Bernardino County Registrar of Voters Joani Finwall from the U.S. attorney’s office in Los Angeles. In it, First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bilal Essayli notes that his office is providing a list of 1,133 names of “likely aliens.”

“Within 48 hours, we ask that you commit to working with DOJ and DHS to identify who on the accompanying list is a citizen and who is not,” Essayli wrote. “I write to make unmistakably clear the legal implications of continuing to send vote-by-mail ballots to those people on the list or tabulating ballots cast by them until citizenship can be verified.”

For those whose citizenship status cannot be confirmed, Essayli asked the county to “immediately instruct the appropriate elections official to segregate — not cancel — those individuals’ vote-by-mail ballots until their citizenship status can be determined.”

“The legal consequences for either facilitating or ignoring federal crimes are significant. An alien voting in a federal election is a federal crime — and knowingly facilitating such conduct is equally unlawful,” Essayli wrote in the letter.

“The letters speak for themselves,” Essayli said in a statement to NBC News. “Any election official who knowingly processes the ballot of a noncitizen is opening themselves to legal jeopardy.”

The New York Times was the first to report the letters.

“Trump’s DOJ has not provided any evidence for their claims of massive voter fraud,” Sen. Alex Padilla, D-Calif., said in a statement late Friday. “They’ve admitted that the data they point to is inaccurate and unreliable. No matter how many lawsuits they file or how many election officials they threaten, they do not have the authority to interfere.”

The Trump administration has made the pursuit of noncitizen voters a priority in the run-up to the midterms and has singled out heavily Democratic California. The administration has sued to block the state from counting more than 20,000 mail-in ballots from voters it suspects are not U.S. citizens. On Thursday, it asked the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals to impose the restrictions before the lower court has ruled in the case.

World.title: How Starlink slowdown hit Ukraine’s front line soldiers pushing Russia back
World.content:
The drone unit he leads has been helping push back Russian troops on the front lines in southeastern Ukraine. Then, late last Tuesday, a drone launched toward Russian troops suddenly lost connection.

“As it was picking up speed, contact with the drone was lost in an instant,” according to the commander, 47, who is serving on the border between the eastern Donetsk and southern Zaporizhzhia regions, and only wanted to be identified by his call sign Flint due to the sensitivity of his service.

The drone fell to the ground, aborting the mission, Flint said in a series of messages on WhatsApp. He fears the technology inside “may have fallen into enemy hands.”

“Only after analyzing the flight, it became clear that the issue was specifically related to the Starlink speed limit,” he added.

Ukraine said last week that limits were imposed without warning on its use of Starshield, the military variant of the Starlink internet service run by Elon Musk’s SpaceX, affecting battlefield missions reliant on it.

President Donald Trump said Thursday that Musk had restored the service in Ukraine, but Kyiv said Friday that it was not seeing any lifting of restrictions. Trump did not say why the limits were in place, though Musk had previously said that “any limits on speed or usage are decided by the U.S. military and ultimately POTUS.” Ukraine had also warned of gaps in intelligence sharing from the U.S., something the White House has denied.

World.title: Vanessa Trump says she is ‘cancer-free’ six months after diagnosis
World.content:
Vanessa Trump, ex-wife of Donald Trump Jr., revealed Friday that she is cancer-free, after beginning treatment for breast cancer earlier this year.

“I am finally cancer-free,” Trump, 48, said in a video posted by her daughter, Kai Trump, who leaned over to hug her mother after she announced the news.

Kai Trump wrote in the caption of the video that they wanted to share her story in part to help raise awareness.

“October is Breast Cancer Awareness Month, a time to raise awareness about early detection, education, and support for those affected by breast cancer,” she wrote.

Vanessa Trump was married to the president’s oldest son from 2005 to 2018. They share five children, with Kai Trump, 19, being the oldest.

Kai Trump said she and her mother sat down with Dr. Nicole Saphier, a radiologist who has been a Fox News medical contributor, to discuss breast cancer prevention and early detection.

“When it comes to breast cancer, it’s not one size fits all. It feels different for everyone,” Saphier, who is President Donald Trump’s third nominee for surgeon general, said in the video.

Vanessa Trump on May 20 first shared that she had been diagnosed with breast cancer, though she said in Friday’s video that she had been diagnosed in April.

In her May post, Trump said she was working on a treatment plan with her medical team and had undergone a procedure earlier that week. In an update the following month, Trump shared that she had been recovering from surgery for the last four weeks and was expected to begin the second stage of treatment soon.

Breast cancer rates for women under 50 have increased faster than the rates for older women in recent years, prompting the recommended age for screening to drop from 50 down to 40. About 16% of women who are diagnosed with breast cancer are under 50, according to the American Cancer Society.

World.title: More candidates are using AI in political ads to get your vote
World.content:
South Carolina Lt. Gov. Pamela Evette appears distressed in a gloomy room as she undergoes a polygraph test that ends with the lie detector catching fire. Although the video clarifies that the “dramatizations” in this political ad are generated with artificial intelligence, some voters still asked her whether what they saw was real, Evette told Noticias Telemundo.

At first, Evette said she thought, “This is ridiculous, right? Like, nobody could possibly believe this?” Later, as she traveled the state during her campaign to become the Republican gubernatorial nominee — a race she lost in June to Attorney General Alan Wilson — she said she encountered voters who were confused about the video’s veracity.

“On the campaign trail, I would have people ask me, like, ‘Oh my gosh, did they really make you take a lie-detector test?’” Evette said. She then had to explain to them that it never happened and it was an AI-generated fake ad.

“So you almost think it’s a joke and you kind of laugh at it, until you realize that there is a group of people out there that can’t tell the difference,” she said, “and then start to question if what they’re saying may be true.”

Evette is not the only one whose image was manipulated in the lead-up to the midterm elections. The Wesleyan Media Project, a group of experts that tracks political propaganda in campaigns, identified at least 220 ads produced or enhanced with artificial intelligence by candidates or political action committees this election cycle. They cost just under $137 million.

It’s a significant leap in the use of this technology compared to 2024, when the investment in AI was less than $50,000 during the presidential election. As of May of this year, the money spent on these AI ads was already $20 million.

“We really saw the growth in AI ads over the summer,” Travis Ridout, a professor at Washington State University and one of the project directors, told Noticias Telemundo. “A lot of them were connected with closely fought primary races.”

The lieutenant governor of South Carolina saw two videos of herself generated with artificial intelligence, or deepfakes, but she also shared one that falsely depicted her opponent, Alan Wilson, rejecting a call from President Donald Trump. According to Evette, her campaign used artificial intelligence after the ads featuring her circulated. “But we said it, ‘This ad is AI-generated,’” she said.

The videos targeting Evette are said to have been paid for by a PAC; the one released against her opponent was funded by the lieutenant governor’s campaign. A request for comment sent to Wilson was not immediately returned.

In response to a query from Noticias Telemundo on social media, nearly 40 people said they had seen political ads generated with artificial intelligence. Some admitted that they have difficulty distinguishing them.

“And that could be deceptive; voters could be basing their decisions on falsehoods in that case,” Ridout said. “That’s, I think, what’s most concerning from a democratic perspective.”

In the absence of a federal law regulating them, the responsibility falls to local governments, said Ridout, who estimates that about 30 states have some type of rule or requirement regarding AI in political campaigns.

Of the 220 ads analyzed by the Wesleyan Media Project, only 27% revealed they used artificial intelligence tools.

The possibilities ‘are endless’

Candidates with smaller campaign budgets rely on artificial intelligence to compete with their rivals, Ridout suggested.

“I think it’s here to stay. I don’t know that it’s going to go away,” said Evette. Campaigns “are extremely expensive,” she noted, and AI reduces many recording and editing costs.

These tools could also “unlock” more creativity in political advertising, said Ridout, “which wouldn’t be the worst thing in the world.”

He said the possibilities are practically endless and include satire. Among the ads he analyzed, he saw candidates emerging from a swamp, boxing against Trump, or appearing alongside physicist Albert Einstein, who died in 1955.

“I do worry about the lasting impact of those images, even if people know that it might not be true,” Ridout said. He noted those images might stick in their mind when they’re voting, or it may even generate waves of misinformation that trigger violence.

AI can “redefine” modern political campaigns, the Brennan Center for Justice, a nonprofit institute whose experts have analyzed the potential impact of this technology on democracy, said in an article.

Mekela Panditharatne, legal adviser and director of the center’s Elections and Government Program, said that without disclosure, “generative AI use in political ads has the potential to distort perceptions of candidates, painting candidates in a flattering light or their opponents in a negative light.”

During the Minnesota primaries, a deepfake circulated showing Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan, the Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate, smiling amid mountains of money.

A spokesperson from her office said that although it didn’t stop them from winning the primary, there was alarm over the impact of the AI-generated video. “There is already too much distrust in our politics, and voters deserve to know what’s real and what’s not,” the spokesperson said.

Minnesota is one of the states with AI regulations; in 2023, its Legislature passed with bipartisan support a ban on its use to influence elections. The AI ad targeting Flanagan elicited debate over whether it was unlawful or whether it was protected under the First Amendment.

Artificial intelligence “should never be used to manipulate voters,” Flanagan’s spokesperson stated.

A matter of transparency

At least two federal bills to regulate AI in politics are pending discussion and approval by lawmakers.

One seeks to ensure that s have conspicuous notices that artificial intelligence tools have been used; the other attempts to prohibit this technology “to generate materially deceptive content falsely depicting federal candidates in political ads to influence federal elections.”

Although local regulations exist, some candidates still violate them, according to Panditharatne from the Brennan Center.

“I think those laws have not had as strong a deterrent effect as we would like,” she said, making a point for the need of a universal federal standard.

When designing any law, legislators take into account the First Amendment, which protects, among other rights, freedom of speech, religion and the press.

World.title: Disappointed primary voters weigh their choices: From the Politics Desk
World.content:
Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail.

In today’s edition, Ben Kamisar and Bridget Bowman have the key takeaways from our latest voter focus groups in Michigan and Texas. Plus, Kristen Welker dives into the downballot effects of this cycle’s key gubernatorial races.

— Adam Wollner

Focus groups: Their candidates lost in the Michigan and Texas primaries. Now what?

By Ben Kamisar and Bridget Bowman

Some voters who backed losing candidates in two key Senate primaries this year are still wrestling with whether to support their party’s nominee on Election Day, with major implications for who controls the Senate majority next year.

Michigan Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and Texas Republican Ken Paxton are both trying to stitch their parties back together for their battleground races after divisive primaries. Two focus groups — one with Michiganders who supported Democratic Rep. Haley Stevens’ unsuccessful Senate bid, and another with Texans who backed Republican Sen. John Cornyn in that primary — reveal how some rank-and-file voters are struggling to process personal concerns about the nominees alongside a desire to be loyal to their party.

The focus groups, produced by Syracuse University and the research firms Engagious and Sago and observed by NBC News, showed Cornyn voters who see Paxton as corrupt but are hesitant to hand Democrats a Senate seat. In Michigan, the Stevens voters worried about whether El-Sayed is too extreme — and some voiced concerns about his Muslim faith and his allegiances.

Both narratives echo how their general election opponents — former Rep. Mike Rogers, the Republican Senate nominee in Michigan, and state Rep. James Talarico, the Democratic Senate nominee in Texas — have sought to define them.

“I’m split down the middle. In this instance, I really feel that I am looking at the lesser of two evils and I’m not sure which that is,” said Kathleen S., a 62-year-old Republican from Comal County in Texas.

In these two 90-minute conversations, the Cornyn voters were more open to looking past ethical concerns about Paxton, the Texas attorney general.

The Stevens voters, meanwhile, included more political independents, and they were more hesitant to back El-Sayed, a former public health official in Michigan.

“In Michigan, I heard undecided Stevens voters growing nervous with El-Sayed, and in Texas I heard Cornyn voters abandoning their preferred candidate, Talarico, in order to put loyalty to the GOP first,” said Rich Thau, the president of Engagious, who moderated the groups. “These undecided voters truly contorted themselves as they struggled to justify a choice they feared they’d later regret.”

Read more →

Ramaswamy ad underscores how governor’s races could affect downballot contests

Analysis by Kristen Welker

The impact of Ohio Republican Vivek Ramaswamy’s controversial ad against Democratic opponent Amy Acton could be felt well beyond the governor’s race.

The ad features Acton’s estranged mother accusing her of lying. Acton has said that she has not spoken to her mother in decades and that she was sexually abused by her mother’s husband when she was a child.

But while Ramaswamy and some of his allies defend the spot, the flood of other Republicans condemning it — including Sen. Jon Husted, who is on the November ballot as well — emphasizes how the controversy could have a ripple effect downballot. One GOP strategist told me there are concerns within the party that the ad could turn off critical women voters in Husted’s race and multiple competitive House districts in the state.

Ohio isn’t the only state where the top-of-the-ticket contests could shift the dynamics in races farther down the ballot.

Pennsylvania has at least four battleground House races this year, and Democratic candidates could get a boost from Gov. Josh Shapiro as he runs for re-election. Shapiro’s contest against Republican Stacy Garrity is not expected to be very competitive, even in the perennial swing state, given his high approval ratings. But he’s been focusing intently on boosting downballot candidates, cutting ads and hitting the campaign trail. Starting tomorrow, Shapiro is going on a 10-day bus tour across the state.

Former Democratic Gov. Roy Cooper appears to be pulling away from Republican Michael Whatley in the North Carolina Senate race, which could help Democrats hold the state’s uber-competitive 1st District, and maybe even flip the redder 11th District.

It’s a similar case in Arizona, where Democrats hope a strong showing by Gov. Katie Hobbs can help them in the 1st and 6th districts, both perennial battlegrounds, and in their push to defeat Rep. Eli Crane in a district Donald Trump won by about 15 points in 2024.

In Iowa, where Democratic Senate and gubernatorial candidates are running strong, Republicans have already retreated from the 1st District. In the 3rd District, Republican Rep. Zach Nunn is running a new ad aimed squarely at winning over Democrats. And Democrats are flooding millions of dollars into the 2nd District, which Trump won by 10 points in 2024.

The fiercely competitive Texas gubernatorial and Senate races, as well as the closer-than-expected Florida governor’s race, have significant downballot implications in two states Republicans made central to their redistricting push.

Republicans have shifted resources away from their bid to defeat Rep. Henry Cuellar, while Democrats are eyeing the redrawn 15th and 35th districts, both of which Trump won by double digits in 2024. And both sides have been pouring money into the seats Florida Republicans redrew to their benefit.

Republicans have a few top-of-the ticket dynamics breaking their way, too. They’re hopeful New Hampshire Gov. Kelly Ayotte’s strong campaign can help former Republican Sen. John Sununu in his Senate race. And in Georgia, the tens of millions of dollars Republican Rick Jackson has poured into his campaign for governor could be felt in other races on the state’s ballot.

Races for Senate and governor could also have down-ticket effects in Michigan, where multiple House races are in play.

We’ll dive into the latest in those Michigan contests on “Meet the Press” this Sunday, with exclusive interviews with Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers and Democratic Gov. Gretchen Whitmer. Sen. Adam Schiff, D-Calif., and our chief data analyst Steve Kornacki will also join me.

World.title: Ukraine says Starlink speed restored after long disruption
World.content:
Ukraine's military has regained full use of Starlink satellite links for its drones and other fast-moving equipment, the defense minister said Saturday, ending speed restrictions that Ukrainian officials said had disrupted front-line operations for more than a week.

The Defense Ministry's monitoring systems in Ukraine reported stable connections on objects traveling faster than 250 mph, Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara told reporters.

The limitations placed on Starshield - SpaceX's military-grade version of the Starlink satellite internet service and the backbone of Ukraine's drone operations and communication - last week alarmed the country's military and government officials, with commanders reporting lost drones and disrupted missions.

President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy awaits the arrival of Prime Minister of Finland Petteri Orpo outside the Mariinskyi Palace, Kyiv, Ukraine, October 22, 2026. Ukrinform/NurPhoto via Getty Images

The restoration comes as U.S. envoys launched a new push to end the war. Russia agreed Wednesday to resume three-way negotiations with Washington and Kyiv next month. On Friday, Kyiv and Moscow also agreed to a localized ceasefire brokered by first lady Melania Trump around Oleshky, a war-ravaged, Russian-occupied town in Ukraine's southern Kherson region.

The episode added to tensions between Kyiv and Washington, a relationship already strained by President Donald Trump's reported deal with Moscow on Russian diesel imports, which Ukraine viewed as a betrayal.

Khmara credited "direct dialogue" and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's diplomacy with Washington, adding that the outcome mattered most "for our front, for the military, the work of drones, logistics and communications."

Zelenskyy on Friday said Ukraine was still experiencing Starlink and Starshield speed limits.

Questions have persisted since last week about who ordered the interruptions to the Elon Musk-made satellite internet system that Ukraine has relied on for years to counter Moscow's attacks.

Trump has maintained that he didn't make the call, while also saying Musk should not be blamed, but on Tuesday CBS News reported the CEO of SpaceX was behind the disruption.

World.title: Paris museums close, shops build barricades ahead of more protests
World.content:
Major museums in Paris closed and authorities deployed a sizable police force for a round of new protests Saturday across France, hoping to prevent a repeat of last week's violent unrest that shocked the country.

France's Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said as many as 70,000 officers will be deployed nationwide, along with helicopters, armored vehicles and water cannons.

A massive turnout is expected again after more than half a million took to the streets last week.

Shops on the Champs-Elysees are barricading themselves in ahead of the planned protests in Paris, France on October 23, 2026. Luc Auffret/Anadolu via Getty Images

Major museums including the Louvre, Orsay Museum, Picasso Museum and Grand Palais — where a Cézanne exhibit is on display — are closed Saturday. Art Basel, one of the world's most prestigious contemporary art fairs, opened to the public Friday, but only for the day, with the threat of unrest prompting organizers to cancel the weekend program.

The first-ever NFL game in France between the New Orleans Saints and the Pittsburgh Steelers remains scheduled for Paris on Sunday, but some associated venues have been shuttered. A pop-up NFL shop and the "NFL House," where the Super Bowl trophy is on display and community sessions and events were scheduled, were closed Saturday. A similar venue for the New Orleans Saints was also postponed until Sunday. Another NFL pop-up shop remains open in Saint-Denis, north of Paris, the league said. NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell said earlier this week that preparations for the game had been made in consultation with U.S. and French authorities.

Parisian shopkeepers have been barricading their stores all week. Near Place de la République in Paris, one of last weekend's hot spots, a bank branch and other businesses were boarded up with wooden panels to deter potential looters.

Some 3,000 shops across France were damaged or looted last weekend. The demonstrations first erupted last month when high school students in the southeast of Paris protested for better conditions, but quickly spread across the country as people took to the streets to demand relief from rising living costs.

Protesters march through central Paris amid fires, smoke, police deployments and clashes during nationwide demonstrations against the high cost of living, on October 17, 2026 in Paris, France. Firas Abdullah/Anadolu via Getty Images

Protest marches are scheduled in Paris and Marseille, but some other rallies, including in Lyon, Nice and Montpellier, have been banned by local authorities. Cities outside Paris were hit hard by the unrest. In Limoges, a suspected arson nearly destroyed the 19th-century city hall.

About 50 organizations have called for a protest against the far right on the sidelines of the two-day congress of Marine Le Pen's nationalist, anti-immigration party ahead of next spring's presidential election. About 50 organizations have called for a protest against the far right on the sidelines of the two-day congress of Marine Le Pen's nationalist, anti-immigration party ahead of next spring's presidential election. Organizers include labor unions, left-wing parties and student groups.

World.title: 1 arrested after fire at Hitler's Eagle's Nest mountain retreat
World.content:
A suspect has been detained in Germany following a fire at Adolf Hitler's mountain retreat, known as Eagle's Nest, German police said.

Authorities were alerted to a fire at the Nazi leader's mountain residence on the peak of Obersalzberg at approximately 9:15 p.m. local time on Friday, Upper Bavaria South police said in a statement.

The building, also known as Kehlsteinhaus, was "completely engulfed in flames" when firefighters arrived, police said, but no one was found inside and no injuries were reported.

Fire trucks had some difficulty accessing the site "due to the local conditions," authorities added.

Still from a webcam of the Kehlsteinhaus early on Oct. 24, 2026, after a large fire broke out in the southern German state of Bavaria. Berchtesgaden /AFP via Getty Images

"Shortly after the fire broke out, a suspect came into the focus of investigators," the statement said, adding that the cause of the fire is now under criminal investigation and one person was taken into custody.

At an elevation of 6,017 feet, Hitler's Eagle's Nest was completed in 1938 and occasionally used by the Nazi leader as a temporary seat of government. The site was spared from Allied bombing during World War II, largely preserving its original state.

Since then, it has become a popular tourist attraction, which also operates as a restaurant and beer garden. According to its website, the Eagle's Nest is "one of the few undamaged monuments of the Hitler era" and it "stands for the insanity of the regime."

World.title: Deadly shooting in Paris suburb investigated as terrorism, officials say
World.content:
A gunman shooting from his car killed one person and at least 5 others, including a 12-year-old girl, in the Paris suburb of Trappes on Friday, in what authorities described as a racially motivated act of terrorism.

President Emmanuel Macron called it "a racist terror attack" and said the suspect's statements suggested it was premeditated.

"These people were targeted because of their skin color or perceived religion, and for no other reason," Macron said following a meeting with officials and residents. "There is no place for this in France."

The alleged shooter was "firing at random, wanting to cause a bloodbath" as he drove through Trappes and neighboring La Verriere, Trappes mayor Ali Rabeh told broadcaster BFMTV.

"This is probably one of the first attempted mass killings motivated by Islamophobia and racism," Rabeh told reporters, The Associated Press reported. "This was a terrorist attack with racist, likely Islamophobic, overtones."

Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said the suspect fired "what appears to have been a military-grade weapon, or at least an automatic weapon." Rabeh called it a "miracle" that there were not more casualties.

Rabeh said that the gunman targeted passersby at three separate locations, including a playground. Forensic investigators were also seen examining evidence at a gas station.

The alleged shooter was arrested in the nearby town of Coignieres. Nuñez said the attack lasted just under 15 minutes and was stopped by five officers from the anti-crime brigade.

Police officers at the scene of a shooting rampage that killed at least 1 in Trappes, a suburb of Paris, France, on Oct, 23, 2026. Dimitar DILKOFF /AFP via Getty Images

Officials initially said four people had been wounded, but Rabeh told reporters there were five, including three who were very seriously injured, with their lives in danger.

A 12-year-old girl was seriously wounded after being shot eight times, but is in stable condition, the mayor of La Verriere, Nicolas Dainville, told the Agence France-Presse news agency.

Rabeh said that the person killed was "of African origin" and one of the wounded, "in critical condition, is of North African origin."

Nuñez said the gunman "clearly" committed "a terrorist crime" that may have been racially motivated. Prosecutors said they were investigating whether the acts targeted the "real or supposed race, ethnicity, nationality or religion" of the victims.

They said they have opened an investigation for "murder in connection with a terrorist enterprise."

Authorities investigate the scene of a shooting in Trappes, France, on Oct. 23, 2026. Mustafa Yalcin/Anadolu via Getty Images

Others in police custody

The National Anti-Terrorism Prosecutor's Office said Saturday that "three additional individuals" from the suspect's "family and circle of friends" were placed in police custody on Friday evening and overnight. The office did not say why those individuals were placed in custody.

The office also said that the suspect's criminal record includes four prior convictions, all of which had been legally expunged. The office did not say what those convictions were for or when they occurred.

Officials have yet to identify the suspect publicly.

Bursts of gunfire and "loud bangs"

A police source told AFP that the gunman had fired in bursts from his vehicle around 10:30 a.m. local time.

Samy, a resident of Trappes, about 13 miles west of Paris, told AFP he saw a body on the ground from his window.

His mother, he said, saw a gray Renault Clio car speeding by and heard "loud bangs."

Writing on X, Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said the case was "very serious" and that "all resources of the security forces and the judiciary are fully mobilised."

President Emmanuel Macron said "the nation is standing with" the victims of this "terrible ordeal."

Trappes previously experienced tensions after a teacher there reported receiving threats after writing that the state did not do enough to protect another teacher, Samuel Paty. Paty was beheaded by a radical Islamist in 2020 in another Paris suburb after he showed his class caricatures of the Prophet Muhammad.

France on edge after street violence and protests

The shooting came with France on edge following riots that erupted amid mass protests over the cost of living, which saw some of the worst street violence in recent years. Demonstrators, including students, labor union members and activists from France's "Yellow Vest" movement, are expected to take to the streets again Saturday.

French police have promised a larger presence to maintain order after a week of overnight curfews across the country. Nuñez said authorities would deploy some 70,000 law enforcement officers and gendarmes. Elite police units will help secure public buildings, he said. Other resources, including helicopters, armored vehicles and water cannons, will also be deployed.

Nuñez said at a news conference that officials will be "absolutely uncompromising" with those involved in violence, looting or vandalism. Police will have a "very firm approach to making arrests, and there will be legal consequences," he said.

Major Paris museums, including the Louvre, will be closed. Art Basel Paris has canceled its weekend program due to safety concerns, the AP reported.

World.title: Iran has "increased efforts to target U.S. personnel," intel chief warns
World.content:
Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton warned Friday that Iran has "substantially increased efforts to target U.S. personnel" abroad, with plots to kill Americans reaching "advanced stages" in the Middle East and other countries.

The warning, contained in an unclassified memo that was sent to Secretary of State Marco Rubio and obtained by CBS News, comes as the State Department adjusts staffing at diplomatic posts across the Middle East, and the U.S. military pares back its footprint in the region, amid concerns about direct threats from Iran and threats from the Iranian-backed Houthi movement in Yemen.

"The lethal plotting efforts by the Iranians against U.S. citizens have reached advanced stages in both the Middle East and certain other countries," Clayton wrote.

The memo, which was issued as the Trump administration weighs resuming military strikes against Iran, does not identify specific targets or countries where the alleged plots are underway, or indicate whether attacks may be imminent.

Clayton said the U.S. intelligence community is working to downgrade sensitive intelligence — received through various channels — so it can be shared more broadly with State Department personnel. CIA Director John Ratcliffe was copied on the memo.

Axios was first to report on the memo.

The warning follows a series of precautions at U.S. diplomatic facilities across the region. Earlier this week, the State Department ordered non-essential U.S. embassy personnel and their families to depart Saudi Arabia. Several other American embassies in the region adjusted their staffing under "restricted operations" status, which allows them to reduce the number of personnel without formally going on ordered departure, CBS News previously reported.

"When it comes to our staffing at embassies, we constantly evaluate new information about the security environment," a U.S. official told CBS News on Friday. "The threat of Houthi attacks and of Iranian terror plots targeting U.S. officials are informing our decisions on staffing adjustments for embassies on RO [Restricted Operations] Status in the region."

A U.S. official and a senior U.S. military official also told CBS News this week that the military has been quietly reducing its footprint at posts in the Middle East due to ongoing threats.

Houthi militants have stepped up drone and missile attacks against Saudi Arabia, targeting oil infrastructure and airports. One strike on Riyadh's King Khalid Airport earlier this month killed at least a dozen people, including a U.S. citizen, and injured hundreds more.

Last weekend, U.S. embassies in Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates and other countries warned Americans to exercise caution due to Houthi attacks.

Although the U.S. and Iran have refrained from striking each other in recent weeks, President Trump has not ruled out restarting hostilities after next month's midterm elections. Iran has also continued to take responsibility for attacks on oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz.

At a campaign rally in Florida on Friday, Mr. Trump suggested the U.S. could launch another operation against Iran if Tehran failed to reach an agreement.

"We may do another little Epic Fury, or they'll agree," the president said, invoking the name of the U.S. military campaign launched in February.

World.title: DOJ demands that some California counties set aside alleged noncitizen ballots
World.content:
Federal prosecutors sent letters to county registrars across California on Friday demanding that local officials set aside and verify ballots that the Justice Department said may belong to noncitizens, according to the Los Angeles County registrar and a letter obtained by The Associated Press.

The letters are the latest escalation in a legal battle between California and President Trump's Justice Department, which has recently focused on the state in its efforts to root out noncitizen voting ahead of the midterm elections. Data shows illegal voting by people who aren't U.S. citizens is incredibly rare, difficult to prove and has not been shown to change the outcome of races.

Earlier this month, the federal government targeted L.A. County and the California Secretary of State's office in a lawsuit that aimed to block them from counting the votes of more than 20,000 people who it alleges are "likely" noncitizen voters. A hearing on the case is scheduled for Tuesday.

The Trump administration on Friday asked the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals to rule on the lawsuit barring a decision from the district judge assigned to the case. They set a deadline for Saturday.

Now, according to the L.A. County registrar's office, at least 18 counties across the state have received similar letters. They have been given a 48-hour deadline to provide identifying information corresponding with ballots that the federal government believes were sent to noncitizens illegally registered to vote. The letter requests that county officials also sequester any ballots where citizenship cannot be verified.

"Any election official who knowingly processes the ballot of a noncitizen is opening themselves to legal jeopardy," said First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli.

The Justice Department is asking counties to send information about the voters it suspects are noncitizens including Social Security numbers, ID information, a copy of their registration and more.

That information can help the government and state quickly assess each person suspected of illegally registering to vote, said the letter sent to San Bernardino County voting officials. The letter says the government's list of suspected noncitizen voters includes 1,133 people from the inland Southern California county.

California's secretary of state and the Los Angeles County registrar have opposed the federal government's demands. In legal filings, lawyers for California say the request threatens to delay the certification of the vote and undermine the legitimacy of the November midterms. They have also argued that the federal government's data is unreliable and that their demands risk disenfranchisement of citizens.

Voting is underway in California, with the state's more than 23 million registered voters receiving ballots in the mail earlier this month. The state said in legal filings that over 330,000 mail-in ballots have already been counted.

The letters on Friday came on the heels of a statewide sweep by federal authorities earlier in the week, where 28 people from the list of 20,000 were charged with illegally registering to vote. Some were also charged with illegally voting and lying on naturalization paperwork. Those charges could lead to years in prison.

The Justice Department's Civil Rights Division has filed 31 lawsuits in an effort to force states to hand over unredacted copies of their voter rolls. The division has said it wants to ensure states are keeping clean voter lists, but it has since acknowledged that it also intends to share the data with the Department of Homeland Security so that the lists can be screened for noncitizens.

Harmeet Dhillon, the assistant attorney general for the Civil Rights Division, sent letters to all 50 states in July threatening to take criminal action if they knowingly allowed noncitizens to remain on their voter rolls.

So far, the Justice Department has lost 26 of those cases, and has not achieved one legal victory to date.

"This is NOT A DRILL: Donald Trump and Todd Blanche are trying to interfere in California elections," Democratic Sen. Alex Padilla of California said in a statement Friday. "Trump's DOJ has not provided any evidence for their claims of massive voter fraud. They've admitted that the data they point to is inaccurate and unreliable. No matter how many lawsuits they file or how many election officials they threaten, they do not have the authority to interfere."

World.title: DOJ sues to block Alaska Senate certification if Sullivan loses
World.content:
The Trump administration is suing to prevent the Alaska Senate election from being certified if Republican Sen. Daniel Sullivan loses to Democrat Mary Peltola because of the other Dan Sullivan who is on the ballot.

Alaskans will choose their senator in a ranked-choice contest with four candidates on the ballot: Sen. Dan Sullivan, Peltola, Gerald Heikes, and a teacher named Daniel J. Sullivan.

The Justice Department argues that if Sen. Sullivan were to lose because of votes unintentionally cast for the Daniel J. Sullivan instead of the senator, the election should not be considered valid.

The government alleges that candidate Daniel J. Sullivan deliberately sought to confuse voters by running with the same ballot name and party affiliation as the incumbent senator. It argues that he is potentially diverting votes and Peltola stands to benefit.

In its court filing Friday, the Justice Department argued that allowing Daniel J. Sullivan to be on the ballot "threatens to mislead Alaskan citizens who want to vote for Senator Sullivan" and said that some of his supporters "likely will inadvertently vote for Daniel J. Sullivan."

Further, the senator's other supporters "likely will be confused as to how to rank the three Republican candidates as to defeat Peltola" and "might not rank Senator Sullivan at all."

Peltola's campaign spokesperson, Harry Child, told CBS News in a statement that the effort was "a despicable political threat to overturn an election."

"We will fight to ensure every single eligible voter in Alaska can make their voice heard and that no bureaucrat or politician from the Lower 48 can interfere with our lawful, secure elections," Child said.

A sample ballot included in the Justice Department's filing shows how the two Sullivans would be listed: Daniel J. Sullivan appears first, as "Sullivan, Daniel J. Jr.," with no party affiliation, while Sen. Sullivan appears next, as "Sullivan, Dan S. (Registered Republican) Incumbent."

Alaska Senate candidates, as shown on sample ballot from Justice Department court filing

In June, the Alaska Supreme Court ruled that Daniel J. Sullivan could remain on the ballot, upholding a ruling from a lower court. The state courts reversed the decision by the state Division of Elections that Daniel J. Sullivan was ineligible because he was allegedly trying to "cause voter confusion."

Daniel J. Sullivan's lawyers argued the state "lacked any basis in Alaska law to exclude Mr. Sullivan from the ballot" and didn't have the power to look into his "private motivations." They said that state law doesn't give officials the power to keep qualified candidates off the ballot due to potential confusion.

If Sen. Sullivan loses in November but would have won had the other Sullivan's votes been counted for him, the Justice Department would ask for an investigation, according to its complaint.

A Justice Department spokesperson said that the DOJ filed the complaint "to ensure that this frivolous candidacy does not undermine the integrity of Alaska's election or the will of its voters."

The department says that Daniel J. Sullivan's candidacy constitutes a violation of the National Voter Registration Act, which was enacted to make the voter registration process more accessible.

President Trump has criticized the dueling Sullivans' presence on the ballot, calling it "totally confusing" and "CHEATING" in a Truth Social post Wednesday, and writing: "It's ridiculous that the Court didn't stop this SCAM." He said his administration was "looking at powerful legal options to remove the fraudulent Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. from the Ballot."

Asked Friday about the Justice Department's lawsuit, Mr. Trump told reporters: "Well, I'm the one that said, 'do it.'"

Alaska's other senator, Republican Sen. Lisa Murkowski, said the department "should never have filed this lawsuit."

"Alaskans don't need any help voting for their preferred candidates, and the State of Alaska has already handled this by clearly distinguishing the candidates on this year's ballot," Murkowski, a frequent Trump critic, wrote on X.

World.title: Melania Trump secures "temporary ceasefire" in Ukrainian city
World.content:
First lady Melania Trump's office on Friday said she — not President Trump or another top official — has secured a temporary ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine for the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky for humanitarian reasons.

In an unusual announcement for a first lady's office, it said both nations agreed to temporarily halt all military action in the southern Ukrainian city "to allow for humanitarian aid to enter and to prepare a civilian evacuation through a designated safe passageway." The localized ceasefire will begin Thursday, Oct. 29.

Russia and Ukraine have not commented on the first lady's announcement. But Ukrainian officials indicated that there has been a tentative agreement in the Russian-occupied territory in southern Ukraine.

The first lady's office says she worked "directly with Russian and Ukrainian leadership to define the terms of the localized ceasefire."

"The situation in Oleshky is dire," the first lady said in a statement. "Oleshky is a front-line war city on the brink of disaster. Oleshky's remaining population is comprised primarily of elderly residents who urgently need medical attention, medicine, food, and clean water. The people of Oleshky have limited electricity, live amid mined roads, and endure regular military attacks. It was abundantly clear that without my intervention, the possibility to bring humanitarian aid into the city and to evacuate the elderly would be impossible."

The first lady's office said she "initiated discussions with both nations and aligned the parties on the agreement's objectives, technical procedures, timing, processes, and terms, in her formal role as Exclusive Intermediary."

"Non-military, civilian leaders from both countries will work together to visit Oleshky residents in their homes and determine the level of assistance they require," the first lady said. "Residents who wish to evacuate will receive coordinated support and transportation to their preferred destination. I anticipate some will want to go to Russia, and some to Ukraine."

The first lady added that she's secured an American media organization to document both Russian and Ukrainian teams. Newsmax, a conservative outlet, said it would be going.

White House communications director Steven Cheung called the announcement "amazing news."

"This is a major, positive step towards peace," Cheung said on X. "History will remember her tireless work to help those in need."

Last week, the Vatican said Pope Leo spoke with Russian President Vladimir Putin on the phone and "expressed his deep concern about the grave humanitarian situation in the city of Oleshky."

Melania Trump has worked to reunite 34 children so far with their families, after Russia forcibly removed children.

Although he said he would bring about an end to Russia's war with Ukraine on his first day back in office, peace has remained elusive for Mr. Trump. The president has grown increasingly frustrated with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in recent days, saying Ukraine should have a new leader and dismissing concerns about Russia's continued slaughter of Ukrainians.

"Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine," Mr. Trump told reporters earlier this week. "They haven't been doing much."

U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff faced backlash for calling Putin a "humanitarian" upon the release of American Stephen Hubbard.

World.title: Is your Medicare Advantage plan ending next year? Here's what to know
World.content:
Is your Medicare Advantage plan ending next year? Here's what to know

toggle caption i Jim Watson/AFP via Getty Images

A slew of Medicare Advantage plans are disappearing for next year, leaving seniors in many areas with fewer options. In 193 counties across the country, no plans are offered at all.

Medicare's annual open enrollment period kicked off October 15 and runs until December 7, and seniors enrolled in those privatized Medicare plans that are closing in certain markets should carefully review their options.

Medicare Advantage means private insurers run Medicare for older Americans who choose it over traditional Medicare, where the federal government itself administers the program. More than half of the 70 million Americans in Medicare choose Medicare Advantage. It's popular because it covers services like vision and dental, often with lower premiums than traditional Medicare. It also often folds in the "Part D" drug benefit, simplifying that decision.

Sponsor Message

But a downside of Medicare Advantage is that companies can pick and choose where they offer plans. If a certain community is not profitable, a company can leave that market. And that has been happening on an increasingly large scale the last three years, according to research published in JAMA.

Who is affected

Big swaths of rural America are losing Medicare Advantage choices and so are some major metro areas.

Last year, 2.9 million seniors were in Medicare Advantage plans that closed up shop, according to JAMA. This year, an analysis of insurance company announcements by An Arm and A Leg podcast, shows at least 2 million people will be affected. Other preliminary estimates range from 3.2 million to 5 million seniors. About 35 million people are enrolled in Medicare Advantage.

According to an analysis of federal data by the health policy research organization KFF, the 193 counties that will have zero Medicare Advantage plans are mostly rural. Last year that number was about 120 counties without a plan offered.

KFF's numbers also show that there will be far fewer plans offered in some metro areas. Dallas, Minneapolis, Seattle, Houston and Portland all have between a quarter and a third fewer Medicare Advantage plans for seniors.

What happens next

If your plan is ending, and you don't choose another, the insurance company will assign you to another Medicare Advantage plan or the government will enroll you in traditional Medicare — but without a supplemental or drug plan.

If you want to switch from Medicare Advantage to traditional Medicare and your plan is ending, you can enroll in a Medicare supplemental plan — also known as Medigap — without the same restrictions that you would normally have. If you have a pre-existing condition that has prevented you from enrolling in Medigap before, that could be good news.

Sponsor Message

Another wrinkle this year is that insurance companies can cap enrollments on some of the Medicare Advantage plans that they do offer.

Which means: If you wait to sign up, a plan you want might already be full.

The companies are supposed to enroll people on a first-come, first-serve basis — and not cherry-pick customers based on health conditions, age, or demographics.

Another reason not to delay is that with so many people on the hunt for new plans, it may take longer than usual to get help.

How and where to find help

Here are some tips for navigating Medicare open enrollment this year:

Find out if your plan is still offered: First, check your mail. Medicare Advantage plans that are closing should have sent letters the first week in October. You can also log in to your account on Medicare.gov to check your plan's status for next year.



First, check your mail. Medicare Advantage plans that are closing should have sent letters the first week in October. You can also log in to your account on Medicare.gov to check your plan's status for next year. Try calling your SHIP: There's a State Health Insurance Assistance Program — known as a "SHIP" — in every state to help seniors with Medicare. The name's not easy to remember or particularly descriptive, but it's free, mandated by the federal government, and the staff and volunteers are required to give you unbiased information on all available options. Find your state in the directory at shiphelp.org. Your county may have a specific number that you can find on your state's SHIP website.

The name's not easy to remember or particularly descriptive, but it's free, mandated by the federal government, and the staff and volunteers are required to give you unbiased information on all available options. Find your state in the directory at shiphelp.org. Your county may have a specific number that you can find on your state's SHIP website. Look for local Medicare counseling services: Friends, family, leaders at your place of worship, and the constituent services of your local elected officials may have the scoop on where you can get one-on-one help. The nonprofit Medicare Rights Center also has a national helpline, and a well-organized library of online guides.

The nonprofit Medicare Rights Center also has a national helpline, and a well-organized library of online guides. Brokers can be helpful, but be savvy: You want a broker who's going to talk with you about all your options — including switching to traditional Medicare and a supplemental plan. Ask if they sell plans from all available insurance carriers. And ask if they answer questions about your plan year-round, because insurance never stops being confusing.

Ask if they sell plans from all available insurance carriers. And ask if they answer questions about your plan year-round, because insurance never stops being confusing. Double check what you see on Medicare.gov : Medicare's Plan Finder allows you to search plans online. But lists of doctors and drugs that are covered can sometimes be wrong. To be safe, double check with your doctor's office or a SHIP counselor, broker, or other Medicare assistor.

To be safe, double check with your doctor's office or a SHIP counselor, broker, or other Medicare assistor. Don't share your personal information with services you find online : Be careful where you share your personal information like your phone number. Some online agencies will sell your information, leading to spam calls and potentially even scam artists.

Be mindful of the deadlines: Open enrollment for Medicare runs October 15, 2026 through December 7, 2026. The coverage starts January 1, 2027. If your plan is ending, you qualify for a "special enrollment period" to give you a little more time — until February 28, 2027. (For coverage that starts January 1, 2027, enroll by December 31.)

World.title: U.S. birth rate drops to record low, but older women are having more babies
World.content:
U.S. birth rate drops to record low, but older women are having more babies

toggle caption i CHARLY TRIBALLEAU/AFP

Sarah Harris was 37 years old when she gave birth to her daughter Bridget last year. She describes motherhood as equal parts joy and exhaustion. "When you have a baby in your mid-30s, what you gain in wisdom and experience you also lose in terms of energy," Harris says with a laugh.

Harris, who lives in Vermont, was laid off from a job four months after Bridget was born. She says she's still figuring out what her career and her life will look like with a child. Harris thinks a lot of women are like her. They're wrestling with financial uncertainty and waiting much later to choose pregnancy.

Sponsor Message

There's also the high cost of raising a child, which Harris said convinced her that one is enough. "I think in another era or another life or another scenario, I might have had more children," Harris says. "I think we're in a difficult societal moment and so that's absolutely affecting people's reproductive choices."

Harris is, in fact, part of a slow revolution in what motherhood and parenting look like in the United States The latest report from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention found the general fertility rate for women fell by 1% to a new record low in 2025. That continues a two-decade trend toward fewer children.

Steep drops in parenting among U.S. women in their 20s

The one-year drop for 20-somethings was even more eye-catching. "Certainly the 6% decline in the birthrate for women age 20 to 24 is noteworthy," said Brady Hamilton, a demographer at the CDC's National Center for Health Statistics who co-authored the report. He noted that women in their late teens also saw a 7% decline.

A separate study released last month by the Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta found Gen Z women, in their late teens and twenties, "are dramatically less likely to want children" compared with U.S. women of previous generations.

Sponsor Message

"Several factors have been identified as contributing to this lower desire to have children, such as increased labor market opportunities and agency among women, rising financial costs, changing priorities, and [concerns about] maternal mortality," the study found.

Dr. Tanise Branche, medical director of labor and delivery at Temple Health, a health, research and training network in Philadelphia, told NPR more of her younger women patients are following a different life script.

"They're starting to focus not necessarily just on what they can bring to kids, but what's going to be best for them," she says.

Women in their 30s and 40s saw "significant" birthrate increase

Meanwhile, the latest CDC data shows a small but significant increase in older women, ages 30 to 45, who are choosing to become pregnant.

Branche says more women, including herself, are building careers and stable lives before becoming mothers.

Branche is currently pregnant with her fourth child. "I will be 43 with my last delivery and I started this reproductive journey at 37," she said. "I see the net positive being that we have a choice."

Fewer children because of choice — and affordability

As a consequence of this shift, there are fewer children now in the U.S. The population under age 18 is falling steadily, according to the U.S. Census Bureau, dropping by more than 1 million from 2010 to 2020.

Some experts also believe women would choose to have more kids if they could afford them and had proper supports that include affordable housing, daycare and health insurance.

"The fact that there are a lot of people who still say they want families, but don't feel like they're able to have them [is a concern]," says Anna Louie Sussman, author of a new book on parenting choices called Inconceivable. "Young people say, I can barely take care of myself I can't imagine taking care of someone else."

Sussman herself is part of the trend toward delayed motherhood. Because of her own concerns about affordability and her career, she froze her eggs and waited to have her child until she was in her early 40s.

Sponsor Message

"I do feel lucky that I'm a little further along professionally than I would have been in my 20s or even 30s," she said.

As women build different lives and birthrates keep falling, the U.S. is changing. The median age is rising rapidly, reaching 39.4 years old in 2025. More states, including Vermont where Sarah Harris lives, are seeing actual population decline, according to the Census Bureau.

"I think about it a lot because I live in a very small place where we're hoping to keep the doors of our elementary school open for as long as we can," she says.

World.title: This decade has been missing its big-impact midterm
World.content:
This decade has been missing its big-impact midterm

toggle caption i Saul Loeb/AFP via Getty Images

Given all that's happened in American politics since 2019, it may be hard to believe there's been anything missing.

But the decade of the 2020s has yet to see a midterm that mattered much — or that ranked among the impact midterms of past decades.

That sets the 2020s apart, as every other decade over the past hundred years has produced at least one midterm that made a big difference in Congress and in national politics more broadly.

These big-impact midterms have also shifted power in the statehouses, often signaling changes in state and national political landscapes that have mattered and lasted.

Midterms do not attract the same level of voter participation or voter interest as presidential elections. When the White House is not at stake, "low propensity voters" tend to tune out. Overall vote totals slide by about one-third.

Sponsor Message

But those voters who show up for midterms elect just as many members of Congress and fill just as many state legislative seats as voters in presidential years. Moreover, midterm voters determine about two-thirds of the nation's governorships.

The big midterms have tended to come in presidents' second terms, when their popularity and political energy may be waning. And just because a president is not on the ballot does not mean he's irrelevant. Historically, each president's detractors have seen midterms as an opportunity, while his supporters have often been complacent — or at least less motivated.

All this contributes to the general expectation that the midterms arriving Nov. 3 will be important, and perhaps momentous.

Flexing midterm muscles

Because this is a decade with three presidential cycles (2020, 2024 and 2028), it is also a decade with just two midterms. One went by in 2022. Some expected at the time that a "big red wave" would sweep then-President Biden's majorities out of Congress.

It did not happen. Democrats held on in the Senate, and the House shifted from barely Democratic to barely Republican. That did bring an end to House Speaker Nancy Pelosi's second (and last) turn with the Big Gavel. But the GOP would spend much of the next two years struggling to unite behind a speaker of their own.

Sponsor Message

That's a far cry from the big midterms that have at times rivaled presidential elections for responding to the mood of the times and rearranging the landscape.

If we take the last hundred years as our sample, we can start with the midterms that followed the Wall Street "Crash of 1929." That financial panic set off a sequence of events that would be called the Great Depression, and the collateral damage included the closing of an era of Republican dominance in Washington.

That era ended with the midterms of 1930, which cost the GOP eight Senate seats and 52 seats in the House in November 1930. Although the GOP initially retained small majorities in both chambers, they lost it in the House with the results of a few special elections early in 1931.

toggle caption i National Archives

The Senate remained nominally Republican but featured a working majority of Democrats and progressive Republicans. A page had been turned, and Democrats would take control outright in 1932 and hold that majority through World War II.

After that war had ended, the period of Democratic hegemony under President Franklin Roosevelt also ended, and abruptly, with the results of the midterm of 1946.

Pendulum swings both ways

Republican numbers in Congress had fallen so far in the FDR years ( below 100 at one point in the 435-seat House ) that it seemed impossible for them to return to power. But in 1946 they stormed back to majority control of both House and Senate in a single midterm cycle.

Midterms have continued to serve as political regulators in the generations since. Dwight Eisenhower won two landslide elections as president in the 1950s, but he lost the House in 1954 and needed the vice president to break ties in the Senate.

In his second term, the re-elected "Ike" did not control Capitol Hill, and in the 1958 midterms saw his party drop to just 35 seats in the Senate .

Sponsor Message

The Senate Democrats first elected in 1958 established a critical mass that would later drive the bipartisan super-majorities needed to break the filibuster and pass the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965.

In the same era, Democrats in Congress enacted a raft of social programs that would become part of the language, such as Medicare and Medicaid. It was all part of President Lyndon Johnson's "Great Society" program.

What goes up …

toggle caption i AFP via Getty Images/AFP

But by the midterm year of 1966, much of the energy from LBJ's landslide election in 1964 had been expended — and much more had been siphoned off by his escalation of the war in Vietnam.

Right on time, the midterm arrived, and while the Democrats only took a haircut in the Senate elections they lost a painful 47 seats to the GOP in the House. It gave the party a new lease on life and encouraged its new emphasis on winning in the South . The redirection would guide the party's 1968 presidential candidate, Richard Nixon, and remain a focus for the onetime "Party of Lincoln" for decades to come.

Also in the midterm of 1966, out on the West Coast, a first-time candidate named Ronald Reagan won the governorship of California. People were starting to use the term "Sunbelt."

Yet another midterm correction

But what the midterms of 1966 gave the GOP, the midterms of 1974 would largely take away. Nixon had been elected president in 1968, pursuing what was called a Southern Strategy, and was reelected in a resounding 49-state landslide in 1972.

But by 1974 it had all gone the other way for Nixon. The "Watergate" scandals emerged from his 1972 campaign's use of burglary and electronic surveillance among other unsavory tactics. An attempt to cover it all up blew back on the White House and forced Nixon to resign on the brink of impeachment in August of 1974 – just three months before the midterm for his second term.

Sponsor Message

The result was a crushing defeat for the GOP, the loss of 48 seats in the House and several more in the Senate (where the Democrats already had more than 60 votes).

While it is tempting to attribute these losses to Nixon's downfall, the country had — to some extent — rallied behind his vice president and successor, Gerald R. Ford. The underlying vulnerability of the GOP was the state of the economy, which was suffering from inflation and the hangover from the oil embargo of 1973 by Arab members of OPEC, the Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries.

That embargo, a side effect of the Arab-Israeli "Yom Kippur War" of 1973, temporarily raised the price of crude oil from $3 to $12 and introduced Americans to the phrases "oil shock" and "energy crisis."

Reagan rises and falls

toggle caption i Consolidated News Pictures/AFP via Getty Images

Reagan became the dominant political personality of the 1980s, defeating incumbent President Jimmy Carter in 1980 and winning a 49-state landslide reelection in 1984. He was able to carry in a majority for Republicans in the Senate and establish a kind of working majority in the House with the aid of conservative Democrats in that chamber.

On the strength of those elections, restrained only marginally by the midterm elections of 1982, Reagan began his second term on top of the world. But he soon learned how hard that height can be to hold. As he neared his second midterm, Democrats were on the march nationally and restoring their strength in the more populous Southern states.

In 1986, Democrats defeated six GOP senators who had been elected with Reagan in 1980. The net gain of eight Senate seats gave them a 55-45 majority. In the session of Congress that followed, the Senate would override Reagan's veto of a highway bill and reject his nomination of Robert Bork to the Supreme Court. Reagan was a spent force.

Yet more dramatic reversals to come

Reagan was able to see his vice president, George H.W. Bush, take the White House in 1988, but the party's hopes for momentum into the 1990 midterms were largely unfulfilled. The presidency was also lost in 1992, when Democrat Bill Clinton won a three-way race with just 43% of the popular vote, defeating Bush and independent candidate H. Ross Perot.

Sponsor Message

Clinton's lack of a majority and list of frustrations in his first term set the stage for a bruising first midterm election in 1994. But what came was beyond bruising. Republicans stormed to their first majority in the House (54 seats net) in 40 years and recaptured the Senate with eight new seats there as well.

The new GOP speaker, Newt Gingrich of Georgia, was a hard-driving partisan who had portrayed the chamber as a House of Ill Repute, the title of a book he and other House Republicans had published.

The use of a "Contract with America" theme promised lower taxes, less corruption and a healthier economy in a compact agenda that had voter appeal as well.

Gingrich explicitly rejected the go-along-get-along attitude of previous GOP leaders in the House and advocated confrontation. The strategy proved less fruitful once he had the Big Gavel, however, and Gingrich spent much of his time as speaker making deals with Clinton. Internal dissatisfaction with him forced him out late in 1998.

Mood swings in the 2000s

In the new century that followed, parties have continued to prosper when their presidential candidates win and give ground in the midterms. George W. Bush was an exception as the president after the terror attacks of September 2001. In his first midterm the following year, theGOP made gains across the board.

But the larger dynamic caught up to him in 2006, when he and his party took what he called "a thumpin'" in elections at all levels. Bush had initially gained popularity with his "War on Terror" and won a second term. But thereafter, his invasion of Iraq had become an albatross. And in 2006 he paid the historic price, losing both his party majorities in the House and Senate. The new majority in the House made Pelosi the first woman speaker in history.

Sponsor Message

That created an atmosphere of optimism for Democrats, who elected Barack Obama president in 2008 and gave him majorities in the House and Senate (the latter briefly reaching 60 seats). But Obama felt the sting of the midterms early — much as Clinton had. Republicans in 2010 capitalized on an economy still experiencing the recession that had aided Obama's win in 2008. The GOP also capitalized on fears and confusion surrounding the enactment of the Affordable Care Act, or "Obamacare," in 2010.

Echoing his predecessor, Obama called this setback "a shellacking," and settled in to work with a much diminished Senate majority and a Republican-dominated House under Speaker John Boehner.

toggle caption i Jim Watson/AFP via Getty Images

Obama managed to thread the needle well enough to win a second term for himself in 2012, but the House remained Republican and the Senate followed suit in Obama's second midterm election in 2014.
