That second midterm revealed continuing GOP strength across the South and Midwest and to some degree augured the Electoral College majorities that would make Donald J. Trump president in 2016 and 2024.

If the 2020s are to have a midterm with the kind of impact others have had, roughly once a decade for a century, the last opportunity for that to happen is Nov. 3.

If the once-a-decade rhythm has any rationale, in fact, the pressure for a meaningful midterm ought to be building substantially. And in fact most pollsters, pundits and other prognosticators now predict Democrats could flip control of the House and even the Senate as well.

Just as in the previous 10 cycles, the current cycle combines economic concerns (including energy prices) and negative stories about incumbents in various offices. It is the party perceived as being in power that is exposed in a midterm, and it pays a price when voters perceive that party to have lost its mandate — or at least its momentum.

World.title: Drinking water supplies dwindle in Yemeni city besieged by Houthi rebels
World.content:
Drinking water supplies dwindle in Yemeni city besieged by Houthi rebels

toggle caption i Abdulnasser Alseddik/AP

Drinking water has been scarce for over a decade in Taiz, but the problem has reached crisis levels in recent weeks as Iran-backed Houthi rebels besiege Yemen's third-largest city in their escalating conflict with government forces.

The needs of Taiz's more than 1 million residents are now barely being met, humanitarian groups say, as access to wells is limited, desalination plants run low on fuel and water delivery trucks are largely prevented from entering the city.

Families are rationing every drop. Before Taiz came under siege, Hadil al-Shahid and her two young children used about 10 liters (about 2.6 gallons) of bottled water per day for drinking and cooking; now they are making the same amount last about four days.

Sponsor Message

"We stopped drinking coffee and tea, which we used to drink daily," al-Shahid said in a phone interview.

Families like al-Shahid's are paying as much as 75% more for bottled water than just a few weeks ago, and some have begun to buy water on credit.

The siege of Taiz — a strategic gateway to southern Yemen — isn't only constricting water supplies. Shortages of groceries have sent food prices soaring. Fuel is also in short supply, making it difficult to maintain basic services such as hospitals and sanitation, which compounds the public health risks.

Amnesty International has called on the Houthis to immediately open roads into the city, saying Taiz is being pushed to "the brink of a severe humanitarian disaster."

Houthis strangle Taiz, cut off residents' access to wells

Yemen descended into civil war in 2014, when the Houthis seized much of the country's north, including the capital of Sanaa, and forced the internationally recognized government into exile. Taiz has been a focal point of fighting ever since.

War-related damage to Taiz's aging water infrastructure magnified the pressures of population growth and frequent droughts that led to shrinking supplies of groundwater. Residents began paying for water delivered by trucks, a mostly reliable alternative — until recently.

Sponsor Message

By August, Yemen had become a widening front in the Iran war. The Houthis ramped up their advance on Taiz last month, after a lightning-fast capture of the port city of Mokha, an area about 130 kilometers (80 miles) away that is vital to controlling shipping through the Red Sea.

As Houthi forces took control of more land and roads surrounding Taiz, residents' access to nearby wells was cut off and deliveries of water from outside the city declined.

The truckers that have managed to ferry water into Taiz have in some cases tripled their rates to make the perilous journey.

As Taiz's fuel supplies dwindle, its water utility is struggling to maintain limited operations and desalination plants are running well below capacity.

The city is also enduring shortages of fuel and food

Since August, Taiz province, which includes the city and surrounding areas, has taken in roughly half of those displaced from other parts of Yemen because of the fighting — an estimated 124,000 people, according to the United Nations' migration experts. That is only compounding the pressure on Taiz's limited supply of water and other necessities.

Some displaced families are now living in makeshift shelters or tents and surviving on one meal a day, said Jens Laerke, a spokesperson for a division of the United Nations that focuses on emergency aid.

Fuel for cooking and transportation has also become scarce — and more expensive. The price of cooking gas has more than quadrupled, according to Hani Bafaqih, a water, sanitation and hygiene expert at the aid organization CARE in Yemen. To get by, some families are cooking over fires made by burning wood, charcoal or cardboard.

These fuel shortages have made it harder for community kitchens to provide free hot meals to families and have also forced waste-collection services to shut down.

"The shortages feed into each other. Without fuel, water pumps, hospital generators and solid-waste collection stop. With less clean water and waste piling up, the risk of disease, including cholera, rises," Laerke said. The health risks are exacerbated by thirsty families tapping into unprotected wells that could be contaminated with waterborne diseases, he said.

Sponsor Message

Food prices are also soaring. Flour and rice are about 50% more expensive than they were over the summer, according to aid groups, and fruits and vegetables are hard to find.

Ahmed Abdel Gaber is living with nine other family members in the ruins of another building after being displaced from their home by the fighting. He used to earn money hauling construction material, but that income is no longer steady and his family is barely scraping by.

"We heavily rely on assistance and donations from people to get food," he said in a phone interview.

Al-Shahid, a hair salon owner, said her income also dried up a few weeks ago. The salon was forced to close as former customers began to prioritize their spending on food and water. Her 10-year-old daughter and 5-year-old son now eat mostly rice, bread and cheese, she said.

Why Taiz matters to the Houthis

While the Yemeni government still controls the center of Taiz, the siege is making it difficult to deliver supplies to its forces there. In the hills surrounding Taiz, the government forces are trying to repel the Houthis but face stiff resistance, especially east of the city.

Gaining control of Taiz city is vital to the Houthis if they seek to advance south toward Aden and Lahj, analysts say, but that won't be easy.

"Any Houthi attempt to seize parts of the city, let alone take it entirely, would likely require a prolonged and costly battle, with significant casualties among Houthi fighters," said Ahmed Nagi, a senior analyst at the International Crisis Group.

Three Houthi officials said the rebel group controls roughly 80% of the countryside surrounding Taiz and several key neighborhoods inside the city. The Associated Press couldn't independently verify the claims by these officials, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because they weren't allowed to brief the media, but Yemen's foreign minister, Afrah al-Zouba, has acknowledged the rebel group's tightening grip on the city.

Sponsor Message

The Houthis' fight for control of the city is made significantly more difficult because of its large civilian population, the officials said.

Earlier this week, missiles fired by the Houthis struck a residential area in Taiz, killing two teenage girls and renewing attention on the dangers faced by civilians.

Abdel Gaber said he can hear loud explosions every day from fighting that is happening roughly 5 kilometers (3 miles) away. The family isn't returning to their home in a mountain village out of concern for their safety.

Leaving Taiz is not an option for al-Shahid because the costs of travel and renting a home in another province are prohibitive.

"Staying in our home is inevitable — whether it be a matter of life or death," al-Shahid said.

World.title: Severe flooding hits Four Corners region, more expected through the weekend
World.content:
Severe flooding hits Four Corners region, more expected through the weekend

toggle caption i South Fork Fire Rescue/AP

Looking out a window on Friday afternoon, Devin Neeley saw light, puffy clouds and a blue sky in San Juan County, N.M. The county's public information officer for emergency management called it "surreal."

Meanwhile, brown rainwaters were flooding homes in low-lying areas of the county and forcing sewage into the San Juan River.

"[The sky] belies really the danger that is coming down the river in historic levels," Neeley says. "We have not seen flooding like this in generations."

Neeley says, emergency responders rescued people on their roofs after floodwater inundated their homes. The county is under an emergency declaration and residents in susceptible areas were told to evacuate Thursday afternoon.

Sponsor Message

"These are communities that have beautiful riverfront places to live," Neeley says. "And unfortunately, that's a problem today."

Rare, heavy rainfall started to hit the Four Corners region — which includes New Mexico, Colorado, Utah and Arizona — on Wednesday.

Since then, severe, brown-colored floodwaters have led to road closures, mandatory evacuations and emergency declarations across the four states.

Thick, brown floodwaters

Areas of southern Utah, southwest Colorado, and the northern parts of Arizona and New Mexico were drenched with rain leading to rapidly rising floodwaters, Thursday and Friday.

In response to a post on X that showed brownish-red floodwaters in Hurricane, Utah, Gov. Spencer Cox, wrote on Thursday: "Our hearts are with the families whose homes and livelihoods have been impacted."

The southern Utah city issued an emergency declaration on Thursday after flooding damaged more than 100 homes and Rvs. People were seen leading horses to safety through ankle-deep water, in a video posted by the National Weather Service.

In Farmington, N.M., at the center of the devastation, Police Chief Steve Hebbe said at a press conference on Friday that "this is singular and this is real."

"So far, we have not had any deaths that is very fortunate, but this is not something that should be played with," Hebbe said.

Sponsor Message

Colorado Gov. Jared Polis declared disaster emergencies for 11 counties. Polis also authorized the use of National Guard members to assist with rescue efforts in southwest Colorado.

The police department for the Navajo Nation, which spans across northeastern Arizona, northwestern New Mexico, and southeastern Utah, said on Thursday that authorities had rescued seven families, 30 people, from their flooded homes. The Hopi Tribe in northeastern Arizona declared a state of emergency on Thursday due to heavy rainfall damaging roads, bridges, homes and other infrastructure.

The Archuleta County Sheriff's office in Colorado warned residents to shelter in place Friday morning, and by the evening had issued an evacuation warning.

The flooding comes after extreme weather hit the Southwest throughout the week. Arizona saw baseball-sized hail and a possible tornado that injured at least one person Wednesday evening.

A record amount of rainfall

The region's mountainous terrain is conducive to flooding. In August, intense flash flooding in the Grand Canyon led to multiple deaths.

Severe thunderstorm warnings started earlier in the week, says Kris Sanders, a meteorologist at the National Weather Service in Grand Junction, Colo. The remnants of Hurricane Trudy, which was active from Oct. 15 to Oct. 18, in the Pacific Ocean formed into a slow-moving low-pressure system that worked its way southwest.

Sanders says a lot of the storms weakened as they came through the region, but the heavy rain did not. Portions of southwest Colorado and southeast Utah saw two to four inches, whereas areas with higher elevations, like the San Juan Mountains, got up to six inches. This caused small creeks and streams and rivers to flood.

"Those rainfall amounts are records in themselves," Sanders says.

While the amount of rainfall is rare, he says, these storms typically happen in the region at this time of year. An event last year caused major flooding in the same spots, "like a carbon copy" of this year, Sanders says.

Sponsor Message

The threat is not over, he says, and thunderstorm watches are active in many of the same areas through Sunday.

Daniel Swain, a climate scientist with the University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources, says the severe thunderstorms are fueled by the large amount of moisture in the air. He says that moisture comes from the record-warm waters off parts of the West Coast, which are driven by a strong El Niño event and a preexisting marine heat wave (which he attributes largely to human-caused climate change).

The flooding isn't a surprise, he says, pointing to a prediction he and others made in the spring — that if El Niño materialized according to forecasts, southwestern U.S. could see extreme precipitation events through October.

Now, "that is exactly what we've seen," he says, "because this isn't even the first event this fall."

Neeley, the public information officer in San Juan County, N.M., says his community will be on alert for more damage and safety risks throughout the weekend.

"People are concerned about their life and their welfare and their property," Neeley says. "This is going to be a long term impact to this community,"

World.title: Russia steps up election influence efforts in final stretch of midterms
World.content:
Russia steps up election influence efforts in final stretch of midterms

toggle caption i Igor Ivanko/AFP via Getty Images

Russian operatives are pumping out fabricated claims about Democratic candidates, AI-manipulated videos of celebrities and fake posts impersonating real news outlets in an effort to influence American voters in the final run-up to Election Day.

Researchers who track online influence operations and lawmakers who've been briefed by the intelligence community say Kremlin-backed groups are renewing familiar tactics they've used to sow distrust and discord in previous elections in the U.S. and around the world.

Sponsor Message

"It's a carnival out there," Rep. Jim Himes of Connecticut, the ranking member on the House intelligence committee, told reporters this week. "They're throwing everything out there to generate a sense of chaos and anarchy."

The goal is to exacerbate divisions, erode confidence in democracy and, crucially, undermine U.S. support for Ukraine.

"At the end of the day, the main issue for Russia is and has to be Ukraine," said Darren Linvill, co-director of Clemson University's Media Forensics Hub, who has tracked foreign propaganda campaigns for years.

Linvill says the Russian playbook is consistent. A false claim or divisive narrative is seeded on social media or on a fake website posing as a news organization or think tank. It's spread by state media, automated fake accounts or, increasingly, paid influencers, in the hopes that it gets seen and repeated by real people.

"In the same way that marketing companies will pay an influencer to disseminate, you know, 'Nike's a great shoe,' the Russians do it with false information and made-up lies," he said. "They use influencers that know their audience, that are part of that audience, and they know how to give that audience a message that they want to hear," Linvill said.

Sponsor Message

A Russian operation put that playbook to work this week to spread a baseless accusation against a Democratic U.S. Senate candidate.

Linvill and several other research groups attributed them to Russian operators the research community has dubbed Storm-1516. It's known for staging fake videos with actors and laundering their claims through influencer accounts with large followings.

Two fraudulent videos targeting the Senate candidate were posted on Tuesday on X by an account created last month that had few followers. The account's X profile said it was based in the U.S. but the social media platform publicly flagged it as possibly using a proxy such as a virtual private network, which could disguise its location.

The videos were likely created using artificial intelligence, according to Graphika, a research company that analyzes online communities. Linvill said a hallmark of Storm-1516 videos is the use of real actors whose faces are swapped using AI to look like someone else.

The post was immediately shared by a network of 15 accounts Linvill flagged as bots. About 12 hours later, one of the videos was shared in new posts by three X accounts with large followings, which researchers said have previously amplified other narratives attributed to Storm-1516. One of them has solicited paid partnerships on X. Soon other X accounts began resharing the large accounts' posts in replies to politicians and journalists.

One of the two fake videos racked up roughly 857,000 views within 24 hours, according to an analysis by Alethea, a threat intelligence company. By late on Wednesday, the account that first posted the videos and one of the large accounts that reshared the claim had been suspended by X, and the two other large accounts that amplified it had taken down their posts.

In the run-up to the 2024 presidential election, Storm-1516 posted fraudulent videos making similar unfounded accusations against Democratic vice presidential nominee Tim Walz and purporting to show ballots for President Trump being torn up.

Sponsor Message

Linvill says the operation tries to glom on to narratives that are already circulating among Americans. "It is hard to persuade anybody of anything, ever," he said. "But what you can do is reinforce beliefs."

This election cycle, Russian operations have also spread messages about Democrats turning away from supporting Israel and fabricated news reports accusing Democratic candidates of corruption.

"I increasingly have come to think of Russia as essentially a dark money PAC," said Lisa Kaplan, who founded Alethea. "You know they're going to be running s. You want to understand what's out there. You want to understand if they're actually effective in moving people in one direction or another."

Intelligence officials have long said Russia has favored Trump and targeted Democrats in its efforts to erode support for Ukraine in the U.S.

On Wednesday, Himes and Sen. Mark Warner, D-Va., vice chairman of the Senate intelligence committee, told reporters they'd seen a recent classified intelligence report on foreign election meddling showing Russia opposes candidates of either party who have backed Ukraine.

Himes stressed that while Russia and other foreign countries have sought to influence voters, there has been no indication that they have been able to interfere with the actual mechanics of voting.

"Nothing out there suggests that there is either the capability or the intent to do interference, whereas there is a pretty robust influence environment," Himes said.

The same Russian operations now active in the U.S. midterms have also targeted elections this year in France, Germany and elsewhere. They've used AI-generated audio and impersonated politicians, celebrities and media outlets, Graphika said in a new report on Friday.

"They have run this playbook in half a dozen other countries in the past six months throughout Europe. We're just the next in line," Linvill said. "They attack with these same themes. Anything that's going to make a candidate seem degenerate, seem corrupt, seem incapable."

Sponsor Message

Kaplan of Alethea says this focus on polarizing issues in the final stretch of the election is less about shaping voter's views and more about inflaming anger or fear to affect turnout.

"In these final posts in the lead up to the election, it's really more about evoking that emotion," she said.

Researchers tracking Storm-1516 and other groups say they expect more false claims and fake videos to come, and for these operations to focus on voting and ballot processing in the period immediately surrounding election day.

NPR's Eric McDaniel contributed to this report.

World.title: The Pentagon's guidelines for "responsible AI" aren't always followed, report shows
World.content:
The Pentagon's guidelines for "responsible AI" aren't always followed, report shows

toggle caption i Government Accountability Office/GAO

The Pentagon is building weapons and projects with artificial intelligence capabilities that officials say don't always closely adhere to the agency's own guidelines for AI, according to a congressional watchdog report published in October.

AI researchers and international organizations have long advocated for strict regulation of AI when used in weapons that could become unpredictable or function with little human control, arguing that those tools could endanger the lives of soldiers and civilians and risk quickly escalating wars. But Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has repeatedly dismissed previous caution of AI tools and encouraged rapid autonomous innovation at the Pentagon.

Sponsor Message

The Pentagon issued a memo in January saying the department would become "an 'AI-first' warfighting force across all components, from front to back." Last month, Hegseth announced a new warfare command focused on autonomous weapon development, including drones.

toggle caption i Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images North America

The watchdog report, published by the U.S. Government Accountability Office on Oct. 14, grants a rare look inside how those kinds of projects are being developed.

The GAO surveyed 10 officials involved with building 10 weapons and tools for the Pentagon that use AI to automatically identify targets on the battlefield, process surveillance and improve tactical decision making, and other tasks. The projects are among more than 300 being built with AI in the Pentagon.

When responding to the GAO survey, six of the 10 officials said their teams had "identified risk(s)" with using the projects "in an operational environment."

To address some of those sorts of risks, in 2021, the Pentagon sent a memo outlining six basic tenets to ensure that weapons built with AI are created responsibly. Those six guidelines mainly stress the importance of Pentagon-wide oversight, verification and "real-time monitoring" of the technology, and cooperation with allies "to advance global norms grounded in shared values."

Alissa Czyz, who directed the GAO review, said the tenets evolved from earlier ethical principles, and while they weren't rules, they were understood to be important by people involved with building AI tools at the Pentagon.

Sponsor Message

"It's a memo, right, at the end of the day, so it's not a department instruction," said Czyz. "It's something that the department has signaled that should be implemented."

Most of the people involved with making the 10 weapons and projects reviewed by GAO had taken "at least initial steps" to follow the six tenets outlined in the memo, according to the report, and some of the projects were in early stages, Czyz clarified.

But some of the responses indicated officials weren't always closely following the guidelines.

Four officials told the GAO that requirements for the weapons and projects they were working on weren't "aligned with Responsible AI tenets." And three of the 10 officials told the GAO they "don't know" if the projects will be continuously monitored after they're deployed, though the six tenets encourage monitoring.

Officials told the GAO that more access to expertise about the agency's guidelines or staff who know about them would increase their ability to incorporate AI responsibly. But the group that helps manage education on the Pentagon's guidelines, the Department of the Responsible AI Division, is understaffed. Although the group was authorized to hire 10 people in 2023, as of February, only three of those positions were filled and the Pentagon "is unlikely to fill vacant positions or increase staffing," the report states.

"That's a very small number of folks tasked with a large responsibility of responsible AI throughout the department," said Czyz.

The GAO issued two recommendations: The Pentagon should more clearly outline the responsibilities and meeting schedules of the office charged with overseeing AI regulation, and address understaffing. Although the Pentagon agreed with those recommendations, as of Oct. 22, the agency had not implemented those changes, a GAO representative confirmed to NPR.

NPR asked the Pentagon when it planned to make those changes, but did not receive a response.

Sponsor Message

When delivering a speech at SpaceX in January, Hegseth indicated he believed AI development at the Pentagon should not be slowed by those sorts of steps.

"Our enterprise currently operates on staffing and committee cycles measured in months and years, and that's unacceptable," said Hegseth. "Military AI is going to be a race for the foreseeable future where the risks to U.S. national security of moving too slowly outweigh the impacts of imperfect alignment."

NPR would like to hear from more people who work with federal agencies or AI companies and have information to share about how agencies are using AI. You can email the reporter of this article, Chiara Eisner, at ceisner@npr.org or contact her on Signal here, username ceis.78.

World.title: Ohio could decide control of the Senate. Its rural voters might decide the winner
World.content:
Ohio could decide control of the Senate. Its rural voters might decide the winner

toggle caption i Keren Carrión/NPR

At the weekday farmers market in Athens, Ohio, colorful vegetables are on display for patrons to purchase, community members interact with each other and vendors and one another. It feels like most people in attendance know one another on some personal level.

For a small town like Athens, the farmers market is a gathering place.

"Our Saturday markets have been fully at capacity," said Paige Walters, the Athens farmers market promotions manager.

Athens, Ohio is home to Ohio University. The city is, like many college towns, pretty liberal. But that's not the case in most of the Appalachian communities in the region.

Sponsor Message

Walters noticed that this year, for the first time in a while, the Athens County Republican Party has set up a table at the market.

"I think that does speak to the political climate right now – that it's pretty competitive," she said.

Despite its past as a swing state, Ohio is now considered to be reliably Republican. This election is a little different. With toss-up races for governor and U.S. Senate, Democrats have a chance to win statewide.

But if Democrats want to win, they have to capture voters who voted for Republicans in the past. That includes the rural Ohio voter base, which historically leans conservative.

While rural voters nationwide have voted red in the past (they backed Trump in 2024 by 40 points), recent polling has shown his approval rating in rural America dropping dramatically amid high inflation, tariffs and the war in Iran.

Democrats are trying to gain ground in the unexpected areas. That's especially true in the competitive Senate match up between Sen. Jon Husted, the Republican nominee, and former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown as both candidates invest in outreach to rural parts of the state.

"There's a lot of people in rural Ohio that are not happy, whether it's gas prices, diesel prices, the tariffs, the war," Matthew White of Athens told NPR at the farmers market.

Sponsor Message

Affordability top of mind

Multicolored bell peppers, onions and squash line the table at the Cowdery Farms booth. While the weekday market usually has slower foot traffic, farmer Larry Cowdery sold a good amount of produce.

He owns a small vegetable farm along the Ohio River in Long Bottom. There are two big concerns at the top of Cowdrey's mind. The first is the cost of healthcare.

"The big, big issue that we run into is since we're self-employed, we have to find health insurance somewhere," he told NPR. "It's going to be much more expensive next year."

Healthcare premiums on the Affordable Care Act marketplace are expected to increase by roughly 15% in Ohio, in part because of the expiration of federal subsidies. Republicans, including Husted, voted to eliminate the subsidies under the Trump-backed "One Big Beautiful Bill." As a result of sticker shock, Ohio saw the biggest drop — tied with Oklahoma for the most in the nation — in the number of people enrolled in the marketplace last year, with a nearly 33% decline in enrollment.

Cowdery's second concern is the survival of his multigenerational family farm. It's becoming too expensive to run. He said the cost of electricity and gasoline is a big factor. Plus, he relies on fertilizer to grow his vegetables.

"I'm not convinced we're even going to be able to get fertilizer next year," Cowdery said.

That's because of the war in Iran. Most of the nitrogen used in fertilizer travels through the Strait of Hormuz, a vital shipping channel in the Middle East controlled by Iran. Travel through the Strait has been volatile.

As a result of the healthcare and business hardships, Cowdery isn't keen on voting Republican this year. He added that he hasn't been happy with the Republican-led Ohio legislature for the last few years and he doesn't like Husted, either.

Sponsor Message

"I don't trust Jon Husted at all. I think he's a crook," Cowdery said.

Dean Ferrell is at the farmers market chatting with people and milling around the market. The 62-year-old man, a lifelong resident of Athens, said the cost of gas, utilities and groceries have become burdensome. He has had to cut back on buying certain foods because he can't afford it.

"I mean, who would ever thought you'd be paying ten bucks a pound for ground beef? That used to be filet mignon prices, not ground beef," he said.

Ferrell tried to look on the upside of his financial reality. Since he's older, Ferrell said he doesn't eat as much as he used to, so he can save some money that way. He added that he wishes politicians could spend "a week or two living like I do."

"Their attitude would be a lot different. I mean, I gotta save money wherever I can, buy reduced and on sale items," Ferrell said. "There's very few things that I pay full price for. You got to, to survive."

Ferrell considers himself to be an independent. While he hasn't decided who to vote for the Senate, Ferrell said he is leaning toward Husted. He doesn't like the direction the Democratic party is headed.

"The far left has basically hijacked the Democrat Party," he said.

A farmer's frustration

On a crisp fall day in rural central Ohio, farmer Chris Gibbs climbs into his John Deere utility terrain vehicle, setting out to survey his land.

"It started in 1983 on our own with $2,500, a pickup truck and a two-year-old daughter," Gibbs said with a chuckle. "So we built that up to 560 acres."

Gibbs, a first generation farmer in Shelby County, grows corn, soybeans, alfalfa hay and has a few dozen cows.

Farming is a tough industry at the best of times. Farms are at the behest of market fluctuations, domestic policy, international relations and mother nature. Tack on high fuel and fertilizer prices, along with Trump's tariffs and the cost of production exceeds the profit.

Sponsor Message

Sitting in his huge combine that used to harvest corn and soybeans, Gibbs said the diesel fuel to run the machinery has increased 50% under the Trump administration and the war in Iran. He fills up the combine about seven times during the harvest season.

"I think about 150 gallons at $7 is $1,000, and that'll run a day and a half," Gibbs said. "That'd be $7,000 worth of diesel fuel."

Politically, farmers tend to vote Republican. Gibbs was one of those Republicans at one point. In a past life, he was the chair of the Shelby County Republicans. He voted for Trump in 2016.

"I'm looking at certainly, buyer's remorse," Gibbs said about voting for Trump.

Gibbs couldn't stand behind Trump's character, his persona on the global stage or the punitive tariffs he said hurt "United States of America's soft underbelly," referring to agriculture. He moved away from Trump in 2018.

Now, in 2026, Gibbs is the chair of the Ohio Democratic Party Rural Caucus and he wants to send Democrat Sherrod Brown back to the Senate.

Brown, Gibbs argued, has the experience necessary to represent rural Ohioans at the federal level.

"We're going to get Sherrod Brown across the line. I have complete confidence in that," Gibbs said.

No career politicians

At a Republican Party event in Guysville, Melissa Jant said she doesn't want a career politician representing her in Congress and that's exactly how she views Brown.

"I absolutely do not want Sherrod Brown back in there. He was there for 30 years. We saw the policies that he put in place. He ran the country down. He ran Ohio down. We just need new blood in there," she told NPR.

Her displeasure toward Brown isn't just because he is a Democrat. Some voters view him as the establishment, despite not being a lawmaker anymore.

Jimmy Williams of Monroe County feels similarly. He said Brown was voted out and shouldn't try and head back to his old stomping grounds. Instead, Williams views Husted as the anti-establishment candidate, despite the fact that he is a sitting senator.

"He's a first-term senator there, and he hasn't even been in there long enough to do everything that they're saying on television," Williams said about ads aimed at Husted. "And people need to be smart enough to look through that."

Sponsor Message

Bob Rouch, of Washington County told NPR he is optimistic that Ohio will stay Republican. He believes Trump has done a lot of good for the county and "it's Ohio's responsibility to keep up with that." If Democrats win control, Rouch thinks they won't doing anything aside from target Trump.

"We're going to have these damn investigations, these attempted impeachments and all the baloney that we went through," he said, referring to the last time Democrats controlled Congress while Trump was president.

Williams argued preserving Republican control of Congress is the goal right now.

"America is at risk," Williams said.

World.title: Canadian privacy watchdogs powerless to hold Crime Stoppers accountable for data breach
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

In the wake of a data breach exposing decades of Crime Stoppers tips that a legal expert called "one of the worst breaches in Canadian history," both federal and provincial privacy watchdogs have suggested their hands are tied.

The true scale of the hack was revealed by an exclusive CBC investigation , which found that more than 1.5 million Canadian tips submitted to Crime Stoppers programs across the country over the past 25 years were compromised.

More than 850,000 tips — about half of all Canadian records identified — included personally identifiable information. We could not determine in every instance whether the information belonged to a tipster, a victim or someone accused of a crime.

Hackers stole the data last March from Navigate360, a U.S. third party that Crime Stoppers hired to manage and secure its anonymous tips.

But CBC has learned that neither the Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada (OPC) nor the Information and Privacy Commissioner of Ontario (IPC) can formally investigate Crime Stoppers for failing to protect tipsters' personal information, due to a glaring gap in Canada's privacy laws.

The federal private-sector privacy law applies to organizations that collect, use, and disclose personal information in the course of commercial activities, the OPC told CBC News in an email — but it "generally does not apply" to not-for-profit organizations like the Canadian Crime Stoppers Association (CCSA) or its local chapters.

Ontario's privacy watchdog also said it does not have the authority to investigate the breach, as it only oversees public-sector privacy law.

WATCH | Crime Stoppers chapters pause programs: More Canadian Crime Stoppers chapters pause program after CBC investigation | Hanomansing Live | Duration closed caption 4:46 At least seven Crime Stoppers chapters have announced they are suspending programs a day after CBC revealed the extent of a massive data leak. Former RCMP superintendent Garry Clement talks to Hanomansing Tonight about how valuable the program has been for law enforcement agencies.

'A significant gap'

The Ontario privacy commissioner said it had already identified this exception "as a significant gap" in 2021, when it called for the adoption of a provincial private-sector privacy law that would more clearly cover the not-for-profit industry.

"The significant volumes of data held by the not-for-profit sector in Ontario are not immune from privacy and security vulnerabilities, yet they remain largely unprotected by federal privacy law," reads the 2021 report, which urged the Ontario government to fix the gap immediately. "No regulator has been given responsibility for this sector."

The issue was first raised in a copy of a CCSA internal memo that CBC News obtained on Thursday.

The June 18 document, signed by CCSA president David J. Forster, urges all chapters to follow a number of guidelines in the wake of the data hack.

WATCH | More on the investigation: Over a million Canadian tips leaked from Crime Stoppers database | Duration closed caption 1:52 A CBC News investigation found more than a million tips submitted to Crime Stoppers in Canada over the past 25 years were exposed in a massive data breach. About half the leaked Canadian tips obtained by CBC contained personal information.

He advised all chapters to direct media inquiries to the CCSA, and not to contact privacy watchdogs.

"We currently do not believe that you are required, nor should you contact the privacy commissioner in your region at this time," instructed Forster, saying his organization has "previously assessed that they [the commissioner] do not have jurisdiction over Crime Stoppers."

CCSA has not responded to CBC's previous request for comment on the contents of the memo.

Cybersecurity expert says Crime Stoppers board could be liable

The legal gap leaves tipsters whose information was exposed with few options for answers.

Still, a lack of formal privacy oversight might not spare the organization or its local chapters from legal threats, said Claudiu Popa, a certified cybersecurity professional with privacy consulting firm Data Risk Canada.

"The accountability trickles up. Where does it go? It goes to the board of directors," Popa said. "These directors are individuals; they are volunteers. They are people who essentially are personally and legally liable for the outcome here."

Crime Stoppers is best known for its public appeals, often partnering with police, for help with unsolved crimes and to advance investigations — all with the promise of anonymity for tipsters who contact them. (Tyson Koschik/CBC)

Popa stressed that the CCSA built its legitimacy on a promise of anonymity that it has now broken.

Regardless of the organization's non-profit status, its leaders could face lawsuits, he said.

"Here's an organization that has made certain claims and these claims established its legitimacy. Those claims proved to be false and therefore this organization could be considered to be illegitimate right back to Day 1."

Memo is 'appalling': Ex-Ontario privacy watchdog

Ann Cavoukian, who served an unprecedented three terms as Ontario’s privacy commissioner, was stunned to find out that the CCSA had advised its local chapters against contacting privacy watchdogs.

"This is appalling!" Cavoukian wrote in an email to CBC News. "I’m not sure if privacy commissioners have jurisdiction here, but if I was still the privacy commissioner, I would go after these folks regardless! This shouldn’t be happening."

In a Friday press release , Navigate360 confirmed its systems had been breached between November 2025 and March 2026 — its first public acknowledgment of the hack, seven months after it happened.

Ann Cavoukian, seen in a screengrab from 2024. (CBC)

Cavoukian also called the organization's apparent failure to de-identify or encrypt its data outrageous, adding that employing a third-party company to manage its information doesn't make the group any less liable.

"You don't just flip your hands and say, 'Well, you know, there's nothing we could do about it.' No, you do that at the outset. The walls should go up; the data should get protected."

The Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada said it "has reached out to Crime Stoppers in order to offer expertise and guidance with regard to responding to [its] privacy breach."

It has also contacted Navigate360 "to obtain more information and determine next steps" and to "ensure that the organizations are taking the necessary steps" to protect Canadians' personal information.

The OPC added that it has not received any complaints about the matter.

World.title: The Marineland belugas keep dying. Was it a mistake to move them?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A few months after a mass relocation effort that stretched across the Atlantic Ocean, six whales have died out of the 30 that were transferred from the now-shuttered Marineland theme park in Niagara Falls, Ont.

The most recent death, a beluga named Cyprus, was announced on Sunday by SeaWorld San Diego — one of five facilities in the U.S. and Spain that took in the marine mammals after Marineland said it could no longer care for them.

The deaths have raised questions about the impact of the transfers on their health and well-being and whether they were fit to travel, and rehashed concerns about the conditions they were living in during the years they spent at Marineland.

But was there ever a better option for the last captive whales and dolphins in Canada?

Advocacy groups such as Animal Justice have pointed to the federal and provincial governments, as well as Marineland, saying they failed to properly plan for the animals' futures. Experts have said they're worried these deaths are just the beginning. Meanwhile, the Department of Fisheries and Oceans maintains the transfers were the best possible rescue plan.

Cyprus, a beluga whale who was rescued from Marineland in Niagara Falls in August, is shown in an undated photo published to social media by SeaWorld San Diego. SeaWorld announced the whale's death on Oct. 18. (SeaWorld San Diego/Facebook)

"This was, I would say, almost kind of a Hail Mary effort in terms of trying to make sure that we could provide a better life for these whales," Dr. Doug Whiteside, the head veterinarian at the Calgary Zoo and a member of the Canadian Veterinary Medical Association's animal welfare committee, told CBC News.

They were already under chronic stress from the conditions they faced at Marineland, Whiteside said. Transferring them caused additional stress, even though international regulations were followed and they went to high-calibre institutions to receive full-time care, he said.

"Is it a risk? Absolutely ... any sort of acute stress may push them over the edge," he said.

While we can't underestimate the stress of the transfers on the whales, that doesn't mean it's not in their best interests to try to give them a better life, said Angela Fernandez, director of the Animal Law Program at the University of Toronto's law faculty.

"People knew that there were stronger and weaker individuals in the mix, just like there would be among a group of 30 human retirees," Fernandez told CBC News.

"You would not evacuate an old-age home and take only the strong individuals if there is capacity to take everyone."

WATCH | Marineland's last living belugas are on 'death watch': Why Marineland's last living belugas are on 'death watch' | Duration 2:42 Marineland transported 34 of its remaining belugas and dolphins to aquariums in the U.S. and Spain over the summer to spare them from euthanasia. But four belugas and one dolphin have since died in their new homes. On Friday, Chicago's Shedd Aquarium released post-mortem details around the deaths of two belugas, indicating the whales were already sick with 'significant gastrointestinal disease.' Necropsy results are still being processed for the other dead animals. CBC News reached out to Marineland for comment but didn't hear back at the time of publication. CBC's Puneet Nijjar explains how the animals got to this point and what scientists suggest could have led to their early deaths.

What happened to Marineland?

Marineland, once Canada's most popular amusement park, has been the subject of controversy for years, with animal rights activists and others vehemently opposed to its practices.

A federal law passed in 2019 that bans keeping whales, dolphins and porpoises for breeding or entertainment in Canada shuttered its business model. Then it never recovered from t he COVID-19 pandemic's tourism slump.

In 2024, the park was put up for sale and began relocating many of its animals. But in 2025, t he federal government blocked Marineland's request to export the remaining belugas to an aquarium in China. Marineland responded by asking for emergency funding from Ottawa, warning that it might otherwise have no choice but to euthanize them.

Releasing them into the wild would lead to certain death for the mammals raised in captivity, marine experts noted. And there was no appropriate seaside sanctuary for them in North America. A proposed sanctuary in Nova Scotia was still years away from being developed.

In May, th e Department of Fisheries and Oceans endorsed a rescue plan to split up all remaining whales between Oceanogràfic València in Spain and four U.S. locations: Georgia Aquarium in Atlanta, Shedd Aquarium in Chicago and two SeaWorld facilities in San Diego and San Antonio, Texas.

By the end of August, the last whale had been shipped out.

PHOTOS | Belugas' journey out of Marineland:

This situation was entirely avoidable, said Camille Labchuk, executive director of Animal Justice, based in Toronto. The animal law advocacy group had pushed for a proactive plan to move the whales to a seaside sanctuary for years, she said, adding there was still time to plan a responsible transition after the 2019 legislation passed.

"It was obvious to everyone that Marineland would one day close, because the public no longer wants to see miserable whales swim in circles in tiny tanks," Labchuk said.

"A seaside sanctuary was always going to be a challenging undertaking ... but these challenges don't excuse the failure to plan for a better option."

Concerns about fitness to travel

Since their transfer, four whales have died at Chicago's Shedd Aquarium, one whale and a dolphin have died at Oceanogràfic València and another whale has died at SeaWorld San Diego — representing one-fifth of the rescued whales.

The first, Peekachu, died on Aug. 25, about two weeks after arriving in Chicago. Rain was next on Sept. 2, followed by Osiris on Sept. 21, both of them also at Shedd. Necropsies for Peekachu and Rain, and preliminary results for Osiris, identified long-standing intestinal and liver issues that began before their rescue, the aquarium wrote in a blog post.

Jelly Bean died on Sept. 17 at Oceanogràfic València, and then Echo, a dolphin, died at the same facility on Sept. 23. They had been experiencing a list of health complications and organ abnormalities that may have developed prior to the transfer, the aquarium said in a news release.

On Oct. 9, Shedd announced the death of Caspian two days earlier, noting it had been concerned about her health for weeks. The aquarium hasn't yet released her necropsy results. Cyprus, the sixth ill-fated beluga, died last weekend. SeaWorld San Diego said an ultrasound determined the animal's intestinal tract did not appear to be functioning normally.

There wasn't much transparency around the condition of the whales and dolphins before they were transferred due to their private ownership, U of T's Fernandez said. "After years and decades in captivity, it would be surprising if they didn’t all have significant health problems."

The deaths raise questions about whether the animals were fit to travel and whether every possible precaution was taken, Labchuk said, adding that the public deserves transparency.

'Heartbreaking,' says former trainer

Kristy Burgess, who worked as a trainer at Marineland from 2022 to 2025, called the deaths "heartbreaking."

Burgess has previously spoken out about the conditions at Marineland, noting that the beluga pools were in desperate need of repair and that the whales were eating paint peeling off the walls.

She now says she wishes there had been more opportunity for independent experts to contribute to the decision-making, as well as greater transparency around the planning, risks and ongoing health of the animals.

"Change has to come with a realistic, carefully considered plan for the animals themselves," Burgess said.

Former Marineland trainer Kristy Burgess says the beluga pools were in desperate need of repair and the whales were eating paint peeling off the walls. (Submitted by Kristy Burgess)

Whiteside, the Calgary Zoo's head veterinarian, said his understanding of the situation is that there simply wasn't a better option.

The belugas were in a "horrible situation" crowded into crumbling pools at Marineland, he said.

At least a transfer gave them a chance for a better life, he said, even if some didn't survive.

The experience is a sad example of what can happen when institutions like Marineland aren't held to account, Whiteside said.

By not being held to account, Marineland allowed the animals to get to a state where they were chronically stressed, crowded in pools and eating paint, he said.

"Right from the get-go, this sets you up for potential failure."

'Their best chance of survival'

Before the animals' transport began, federal Fisheries Minister Joanne Thompson said she had taken reasonable steps to ensure their safety, including individual health assessments for each animal.

In a statement to CBC News on Wednesday, Thompson said she was still confident in the rescue plan, noting that the transfer was "a significant and complex undertaking."

"Marineland was no longer able to care for these animals. I remain confident that this rescue plan gives these belugas their best chance of survival and that they are being cared for by experienced professionals who are deeply committed to their welfare," she said.

The experts and advocates who spoke to CBC News say their concern now is for the fate of the remaining Marineland whales.

"It's almost a certainty that more belugas and dolphins will die," Labchuk of Animal Justice said.

But Fernandez said "that means 24 are safe, at least for now."

CBC News has reached out to Marineland for comment but has not received a response.

World.title: Will the Alberta referendum feed a more polarized immigration debate?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Referendums tend to raise as many questions as they answer. And so it may be for the 10-part questionnaire that Alberta Premier Danielle Smith put to her province — although with a series of no's Albertans have seemingly foreclosed on a number of possibilities.

"I am well aware that not every grievance Alberta has with Ottawa has been resolved," Smith told Albertans on Tuesday night. "There are still many political and constitutional battles ahead of us."

On the question of whether Alberta should remain in Canada the answer was not close. The 75 per cent of voters who chose the first option is decidedly more decisive than the 1980 referendum in Quebec.

Of the 25 per cent who voted for another referendum, it is also fair to ask how many genuinely want secession. According to Abacus Data, making Alberta an independent country was the primary motivation for just 32 per cent of Albertans who favoured Option 2.

Whatever Smith's appetite for future constitutional battles, Albertan voters also proved to be unenthusiastic: all four questions about whether Alberta should pursue constitutional amendments were answered with a "no."

Not even a question about abolishing the Senate — possibly the most-maligned public institution in Canada history — was able to muster even a simple majority of Albertans.

"There's a reason to be skeptical that some constitutional amendments would be worth the effort and ... what I'm seeing is that Albertans would just rather that we spend our time focusing on things where we can make some meaningful change," Smith said at a news conference on Wednesday (at the time, two of the four constitutional questions were being answered in the negative as results were still being tallied).

"That's why I think the numbers were so different on the immigration questions versus … perhaps the constitutional ones."

Beside Smith's own political future, the most unresolved questions raised by her referendum concern immigration — and one of the questions now is whether they will feed into a more polarized national debate on Canada's immigration policy.

Immigration on the ballot in Alberta

Of Smith's 10 questions, four concerned either immigration or potential new rules for newcomers. On its official referendum website, Smith's government claimed that "unsustainable immigration levels over the past 10 years" had "a profound impact" on Alberta's ability "to fund and effectively deliver social services like health care and education — directly impacting Albertans' access to these services and costing taxpayers billions of dollars."

Alberta NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi argued Smith was "scapegoating" immigrants.

"The reality of the matter is even if you took all the young, healthy temporary foreign workers out of the health-care system, even if you denied public education to refugee children, it's not going to make the emergency room lineups any less," Nenshi told CBC's Power & Politics this week. "It's not going to make your classrooms any smaller. It's not going to make anyone's life better."

Just under 55 per cent of voters supported the proposition that the Alberta government should take "increased control over immigration for the purposes of decreasing immigration to more sustainable levels."

WATCH | Smith on what comes next: Danielle Smith says Alberta separatist UCP members can 'join a different party' | Duration closed caption 2:44 Alberta Premier Danielle Smith said her governing United Conservative Party must support the will of Albertans who voted overwhelmingly to remain in Canada, and that disaffected pro-separatist members are free to 'join a different party.'

Three questions that floated possible limitations on how or when newcomers or temporary residents can access health care, education and other social services in Alberta were supported by narrower majorities of 52.4, 53.1 and 52 per cent.

Smith's government has a majority in the Alberta legislature and it didn't need a referendum to pursue any of these initiatives. But the results — notably, none of the immigration questions won a majority in Calgary — may give Smith reason to hesitate.

At her news conference on Wednesday, the premier suggested she was prepared to act quickly on the first question, but she would "proceed with caution" in response to questions two, three and four. She said she did not want to impact anyone who was already residing in Alberta.

While Prime Minister Mark Carney raised some eyebrows when he repeated the "no to the nine" slogan before Alberta's vote, he had also suggested he was inclined to give all provinces more input on immigration.

"To be candid, I don't need a referendum to tell us to co-operate more with the provinces on immigration," Carney told Global News a few days before Alberta's vote. "I think that's where we're headed."

But Alberta's immigration questions also caught the attention of Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre.

An increasingly polarized debate

"I thought it was inappropriate for the prime minister to tell Canadians and tell Albertans that they should vote to continue to give deluxe taxpayer benefits to people who are illegally here," Poilievre said. "And for the prime minister to suggest that Albertans vote in favor of continued mass, unvetted, out of control immigration was a mistake."

The Conservative Party also sent a fundraising appeal to supporters on Tuesday that promised a Conservative government would "dramatically reduce immigration."

The Carney government argues that it has immigration "under control" after steps were taken to curb the intake of international students and temporary workers. The Conservatives obviously disagree.

But the Alberta referendum also landed between two triggers for renewed debate about immigration to Canada.

First, in discussing immigration policy during an interview with the New York Times last month, Carney said, "now the question starts to become: When do we resume some controlled increase in the population, which is the nature of Canada? So that will happen, and we just want to make sure that we've got it under control."

Now the federal government is due to table its latest immigration levels plan, which sets out targets for the next few years for both permanent and temporary arrivals (technically, a new plan is due by Nov. 1, but last year's plan was included in the fall budget).

Speaking to reporters on Wednesday, Carney said his government "will not budge from overall levels that are sustainable." But what constitutes "sustainable" is likely a matter of debate.

At a news conference on Thursday, Conservative immigration critic Michelle Rempel Garner argued "mass immigration" was suppressing wages and driving up rents, to the benefit of corporate profiteers. Conservatives, she said, will "vigorously oppose any attempt by Mark Carney to continue to raise and sustain high immigration levels" and "will push him to lower them."

Claims that the "Canadian consensus" on immigration has been broken are sometimes overstated. Canadians still believe immigration is a net-positive for the economy, but they also believe recent immigration levels have been too high, driven in large part by concerns about the availability and affordability of housing.

Polling by the Environics Institute has also shown a growing gap along the political spectrum, with Conservative voters much more inclined to say there is too much immigration. And the parties themselves may be getting further apart.

That is not the most stable foundation on which to build significant new increases in immigration, however much such increases might be necessary.

If the goal remains to be as open and welcoming as possible — if there is an economic imperative to being so — "proceed with caution" might be good advice for all sides.

World.title: Can millions of people live on the moon? These scientists say yes — but not for very long
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Humans have long dreamed about reaching out and exploring space. Most science fiction, more often than not, portrays cities on the dusty lunar surface and Mars.

And if you listen to some billionaires like Elon Musk and Jeff Bezos, cities on the moon are coming soon.

In fact, in February, SpaceX CEO Musk posted on social media that the company was shifting its focus away from settling on Mars — something Musk has been passionate about for the past decade.

“For those unaware, SpaceX has already shifted focus to building a self-growing city on the moon, as we can potentially achieve that in less than 10 years, whereas Mars would take 20+ years,” he wrote.

For those unaware, SpaceX has already shifted focus to building a self-growing city on the Moon, as we can potentially achieve that in less than 10 years, whereas Mars would take 20+ years. The mission of SpaceX remains the same: extend consciousness and life as we know it to the stars. It is only possible to travel to Mars when the planets align every 26 months (six month trip time), whereas we can launch to the Moon every 10 days (2 day trip time). This means we can iterate much faster to complete a Moon city than a Mars city. That said, SpaceX will also strive to build a Mars city and begin doing so in about 5 to 7 years, but the overriding priority is securing the future of civilization and the Moon is faster. —elonmusk

This statement — and those of Blue Origin CEO Bezos, who has claimed “millions of people” will be living in space by 2045 — intrigued Martin Elvis, senior astrophysicist at Harvard University’s Smithsonian Astrophysical Observatory.

He, along with astrophysicist Jonathan McDowell, honorary professor at the Durham University Space Research Centre in England, decided to take a look at the numbers.

But their findings, it turns out, aren't great for a lunar civilization, so don’t start packing just yet.

In their paper , published in the journal Frontiers in Space Technologies, the pair decided to examine power and water needed to sustain humans on the moon.

When it comes to power, they found that solar and nuclear would be enough to sustain one million people on the lunar surface.

But then there's water.

It may be surprising to some, but there is water on the moon. It’s believed that most of it is contained in permanently shadowed regions (PSR), areas at the poles that never see sunlight.

But in this study, they found that there’s not enough on the moon to sustain a large human presence on the lunar surface.

WATCH | NASA shares plans for Moon Base: NASA shares plans for moon base | Duration closed caption 2:04 NASA has outlined its plans to build a base on the moon that will first be occupied by rovers and drones, but the longer-term goal is human habitation.

“Our work shows that, yeah, if you want to have an Antarctic base on the moon for the next few hundred years, no problem. If you want to have a small town, that's doable. If you want to cover the face of the moon with cities, like in the best science fiction, then you have to find a way to get the water there, because it's not there right now,” McDowell said.

Assuming that there is roughly one billion tonnes of water on the moon, which is in line with current estimates, they found that a civilization of one million people would only be able to live on the moon for roughly 100 years. And that’s only if we can recycle 98 per cent of the water, which is what is done on the International Space Station.

'A small lake'

Elvis said that while one billion tonnes of water sounds like a lot, you have to put it in perspective.

“If you had a huge aquarium the size of Central Park in Manhattan, you could fill it up to where the Statue of Liberty was just underwater and that's the amount of water you've got. So it's huge in one way, but … it's a small lake. And a small lake is not going to supply a big city for very long.”

That’s not to say that humans can’t ever live on the moon. If it were a town of 10,000, they found that would be sustainable for centuries.

However, that's assuming that the one billion tonnes of water is an accurate estimate.

"Very likely a billion is way overestimating. It's probably 20 or 30 times too big," Elvis said.

WATCH | How Artemis II is setting up the next stage of space exploration: How Artemis II is setting up the next stage of space exploration | Duration closed caption 4:42 Jacob Bleacher, NASA's chief exploration scientist, says the first two Artemis missions have set the stage for the next moon landing, a moon base and eventually, human exploration of Mars, missions so challenging that only international co-operation makes them possible.

He also said that it's unlikely that we'd be able to recover all the water that's available. Instead, it would be more like one-third to half of what is present.

"So my best guess is the real amount of water available that we can be fairly confident about is one per cent of what we said before. So instead of 100 years, it's one year."

And there's one other thing: We don't know in what form that water exists. And we need to figure that out.

"It's one thing to detect it from satellites, but ... there are uncertainties in those measurements," said Gordon Osinski, a professor in planetary geology at Western University in London, Ont.

" I think it is there, but let's go and ground-truth that and confirm it. And then there's the bigger unknowns of what form it's in…. Is it more like the permafrost up in the Arctic, where it's basically soil with, you know, sub-millimetre size ice crystals, which are hard to get out of?"

While this may sound like pessimistic news for humanity's plans to explore the cosmos, McDowell said it's best to know what you're dealing with.

"The truth is never negative," he said. "What's negative is to actually go and try and do something that isn't going to work."

World.title: Black Sea sailors thought a rescue boat was racing toward them. Instead, it was a drone that sank their ship
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

In the early hours of Oct. 13, the crew from the HS Dignity gathered on the deck of the cargo ship and put on life jackets as the vessel rocked in the churning waves of the Black Sea. The captain had given the order to abandon the vessel because it was sinking after a sea drone struck its hull.

As the 16-man crew, made up of Syrian and Egyptian nationals, peered into the darkness, they spotted the outline of a boat moving quickly toward them. They shone their flashlights, thinking rescuers might have already responded to their distress call.

But what they saw alarmed them.

No one was driving the boat.

“We realized that this boat was also part of the group that was attacking us. Of course, we all ran,” said Ashraf Mamdouh, the vessel's 42-year-old chief officer.

The sea drone rammed directly into the ship.

“The vessel began sinking rapidly into the water. The whole crew was falling to the deck; nobody could stand properly because of the impact and the chaos,” he said.

“We didn't have time to finish launching the lifeboats.”

WATCH | How the dramatic rescue happened: Inside dramatic rescue as drones hit hundreds of ships in Black Sea | Duration closed caption 4:58 The Black Sea is a key shipping corridor in the escalating war between Russia and Ukraine. Maritime analysts believe there have been more than 500 attacks on commercial ships in the region in the past year, killing mariners and leading to dramatic rescues at sea. Briar Stewart and CBC’s visual investigations team take you inside a strike and speak with one of the survivors.

The Dignity is one of nearly 50 commercial vessels that maritime analysts say have been attacked in the Black Sea this month as the conflict between Russia and Ukraine escalates at sea.

The strikes have brought much of the traffic through the key shipping corridor to a halt and prompted NATO to step up maritime security , including by deploying more patrol boats and radar.

More than 30 killed or missing

At least 31 seafarers have been killed or are missing in the attacks.

Many of the vessels that were recently attacked were travelling through the western Black Sea, including some that were struck off the coasts of NATO members Bulgaria and Romania.

On Friday, a search-and-rescue operation was underway after a ship flagged to Comoros, a small archipelago off the coast of East Africa, was struck by drones just outside Romania's territorial waters.

The crew of 13 included Ukrainian and Azerbaijani sailors. One body has been recovered, while officials say three people remain missing.

Romanian President Nicușor Dan blamed Russia for the attacks.

Data shared with CBC News by maritime risk management firm Ambrey suggest there have been more than 500 attacks on commercial vessels this year in the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov, which are connected by the narrow Kerch Strait.

Of the 45 attacks recorded in October, Ambrey believes Russia was responsible for 40.

Russia's Ministry of Defence has acknowledged striking dozens of ships this month alone in social media posts, almost always claiming the vessels were supporting Ukraine's military.

But Mamdouh, who spoke to CBC News from a hotel in Varna, Bulgaria, said the Dignity had sailed from Algeria and was headed for Romania, where it was scheduled to pick up grain.

Ashraf Mamdouh, the chief officer aboard the HS Dignity, arrives in Varna, Bulgaria, on Oct. 13 after his ship sank when it was hit by two sea drones. (Nikolay Doychinov/AFP/Getty Images)

Adrift in the Black Sea

The Dignity had already been at sea for more than a month when the drones struck at about 1:30 a.m.

Mamdouh and other experienced crew members urged everyone aboard to get as far away from the ship as possible to avoid being pulled under as the 123-metre vessel sank beneath the churning waves.

“We tried to gather together to reduce everyone's fear and panic. We wanted to remain in one group so that, if a rescue team arrived, it would be easier for them to rescue as many people as possible,” Mamdouh said.

This undated image of the HS Dignity shows the ship before it sank in the Black Sea on Oct. 13. (Submitted by Ashraf Mamdouh)

He began calling out to other crew members, but the strong winds drowned out their voices.

“I started asking everyone, ‘Why are you moving away from each other?’ I hadn't realized that I was drifting away, too. The sea currents were separating us.”

At one point, a life raft suddenly appeared beside him. He climbed aboard and lay there for four hours, until another commercial vessel appeared nearby.

Still clutching his cellphone, he switched on its flashlight to attract the attention of the crew aboard the Azov Concord.

Cargo ships are seen in the Black Sea from Port Varna, in Varna, eastern Bulgaria on October 13. (Nikolay Doychinov/AFP/Getty Images)

18-year-old among the missing

Mamdouh was pulled from the water and is one of five crew members who survived. Eleven remain officially listed as missing, including 18-year-old Hamza Suleiman, a Syrian who was on his first voyage aboard a ship.

“The last phone call between Hamza and me was on the night of Oct. 12,” said his father, Basel, who spoke to CBC News via Zoom from Tartus, Syria.

“Hamza contacted us and said hi to his mother and reassured us. He said, ‘Dad, we're in Bulgaria now.’”

Basel said his son had taken the job aboard the Syrian-owned ship because he expected to work in the engine room, where he hoped to learn more about engineering.

Hamza Suleiman, 18, boarded the HS Dignity in August for his first job as a seafarer. He has been missing since the vessel sank on Oct. 13 off the coast of Bulgaria. (Submitted by Basel Suleiman)

But he became disillusioned when he was assigned to work on the deck. He grew increasingly fearful after learning that another vessel, the Alfa Watan, had been struck by drones on Oct. 6.

Ten crew members aboard that ship, most of them Syrian, have yet to be recovered.

After the Alfa Watan attack, Suleiman spoke with his son, who said he wanted to leave the vessel.

Basel Suleiman told CBC News he tried contacting the ship's owners to arrange for his son to disembark in Turkey, but the young man remained aboard.

Mamdouh, who spoke with Suleiman's father, told him that the last time he saw his son, the young man was aboard the ship wearing a life jacket. That detail has helped sustain his father's hope that he might still be alive.

Basel agreed to speak publicly about his son despite the uncertainty surrounding his fate.

“We don't have the ability to reach the [Bulgarian] authorities or to go and look for our children with our own hands,” he said.

Khaldoun Nabelsi, head of the Syrian Seafarers Association of the U.K., said he had been in contact with several families whose relatives had been killed in strikes on commercial vessels. He said he had counted at least 18 Syrian seafarers killed.

“Nobody is forced to take these jobs, but in other ways you are forced. If you want to work, you have to go,” Nabelsi said.

“They have to find a deal to stop this. But from our side, as a seaman or as a shipping company, we can do nothing.”

The deteriorating security situation has prompted the Philippine government to issue a directive prohibiting its citizens from boarding vessels navigating the northern stretches of the Black Sea.

In an image supplied by the Romanian government, the fire-damaged Royad Mammadov ship sits in the Black Sea on Oct. 5 after a suspected drone strike that killed two people. (Romanian Interior Ministry/Handout/Reuters)

Shipping companies scale back operations

Some shipping companies that normally operate in the region are avoiding it altogether or have sharply reduced the number of vessels they deploy there.

Turkey-based ED Shipping has a fleet of 26 vessels, but 19 are currently “laid up,” meaning they are temporarily out of service and not operating at sea, said the company's chief financial officer, Demre İşcen.

One of the company's ships, the Circon, was struck on June 5 while transiting the Sea of Azov. Two crew members were killed.

Ukraine carried out the attack, acknowledging that it had targeted five vessels that night, including ships stationed at occupied Ukrainian ports. Ukraine said the vessels were involved in transporting stolen Ukrainian grain, as well as military cargo and fuel .

İşcen disputes that account, saying the Circon was on its way to a port in the Sea of Azov near Rostov-on-Don, Russia, where he said the company had a contract to load Russian grain.

“Our crew members are Azeri and Turkish nationals. We didn't have anything to do with Ukraine. We didn't have anything to do with occupied-area grain … stolen grain, whatever,” he told CBC News in an interview from Istanbul.

“Ninety per cent of the time, we carry grain cargo from Russia to Turkey, Bulgaria, Romania, Moldova, Georgia, Greece, all around the Mediterranean, Aegean Sea, Red Sea, Black Sea. This is our main trading area.”

İşcen said the company was losing millions of dollars every month and that some of its seafarers were out of work because its ships were no longer travelling to Black Sea ports.

Other mariners say they will refuse any work in the region.

Mamdouh remains in Bulgaria with the other surviving members of the Dignity's crew. They are waiting for new documents so they can leave Europe and fly home.

“I will not go back to the Black Sea again. Never,” he said.

“This situation is too dangerous.”

World.title: Why a new round in the U.S.-Iran conflict could be the most devastating yet
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The warning signs are flashing red with indications that once the ballots are counted in the U.S. midterm elections, the United States and Israel will relaunch their war with Iran.

The next round of attacks could be more devastating than the first, warn analysts.

"A renewed war seems almost inevitable," said Danny Citrinowicz, an Israeli Middle East and Iran analyst whose earlier warnings and cautions about the risks of a direct conflict with Iran were largely borne out by events.

Citrinowicz, who worked for Israel's military as an intelligence official for more than two decades, had initially warned that any U.S. and Israeli attack on the Islamic regime would not likely lead to regime change but would instead end up engulfing the entire region in a wider conflict — an assessment that proved true.

In an interview with CBC News, he said that assessment still holds.

"The problem is there is no silver bullet solution to the impasse we are now at in the Persian Gulf and in front of Trump he has only bad and worse options."

Under U.S. President Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, their countries broke with decades of restraint and shadow warfare and launched two distinct wars with Iran over the past 18 months.

Iranian women look at a building, which was damaged in a U.S. and Israeli strike in March, in Tehran on Aug. 22. (Reuters)

The first in June 2025 began with U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iranian nuclear facilities, lasted 12 days and ended with a fragile ceasefire.

The conflict roared back to life in February of this year following a massive U.S. military buildup in the region. It began with Israel's strikes against Iran's senior leadership, including Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.

Worst round yet

Citrinowicz, who's with Israel's Institute for National Security Studies, said a third round of war could be the worst yet, based on what Iranian officials are telegraphing.

"They will attack the energy facilities in the Gulf. But more than that, they will cause significant damage to civilian infrastructure, communications, as well as cutting off the internet lines going under [the] Hormuz Strait," he said.

He said there is even a possibility that Iran could push some of its massive land army into the fight with limited assaults against Gulf countries that house U.S. bases, such as Kuwait and Bahrain.

"We'll see a regional war with Iran investing a lot in attacking the U.S. presence in the region to cause maximum economical damage to the U.S. international economy."

Smoke rises from a burning vessel, following what the U.S. Central Command said was a strike on an Iranian-affiliated dhow, at a location given as the Gulf of Oman, in this still image taken from a video released on Oct. 14. (U.S. Central Command/Reuters)

Midterm dynamics

While both sides have largely avoided fresh strikes against each other's bases or territory since the summer truce collapsed, the conflict remains active. The U.S. imposed a naval blockade of Iranian ports and Iran has continued to target commercial shipping traffic in the Strait of Hormuz, driving up global energy costs.

Posting on Truth Social Thursday, Trump blamed Iran for trying to artificially drive up oil prices ahead of the midterms on Nov. 3, elections that many pollsters believe will see Trump's Republicans lose control of the House of Representatives and possibly the Senate as well.

"They are even making up fake hits, mines and everything else," said Trump, implying that Iran is exaggerating the extent of the damage it's causing.

A report published this week by the Washington, D.C.,-based Critical Threats Project alongside the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) also suggested Iran is trying to use strikes on shipping to weaken Trump's position heading into the elections.
