"The increase in Iranian attacks on vessels is part of the ongoing Iranian campaign to pressure the United States to meet Iranian demands, including control over the Strait, by driving up global prices," the report said.

People walk on the beach, with vessels in the Strait of Hormuz visible near the beach of Bandar Abbas, Iran, on Oct. 13. (Razieh Poudat West Asia News Agency/Reuters)

Iran's demands

Iran's government wants relief from punishing sanctions, reparations for the damage caused by earlier U.S.-Israel strikes, the release of billions of dollars in frozen Iranian assets and the right to keep its supplies of enriched uranium.

Mediators with Pakistan and Qatar have spent weeks trying to push diplomatic solutions to get the two sides talking again, but to no avail.

For both Netanyahu and Trump, the war with Iran remains unfinished business.

The Islamic regime not only remains in power, but its leadership has also proven remarkably adept at adapting to both the military strikes and the economic blockade imposed by the West.

"The war in some respects has probably persuaded Iran's leadership to double down on their commitment to the revolutionary ideology that has really forged this regime," said Suzanne Maloney, a vice-president and director of the foreign policy program at the Washington, D.C.,-based Brookings Institution.

Like Citroniwicz, she said if war resumes, Trump won't be able to easily contain it.

"The retaliation as we've seen will come not just from Iran, but from its proxies and partners in the region," she said, referring to the Houthi militias in Yemen and Hezbollah in Lebanon.

Iran's goal won't just be to hit back at U.S. military targets but also soft economic targets, such as airports, that could undermine Gulf countries for years to come, she said.

WATCH | How one conflict plays into another: How the Houthi-Saudi Arabia conflict plays into broader Middle East war | Duration closed caption 8:02 Saudi Arabia has recently been rocked by attacks from Yemen's Houthi rebels. The weekend strikes came in response to Saudi's own ongoing attacks on Houthi-controlled parts of Yemen, which resumed in July amid the U.S. and Israel's war with Iran. Analyst Sina Toossi explains how the conflict between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis plays into the broader war in West Asia.

Maloney and Karim Sadjadpour, a prominent Iran expert with the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, were speaking on an online Carnegie panel about the future of the war in Iran.

"I genuinely don't think that President Trump has a clear idea in his head what he's trying to achieve," said Sadjadpour.

"I don't see any possibility of what Trump is looking for — which is like a knockout punch, a military strike — which will essentially force the Iranians into a compromise or capitulation."

Nuclear timeline?

Trump claimed his justification for the initial attacks on Iran was to ensure the country doesn't get a nuclear weapon.

At the time, while Iran possessed enough enriched uranium to theoretically pursue a weapon, many independent experts and U.S. intelligence sources believed it was still likely months away from doing so — and perhaps more importantly, that the regime's supreme leader had not yet made the definitive political decision to cross the nuclear threshold.

Since those initial June 2025 strikes, the human cost of the war has been severe.

Western NGOs claim the death toll in Iran is well over 7,000, including civilians and government figures who have been killed in the joint U.S.-Israeli strikes.

Lebanon has also suffered an especially heavy toll, with local media reporting more than 4,000 fatalities.

Twenty-one U.S. service members were killed, mostly by Iranian strikes on U.S. bases in the Persian Gulf, while more than 70 Israelis have died.

People drive near a billboard depicting U.S. President Donald Trump on a building in Tehran on Sept. 16. (Majid Asgaripour/WANA/Reuters)

There have also been deaths throughout the Gulf countries, including the UAE and Saudi Arabia, as well as in Iraq and Yemen.

The New York Times and other U.S. media are reporting the Pentagon is working on a new battle plan for the possible next round of attacks — but whether Trump will ultimately authorize it is unknown.

'Finishing the job'

Israel's leadership, on the other hand, has made no secret of its push to restart the conflict, with Netanyahu explicitly stating his desire to bring down the Iran regime by "finishing the job."

Netanyahu faces Israeli voters in the coming days, and whether he hangs onto his job could end up in a photo finish.

Relaunching the war with Iran could offer him a tactical way to stay in power; even if his party loses seats, a widening security crisis could lead to the creation of an emergency unity government with members of the opposition, said Citrinowicz.

"The real risk is that Netanyahu will involve his political considerations together with some other operational development in Iran that he is going to not necessarily invent, but probably [inflate]," he said.

A shopkeeper works at his shop in a local market in Tehran on Sept. 26. (Majid Asgaripour/West Asia News Agency/Reuters)

"And this combination will lead to an unnecessary attack against Iran."

Sadjadpour from the Carnegie panel said there is no obvious military way out of the impasse and says Trump's maximalist goals have closed down diplomatic options as well.

"I believe there's a pretty clear formula under which it [Iran's government] compromises," said Sadjadpour. "It's when it faces what I would describe as existential economic pressure, coupled with a clear, limited diplomatic exit.

"If you're asking them to change their identity, that's not going to succeed."

World.title: Brewers withstand Rays' comeback attempt to win Game 1 of World Series
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Trevor Megill struck out Jonny DeLuca with runners on second and third to wiggle out of a ninth-inning jam as the Milwaukee Brewers escaped with a 3-2 victory over the Tampa Bay Rays in Game 1 of the World Series on Friday night in Milwaukee.

DeLuca's strikeout came after Tampa Bay's Liam Hicks had grounded into an apparent game-ending double play that was overturned after a video review. Replays determined that Brewers shortstop Cooper Pratt's right foot was slightly off the bag when he reached to catch a high throw from second baseman Brice Turang.

"You have a big range of emotions," Milwaukee captain Christian Yelich said. "It's a big credit to Trev for locking back in right there and making some huge pitches after you have that emotional dump and then have to get back on it."

Jacob Misiorowski allowed one run and four hits over five innings to earn the victory.

Abner Uribe and Aaron Ashby combined for five strikeouts in three scoreless innings of relief before handing the ball to Megill.

"Not perfect, but good enough to get a win," Misiorowski said.

Yelich hit an RBI triple to spark a two-run rally in the first that put the Brewers ahead for good and delighted a sellout crowd reveling in Milwaukee's first World Series game since 1982. Jackson Chourio and William Contreras each had two hits, including an RBI single. Contreras also threw out two runners trying to steal.

This marks the first World Series featuring two teams seeking their first championship since 1980, when the Philadelphia Phillies beat the Kansas City Royals in six games. The only other major league clubs without a World Series title are the Colorado Rockies, San Diego Padres and Seattle Mariners.

The Game 1 winner has gone on to win the World Series 62.8% of the time.

Tampa Bay trailed 3-1 and hadn't put a runner on since the sixth inning until it mounted its comeback attempt in the ninth.

Jonathan Aranda and Chandler Simpson hit consecutive one-out singles off Megill. A double steal involving pinch-runner Jorge Mateo and Simpson put the potential tying run in scoring position with Rays slugger Junior Caminero at the plate. Caminero walked on a 3-2 pitch in the dirt to load the bases.

Hicks hit a grounder to the right side, and Turang ranged well to his left to field the ball before throwing to Pratt to start what initially was ruled a game-ending double play.

Fireworks went off, players poured onto the field and Milwaukee fans roared — before the crowd hushed as it watched the play again on the videoboard.

A replay review determined Pratt's right foot came off the bag as he caught Turang's throw. Hicks was still out at first, but the Rays now had runners at second and third with the score 3-2.

"I thought Coop had him, and obviously I was wrong," Misiorowski said.

Megill finally closed the deal as DeLuca struck out swinging.

"You just have to lock it back in," Yelich said. "It's the World Series — you have to do what you have to do to make things happen."

By sweeping the two-time defending World Series champion Los Angeles Dodgers in the National League Championship Series, the Brewers had time to set up their rotation the way they wanted by handing the Game 1 start to Misiorowski, the hard-throwing NL Cy Young Award favorite.

Misiorowski opened the game by throwing the fastest pitch ever delivered in a World Series, a 103.5 mph ball to Yandy Diaz. The right-hander finished with a season-low three strikeouts.

"Look, he's so talented. He's such a special pitcher. I felt like for him to be out of the game at five innings, there's a small win in that," Rays manager Kevin Cash said. "The problem is when you knock him out of the game, you've got just an elite bullpen that can match up and come in the ballgame like they did and kept us quiet there."

While Milwaukee started with its ace, Tampa Bay countered with Nick Martinez to give two-time All-Star pitchers Drew Rasmussen and Freddy Peralta an extra day of rest. Martinez struck out five and allowed two runs over five innings, but a slow start proved costly.

Chourio lined a single to right field on Martinez's first pitch, and Yelich drove him home with a one-out triple to center. DeLuca covered 85 feet to track down Yelich's drive but just missed making a diving catch as the ball glanced off his glove.

"I thought Jonny covered a lot of ground right there to even make that play close," Cash said. "I don't think we did too many things wrong. They did some things right. Squared some balls up."

Yelich was batting third in the lineup for the first time since Aug. 3. The three-time All-Star and 2018 NL MVP posted the lowest on-base percentage (.315) and OPS (.692) of his career, but he has stepped up his since being named the first team captain in franchise history the final week of the regular season.

He was the seventh player to triple in his first World Series plate appearance, and the first since Kansas City's Lynn Jones in 1985, according to the Elias Sports Bureau.

Contreras knocked home Yelich with a line-drive single to left that was deflected by shortstop Taylor Walls with the infield playing in.

Tampa Bay got a run back in the fourth.

Aranda drew a leadoff walk and advanced to third when Caminero doubled on a one-out liner with a 112.7 mph exit velocity that sailed over center fielder Garrett Mitchell and off his outstretched glove. Aranda came home on Hicks' groundout to the right side.

Milwaukee extended the lead to 3-1 in the seventh. Pratt drew a leadoff walk from Steven Matz and scored from second when Chourio greeted Kevin Kelly with a two-out single.

That insurance run proved critical.

"The guys settled in right away and did a great job," Yelich said. "We still have a ways to go, but it's nice to get that first one."

World.title: Canadian cybersecurity exec arrested by FBI accused of working with criminals to defraud his own clients
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A Toronto-area cybersecurity executive arrested by the FBI amid a high-profile hacking probe colluded with cybercriminals to extort money from his own clients, according to U.S. prosecutors.

The explosive allegations laid out in a U.S. court provide a clearer indication of how Edward Dubrovsky is suspected of being involved with "threat actors" linked to the notorious ShinyHunters cyber-gang.

ShinyHunters claimed responsibility last month for hacking an FBI jobs portal and stealing a massive trove of data. The group typically demands ransom payments in exchange for not releasing the sensitive data it's obtained.

"The defendant was actually working on behalf of the threat actors," assistant U.S. attorney Anthony Carissimi claimed before a federal magistrate judge in Philadelphia on Oct. 8, according to a court transcript obtained by CBC News.

"Given that those are the charges and that is what he's been arrested for, I suspect that his business will dry up," the federal prosecutor added.

Dubrovsky will contest the charges, his court-appointed defence said.

Dubrovsky, 54, was detained earlier this month during a trip to Philadelphia for a cybersecurity conference. He was charged with an extortion conspiracy offence and "interference with commerce by threats," according to a public docket.

At the time, FBI director Kash Patel said the agency had arrested a "suspected co-conspirator" of ShinyHunters. The RCMP said it was aware a Canadian had been arrested in connection with the case.

FBI director Kash Patel confirmed on Oct. 9 the agency had in recent days 'arrested another suspected co-conspirator of the ShinyHunters group,' the notorious cyber-gang linked to a hack targeting an FBI jobs portal. (Kylie Cooper/Reuters)

During Dubrovsky's 14-minute initial hearing in U.S. District Court, the federal prosecutor provided a brief overview of the case against the Canadian. He did not directly reference ShinyHunters or the FBI cyberattack.

"The reason [Dubrovsky] is sitting here is because he was engaging in essentially a fraud involving his own clients, his own business partners," Carissimi said.

He said Dubrovsky was "clearly engaged in cryptocurrency exchanges with, among other people, a criminal element."

Carissimi told the court that Dubrovsky had been dealing in the cryptocurrency Monero, which the prosecutor said is "renowned for being untraceable." He told the court that, while Dubrovsky has a Canadian passport, he's originally from Latvia and at one point also held an Israeli passport.

Tim Wright, a court-appointed federal defender, described the allegations against Dubrovsky as "completely untested."

"He wants to fight this to clear his name because of his reputation, because he's a businessman," Wright said.

Canadian firm CyberSteward shared this picture of Edward Dubrovsky signing copies of his book Cyber Extortion: Strategic Response at the NetDiligence conference in Philadelphia on Oct. 6. (CyberSteward/LinkedIn)

Self-described 'globally recognized' expert

On his LinkedIn profile, Dubrovsky describes himself as a "globally recognized cybersecurity expert" who helps clients negotiate with ransomware attackers. He recently published the book Cyber Extortion: Strategic Response, intended for victimized companies.

The day before his arrest, Toronto-based tech firm CyberSteward posted a picture of Dubrovsky signing copies of his new book at the NetDiligence conference in Philadelphia.

Heather Osborne, NetDiligence's director of global events and programming, told CBC News in an email that "to our knowledge," Dubrovsky's arrest "did not occur at our event, which ended at 11:30 a.m. on Oct 7."

CyberSteward has not responded to multiple requests for comment on the firm's ties to Dubrovsky, and his employment status.

Wright, the defence lawyer, said in court that Dubrovsky had planned to attend another conference in Canada on Oct. 15, then return to the U.S. for an event in South Carolina.

"He is a very well known and well respected businessman in cybersecurity," Wright said.

The FBI's criminal complaint remains under seal. The document would typically contain further details of the agency's investigation into a defendant and specifics of any alleged offence.

U.S. Magistrate Judge Scott W. Reid ordered Dubrovsky held in custody until he is transported to Texas, where the charges were filed and where he will appear for a formal detention hearing.

As of Friday, public records from the U.S. Federal Bureau of Prisons showed Dubrovsky was still being held at the Philadelphia detention centre where he was taken on Oct. 7.

WATCH | Dubrovsky arrested amid FBI hacking case: Canadian ransomware negotiator arrested in connection to FBI hacking case | Duration closed caption 1:57 Edward Dubrovsky, a Canadian cybersecurity executive who negotiates with ransomware hackers has been arrested in Pennsylvania as authorities investigate a hacking group that claims to have stolen FBI employee information.

'Every system' is vulnerable, Dubrovsky once told CBC

Dubrovsky previously served as managing director at CYPFER, the firm tasked with helping the city of Hamilton, Ont., recover from a 2024 cyberattack.

The company recently told CBC News that Dubrovsky wasn't involved in the Hamilton file.

Once hired as a York University cybersecurity instructor, he appeared in Canadian media as a commentator on related issues and was previously interviewed by CBC News.

"Every organization uses vendors and service providers to do some of their business," Dubrovsky said in 2018, "so every single system in the world has vulnerabilities."

David Shipley, CEO of the Fredericton-based firm Beauceron Security, told CBC News in an interview earlier this month that Dubrovsky's case highlights his own longstanding reservations surrounding ransomware negotiators.

"We have seen people fall from grace before," Shipley recalled.

He urged ransomware victims who have backed up their data to seek to restore uninfected files, rather than paying a ransom.

"There's no guarantee that paying [the attackers] gets you out of the pain," he said.

If you have a news tip related to this story, contact CBC News senior reporter Thomas Daigle by email: thomas.daigle@cbc.ca.

World.title: Adam Pankratz: David Eby thought this would be easy
World.content:
Article content

Finally, came the daycare bombshell. At a campaign stop on Oct. 12, Eby was asked if his family had taken advantage of B.C.’s notoriously hard to access $10 a day daycare spots. “Yes” he had, said Eby. Perhaps this, more than any other campaign misstep, could prove to be the killer blow for the NDP leader. While the other campaign misfires were ludicrous and hypocritical in their own right, his daycare blunder has serious “cut through.” That is to say, normal people going about their lives who may ignore other political disagreements, will definitely notice the hypocrisy here. Eby, who is married to a doctor and whose family likely has a household income north of $500,000, is taking a $10/day spot, which everyone knows is intended for families in need. That cuts through all other election noise and it sticks precisely because it stinks.

World.title: Conrad Black: Alberta referendum should spur Canada to do better
World.content:
Article content

This is an opportunity for Canada. U.S. President Donald Trump raised again recently his rather tedious refrain about Canada being the 51st state, and being unable to function otherwise should be used by Prime Minister Carney as a stimulus for completing reforms to Confederation and not just as the cue for a reprise of his Churchillian shtick opposite the great orange beastly ogre on the other side of Lake America. Canadians should understand that Trump does not dislike Canada and is not threatening to invade or attack it. But he has concluded that an independent Canada won’t succeed, despite the best efforts of many, this writer included, to convince him that most Canadians don’t wish to be Americans and don’t have unlimited admiration for the violence, corruption, extreme disparities of wealth, contentiousness and vulgarity of American life, though almost all Canadians would acknowledge there’s much to admire about the United States. The strength, success and influence of that country and its contribution to the advancement of democracy, human rights and the free market are beyond question.

World.title: De la Espriella sacks interior minister after Congress bungles Colombia’s 2027 budget
World.content:
Colombia President Abelardo de la Espriella sacked Interior Minister Rodrigo Lara hours after Congress found a procedural flaw in the passed 2027 budget, which makes the law invalid.

In a post on social media platform X, De la Espriella briefly thanked Lara and announced he would be replaced by the ambassador to the Organization of American States, Alejandro Ordoñez.

The news surprised the interior minister, who suddenly left a congressional debate on a law to facilitate the demobilization of illegal armed groups after receiving a message on his phone.

Lara was apparently held responsible for the blunder of Congress, whose two houses approved the 2027 budget but with conflicting versions of an article on financial risk-coverage mechanisms for the Ministry of Finance.

By the time the error was detected, the budget debate had passed its October 20 deadline, forcing De la Espriella to issue a decree that would convert an older version of the budget bill into law.

The interior minister was the administration’s primary political liaison responsible for managing legislative procedure and whip operations in Congress.

Lara’s job was already under pressure after he failed to convince Congress to cede its presidency to the president’s candidate.

While Ordoñez returns from Washington, Justice Minister Ivan Cancino will assume the role of interior minister.

The incoming interior minister is an ultra conservative Catholic with ties to the Society of St. Pius X, which considers the modernizing reforms of the Catholic Church heresies and errors, and was declared in a schism with the church in June.

In Colombian politics and particularly among the opposition, Ordoñez is mainly remembered as the inspector general who illegally removed former President Gustavo Petro from his post as mayor of Bogota in 2013.

Petro was ultimately reinstated and would become president of the country in 2022.

World.title: Colombia’s Congress approves De la Espriella’s 2027 budget
World.content:
Colombia’s Congress agreed to increase the government’s 2027 budget despite promises by President Abelardo de la Espriella to reduce public spending.

Next year’s budget will be COP634.9 trillion, almost $204 billion, which is 16% more than last year’s budget and 10% higher than the proposal made by former President Gustavo Petro.

According to Finance Minister Miguel Gomez, the budget seeks to bring the State’s finances in line with reality.

The budget was approved in both the Senate and the House of Representatives with the support of De la Espriella’s government coalition.

The Historic Pact, the only leftist opposition party, rejected the budget and boycotted the vote.

On behalf of the national government, I would like to thank you all for your work over the past few months in passing the budget. I would also like to thank the opposition for the strength with which they defended their views. The message that Congress has sent today regarding the government’s economic policy is very important. It is the first step toward putting the country’s economy back on track toward growth, fiscal responsibility, and addressing the nation’s needs. Finance Minister Miguel Gomez

The budget seeks to reimpose the neoliberal model that had been abandoned by Petro and reduce public debt.

According to Green Party representative Jaime Raul Salamanca, who opposed the budget, funding for free higher education was cut in half from COP800 billion ($254 million) to COP400 billion (127 million).

“This cut raises concerns about its potential impact on the continuity and scope of this policy, which has enabled thousands of young people to enroll in public institutions of higher education,” said Salamanca.

The budget also cut the budget for the war crimes tribunal JEP, which could endanger the future of the peace process with the FARC and is opposed by the government.

World.title: De la Espriella announces “open, resolute, and patriotic struggle against wokeism”
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella announced an “open, resolute, and patriotic struggle against wokeism” as part of his “cultural counterrevolution.”

During a visit to the Culture Ministry, De la Espriella described wokeism as “an ideological paradigm that aims to transform moral, cultural, and social foundations in the West, perverting values, family tradition, and national identity.”

According to the president, Culture Minister Paola Holguin was a general in the “cultural counterrevolution.”

Culture has an enormous capacity to shape society, and that is why the State has a moral, inescapable, and political duty to prevent cultural spaces from being taken over by social communism, which is atheist and an enemy to the fundamental values upon which the nation of Colombia is built. This is where that cultural counterrevolution will begin. President Abelardo de la Espriella

De la Espriella said that Holguin, the daughter of a reported money launderer, would lead the “Culture War” against the “extreme left,” which has “permeated all parts of society, particularly the cultural and academic spheres.”

I want to be clear about this: we are going to wage an open, resolute, and patriotic struggle against wokeism, which is nothing more than an ideological movement that aims to transform the moral, cultural, and social foundations of the West, corrupting values, family tradition, and national identity. President Abelardo de la Espriella

Earlier in the day, the National Museum removed all references to members of the exterminated Patriotic Union party, slain guerrilla leader and presidential candidate Carlos Pizarro, and the struggle for the rights of Colombia’s LGBT+ community.

References to Colombia’s former guerrilla movements was “terrorism apology, which is “exactly what we have come to confront” in an attempt to “recover pride for Colombian culture.”

Atheists, the Pizarro family and gay rights activists rejected the president’s attempts to remove them from mainstream culture.

World.title: Colombia’s first lady promises transparency over earthquake donations
World.content:
Colombia’s first lady, Ana Lucia Pineda, vowed to reveal how much money she collected and spent in response to the August 10 earthquake that affected hundreds of thousands of people.

Amid mounting public pressure about where the money had gone, Pineda went on the morning program of public television channel Nuestro Caribe to promise that her foundation, Luz y Sonrisas, will take its finances public on Friday.

Carrying a white folder, the wife of President Abelardo de la Espriella stressed that “in the foundation’s accounts rest all, absolutely all of the monies from the donations we received during the ‘Colombia One Single Heart’ campaign” that was announced on August 12.

“A lie is not going to tear down the truth of who I am or what I represent, or how my children recognize me,” said Pineda.

Luz y Sonrisas was one of three NGO’s that were promoted by the De la Espriella government to collect contributions for victims of the earthquake.

Pineda’s foundation was the only one that could receive contributions from abroad.

Earlier in the week, news program Noticias Uno revealed that her foundation that was founded on July 7 lacked the tax exemption that would allow it to accept donations, a process that usually takes months.

In a press statement, tax office DIAN subsequently said that it had granted the tax exemption to the first lady and that she could legally accept financial contributions.

Pineda did not say how much money she had received, but said that she stopped supporting the initial relief efforts “because the humanitarian aid was sufficient, it was huge.”

The first lady vowed she had saved the donations for the reconstruction phase “because I have also taken the initiative to build and return to the victims a house that is durable for the families who lost everything.”

World.title: Colombia’s opposition takes to the street to protest De la Espriella
World.content:
Despite intimidation attempts by the national government and the police, tens of thousands of people took to the streets throughout Colombia to protest the far-right government of President Abelardo De la Espriella.

The protest had been organized by social organizations, labor unions and the country’s largest opposition party, the Historic Pact.

Opposition leader Ivan Cepeda, who joined the protests in Bogota, told a reporter that the government is “exercising a mafia-style rule in the service of the worst elements of Colombian politics—the drug trade.”

Contrary to what De la Espriella is saying, this is not a government that opposes drug trafficking; it is a government that supports the drug trafficking cartels, the paramilitaries, and the ultra-conservative forces that want to destroy people’s rights, the democratic advances made by President Gustavo Petro, and the progress achieved by the popular movement over the past four years. Senator Ivan Cepeda

“That’s why we’re here; we won’t allow people’s rights to be violated or trampled upon,” said the senator.

Hours ahead of the protest, the president signed off on a decree that changed the police response to protests and accused the organizers of being “instigators of evil” who “seek to once again cause chaos.”

Human rights organizations denounced that the security forces put snipers on the roofs of buildings in Bogota and in Cali, a helicopter flew over the heads of the protesters.

The protests sought to test the waters for an even larger “national strike” that is set for November and shut down parts of the country in 2021.

“We are only warming up,” warned Cepeda, who has yet to recognize De la Espriella as Colombia’s legitimate president after losing the elections in July.

World.title: Colombia’s national strike organizers “are instigators of evil,” claims De la Espriella
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella called labor unions and social organizations who organized anti-government protests for Wednesday “instigators of evil” who “seek to once again cause chaos.”

In an address to the nation, De la Espriella stressed that the security forces were instructed to allow peaceful protests, but warned the protesters that “if they intend to set Colombia ablaze, they will face the determination of the tiger and his government to do what is lawfully required—which is to defend the lives, honor, and property of all Colombians.”

Wednesday’s protests are a preparation for a national strike that is set to take place in November and is supported by the country’s political opposition to the far-right government.

According to the president, “those who are promoting the strike and seeking to use it to once again cause chaos and destabilize the government are the very same people who left the country bankrupt, on the brink of a blackout, with the healthcare system in intensive care, energy sovereignty compromised, and public resources plundered and looted.”

“They are instigators of evil, not fighter for freedom,” said De la Espriella.

If they intend to set Colombia ablaze, they will face the determination of the tiger and his government to do what is rightfully required—which is to defend the lives, honor, and property of all Colombians. President Abelardo de la Espriella

The president stressed that he would be signing a decree that regulates public protests in an attempt to avoid the chaos that erupted during massive strikes in 2019 and 2021 an killed 80 people.

De la Espriella additionally is expected to present an “anti-terrorism stature” to Congress, which could see the prosecution of protest organizers on terrorism charges, according to opposition leaders and security experts.

World.title: Colombia declares official start of El Niño, warns of strong impacts
World.content:
Colombia’s meteorological institute IDEAM officially declared the arrival of El Niño, and warned that the climate phenomenon could trigger water shortages and forest fires.

In a press statement, the IDEAM said that its “confirmation reflects the sustained warm conditions in the Pacific Ocean, which, according to the latest measurement, broke records, reaching a sea surface temperature anomaly of +3.49°C.”

The meteorological institute said it expected that this year’s “Godzilla El Niño” could continue to disrupt local climate patterns until March next year.

Initially, the weather phenomenon is expected to reduce rainfall between October and December, which is normally the rainy season in large parts of the country.

“Given this situation, and in light of the alerts issued since the beginning of the year, the national government launched an interagency response,.. with specific instructions for the responsible agencies to have their contingency plans formulated and activated by November 30 at the latest,” said the President’s Office in a statement.

The National Unit for Disaster Risk Management (UNGRD) coordinates response capabilities across the country and enhances the monitoring of wildfires using satellite technology. For its part, the Ministry of Environment and Sustainable Development is taking steps to protect strategic ecosystems, water sources, and the most vulnerable areas. President’s Office

The Mining Ministry “is implementing an emergency plan aimed at ensuring the country’s energy security by strengthening thermal power generation, securing fuel supplies, and implementing efficiency and conservation measures,” according to the President’s Office.

EPM, the local utilities firm in Medellin, has been testing the effectiveness of water rations as they fear the lack of rain could affect the hydro-electric power plants that provide the northwest of Colombia much of its energy.

Before leaving office on August 7, former President Gustavo Petro ordered the mass purchase of solar panels to reduce the pressure on the electric grid.

World.title: Colombia’s draft counterterrorist statute “creates foundations of dictatorial and inquisitorial regime:” opposition
World.content:
President Abelardo de la Espriella’s antiterrorist statute would criminalize political opposition, social movements, and social protest, and essentially form a dictatorial regime, said opposition leader Ivan Cepeda on Wednesday.

In a video, Cepeda said that the true purpose of the bill that was leaked earlier seeks “to advance in the formation of essentially a dictatorial regime,.. which, moreover, has such a regime prostrate to drug trafficking.”

“The true objectives of this statute are to wage a crusade against the political opposition, social movements, and social protest, which is a legitimate right of citizens,” said the Senator of the Historic Pact party.

“Most of the articles in this draft are devoted to provisions that seriously undermine civil liberties, human rights, and the right to protest—not to illegal armed groups,’ according to Cepeda.

The broad legal definition of the word terrorism would allow the government to prosecute protest organizers on terrorism charges if any clashes occur between protesters and police.

This law could serve to intensify the persecution already underway in Colombia against journalists, judges, students, teachers, union members, peasants, indigenous people, people of African descent, LGBTIQ+ individuals—in short, any person or group that criticizes the citizen Abelardo de la Espriella, his government, law enforcement, or any state institution. Such a person could be taken to prison—without even prior warning—and subjected to abuse and torture. Senator Ivan Cepeda

Furthermore, the creation of a National Registry of Terrorist Organizations and Actors would allow the government to criminalize citizens based on an administrative rather than a legal basis, and “grants extraordinary powers to the president to regulate a statutory judicial procedure, specifically the expedited preventive detention proceeding,” said the opposition leader.

The aim is to criminalize social protest; the alleged crime of “manipulating the civilian population” punishes anyone who promotes, finances, organizes, or leads crowds—this is the language of the draft statute—and this is nothing less than the institutionalization of political persecution and the criminalization of free speech. Senator Ivan Cepeda

The antiterrorism statute will be facing opposition when the government tries to push the legislation through Congress, Cepeda said.

“The Historic Pact rejects this and will do whatever is necessary to ensure that the opposition’s rights and guarantees are respected,” said the opposition leader.

World.title: Burnham tells Trump of the “economic consequences” of Argentina’s Falklands measures
World.content:
Burnham tells Trump of the “economic consequences” of Argentina’s Falklands measures

24th Saturday, October 2026 - 08:32 UTC Full article

Trump has said in recent weeks that the US position of neutrality on sovereignty over the archipelago is under review

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham set out to US President Donald Trump on Friday “the economic consequences that Argentina’s coercive measures have for the United Kingdom and the United States”, in a phone call focused on the Sea Lion oil project north of the Falklands, according to a Downing Street statement quoted by the EFE news agency. Burnham reiterated the islanders’ right to develop their natural resources.

The call came a day after US Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau acknowledged in Buenos Aires that Washington is closely watching the impact Argentina’s National Sovereignty Defence bill could have on its companies. The bill, still stalled in the Chamber of Deputies, extends sanctions to affiliates, shareholders, financiers and suppliers of companies operating in the islands. Trump has said in recent weeks that the US position of neutrality on sovereignty over the archipelago is under review.

The same day, Burnham spoke with Chilean President José Antonio Kast, to whom he raised “the UK’s interest in ensuring that Falkland Islanders retain the ability to exercise their right to self-determination”, according to Downing Street. The two agreed on the need to work together to modernise their defence capabilities and that there are “untapped trade opportunities” between their countries. Kast reiterated Chile’s support for Argentina’s sovereignty claim during a state visit to Buenos Aires in April, while his government described the new commercial route between Punta Arenas and Stanley in September as “a business between private parties”.

Argentina launched sanctions proceedings in September against dozens of people and companies linked to Sea Lion, operated by Navitas Petroleum and Rockhopper Exploration, and asked the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea to order a halt to the project. The tribunal will hold its hearing on November 10 and 11 in Hamburg. The United Kingdom has announced measures to protect its companies from Argentine sanctions and maintains that the islanders’ decision to remain British, expressed by 99.8% of voters in the 2013 referendum, must be respected.

World.title: Eight in ten Argentines barely make it or fall short by the end of the month, survey finds
World.content:
Eight in ten Argentines barely make it or fall short by the end of the month, survey finds

24th Saturday, October 2026 - 02:00 UTC Full article

Some 79% of respondents have a credit card

Some 45% of Argentines just about reach the end of the month and 34% fail to cover their expenses, according to a survey by consultancy Brain Network carried out in September, which describes a picture of financial stress, rising debt and little capacity to save. Among those who had trouble paying, 40% use their credit card to cover shortfalls.

The study classifies respondents into three groups. The “Jugglers”, 57%, keep up with payments through frequent adjustments and a fragile balance; the “Up to date”, 22%, are more stable; and the “Overwhelmed”, 21%, have insufficient income and recurring arrears. People over 50 predominate in the first group, and those aged 30 to 39 among those facing the most severe difficulties.

Some 79% of respondents have a credit card. Besides using it to cover shortfalls, those who had trouble paying resorted to cutting spending, 31%; borrowing from family or friends, 23%; delaying payments, 17%; and taking out loans, 16%. In the past six months, 60% of those with bank debts and 65% of those owing digital finance platforms had difficulty paying. Among the “Overwhelmed” with problems, 21% took out a new loan to cover another debt.

“The market is not in default, it is juggling,” said Lionel Holzman of Brain Network, who recommended that lenders offer refinancing before the situation worsens. Some 45% of those in arrears say they have not received any such offer.

President Javier Milei recently challenged the idea that people cannot make ends meet: “If they really run out of money on the 20th, how do they live ten days without eating or drinking?” he said in Neuquén. According to the survey, 44% believe their situation will improve next year, 36% that it will stay the same and 20% that it will worsen.

World.title: Bolsonaro apologises twice to Lula in a calmer final debate as polls show a dead heat
World.content:
Bolsonaro apologises twice to Lula in a calmer final debate as polls show a dead heat

24th Saturday, October 2026 - 01:39 UTC Full article

The first apology came when Lula asked why he had voted against extending maternity leave as a state deputy in Rio de Janeiro. “It was a mistake,” Bolsonaro replied

Senator Flávio Bolsonaro apologised twice to President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva during the last televised debate before Sunday’s runoff in Brazil, held on Friday night on TV Globo, which was more measured in tone than the first. The candidates arrived level: the latest Datafolha poll, published on Thursday, gives each 50% of valid votes.

The first apology came when Lula asked why he had voted against extending maternity leave as a state deputy in Rio de Janeiro. “It was a mistake,” Bolsonaro replied. “Today, after having children, I would vote completely differently.” Lula retorted: “When you had the chance to vote in favour, you didn’t.” The second came after the senator called the president “nine fingers”, a nickname referring to the finger he lost in a workplace accident as a metalworker. “I will not allow a militiaman to call me nine fingers,” Lula replied, contrasting his working-class background with his rival’s. Lula also asked him about having once referred to Bolsa Família as “Bolsa Fodder”.

Argentine President Javier Milei featured again. Lula compared his rival’s proposals with those of the Argentine government, and Bolsonaro turned the argument around: “In Argentina, the left governed for 20 years and destroyed the country. Milei began his government with 200% inflation.”

Bolsonaro, who won the first round with 47.03% of the vote against Lula’s 45.16%, focused on the cost of living and public debt. He promised to cut taxes, raise the minimum wage and pensions above inflation and not to privatise oil company Petrobras or Banco do Brasil, and challenged Lula for the vote in the northeast, his main stronghold: “I will be the most northeastern carioca you have ever seen.” Lula defended his investment in infrastructure and in that region, accused his rival of not knowing the country and recalled the oxygen shortage in Manaus hospitals during the pandemic.

The debate was held under new rules barring candidates from entering each other’s space, requested by Lula’s campaign after the first encounter. On Saturday, candidates may take part in events but can no longer ask for votes.

World.title: Lula accuses Bolsonaro of “licking Trump’s boots” in the final debate
World.content:
Lula accuses Bolsonaro of “licking Trump’s boots” in the final debate

24th Saturday, October 2026 - 01:30 UTC Full article

Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva on Friday accused his runoff rival, Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, of “licking the boots” of US President Donald Trump during the last televised debate before Sunday’s election.

Lula said Bolsonaro was behind Trump’s decision to impose tariffs on Brazilian imports, a recurring accusation the senator has repeatedly denied. “But I wasn’t worried; if Trump doesn’t want to buy from Brazil, I’ll sell elsewhere,” he said in the TV Globo debate, referring to the opening of new markets during his term. Brazil “has never exported so much” as it does now, he added.

Bolsonaro, for his part, accused Lula of “massacring” the farm sector with high interest rates and reminded him that he had recently said farmers should “kneel” before him for his government’s investment. “Why do you humiliate people, why do you treat the farm sector so badly?” he asked. Lula replied that his rival “memorises but doesn’t learn” and that agriculture received more resources under his government than under former president Jair Bolsonaro, the candidate’s father.

Bolsonaro won the first round with 47.03% of the vote against Lula’s 45.16%, and the latest Datafolha poll puts them level at 50% of valid votes each.

World.title: The Pope cancels a visit to Assisi as a medical precaution, two weeks before his South American tour
World.content:
The Pope cancels a visit to Assisi as a medical precaution, two weeks before his South American tour

23rd Friday, October 2026 - 18:19 UTC Full article

According to a medical bulletin released by the Vatican on Friday, a follow-up chest X-ray “confirmed his optimal post-operative recovery”

Pope Leo XIV has cancelled a visit planned for Tuesday, October 27, to Assisi, in central Italy, after his doctors advised against helicopter travel so soon after the lung surgery he underwent on October 13. It is the first engagement on his schedule to be called off since the operation, two weeks before the start of his tour of Uruguay, Argentina and Peru.

According to a medical bulletin released by the Vatican on Friday, a follow-up chest X-ray “confirmed his optimal post-operative recovery”. “However, given the short time that has elapsed since surgery, the attending physicians considered it appropriate to advise against the helicopter flight planned for October 27 as a precautionary measure,” it added.

In Assisi, the Pope was due to take part in a peace gathering marking the 40th anniversary of the World Day of Prayer for Peace convened by John Paul II. He will send a message to the organisers and participants.

Leo XIV, 71, underwent surgery at Rome’s Gemelli hospital to remove the lower lobe of his right lung, where he was diagnosed with adenocarcinoma. On Wednesday, the Vatican said the tumour was localised and that he will not need further treatment. On Sunday, in his first appearance before the faithful since the operation, the Pope said he would resume his activities “gradually”.

The Vatican has announced no changes to the South American tour, scheduled from November 6 to 17, which will begin in Uruguay, from the 6th to the 8th, and continue in Argentina, until the 11th, and in Peru.

World.title: US confirms concern over the impact of Argentina’s Falklands bill on its companies
World.content:
US confirms concern over the impact of Argentina’s Falklands bill on its companies

23rd Friday, October 2026 - 10:25 UTC Full article

Landau also defended the US proposal to end the UN Decolonisation Committee, before which Argentina presents its claim every year

US Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau acknowledged in Buenos Aires on Thursday that Washington is closely watching the impact that Argentina’s National Sovereignty Defence bill, which toughens sanctions against those involved in hydrocarbon exploitation in the Falklands, could have on its companies. Argentine Foreign Minister Pablo Quirno defended the initiative.

“We are obviously looking at the interests of our companies. It is natural for any country to be concerned about that, but I want to stress that we respect the legislative process of the great Argentine nation,” Landau said at a joint press conference at the San Martín Palace, after meeting Quirno together with Assistant Secretary for Western Hemisphere Affairs Juan Pablo Segura. The US concern centres on the bill’s extension of sanctions to affiliates, shareholders, financiers and suppliers of the companies involved, as the newspaper Clarín reported on Sunday.

Quirno said current legislation needs changes to give the country better tools and denied that the bill targets anyone in particular: “This law is not against anyone in particular, it is not against any company in particular.” He explained that it seeks to make companies choose between investing on the mainland or in the islands. “We hope they will always choose the Argentine mainland over the illegitimate licences of the Malvinas Islands,” he said. The bill remains stalled in the Chamber of Deputies.

Landau also defended the US proposal to end the UN Decolonisation Committee, before which Argentina presents its claim every year, as part of a broader reform of multilateral bodies, and asked that it not be read in light of any specific dispute. Quirno replied that its possible disappearance would not weaken Argentina’s claim or UN resolutions: “Our claim is global, in every international forum and above all at the United Nations.” He reiterated that Argentina seeks a peaceful negotiation with the United Kingdom.

On bilateral matters, Quirno announced US funding against drug trafficking and child trafficking and for a cybersecurity centre, and a framework with the Export-Import Bank to explore up to US$7 billion in financing for the Andes-Atlantic Corridor. On the conditions of Washington’s support, he said: “The only condition is that we keep doing what we are doing.” US Vice President JD Vance is expected to visit Argentina in November.

World.title: Lula and Bolsonaro agree to open their bank and phone records days before the runoff
World.content:
Lula and Bolsonaro agree to open their bank and phone records days before the runoff

23rd Friday, October 2026 - 10:13 UTC Full article

The initiative arose from a challenge Lula issued to his rival during Sunday’s televised debate

Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Senator Flávio Bolsonaro signed an agreement at the Superior Electoral Court on Thursday to simultaneously lift the secrecy of their bank, tax and phone records, and those of relatives and linked companies, three days before Sunday’s presidential runoff. Release of the data now depends on a decision by Judge André Mendonça, the case rapporteur.

The document covers the past eight years and provides for the information, requested from the Central Bank, financial institutions, the tax authority and phone companies, to be published on a public portal of the electoral courts. Lula signed in person; Bolsonaro did so through his lawyer, Maria Claudia Bucchianeri, who had sought to extend the period covered. Allies of the president expressed doubts about whether the senator would comply.

The initiative arose from a challenge Lula issued to his rival during Sunday’s televised debate. On Tuesday, the president filed authorisation with the court to open his data if Bolsonaro did the same. The senator made his acceptance conditional on including presidential corporate card spending since 2023, the schedule of First Lady Janja Lula da Silva, visits by the president’s children to the official residence, the use of official helicopters and the government’s links with former banker Daniel Vorcaro. Lula’s campaign accepted the conditions, according to its coordinator, Senator Camilo Santana.

The agreement comes amid mutual accusations of corruption. Bolsonaro is under investigation for alleged corruption and money laundering in connection with the Banco Master case, and one of the president’s sons, Fábio Luís Lula da Silva, for alleged influence peddling. Both deny the accusations.

Polls show a statistical tie between the two candidates, who hold their final debate on Friday on TV Globo.

World.title: Lula and Bolsonaro chase non-voters in the final stretch of Brazil’s campaign
World.content:
Lula and Bolsonaro chase non-voters in the final stretch of Brazil’s campaign

23rd Friday, October 2026 - 10:02 UTC Full article

The latest Datafolha poll gives Bolsonaro 51% of valid votes and Lula 49%, within the margin of error, while Quaest puts them at 46% and 44% of total voting intentions

Two days before Brazil’s presidential runoff, President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Senator Flávio Bolsonaro are focusing their final efforts on the same target: the roughly 33 million voters who stayed away in the first round. With polls showing a statistical tie and just 1% or 2% undecided, mobilising those who stayed at home on October 4 could decide the outcome.

The latest Datafolha poll gives Bolsonaro 51% of valid votes and Lula 49%, within the margin of error, while Quaest puts them at 46% and 44% of total voting intentions. In the first round, Bolsonaro won 47.03% and Lula 45.16%. Since direct elections returned in 1989, no candidate who came second in the first round has won the presidency.

Both campaigns are targeting two groups for whom voting is optional: people over 70, who have high abstention rates, and 16- and 17-year-olds. Lula’s campaign has mobilised activists and supporters on the streets and online, with large events such as the rally on São Paulo’s Avenida Paulista and the “Lula’s Army” WhatsApp channel, with millions of followers. This week the government began paying the 15% increase in Bolsa Família, and the Senate approved the 40-hour working week, one of the president’s flagship pledges.

Bolsonaro, for his part, has the backing of almost all right-wing and centre-right parties and of ten governors elected in the first round. He has centred his message on security and the economy, promises to create a Ministry of Prosperity and keep social programmes, and has also called his supporters to Avenida Paulista and mobilised them online through channels such as “Flávio’s Troop”.

The digital battle has reached the courts: both campaigns accuse Meta of unequal treatment on its platforms, and the Superior Electoral Court has ordered it to guarantee equality between the candidates. Lula and Bolsonaro face each other on Friday in their final debate, on TV Globo, before Sunday’s vote.

World.title: Sunday’s Binational Race San Diego-Tijuana will feature a cross-border course
World.content:
The third edition of the Binational Race San Diego-Tijuana takes place on Sunday and, for the first time, features three separate distances, two of which are cross-border events.

Participants can choose between the 21-kilometer half marathon, the 12-kilometer race — both starting at the Las Américas shopping center in San Diego’s San Ysidro neighborhood — or the 10-kilometer race, which starts in Tijuana.

Organizers Benjamin Castillo and Valeria Rivera anticipate that 4,500 runners from both sides of the border will participate, twice as many as took part in 2025 and three times as many as the 1,500 entrants in the inaugural event in 2024.

Approximately 3,000 runners will compete in the half marathon, another 1,000 in the 12K and 500 others will run the 10K. Also, about 150 volunteers (50 on the U.S. side and 100 in Mexico) will be on hand to assist participants throughout the day.

Castillo voiced confidence that the event will become a permanent fixture on the race calendar. Registration for next year’s race on Oct. 24, 2027, will open this weekend.

More than a race, organizers say the Binational Race was created to celebrate cross-border culture, unity and friendship and seeks to promote social, athletic and community exchange between San Diego and Tijuana.

San Diego city officials enthusiastically endorsed the idea when first promoted by local runners, community organizers and advocates. Their support was mirrored in Tijuana, where local leaders and organizations jumped on board to ensure the race could showcase the best of both cities.

Castillo told MND that the support of local officials on both sides of the border has been “fundamental” in arranging race logistics, adding that “at no point have they presented obstacles.”

The event partners with regional nonprofits and charities on both sides of the border, including Laboratorios Delia Barraza, the Xolos de Tijuana soccer club, Coca-Cola, Univisión, Casa Familiar, Fundación Castro Limón, the Emilio Nares Foundation as well as “mile sponsors.”

Where will they be running?

The half marathon begins at 6:50 a.m., while the 12K and the 10K start at 8:30 a.m. The finish line for all three races is at the Playas de Tijuana Lighthouse.

After starting outside the Las Americas Premium Outlets, the half-marathon course enters San Diego’s scenic Tijuana River Valley Regional Park around the 5-kilometer mark (allowing participants to run amid rare coastal sand dunes, salt marshes and riparian forests), before reaching the border at kilometer 10.

Here, runners utilize a designated lane to pass through the San Ysidro–El Chaparral international checkpoint into Mexico — the busiest land border crossing in the Western Hemisphere — where they will be greeted by a traditional mariachi band.

From the Tijuana Viaduct, runners are rewarded with panoramic views of San Diego before facing the biggest physical challenge of the course: Enchilada Hill. Once conquering that climb, the final 5 kilometers are a fast, downhill run to Playas de Tijuana.

The San Diego-Tijuana Binational Race is the longest U.S.-Mexico cross-border race.

El Paso, Texas, and Ciudad Juárez, Chihuahua, hold an annual 10K race (the 8th edition will take place on April 4, 2027), while Laredo, Texas, and Nuevo Laredo, Tamaulipas, sponsored the Dos Laredos Binational Marathon in 2024 and 2025, but have not held another race.

With reports from SanDiego.org, San Diego Magazine, Zeta and KSDY Noticias

World.title: Public perception of insecurity hits its lowest level in 13 years
World.content:
Listen to this article

Security Minister Omar García Harfuch said the perception of insecurity in Mexico has fallen to its lowest levels since the national statistics agency INEGI began collecting the data in September 2013 — and yet, 58.1% of people aged 18 and older still consider it unsafe to live in their city.

“The survey also shows important advances in what people observe and hear in their communities,” García Harfuch said in a social media post, adding that those surveyed reported fewer robberies and fewer instances of gunfire.

The quarterly security survey is carried out by INEGI in approximately 28,000 homes across 91 cities spanning all 32 states. Individuals aged 18 years and older who permanently reside in private housing units within designated urban areas are asked about the principal problems affecting their neighborhood.

García Harfuch said the results showed that, compared to September 2025, residents in 28 of the 91 cities felt that there were significant improvements.

The survey reflects the public’s perception of security and does not, in itself, constitute a measurement of crimes committed in the country.

Instead, the survey measures how safe or unsafe citizens feel in their cities generally as well as in specific public spaces, such as at ATMs, on public transit or in the streets.

In general terms, the survey found that 68.7% of the population reported feeling unsafe at ATMs located on public roads, 61.8% felt unsafe on the street, 61.1% felt uneasy on public transport and 55.3% felt unsafe on the highway.

Irapuato, Guanajuato, holds the ignominious claim to being the least safe city in Mexico, as 90.5% of its adult population consider it unsafe. Residents of Chilpancingo, Guerrero, followed with 86.9%, and Mazatlán, Sinaloa, was next with 85.8%.

At the other end of the spectrum, San Pedro Garza García (an affluent suburb of Monterrey, Nuevo León), registered the lowest percentage, with 5.8%, while the borough of Benito Juárez in Mexico City reported reduced levels at 13.8%.

With regard to comparative statistics, cities that saw a significant increase in the perception of public insecurity between June and September 2026 were Hermosillo (the capital of Sonora), which rose from 43.2% to 53.2%; Lázaro Cárdenas (a major port city in Michoacán), from 33.0% to 42.3%; and Ciudad Victoria (the capital of Tamaulipas), from 47.5% to 56.5%.

World.title: Mexico’s best-known ufologist’s latest claim is a humanoid ‘being’ near the northern border
World.content:
A camera-trap video from the Juárez Valley in Chihuahua has given Mexico’s best-known ufologist, Jaime Maussan, a new mystery: a pale, long-limbed creature that he describes as an agile, intelligent, humanlike predator capable of walking on two legs.

To online commenters, the figure looks more like a pigment-deficient iguana, an albino lizard or an escaped exotic pet.

😱 De acuerdo con los investigadores algunas de las imágenes fueron obtenidas mediante cámaras trampa 🫣🔍

https://t.co/p10Wwp3s6b — El Heraldo de Juárez (@heraldodejuarez) October 22, 2026

Maussan’s team said the footage was recorded Oct. 14 between 7 and 8 p.m. in the rural farming area southeast of Ciudad Juárez, along the Rio Grande near the U.S.-Mexico border.

The images show what the group describes as a hairless, reptilian-looking creature with a long tail and elongated limbs.

The team says it has documented or received reports of three sightings since July. In the latest images, the creature appears to climb a brick wall and descend a tree.

Researchers working with Maussan estimated it measured about 1.8 meters (nearly 6 feet), including a tail they said was about 90 centimeters (3 feet) long. However, their estimates were reportedly based on the comparative size of the wall in the video.

Maussan has called the being “El Ser del Valle de Juárez” — the Creature of the Juárez Valley. His team has linked it to reports of dead chickens, rabbits, roosters and other animals, including two horses in the Samalayuca area.

He compared it to “El Ser de Metepec,” a purported alien creature said to have been caught in a rat trap near Toluca in 2007 — and later identified as a taxidermy-altered squirrel monkey.

All of this has revived talk of the chupacabra, a folkloric creature blamed for attacking animals, especially livestock. The name means “goat sucker” in Spanish, although no scientific evidence has established the existence of such a being.

Maussan also floated the unsupported possibility that the being in the footage is an interdimensional being.

“It’s a predator,” he told NetNoticias.Mx, according to the El Paso Times. “I’m not saying it’s extraterrestrial, but it is something scary.”

However, publicly available evidence so far consists only of blurry video, photos and unidentified witness accounts. No carcass, DNA sample or other biological evidence has been released for independent examination.

Juárez Civil Protection director Sergio Rodríguez said his agency had received no official reports or evidence of a mysterious animal attacking livestock or pets in the valley. The department’s recent responses in the area have been related to rain damage, not animal attacks.

The El Paso County Sheriff’s Office told the El Paso Times it had received no reports on the Texas side of the border involving unusual farm-animal deaths or sightings of a strange creature.

Maussan, a journalist and self-described ufologist, has spent decades promoting UFO and paranormal claims. His fame in Mexico is such that Mexican pop star Belinda enlisted him this week for a mock emergency broadcast from a “spaceship” to announce that her annual Beliween Halloween party will have an extraterrestrial theme this year.

Maussan hosts “Tercer Milenio,” a long-running Mexican TV program focused on UFO sightings, extraterrestrial claims and other paranormal phenomena. In 2024, he was part of a promotion offering guests an overnight Airbnb stay at his home and research bunker in the forest.

In 2023, he appeared twice before the lower house of Mexico’s Congress, the Chamber of Deputies, with mummified remains he claimed were nonhuman. Experts challenged the extraterrestrial claim, pointing to studies of similar specimens that found assembled human and animal remains.

With reports from Infobae, El Paso Times, La Opción de Chihuahua and Daily Mail

World.title: Opinion: China’s model is cracking and Mexico (and the world) should get ready now
World.content:
In the last couple of months, I had the great opportunity to moderate three conversations about trade in international forums. The first was with Kate Kalutkiewicz, who served as Special Assistant to President Donald Trump and Senior Director for International Trade at the National Economic Council. The second, with Daniel Watson, who until very recently was Assistant U.S. Trade Representative for the Western Hemisphere (USTR). The third, with Michael Pettis, professor at Peking University and co-author of the well-known book Trade Wars Are Class Wars.

I won’t disclose what any of them said specifically. I will, however, share some of the ideas we discussed and my conclusions in the following lines.

Let me start with a few “stylized facts”. First, the new era in trade policy is built on economic security. The free movement of goods and services is no longer the guiding principle.

The easiest way to understand this new dynamic is as a managed trade system that limits non-aligned countries (read: enemies) from accessing the supply chains of critical industries and favors local production, or at least production among allies, of those goods and services.

In plain English: separating as much as physically possible from China and its allies, and from their exports of steel, aluminum, critical minerals, energy, vehicles, and technology, while bringing that production back to the neighborhood.

Which leads me to the second stylized fact: China is the enemy of the United States. Every conversation about trade comes down to how, when, and who is going to decouple from China, and what they can do to support re-industrialization and job creation in the United States. That is, of course, if your interest is to stay close to the Americans.

The third and last one is tariffs. They’re not the answer. Tariffs on countries such as Mexico and Canada have the immediate effect of increasing the overall deficit the United States absorbs. They have even become unpopular among American voters and will most likely play a significant role against Republicans in the upcoming midterm elections. As a tool to reach the first two objectives, economic security and decoupling from China, tariffs are, besides being erratic, a misguided policy.

China and the opportunities ahead

When we look at the numbers, China isn’t as strong as some might think. Its debt-to-GDP ratio is above 300%, and debt continues to grow at more than 10% per year. Its unemployment rate is in the double digits (the exact number is hard to know), wages are suppressed, productivity is artificially boosted by subsidies, and the country lacks the capacity to consume what it produces. So the excess supply gets shipped at very low prices all over the world. That’s basically their growth model. But when the biggest consumer market in the world and its allies are looking for ways not to buy China’s excess production, the conditions for a collapse get closer, and fast.

This is a serious threat to China and to the world’s economy. We’ve all relied on this system for the past three decades. The sirens are on, and it’s up to the rest of us to get ready.

So, how do we get ready?

Each country has to do its part, and there are two sides to it: one international and another national.

On the international front, it’s about picking sides and coordinating. This is not a party where two superpowers “fight” while the rest of the world sits and watches. Everyone plays a part. This is a continental battle. The U.S. and its allies should present a united front to bring the production of semiconductors, medical devices, drugs, critical minerals, energy, data centers, ships, and vehicles back to “safe harbor.” Just to state the obvious: the opposite is happening.

At the national level, at least in Mexico, the opportunity is to be ready for the hit. Let me put it less dramatically and more as an opportunity. When China collapses, if it does and as it does (it won’t be overnight), Mexico should have the installed capacity to absorb part of the production China will no longer be able to deliver. Mexico must focus on domestic policies that would enable it to welcome a tsunami of investment: sufficient energy, first-class infrastructure, a trained workforce, and a seamless, trustworthy bureaucracy.

The United States should match this with its own industrial policy, ideally twinned with or planned alongside Mexico and its other allies. That way, those policies get reinforced and multiplied with resources from its partners.

I’ll say it one more time: you don’t win a trade war alone, and even less by beating your allies and friends. The way forward is together, or it simply isn’t.

Pedro Casas Alatriste is the Executive Vice President and CEO of the American Chamber of Commerce of Mexico (AmCham). Previously, he has been the Director of Research and Public Policy at the US-Mexico Foundation in Washington, D.C. and the Coordinator of International Affairs at the Business Coordinating Council (CCE). He has also served as a consultant to the Inter-American Development Bank. Follow his Substack here.

World.title: 20 new industrial parks delivered, bringing to 40 the total under Sheinbaum’s Plan México
World.content:
Less than two years after its launch, President Claudia Sheinbaum’s Plan México has delivered 40% of the 100 industrial parks projected in the economic and industrial strategy’s six-year blueprint.

Alongside representatives of the Mexican Association of Private Industrial Parks (AMPIP) at the National Palace on Thursday, Sheinbaum announced the delivery of 20 new industrial parks, with a reported investment of between US $670 million and US $763 million.

This brings to 40 the total number of these factory districts completed since Plan México was launched in January 2025.

The new developments are located in eight federal entities (the states of Baja California, Coahuila, Nuevo León, México state, Aguascalientes, Guanajuato and Querétaro, along with Mexico City) and 17 municipalities.

The new industrial projects are distributed in four strategic corridors, with a greater concentration on the northern border and the region linked to the Felipe Ángeles International Airport located outside of Mexico City. Ten of the new properties are located in Coahuila and Nuevo León.

The new parks comprise a total surface area of ​​4.6 million square meters, with the capacity to house approximately 175 companies. President Sheinbaum said the new projects hold the potential of creating 32,127 jobs.

David O’Donnell, president of the AMPIP Board of Directors, said the industrial parks are a key part of the infrastructure that makes it possible to attract capital, strengthen supply chains and connect workers, suppliers, universities, communities and markets.

“Mexico’s industrial base is a great strategic asset for the country,” he said, adding that the country’s geographic location, talent and manufacturing experience allow it to participate in global value chains.

The new parks — all 20 of which already have companies installed and in operation — will house industrial activity in key markets such as electronics, medical devices, logistics and e-commerce, sectors that have been expanding in Mexico.

O’Donnell said the AMPIP and its associates will have invested US $4.6 billion this year in the development of industrial infrastructure.

The investments are expected to increase Mexico’s competitiveness, as well as boost formal employment, training, security and development opportunities for families.

“We believe that industrial growth should translate into well-being for Mexican families and opportunities for young people,” he said.

With this second delivery, AMPIP now has 40 industrial parks in operation, developed by 26 industrial real estate companies and distributed across 14 states.

Together, they represent an investment of over US $1.4 billion and more than 8.2 million square meters of industrial infrastructure.

With reports from El Economista, Obras por Expansión and Excelsior

World.title: Uber launches ride-hailing service in Tulum and Playa del Carmen
World.content:
Uber has begun offering rides in Tulum and Playa del Carmen, Quintana Roo, expanding its operation in the state beyond Cancún and Chetumal.

According to reports from news outlets Uno TV and Excelsior, the ride-hailing app began operations on Oct. 20, offering introductory promotions including rides at zero cost.

The company’s website confirms that rides can now be booked via its app.

Uber’s arrival occurs amid dissatisfaction with the costs of traditional transport in Tulum and Playa del Carmen.

In Tulum, a merchant named Mauricio Morales told Uno TV that he viewed the competition as a positive development, noting that the apps offer an affordable alternative to taxis. He said a 10-minute taxi ride from town center to the archaeological site ranges between 150 and 200 pesos (US $8 and about $10.70). Meanwhile, apps like DiDi — which was already operating in the area along with inDrive and Itaxi — charged between 60 and 80 pesos (US $3 and $4).

Among traditional transport operators, however, the reaction was different.

Brigadier Hernández, a taxi driver with the “Tiburones del Caribe” union in Tulum, told newspaper Excélsior that the sector is struggling due to a lack of passengers and warned that new platforms could further diminish their work opportunities. The driver recounted that on the day of the interview, he had gone about an hour without securing a fare.

His concern highlights the contrast between the expectations of users — who seek to pay less — and those of workers who rely on every single trip to sustain their income.

Reports also revealed that the company is preparing to expand into Tulum and Playa del Carmen with Uber Taxi, which connects app users to tradtional taxis, and the ultra-low-cost Uber Moto, where users can hop on the back of a driver’s motorcycle. The combination of services would replicate the model that is already in place in Cancún, as well as in cities like New York and Paris.

The ride-hailing company has already opened driver registration for both options, El Heraldo de México reported.

This development comes three years after Uber won the right to operate in Quintana Roo.

With reports from Excelsior and Grupo Animal

World.title: El Jalapeño: Departed spirits tiring of same old Día de Muertos altar offerings
World.content:
All stories in El Jalapeño are satire and not real news. Check out the original article here.

Ancestral spirits traveling across the spiritual plane for Mexico’s annual Día de Muertos celebrations expressed growing fatigue Thursday with the repetitive selection of altar items, requesting that surviving relatives consider modernizing their ofrendas for the upcoming holiday.

According to a nationwide survey conducted by the Trans-dimensional Cultural Ministry, over 78% of visiting souls reported that while they appreciate the sentiment of marigolds, water and salt, three consecutive centuries of pan de muerto and cold tamales have left the spirit realm desiring more culinary variety.

“Look, I love my great-great-granddaughter, and the copal incense smells lovely, but I died in 1994, not the Middle Ages,” said former Oaxaca resident Héctor Morales, speaking through a spiritual medium in Mexico City. “Every November 2, I make a 12-hour journey across the void only to find the exact same clay bowl of mole and a bottle of cheap tequila. Just once, I’d like to cross over and find a sparkling water and some avocado toast.”

The study noted that while traditional symbolism — such as papel picado representing wind and candles lighting the pathway — remains popular among older generations of the deceased, spirits who passed away in recent decades are requesting items that reflect their actual earthly habits.

“My family still puts out a pack of unfiltered cigarettes and a glass of warm pulque every single year,” said Sofia Reyes, who passed away in Guadalajara in 2011. “I spent the last years of my life drinking oat milk lattes and listening to podcasts. If they really want to honor my memory, they can leave some Starbucks coffee and an active Wi-Fi password on the second tier of the altar.”

Cultural historians observe that the mismatch stems from a misinterpretation among the living, who often view ofrenda guidelines as rigid doctrine rather than dynamic personal tributes. This has led to widespread spiritual dissatisfaction regarding what are often perceived as outdated mementos.

“Tradition is vital, but we are seeing a clear structural divide between living expectations and deceased preferences,” said Dr. Elena Vasquez, a researcher in folkloric logistics at the National Autonomous University of Mexico. “The living treat the altar as a museum exhibit, while the dead view it as a room service menu.”

As the holiday approaches, municipal authorities have advised families to consider minor adjustments to their customary setups, suggesting that an occasional craft beer or artisanal pastry placed beside the traditional sugar skulls could significantly improve spirit satisfaction scores across the country.
