World.title: Hurricanes? Above-average rainfall? They weren’t enough to prevent more drought in Mexico
World.content:
Despite above-average rainfall in much of the country during the first half of October 2026, the overall area affected by moderate to severe drought increased compared to the same period of the previous year.

According to Mexican Drought Monitor data through Oct. 15, a dry spell has impacted Mexico’s southeast and just over 35% of the country’s territory registered abnormally dry conditions (tagged as “D0”), moderate drought (D1) or severe drought (D2). A small area in northeasternmost Mexico is experiencing extreme drought (D3).

The Monitor did in fact report that recent rains helped reduce the affected areas in some “abnormally dry areas and areas with moderate to extreme drought in portions of the states of Chihuahua, Nuevo León and Tamaulipas,” particularly in Tamaulipas where the elimination of extreme drought was notable.

It attributed the above-average rainfall during the first half of October to the steady arrival of low pressure troughs and monsoon troughs. Additionally, the influence of Hurricane Simon and Hurricane Trudy in the Pacific and Tropical Storm (later Hurricane) Isaias in the Gulf of Mexico was significant.

However, the rains were “not enough to reverse the accumulated precipitation deficits from previous months in the south and southeast.”

In the state of Tabasco, 56.1% of the surface area registered moderate drought and another 19.3% is suffering from severe drought, while 35.9% of the state of Chiapas registered moderate drought and 8.4% is seeing severe drought.

In Guerrero, 15.9% of the state experienced moderate drought and 2.1% severe drought, whereas in Oaxaca, the proportions were 17.5% and 4.8%, respectively.

The Monitor also reported below-average rainfall in the east and in specific areas of the northwest.

The data for the first half of October showed slight improvement when compared to the second half of September. September ended with 64.6% of Mexico’s territory free from drought and by Oct. 15 that figure had inched upto 64.9%.

But using year-on-year comparison, the moderate to severe drought categories — D1 to D2 — that covered 12.7% of the national territory as of this October 15 represented an increase of 5.2 percentage points compared to the 7.5% reported on Oct. 15, 2025. The affected proportion was almost 70% higher than a year earlier, the Monitor said.

The conditions are in keeping with the projections that the El Niño phenomenon would produce increased temperatures in northern regions of the country in September and increased oceanic heat content in the Mexican Pacific between September and December.

With reports from El Economista, Gaceta UNAM and Crónica Veracruz

World.title: US Justice Dept Sues Over Alaska Ballot
World.content:
The west front of the US Capitol in Washington, where the House of Representatives and the Senate meet (file photo; Photo: Architect of the Capitol, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons)

Key Facts Lawsuit: The US Justice Department asks a federal court to block Alaska from certifying its Senate result if Sen. Dan Sullivan loses.

Why: It says a candidate with the same name, Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., could mislead voters.

Next: No hearing or ruling has been reported; Election Day is Tuesday, 3 November.

Prediction markets: Polymarket prices Democrat Mary Peltola at 74.5% to win Alaska and Democrats at 67.5% for the Senate (as of 6:22 a.m. ET, 24 October).

This story is part of our coverage of the 2026 US midterm elections. Dates, times and how to follow it are in our guide. Latest: US House Odds Favour Democrats at 91%

The US Justice Department has sued to stop Alaska from certifying its Senate election result if Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan loses on 3 November, according to reports on 23 October. The case is one more flashpoint in the 2026 US midterm elections, where control of the Senate is still open.

The department argues that another man named Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. is on the ballot to confuse voters. President Donald Trump told reporters on Friday that he was the one who said to bring the case.

What the Lawsuit Asks For

The suit was filed in the US District Court for the District of Alaska and asks the court to bar certification of any result affected by voter confusion. The department says it should apply if Sullivan does not win.

Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. appears on the ballot with no party label. State election officials tried to remove him in June, but Alaska courts kept him on.

Voters wait in line for early voting in Metairie, Louisiana, in October 2024 (file photo; Photo: Infrogmation, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons).

Reactions and What Is Unclear

Peltola, the Democratic nominee, has called the suit a political threat to overturn an election. Sen. Lisa Murkowski, a Republican, said the department should not have filed it.

No judge has set a hearing, and no court has ruled. It is also unclear whether federal law lets the department stop a state from certifying a result after voters have cast their ballots.

What Prediction Markets Say

Alaska Senate winner (Polymarket, about US$1.6 million traded): Peltola 74.5%, Sullivan 25.5%.

Control of the US Senate (Polymarket, about US$8.9 million traded): Democrats 67.5%, Republicans 32.5%.

Control of the US House (Polymarket, about US$21.2 million traded): Democrats 91.5%, Republicans 8.5%.

Prices are the implied probability of each outcome as of 6:22 a.m. ET on Saturday, 24 October. They are real-money bets, not polls.

Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

Polls Before Election Day

The New York Times/Siena poll released on 21 October showed Democratic House candidates ahead 52% to 41% among likely voters. An ABC News/Washington Post/Ipsos poll found Democrats ahead 52% to 44% among likely voters.

The Senate is closer than the House, which is why one state with a legal fight can matter. For the wider numbers, see our midterm polls data room.

What It Means for US Readers

If the Alaska race is close, a court fight over certification could delay the final result in a Senate seat that helps decide control of the chamber. Investors who watch Washington for tariff and sanctions policy would then wait longer to know who sets the agenda in 2027.

Voters in Alaska use ranked-choice voting, so the order of choices counts if no one wins a majority. Results are not expected to be certified until after Election Day.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why is the Justice Department suing over Alaska’s Senate election?

It argues that a candidate with the same name as Sen. Dan Sullivan could mislead voters. It asks a court to block certification if Sullivan loses.

Who is Daniel J. Sullivan Jr.?

He is a candidate on Alaska’s Senate ballot with no party label. Alaska courts kept him on the ballot after officials tried to remove him.

Has a court ruled on the lawsuit?

No ruling or hearing had been reported as of 24 October. We will update when the court acts.

What do prediction markets say about Alaska?

On Polymarket, Peltola was at 74.5% to win the seat at 6:22 a.m. ET on 24 October. These are bets, not polls, and prices can move quickly.

When is Election Day?

Election Day is Tuesday, 3 November 2026. Polls open and close under each state’s rules.

World.title: Paris Unions Accept Police March Route
World.content:
Protesters hold up placards in Paris on 17 October 2026, the day the cost-of-living protests turned into riots. (Photo: FreCha, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

Key Facts What happened: A Paris court rejected the unions’ appeal, and they accepted the police route.

Who decided: The Paris administrative court backed the police prefecture’s route.

The route: Porte d’Italie to Porte de Vincennes, the only authorised Paris march.

What happens next: The march starts at 8:00 a.m. ET (2:00 p.m. Paris) today.

Prediction markets: Polymarket puts a French state of emergency by 31 October at 8.5% (24 October 2026, 6:05 a.m. ET, 12:05 p.m. Paris).

This story is part of our coverage of the why France is in crisis. Dates, times and how to follow it are in our guide. Latest: Limoges Under Curfew After City Hall Fire

Published Saturday, 24 October 2026, 6:25 a.m. ET (12:25 p.m. Paris) · Source: Franceinfo, BFMTV

Unions in Paris have accepted a police-set route for Saturday’s France protests after the Paris administrative court rejected their appeal. The march between Porte d’Italie and Porte de Vincennes is due to start at 8:00 a.m. ET (2:00 p.m. Paris), Franceinfo reports.

The coalition of unions and student groups had called the route impossible to secure on Friday. Franceinfo and BFMTV, two French news outlets, report that organisers agreed to march after the ruling.

In plain English France’s unions called a national day of protest over living costs. The Paris police chief, called the prefect, chooses which streets a march may use. Unions went to court to change the route, lost, and have now agreed to follow it.

How the Route Dispute Ended

The Paris police prefecture first agreed a march from Place de la Bastille to Place de la Nation with the unions. On Friday, 23 October, it banned that route and offered a march from Porte d’Italie to Porte de Vincennes instead.

The prefecture pointed to violence and damage seen at earlier protests, in particular on 13 October. The Île-de-France union coalition filed an urgent appeal on Saturday morning, and the Paris administrative court rejected it.

File photo: riot police in Paris after the 17 October 2026 unrest.

Who Said What

Karl Ghazi, co-secretary general of the CGT in Paris (one of France’s largest unions), had called the new route impossible to secure. The Paris police prefect, Patrice Faure, has said the earlier violence calls for great caution in choosing routes.

France 3 reports a reinforced deployment with elite police units and armoured vehicles. The interior minister has also announced helicopters and water cannon. A separate Bastille to Opéra march, declared by Interfac Île-de-France and the Yellow Vests (a protest movement over living costs), was banned by the prefecture.

What Prediction Markets Say

On Polymarket, a state of emergency in France by 31 October trades at 8.5% and by 31 December at 14.5%, with about US$668,000 traded. On Kalshi, a US exchange regulated by the CFTC, the same question trades at 11.0% for before 1 November (24 October 2026, 6:05 a.m. ET).

Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

What It Means for US Readers

Anyone in Paris today should expect heavy policing and crowds along the southeastern edge of the city. The march starts early on the US East Coast, so first reports will come in the morning.

The route fight shows how tightly the government is managing protests after a week of unrest. Calm marching would ease pressure, while clashes would test the state’s tougher line.

What Is Not Known

No turnout figures, arrests or damage reports are available yet. The march’s end time and the number of people who will join it are not confirmed.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the authorised Paris protest route on 24 October?

The only authorised route runs from Porte d’Italie to Porte de Vincennes. It starts at 2:00 p.m. Paris time, which is 8:00 a.m. ET.

Why did the unions change course?

The Paris administrative court rejected their appeal against the police route. After the ruling, organisers agreed to march along it.

Why was the Bastille to Nation route banned?

The prefecture cited violence and damage at earlier protests, in particular on 13 October. It announced the ban on Friday, 23 October.

Is it safe to be in Paris today?

Expect heavy policing and disruption near the march. Follow police instructions and check official transport updates.

World.title: Pemex Denies Mass Layoffs, Cites 0.21% Cut
World.content:
A Pemex industrial workshops site at Naranjos, Veracruz, file photo from December 2021 (Photo: Isaacvp, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

MEXICO · ENERGY

Key Facts — The country Mexico, the US southern neighbour, runs its oil industry through the state company Pemex.

— Why it matters Staff cuts at Pemex touch its finances, its workers and the bond investors who watch its rating.

— Why now Pemex issued its denial on Thursday 22 October 2026, a day after workers made dismissal letters public.

— What happened Pemex called mass layoffs and pay-scale cuts false, but said its 2026 staffing is down 0.21%.

— The numbers The union counts 11 dismissals in Reynosa on 5 October and a worker cut from level 39 to 30.

— What it means for you US investors and suppliers should expect more Pemex cost-cutting and a court fight over a 5,000-member union.

— Still open How many jobs went, and whether the Supreme Court will recognise the union.

— Power Index Mexico ranks 2nd of 14 in Mexico ranks 2nd of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 71.4 points (October 2026 edition).

In Plain English Pemex is Petróleos Mexicanos, the state-owned oil company that runs much of Mexico’s oil and fuel business. Its large union, the STPRM, holds the main labour contract for its rank-and-file workers. Trusted staff, called personal de confianza in Spanish, are employees to whom that main contract does not apply, which means fewer protections. A pay level is a grade on Pemex’s salary scale, so a move from level 39 to level 30 means a lower grade and lower pay.

Pemex denies mass layoffs, the Mexican state oil company said in a statement on Thursday 22 October 2026, calling reports of widespread dismissals and cuts to pay scales false. It also confirmed a restructuring that has trimmed its workforce by 0.21% so far this year.

For US readers the dispute matters because Pemex is a state company whose finances are watched by bond investors, and the first dismissals the union reported were in Reynosa, across the border from McAllen, Texas. Pemex said on 15 October that the agency HR Ratings had kept its national rating at the top level and set its global rating at BBB with a stable outlook.

The row went public on Wednesday 21 October, when the business magazine Expansión published dismissal letters shared by the UNTyPP, a union of oil technicians that Pemex does not recognise. On Friday 23 October Expansión reported that the same group has taken its fight for recognition to Mexico’s Supreme Court.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Mexico ranks 2nd of 14 with 71.4 points. Strongest pillar: economic relationships (90); weakest: state capacity & security (46). Alignment group: Hedging. Watch21 homicides per 100,000; organised crime at 7.7 of 10. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

What Pemex Said on Thursday Night

Pemex posted its statement on its press page on Thursday 22 October, saying that versions of mass layoffs and of cuts to pay scales are false. The company, led by Director General Juan Carlos Carpio Fragoso, did not name any outlet or union in the text.

It said it runs continuous performance reviews and an organisational restructuring to remove duplicated functions, duplicated posts and unnecessary levels of hierarchy. In 2026 those steps amount to a 0.21% reduction of the workforce, carried out with severance and benefits, the company said.

The statement gives no headcount, no list of units affected and no savings target, and El Universal put Pemex’s workforce at about 130,000 people. If 0.21% applies to that total it would be about 270 jobs, which is our own arithmetic and not a Pemex figure.

Industry & Energy Magazine said that moving one worker to a lower level is not the same as cutting the general pay scale, so the two claims must be kept apart. Pemex’s statement does not mention individual level changes or the dismissal letters.

What the Union Says Happened

The UNTyPP says 11 workers were dismissed in Reynosa, Tamaulipas, on 5 October, two of them its members, including one with 35 years at Pemex. Those figures come from the union, and Pemex has not confirmed them.

Union official Silvia Ramos told Expansión that Pemex began with selective dismissals and last week moved to lowering pay levels, citing one worker cut from level 39 to level 30, which she said means earning less than half. Expansión found no overall figure for dismissals or level cuts.

The dismissal letters seen by Expansión promise severance within 60 days under Pemex’s rules for trusted staff. They also ask the worker to accept the payment and not to sue Pemex in any labour, civil, commercial, criminal or administrative court.

Ramos said word was also circulating of at least 800 dismissals among members of the STPRM, but Expansión could not confirm that or tie it to the same restructuring. The UNTyPP asked the Energy Ministry for a meeting and, with no reply, said it would protest outside the ministry.

Key Dates in the Dispute — 14 April: Pemex changes its rules for trusted staff

— 3 June: a labour appeals court rejects the union’s collective action

— 7 August: the Supreme Court accepts the union’s review appeal, its lawyer says

— 4 September: Pemex and the STPRM agree a 4% pay rise

— 5 October: the union counts 11 dismissals in Reynosa

— 21 October: dismissal letters published; union marches in Mexico City

— 22 October: Pemex denies mass layoffs and pay-scale cuts

Why the Union Is Not Recognised

The UNTyPP was founded on 18 March 2008, holds registration with Mexico’s labour ministry and says it groups more than 5,000 oil technicians and professionals. Pemex does not treat it as a union and classes its members as trusted staff, which the union says limits their protections.

Article 3 of Pemex’s trusted-staff rules, changed on 14 April, says anyone hired under those rules is outside the union contract. The union argues that Mexican labour law looks at what a person actually does, not at the job label Pemex chooses.

Expansión reported that the union wants the same working conditions as the STPRM and an end to what it calls an employer sham. Lawyer Enrique Guerrero said the union has been told that the lack of a pay rise will probably last the whole six-year presidential term.

The Supreme Court Case Explained

On 3 June the Eleventh Collegiate Tribunal in Labour Matters of the First Circuit rejected the union’s collective action, Expansión reported. It gave three reasons: the collective route was wrong because each worker’s duties must be judged one by one, there was no discrimination because the workers were hired as trusted staff, and there was no direct clash between Article 3 and the Federal Labour Law.

The union appealed for review to the Supreme Court, arguing that Article 9 of the Federal Labour Law makes trusted status depend on a person’s functions and that Pemex’s director general cannot decide it alone. Guerrero said the Court accepted the appeal on 7 August and notified it recently, while the union announced the admission on 20 October, according to Industry & Energy Magazine.

Justice Loretta Ortiz Ahlf will prepare a draft ruling for the full court, Expansión said, and no deadline applies. Admission of the appeal does not mean the Court has sided with the workers, the magazine stressed.

The Pay Gap Behind the Dispute

On 4 September Pemex and the STPRM signed a 2026-2027 wage deal with 4% more ordinary pay and 2% more benefits from 1 August, plus 3.12% on gas and gasoline benefits. From 1 January 2027 tabulated wages rise a further 5%, which Pemex says adds about 1.5% on average once knock-on payments are counted.

The UNTyPP says those gains have not reached its members, as it said of a 4.5% rise last year. Guerrero called the Court the only authority that can stop what he described as systematic violations of labour rights at Pemex.

What It Means for You

US bond investors and Pemex suppliers should read this as a sign that the company is trimming costs while keeping its pay deal with the main union. Pemex said on 15 October that HR Ratings credited it with lower financial debt and better liquidity, yet its staffing statement offers no savings figure.

People in Texas border towns have a stake because Reynosa, where the union places the first dismissals, sits across from McAllen. The sources reviewed report no fuel-supply or production impact from the staffing changes.

Our explainer What Is Pemex covers the company’s role and debt, and our earlier report Pemex Fires 11 Workers and Cuts Pay Levels covers the first dismissals. Our Mexico power structure guide shows who runs the state, and Pemex Says Debt Fell US$20 Billion covers its finances.

What Is Not Known

Even as Pemex denies mass layoffs, it has not said how many people were dismissed or moved to lower levels, and Expansión found no overall count. The 0.21% figure comes with no stated base, so the number of jobs is unknown.

The claim of at least 800 dismissals among STPRM members is unconfirmed. The sources reviewed do not say whether any court has ruled on the level cuts.

No date is set for the Supreme Court ruling, and the Court has not said how it will decide. Expansión’s source dates the admission to 7 August while the magazine dates the union’s announcement to 20 October, so the sequence is not fully clear.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does Pemex deny mass layoffs?

Pemex says mass layoffs are false but confirms a 0.21% cut in its workforce in 2026 from restructuring. A union counts at least 11 dismissals in Reynosa on 5 October.

Is Pemex cutting salaries?

Pemex says pay scales are not being reduced. The union says individual workers have been moved to lower levels, one from 39 to 30, so that the worker earns less than half.

What is the UNTyPP?

It is a union of more than 5,000 oil technicians and professionals, founded in 2008 and registered with Mexico’s labour ministry. Pemex does not recognise it and treats its members as trusted staff.

What will the Supreme Court decide?

It will review whether Pemex can classify workers as trusted staff by contract rather than by their duties. No deadline applies, and Justice Loretta Ortiz is to prepare the draft ruling.

What does it mean for US readers?

Bond investors and suppliers see Pemex trimming costs while a labour dispute heads to court. The sources reviewed show no effect on fuel supply or production.

Sources: Pemex press release 85, 22 October 2026; El Universal, 22 October 2026; Expansión, 23 October 2026; Expansión, 21 October 2026; Industry & Energy Magazine, 20 October 2026; Industry & Energy Magazine, 23 October 2026; Pemex press release 74, 4 September 2026; Pemex press release 84, 15 October 2026.

World.title: Salvadorans Say Pensions Stopped in October
World.content:
A person wrapped in a Salvadoran flag at a "Day Without Immigrants" rally in Washington, DC, in February 2017 (Photo: Lorie Shaull, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

EL SALVADOR · SOCIAL SECURITY

Key Facts — The country El Salvador is in Central America; about 170,000 of its citizens in the US hold TPS.

— Why it matters US law bars Social Security checks to non-citizens who are not lawfully present.

— Why now Reports of stop-payment letters spread again on 22 and 23 October.

— What happened Some Salvadoran TPS holders say Social Security letters stopped their retirement pay.

— What it means for you Lawyers quoted say to read any letter closely and not ignore its deadlines.

— Still open Why the agency acted, how many letters went out, and whether payments resume.

Some Salvadorans who hold Temporary Protected Status (TPS) in the United States say the Social Security Administration (SSA) has told them in letters that their monthly retirement pay is suspended for lack of legal presence. Univision first reported cases on 13 and 14 October, La Nación and elsalvador.com repeated them on 22 and 23 October 2026, and none of the reports we reviewed carries an explanation from the agency.

For US readers the story matters because about 170,000 Salvadorans hold TPS, according to Los Angeles Times en Español, and the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) said on 9 September that they keep their protection until a new announcement. If the SSA is acting as though that protection ended on 9 September, retirees with decades of US work say they are already feeling it, though no source has confirmed that explanation.

In Plain English TPS: a temporary US permit that lets people from a country hit by disaster or conflict live and work legally; Salvadorans have held it since 2001.

a temporary US permit that lets people from a country hit by disaster or conflict live and work legally; Salvadorans have held it since 2001. Social Security Administration (SSA): the federal agency that pays monthly retirement checks to people who paid into the system.

the federal agency that pays monthly retirement checks to people who paid into the system. Legal presence: a non-citizen’s lawful right to be in the US, which federal law ties to Social Security payments.

a non-citizen’s lawful right to be in the US, which federal law ties to Social Security payments. DHS: the US department that runs the immigration agencies, including USCIS, which handles TPS.

What the Letters Tell Salvadorans

A lawyer in the Washington, DC area told Telemundo 44 on 17 September that some clients were receiving a letter saying “Based on the information we have, we cannot pay benefits starting September 2026.” The letter, as she quoted it in Spanish and as we translate it, adds that the payment would normally arrive in October 2026 and that a person must be a US citizen or legally present to receive benefits.

The lawyer, Cristina Paoli, said the letter asks recipients to call within 10 days and gives 60 days to appeal, and she urged clients not to ignore it. Telemundo said it had asked the SSA and DHS about the letters and was still waiting for replies when it published.

On 14 October Univision in Tampa, Florida, reported that other Salvadorans with TPS had received similar letters about their retirement payments. The station said it was not clear whether every letter used the same reasoning or how each person’s immigration status had been checked.

Francisco Semiao, president of the Asociación Nacional Salvadoreña Americana, told Univision the measure is also affecting relatives who are US citizens. The reports we reviewed do not say how many people have received letters.

A Retiree’s Account From Los Angeles

Juan Cerén, a 69-year-old Salvadoran with TPS, told Univision in Los Angeles that he has worked and paid taxes in the United States since 1990. A letter from the SSA told him his retirement benefits were suspended, and his family said it also asked him to return the October payment.

He told the station he had been informed that his health coverage would be cancelled, though the reports do not say which program or whether that has happened. His wife described opening the letters as a bucket of ice water, and the couple said they had relied on the income.

Immigration lawyer Alex Gálvez told Univision that denying the benefit “simply because TPS formally was not extended is a violation and a contradiction” of what the government published on USCIS.gov, in our translation from Spanish. Univision reported that he suggested affected people seek legal advice, call members of Congress and consider federal lawsuits.

What the Law Says About Legal Presence

Section 202(y) of the Social Security Act says no monthly benefit is payable to a non-citizen in the United States for any month in which that person is not lawfully present, as determined by the Attorney General. The printed text does not mention TPS, so the question in these cases is how agencies count TPS holders after the last formal period has ended.

The TPS law, section 244 of the Immigration and Nationality Act, tells the government to review a country’s conditions at least 60 days before a designation ends and to publish its decision in the Federal Register. If it does not find that the conditions have stopped being met, the designation is extended for six months, or for 12 or 18 months at its discretion.

UnoTV, quoting immigration lawyers, and La Nación read that rule to mean Salvadoran TPS could run to 9 March 2027, six months after 9 September. That is a legal interpretation and not an announcement, and none of the reports we reviewed quotes DHS or the SSA confirming it.

Where Salvadoran TPS Stands After 9 September

The last formal extension, published in the Federal Register on 17 January 2025, ran 18 months from 10 March 2025 to 9 September 2026. A Federal Register search on 24 October found no later notice on El Salvador TPS.

On 9 September a DHS spokesperson said in writing, as quoted in Spanish by Los Angeles Times en Español, that an announcement on Salvadoran TPS would come “at the appropriate time” and that until then covered Salvadorans “retain protection.” UnoTV reported on 7 October that a USCIS notice says the same, including work authorization, while the page still lists 9 September 2026 as the last date and no official document names a later one.

An immigration lawyer told Univision, as quoted by La Nación, that because the immigration agencies placed no new notice in the Federal Register, other offices such as the SSA may be sending letters as if everything expired on 9 September. The SSA has not confirmed that explanation, according to La Nación and elsalvador.com.

What It Means for You

If you or a relative holds Salvadoran TPS and receives a Social Security letter, lawyers quoted by Telemundo and Univision say not to ignore it, to check the call and appeal deadlines printed on it and to speak to an immigration lawyer. One retiree showed Univision his TPS renewal cards and work permits as proof of his work history.

This article is news reporting and not legal advice, and each case depends on the person’s own record. For wider context see our guides El Salvador Explained 2026, El Salvador Geopolitics Explained 2026 and El Salvador in Latin America, Its Role, Weight and Alliances.

Readers who follow US status decisions can also see our report Supreme Court Voids Ruling Shielding Venezuelans in US, which covers a different country’s TPS case. Salvadoran families in the US and their relatives at home will be watching whether DHS announces a decision soon.

What Is Not Known

No report we reviewed says how many Salvadorans have received letters or how much money is involved. It is also unclear whether every letter cites the same reason or only the lack of legal presence.

The SSA has not been quoted explaining the letters, and the explanation offered by lawyers, a gap between agency records, is unconfirmed. Telemundo said in September that it was waiting for replies from the SSA and DHS.

It is not known when DHS will announce a decision on Salvadoran TPS, or whether payments suspended in the meantime will be restored. Whether the six-month extension to 9 March 2027 applies is a legal question that DHS or the courts would have to settle.

The USCIS, SSA and DHS websites refused our requests on 24 October, so we relied on the Federal Register, published statute text and the Spanish-language reports. We could not see a letter ourselves, and the quotes from letters come from lawyers and recipients.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why are some Salvadorans losing Social Security payments?

Some retirees with TPS say SSA letters cite a lack of legal presence, which federal law requires for monthly payments to non-citizens. None of the reports we reviewed carries an SSA explanation.

Does TPS for Salvadorans still apply?

DHS said on 9 September that Salvadorans covered by TPS retain protection until a new announcement. The last formal period ended on 9 September 2026, and no decision has been reported since.

What should someone do after getting such a letter?

Lawyers quoted by Telemundo and Univision say not to ignore it and to check the call and appeal deadlines on the letter. They also advise speaking to an immigration lawyer.

How many Salvadorans hold TPS?

About 170,000 people are covered, according to Los Angeles Times en Español, and the status dates from 2001. The number who received SSA letters is unknown.

Is the SSA letter confirmed as agency policy?

The reports rest on letters shown by recipients and lawyers, not on a published SSA rule. None of them quotes the agency explaining one.

Sources: Federal Register, Extension of the Designation of El Salvador for TPS, 17 January 2025 (90 FR 5953); US Code, 42 U.S.C. 402(y); US Code, 8 U.S.C. 1254a; Telemundo Washington DC, 17 September 2026; Univision Tampa, 14 October 2026; Univision Los Angeles, 13 October 2026; La Nación, 22 October 2026; elsalvador.com, 23 October 2026; UnoTV, 7 October 2026; Los Angeles Times en Español, 9 September 2026.

World.title: Guatemala Arrests 7 Police in Killing Probe
World.content:
The Supreme Court building and the Torre de Tribunales tower in Guatemala City, where the seven officers were taken (file photo, 2011; Photo: Sistematización y Co…, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

GUATEMALA · JUSTICE

Key Facts — The country Guatemala is a Central American country led by President Bernardo Arévalo, with strong US trade and migration links.

— Why it matters The case tests whether Guatemala can solve a killing that the US Embassy condemned.

— Why now The Interior Ministry put seven police officers before the courts on Friday 23 October 2026.

— What happened Seven police officers face a judge over the arrest of two brothers who were later freed.

— The numbers Seven officers, two freed brothers, two men killed, and no suspect yet held for the shooting.

— What it means for you US investors and expats get a test of how Guatemala handles police misconduct and a high-profile killing.

— Still open Who fired the shots, who ordered them, and whether officers planted the carbine.

Guatemala arrests 7 police officers over the detention of two food-delivery brothers who were named as suspects in the murder of anti-corruption lawyer Juan Francisco Solórzano Foppa, the Interior Ministry said on Friday 23 October 2026. The seven, a commissioner, an inspector, a third-grade officer and four agents, were taken to the Torre de Tribunales courthouse that night to give a first statement to a judge.

For US readers the case matters because the US Embassy in Guatemala condemned the killing on the day it happened and called for a complete and transparent investigation. A source told Prensa Libre that FBI agents are helping prosecutors, although the Public Ministry has said only that it has technical support from international allies.

The arrests do not solve the murder, because nobody has been detained for the shooting that killed Solórzano Foppa and a second man, Gustavo Adolfo Aguilar Gamarro, at a Guatemala City sports complex on Saturday 17 October. They deal with the first arrest in the case, which police presented as the capture of the suspects and which a judge undid within a day.

In plain English — Solórzano Foppa A 43-year-old lawyer who worked as a state prosecutor and later led Guatemala’s tax agency, SAT.

— PNC The National Civil Police, Guatemala’s main police force, which answers to the Interior Ministry.

— Comisaría 13 The police unit whose officers arrested the two brothers on the day of the killing.

— Torre de Tribunales The courthouse tower in Guatemala City where suspects are brought before a judge.

— Falta de mérito A judge’s ruling that the evidence is too thin to continue a case, so the suspect goes free for now.

— Public Ministry Guatemala’s prosecutor’s office, known as the MP.

How the First Arrest Fell Apart

Gunmen shot Solórzano Foppa at the Campo Marte sports complex in zone 5 of Guatemala City on the morning of Saturday 17 October, in an attack that also killed Aguilar Gamarro. Police said they caught two brothers, Rigoberto and Daniel Zaqueo Choc Toz, in zone 16 soon afterwards and showed a carbine as evidence.

The brothers, who deliver food by app, denied any role, and a judge freed both for lack of merit on Sunday 18 October. Prensa Libre reported that police say the carbine is registered to a private individual and has no theft report, and Plaza Pública reported that its owner is under investigation.

What Police Leaders Told Lawmakers

On Wednesday 21 October the deputy director of police operations, Esvin Jacinto, told lawmakers that the arresting officers took the brothers to a police station instead of straight to the Torre de Tribunales, as the rules require. He said patrol cars were swapped and routes changed without telling senior commanders, which he called a break in the chain of command.

Plaza Pública counted nine irregularities in about three hours and reported that, at the station, the captors made the brothers kneel and pose for photos in front of the weapon. On Thursday 22 October police director David Custodio Boteo said several officers and the station chief had been removed from their duties, and prosecutors inspected patrol car GUA 13190 the same day.

What the Seven Officers Face

The Interior Ministry said the officers were put before the courts for alleged irregularities in the detention, on arrest warrants from the Third Criminal Court of First Instance in Guatemala City. Publinews described the accusation as abuse of authority and the alleged planting of a firearm.

La Hora reported that the weapon was said to have been planted by the officers themselves and did not match the one used in the attack, a claim the ministry has not made and that no court has tested. The brothers also say the carbine was planted, and the officers have not been heard by a judge.

The ministry withheld the officers’ names, citing the presumption of innocence, although police published the brothers’ names, ages and photos on the day of their arrest. One officer told reporters at the courthouse that the case reflected political exploitation and that organised crime was to blame.

At the first hearing a judge hears each officer and then decides whether there is enough evidence to continue the case. No ruling had been published in the outlets reviewed by Saturday morning.

Why Guatemala Arrests 7 Police Matters Now

Solórzano Foppa was known for criminal analysis at the Public Ministry, including expert work in the La Línea corruption case that forced President Otto Pérez Molina to resign in 2015, and in 2022 he took on the defence of jailed journalist José Rubén Zamora. Prensa Libre also recalled that he was convicted in three cases during the term of then attorney general Consuelo Porras, and that in one of them, in June 2023, he accepted the charges.

President Arévalo said at the funeral on Monday 19 October that he demands justice, ruled out a state of emergency and warned against political use of the killing. The Interior Ministry announced on Tuesday 20 October a deep review of the police, and Interior Minister Marco Antonio Villeda has said officers could be dismissed if illegality is proven.

The US Embassy called Solórzano Foppa a firm defender of the fight against corruption and organised crime. The Organization of American States also demanded that the crime be clarified.

What It Means for You

US companies, aid groups and diplomats follow cases like this as a gauge of whether Guatemala’s police and prosecutors can investigate themselves and protect critics. We found no change to travel rules or business regulations announced with the arrests.

Our guides Guatemala Geopolitics Explained 2026 and Guatemala Explained 2026 explain how the country’s politics and security forces fit together. We also looked at Who Runs Guatemala’s Economy earlier this week.

Our earlier report Guatemala Probes 7 Police in Foppa Killing covered the internal police inquiry that preceded these arrests. This article follows the case into the courts now that Guatemala arrests 7 police officers over it.

What Is Not Known

Nobody has been named or detained for the shooting, and the sources reviewed do not say who fired the shots, who ordered them or why. The Public Ministry has not confirmed that the FBI is involved, and the name comes from one source quoted by Prensa Libre.

The officers’ names have not been released, and the judge’s decision after their first statements was not public when this article was written. Whether the carbine was planted is an allegation that no court has decided.

The sources also do not agree on the number of spent cartridge cases at the scene, with reports ranging from more than 50 to at least 57. The brothers have threatened legal action against the state, and it is not known whether they will file a claim.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who are the seven police officers arrested in Guatemala?

They are a commissioner, an inspector, a third-grade officer and four agents of Comisaría 13, according to the Interior Ministry. Their names have not been released.

Who was Juan Francisco Solórzano Foppa?

He was a 43-year-old lawyer, former prosecutor and former head of the tax agency SAT, shot dead on 17 October 2026. In 2022 he took on the defence of jailed journalist José Rubén Zamora.

Has anyone been arrested for the murder itself?

No suspect has been detained for the shooting, according to EFE on 24 October. The two brothers first accused were freed for lack of merit.

Is the FBI helping in Guatemala?

A source told Prensa Libre that FBI agents are supporting the Public Ministry. The ministry has said only that international allies provide technical support.

What does the case mean for US readers?

The US Embassy condemned the killing and called for a transparent investigation, so the case tests Guatemala’s police and prosecutors. No change to travel or business rules has been announced.

Sources: Agencia Guatemalteca de Noticias (Interior Ministry statement), 23 October 2026; La Hora, 23 October 2026; Prensa Libre, 23 October 2026; Plaza Pública, 22 October 2026; EFE via Infobae, 24 October 2026; Publinews, 23 October 2026; Prensa Libre on international support, 18 October 2026; La Hora on the US Embassy statement, 17 October 2026.

World.title: Falabella Rewards Plan Has 12M Chile Clients
World.content:
A Falabella department store in Viña del Mar, Chile. File photo, 2009. (Photo: Carlos yo, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

CHILE · RETAIL

Key Facts — The country Chile, in South America, is home to Falabella, one of Latin America’s largest retail groups.

— Why it matters Falabella’s points tie its stores, bank and shoppers together, so rule changes shape spending.

— Why now Fpuntos began 14 September, Cencosud has announced changes too, and earnings land 10 November.

— What happened Falabella renamed CMR Puntos as Fpuntos; each point is worth CLP 1 (about US$0.001) when spent.

— The numbers 12 million clients in Chile; a CMR card earns 1 point for every CLP 150 (about US$0.15).

— What it means for you Investors see Falabella’s loyalty engine; Elite cardholders earn from triple points.

— Still open Whether richer earn rates lift sales or squeeze margins shows in 10 November earnings.

— Power Index Chile ranks 3rd of 14 in Chile ranks 3rd of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 63.6 points (October 2026 edition).

The Falabella rewards plan, renamed Fpuntos on 14 September 2026, now serves 12 million clients in Chile, the company says. Each point is worth CLP 1 (about US$0.001) when spent, and card holders earn points faster than under the old CMR Puntos scheme.

For US readers the story is about how a Chilean retailer with its own bank and shopping malls keeps customers close, which feeds the sales and card income that investors follow. Falabella’s newsroom puts its net profit at US$497 million so far in 2026, up 17.9% from the first half of 2025.

Rival Cencosud and Latam Airlines have also changed their loyalty rules, The Clinic reports, so points are in play across Chilean business. This report sets out the Falabella rules, the money they imply and what to watch before earnings on 10 November.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Chile ranks 3rd of 14 with 63.6 points. Strongest pillar: state capacity & security (86); weakest: diplomatic & cultural influence (38). Alignment group: Closer to Washington. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

In Plain English Loyalty programme: points a shop or bank gives you for spending, which you can spend later like a small discount.

points a shop or bank gives you for spending, which you can spend later like a small discount. Fpuntos: Falabella’s new name for its points, where one point is worth CLP 1 (about US$0.001) when spent.

Falabella’s new name for its points, where one point is worth CLP 1 (about US$0.001) when spent. CMR card: Falabella’s store credit card, issued by Banco Falabella, in Classic, Premium and Elite versions.

Falabella’s store credit card, issued by Banco Falabella, in Classic, Premium and Elite versions. Cencosud: Chile’s other big retailer, owner of Jumbo supermarkets and the Paris and Easy stores.

Chile’s other big retailer, owner of Jumbo supermarkets and the Paris and Easy stores. Exchange rate: all US$ values here use the Banco Central de Chile observed rate of CLP 986.58 per US$ on 23 October 2026.

What Changed in the Falabella Rewards Plan

Falabella confirmed on 11 September that CMR Puntos would become Fpuntos on Monday 14 September, and redemptions were switched off the weekend before, The Clinic reported at the time. The group’s newsroom says each Fpunto equals CLP 1 (about US$0.001) and that four categories, Standard, Classic, Premium and Elite, depend on the payment method.

CMR cardholders now earn from 1 Fpunto for every CLP 150 (about US$0.15) spent in Falabella group shops and partner shops, against 1 for every CLP 200 (about US$0.20) in the old programme, Banco Falabella’s programme page says. That is one third more points for the same spending by our arithmetic, though the page does not say what a point was worth before.

Premium cardholders can double their points and Elite cardholders at least triple them, and the heaviest users can reach five times the base rate, the newsroom says. Falabella also lists a wide range of redemptions and events across the group and more than 100 partner shops.

What Each Point Earns

The list below turns the published earn rates into a rough share of spending, using the stated CLP 1 per point. It is our arithmetic, and the Classic, Premium, Elite and no-card rates come from The Clinic’s review of 23 October.

Earn Rates at Falabella Group and Partner Shops CMR Classic: 1 point per CLP 150 (about US$0.15), roughly 0.67% of spending back.

1 point per CLP 150 (about US$0.15), roughly 0.67% of spending back. CMR Premium: 2 points per CLP 150 (about US$0.15), roughly 1.33%.

2 points per CLP 150 (about US$0.15), roughly 1.33%. CMR Elite: from 3 points per CLP 150 (about US$0.15), roughly 2.0% or more.

from 3 points per CLP 150 (about US$0.15), roughly 2.0% or more. Banco Falabella debit card: 1 point per CLP 500 (about US$0.51), roughly 0.2%, or per CLP 1,500 (about US$1.52) at other shops.

1 point per CLP 500 (about US$0.51), roughly 0.2%, or per CLP 1,500 (about US$1.52) at other shops. No card, Chilean tax ID only: 1 point per CLP 750 (about US$0.76), roughly 0.13%.

Outside group and partner shops, a CMR Classic card earns 1 point per CLP 300 (about US$0.30), with Premium and Elite multiplying that, The Clinic says. The real worth of a point still depends on what it buys at redemption.

Fee Cuts for Heavy Card Users

Banco Falabella says CMR cardholders who collect more than 80,000 Fpuntos (about US$81) or spend more than CLP 6.6 million (about US$6,690) in a calendar year pay half of the card’s administration cost. Above 220,000 Fpuntos (about US$223) or CLP 18 million (about US$18,245) of spending, that cost falls to zero.

Customers who held a category by December 2025 keep it until December 2026, and those who reach one by December 2026 keep it through 2027, the same page says. Customers without a points-based category get one that depends on the card they hold.

For investors, the fee waivers are card income that Falabella gives up for its heaviest spenders. The third quarter, which ends 30 September, covers only 17 days of the new scheme, so the 10 November earnings will be an early look at best.

Cencosud and Latam Also Changed Rules

Cencosud, owner of the Jumbo supermarkets and the Paris and Easy stores, now gives 1 point for every CLP 150 (about US$0.15), against 1 for every CLP 300 (about US$0.30) before, The Clinic reported on 23 October. It also cut the minimum redemption from 6,000 to 2,000 points and says anyone can earn without a bank card, while the price of a redemption stays the same.

Latam Airlines will move elite members of its Latam Pass programme to automatic requests for free cabin upgrades from April 2027, so they no longer ask flight by flight, The Clinic said. The airline puts the programme at more than 57 million members and says they received more than 760,000 courtesy upgrades in 2025.

Each change is a separate company decision announced on its own date. We rely on Falabella’s own pages for its rules and on The Clinic for Cencosud and Latam, which we could not confirm on their own sites.

What It Means for You

Investors in Falabella shares or bonds can read the plan as a bet that richer points keep customers spending across its stores, bank and malls. Fitch Ratings raised the group’s international rating to BBB from BBB- with a stable outlook on 14 October, which our earlier report on the Fitch upgrade covers.

The Clinic says shoppers without a CMR card can still earn by giving their RUT, the Chilean tax ID, though at a lower rate. The sources do not say whether foreign visitors without a RUT can earn, so tourists should ask at the till before counting on points.

Our Falabella company profile tracks the group’s businesses and results, and our guide Who Dominates Chile, Elites and Regions Explained covers the wider business world. Shoppers comparing offers before the sales season can also read our Black Friday in Latin America 2026 guide.

What Is Not Known

Falabella’s pages do not say how much a CMR Puntos point was worth before 14 September, so the true gain from the new CLP 1 value cannot be calculated. Headlines from BioBioChile and Diario El Día on 13 August said the consumer agency Sernac had sent Falabella a formal request about the earlier changes, but we could not open the agency’s own statement.

It is not known how many of the 12 million clients are active or how many points are outstanding. No figure for the cost of the richer earn rates has been published.

We could not open the Cencosud or Latam pages, so their rules rest on The Clinic’s account of what the companies told it. Falabella lists its third-quarter earnings release for 10 November 2026 and a call for 12 November.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Fpuntos?

Fpuntos is the name of Falabella’s loyalty programme, which replaced CMR Puntos on 14 September 2026. Each point is worth CLP 1 (about US$0.001) when spent.

How many clients does the Falabella rewards plan have?

Falabella says it has 12 million clients in Chile, up 65% in five years. The figure is the company’s own and does not say how many are active.

How fast do CMR cardholders earn points?

CMR cardholders earn from 1 Fpunto per CLP 150 (about US$0.15) at group shops and partners. Premium cardholders earn double and Elite cardholders at least triple.

Did Cencosud change its points too?

Yes, Cencosud told The Clinic it now gives 1 point per CLP 150 (about US$0.15) instead of 1 per CLP 300 (about US$0.30). Its minimum redemption fell from 6,000 to 2,000 points.

When are the next Falabella results?

Falabella lists its third-quarter earnings release for 10 November 2026 and an earnings call for 12 November. That quarter covers only 17 days of the new programme.

What does it mean for US readers?

It shows how a large Chilean retailer uses points to keep shoppers across its stores and bank, which investors in the group follow. The 10 November results are the next check.

World.title: Bancolombia Chief Backs 8% to 9% Wage Rise
World.content:
The Bancolombia headquarters in Medellín, the home of Grupo Cibest (Photo: Petruss, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

COLOMBIA · BANKING

Key Facts — The country Colombia sets one national minimum wage each year, negotiated by the government, unions and employers.

— Why it matters A big wage rise can lift inflation and interest rates, and Bancolombia’s parent trades in New York.

— Why now Talks for 2027 are warming up, and Colombia’s largest bank named its range on Friday 23 October.

— What happened Juan Carlos Mora, president of Grupo Cibest, said the 2027 minimum wage should rise 8% to 9%.

— The numbers That would lift the monthly wage from about US$554 to between US$599 and US$604.

— What it means for you Holders of the CIB shares and employers in Colombia face a higher pay floor if the range holds.

— Still open The final figure, which the government must set by 30 December at the latest.

— Power Index Colombia ranks 6th of 14 in Colombia ranks 6th of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 51.9 points (October 2026 edition).

Bancolombia minimum wage talk moved on Friday 23 October 2026, when its president said Colombia’s minimum wage should rise 8% to 9% for 2027. Juan Carlos Mora, who runs parent company Grupo Cibest, spoke at the Camacol construction congress in Cartagena.

For US readers the signal matters because Grupo Cibest shares trade on the New York Stock Exchange as American depositary receipts under the ticker CIB. A wage rise of this size can feed into inflation, interest rates and payroll costs for any firm that hires in Colombia.

We covered the opening of this year’s pay talks in Colombia Wage Commission Opens Early 2027 Talks and an economist’s forecast in Colombia Minimum Wage: Economist Sees 9% to 10% Rise for 2027 as Talks Begin. This report adds the view of the head of Colombia’s largest bank, a lender to the households and firms that live with the decision.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Colombia ranks 6th of 14 with 51.9 points. Strongest pillar: military means (91); weakest: diplomatic & cultural influence (28). Alignment group: Closer to Washington. WatchRating below investment grade (BB-); 26 homicides per 100,000; organised crime at 7.8 of 10. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

In Plain English Minimum wage: the lowest monthly pay allowed by law, set once a year for the whole country.

the lowest monthly pay allowed by law, set once a year for the whole country. Productivity: how much more each worker produces, one of two inputs in the traditional pay formula.

how much more each worker produces, one of two inputs in the traditional pay formula. Grupo Cibest: the holding company that owns Bancolombia, Colombia’s largest bank.

the holding company that owns Bancolombia, Colombia’s largest bank. Camacol: Colombia’s construction industry chamber, host of the congress where Mora spoke.

Colombia’s construction industry chamber, host of the congress where Mora spoke. Transport allowance: a separate payment to low earners, left out of the wage figures here.

The Bancolombia Minimum Wage Proposal

Mora said Colombia should go back to the older rule that builds the minimum wage from inflation and productivity, plus perhaps a few small points. He told the congress the main aim is to stop workers losing buying power.

Valora Analitik gave his range as 8% to 9%, while Semana wrote 8.5% to 9% and quoted his sum of inflation of 6.29% plus 1.5 or 2 points of productivity. Those two inputs add up to about 7.8% to 8.3%, so the rest is the small margin he mentioned, which is our calculation.

Mora also called the minimum wage a social matter, because families depend on that income. He said the answer must balance what suits the economy with what suits workers.

The 2026 rise is the backdrop to his remarks. The government of former president Gustavo Petro raised the wage by about 23%, far above inflation at the time, and Corficolombiana, a bank, estimated it explains 53% of the acceleration in prices between December and September.

The Numbers in Pesos and Dollars

Colombia’s minimum wage for 2026 is COP 1,750,905 a month (about US$554), not counting the transport allowance. We convert at the official rate of COP 3,158.43 per US$, valid for 24 to 26 October and published by Colombia’s financial regulator.

Monthly Minimum Wage Scenarios 2026 wage: COP 1,750,905 (about US$554)

COP 1,750,905 (about US$554) Inflation only, 6.29%: COP 1,861,037 (about US$589)

COP 1,861,037 (about US$589) Mora low end, 8%: COP 1,890,977 (about US$599)

COP 1,890,977 (about US$599) Mora high end, 9%: COP 1,908,486 (about US$604)

COP 1,908,486 (about US$604) Union idea floated, 38.5%: about COP 2.43 million (about US$768)

Valora Analitik calculated that 8% would lift the wage to COP 1,890,977 (about US$599) and 9% to COP 1,908,486 (about US$604). The monthly gain would be COP 140,072 to COP 157,581 (about US$44 to US$50), which is our calculation.

DANE, the national statistics agency, put annual inflation at 6.29% for September, released on Wednesday 7 October 2026. Prices are up 5.74% since December, and the central bank’s policy rate stands at 12.25% after its 30 September decision.

What Grupo Cibest does. Grupo Cibest S.A., together with its subsidiaries, provides various banking products and services in Colombia and internationally. It offers deposit products, including checking and savings accounts, fixed-term deposits, and investment products; credit alternatives solutions such as trade financing, working capital loans, mortgages, credit cards, personal, vehicle, payroll, and small business loans, and…

Who Decides and When

The figure is negotiated by the government, unions and employer groups. The Labour Ministry, led by Natalia López Fuentes, held the first session of its wage commission on 1 October, with comments due by 9 October.

IFM Noticias reported that the formal table is expected to be installed toward the end of November. Under Law 278 of 1996 the commission should decide by 15 December, and if there is no consensus the government sets the wage by 30 December.

Unions may ask for far more than Mora. Fabio Arias, a former president of the CUT union federation, said workers plan to bring a 38.5% rise to the table, although he stressed the figure is not final.

Corficolombiana, the financial group, proposed 8% on the traditional rule, using projected 2026 inflation of 6.8% and productivity of 1.2%. In July, Miguel Gómez Martínez, then the designated finance minister of President Abelardo de la Espriella, said the wage cannot rise far above inflation and should grow with productivity.

What Else Cibest Said on Growth

At the same event Mora said Colombia’s potential growth is close to 3% and could reach 6% only gradually, which needs more national and foreign investment. The 6% goal is the government’s, according to La FM.

He called public finances one of the country’s most important economic issues and backed seeking International Monetary Fund support to give fiscal measures credibility. Other bankers on the panel also asked the government for a credible fiscal adjustment and incentives for investment, El Colombiano reported.

Cibest’s own research team had already cut its 2027 growth forecast to 2.4%, as we reported in Colombia’s Largest Bank Sees 2027 Growth Slowing to 2.4% on Spending Cuts. Our explainer Bancolombia Explained, Colombia’s Largest Bank in 2026 describes the bank itself.

What It Means for You

Investors in the CIB receipts can watch the company’s own calendar, which lists the third-quarter results call for Tuesday 10 November 2026. A high wage outcome would add to the cost pressures behind the central bank’s 12.25% rate, whose next decision is due on 30 October (see Colombia’s 12.25% Rate Faces 30 Oct Vote).

Employers with staff in Colombia should watch whether the Bancolombia minimum wage range sets the tone, since pay scales tied to the minimum wage move in January 2027. Our guides Who Runs Colombia’s Economy, the Key Players in 2026 and Colombia Explained give the wider picture.

Visitors and residents in Bancolombia’s home city can read our Medellín expat city guide for day-to-day costs. A higher minimum wage lifts the pay floor for domestic and service workers, though prices also respond.

What Is Not Known

The final 2027 wage is not known, and the Bancolombia minimum wage range is one voice among many. Reports of his remarks differ slightly, giving 8% to 9% in one outlet and 8.5% to 9% in another.

The sources reviewed do not say whether the range is a formal Cibest position or a personal view, and no Cibest research note with the same figure was found. They also do not show whether other business leaders at the congress agreed.

The Council of State has admitted a lawsuit against the 2026 decree, and the retail group Fenalco has also asked it to annul the rise, but no ruling is known. The table has not formally opened, so unions, employers and the government may still change their positions.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did the Bancolombia president say about the minimum wage?

Juan Carlos Mora said the 2027 minimum wage should rise 8% to 9%, based on inflation, productivity and perhaps a few extra points. He spoke on Friday 23 October 2026 at the Camacol congress in Cartagena.

How much would 8% to 9% add to the monthly wage?

It would add COP 140,072 to COP 157,581 (about US$44 to US$50) to the current COP 1,750,905 (about US$554). That brings the wage to roughly US$599 to US$604, our calculation.

Who decides Colombia’s minimum wage?

The government, unions and employer groups negotiate it, and the government can decree it if they fail to agree. The legal deadline for a decree is 30 December.

Is Bancolombia part of the pay negotiation?

Bancolombia and its parent Grupo Cibest are not named among the negotiators in the reports reviewed. The talks involve the government, unions and employer groups.

Why does a Colombian wage rise matter in the US?

Grupo Cibest shares trade in New York as CIB receipts, and a larger wage rise can affect inflation and interest rates. US firms with Colombian staff would also face higher pay floors.

Sources: Valora Analítik, 23 October 2026; Semana, 23 October 2026; La FM, 23 October 2026; El Colombiano, 23 October 2026; DANE consumer price index, September 2026; Banco de la República, September 2026 decision; Grupo Cibest financial calendar; Grupo Cibest share information; Bancolombia research on 2027 growth.

World.title: Jamaica Remittances Reach US$3.1 Billion
World.content:
A National Commercial Bank branch in Montego Bay, Jamaica, photographed in 2015 (Photo: Balou46, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

JAMAICA · REMITTANCES

Key Facts — The country Jamaica is a Caribbean island nation whose relatives abroad send home billions of dollars a year.

— Why it matters Most of that money comes from the United States, so American wages reach Jamaican family budgets.

— Why now A Jamaican minister gave the figures to more than 300 delegates in Philadelphia on Friday 23 October 2026.

— What happened Jamaicans abroad sent home US$3.12 billion in the year to March 2026, up 6.7% on the year before.

— The numbers December 2025 set a monthly high near US$297 million, and the US supplied 68% of the year.

— What it means for you US families, banks and transfer firms start a flow that keeps growing after Hurricane Melissa.

— Still open Whether monthly flows stay near US$280 million to US$290 million, as in July and August 2026.

Jamaica remittances reached US$3.12 billion in the fiscal year 2025/26, Minister of State Alando Terrelonge told Jamaicans in Philadelphia on Friday 23 October 2026. Remittances are money that people living abroad send home to family, and for Jamaica most of it comes from the United States.

For US readers the Jamaica remittances story runs both ways, because about 68% of the money travels from the United States, according to monthly Bank of Jamaica figures. What Jamaican families abroad earn and spend in American cities therefore matters to the island’s recovery from Hurricane Melissa.

Terrelonge spoke at the opening of the second Jamaica Diaspora Northeast USA Conference at Temple University, which runs on 23 and 24 October. Our report 63 Jamaica Schools Rebuilt After Melissa covers another part of the island’s recovery.

In Plain English Remittances: money that people living abroad send to relatives at home.

money that people living abroad send to relatives at home. Diaspora: people from a country who now live elsewhere, here Jamaicans in the United States and other countries.

people from a country who now live elsewhere, here Jamaicans in the United States and other countries. Fiscal year: Jamaica’s budget year, which runs from 1 April to 31 March.

Jamaica’s budget year, which runs from 1 April to 31 March. Bank of Jamaica: the island’s central bank, which publishes monthly remittance figures.

the island’s central bank, which publishes monthly remittance figures. Hurricane Melissa: the storm that struck Jamaica in late October 2025.

What the Minister Said in Philadelphia

Terrelonge is the minister of state in Jamaica’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Foreign Trade, with responsibility for diaspora affairs. He gave the figures to more than 300 delegates, who included government officials, diplomats, business executives and community leaders.

He said Jamaicans abroad sent an extra US$93 million in the three months after Hurricane Melissa, compared with the same period a year earlier. He added that December 2025 recorded a monthly high of US$296 million.

He called the storm’s impact “devastating” and said the diaspora’s contributions deserved to be acknowledged. The government wants to move from individual acts of goodwill to lasting programmes with measurable results, he said.

The conference runs under the theme “One Diaspora, One Vision: Advancing Jamaica Together” and follows an inaugural Northeast edition in Philadelphia in 2025. Michelle Tulloch-Neil, the Global Jamaica Diaspora Council representative for the northeastern United States, leads the organising.

What Bank of Jamaica Data Shows on Remittances

The Bank of Jamaica publishes a monthly table of inbound remittances by country, in millions of US dollars, based on reports from licensed remittance companies. Adding the named country lines for April 2025 to March 2026 gives US$3.124 billion, which matches the minister’s US$3.12 billion.

Jamaica remittances in the previous fiscal year came to US$2.929 billion, so the latest year is up 6.7%. The United States line alone came to US$2.125 billion, or 68% of the total.

The United Kingdom came next at US$360 million, or 11.5%, followed by Canada at US$299 million, or 9.6%, and the Cayman Islands at US$195 million, or 6.3%. These shares are our calculation from the bank’s monthly lines.

November 2025 to January 2026 brought in US$806 million, against US$712 million a year earlier, a gain of about US$93.5 million. That matches the minister’s US$93 million, although he did not say which three months he meant.

December 2025 was the strongest month in the table, at US$296.9 million, and the table starts in January 2012. The next highest was July 2026, at US$290.0 million.

Jamaica Remittances Stay Higher in 2026

From January to August 2026 Jamaica remittances add up to US$2.130 billion on the named country lines, against US$2.018 billion in the same eight months of 2025. That is a rise of 5.5%.

July 2026 brought US$290.0 million, the second-highest month in the table after December 2025, and August brought US$280.8 million. The figures rest on estimates that remittance companies submit to the central bank.

Why Diaspora Money Matters After Melissa

The Jamaica Observer reported on Friday 23 October that the government has halted official overseas travel across the public sector until 31 March 2027, to contain spending and redirect money to recovery after Hurricane Melissa. The sources reviewed do not link that decision to remittances.

Terrelonge said diaspora donors supported 37 of the 59 health clinics adopted under a Ministry of Health and Wellness programme as of October 2025. He also named Farm Up Jamaica, a New York-based nonprofit that backs local farming.

The government is exploring ways to cut barriers to trade, business, investment and philanthropy for Jamaicans abroad, he said. It also wants more diaspora members on advisory boards and policy committees.

Our guides Jamaica Explained 2026 and Jamaica Geopolitics Explained 2026 set out how the island’s economy and its place in the Caribbean fit together. Our report Most Jamaican Tourism Jobs Are Back After Hurricane Melissa, Minister Says covers the tourism side of the rebuilding.

What It Means for You

Jamaican Americans who send money home use the same licensed remittance companies that report to the Bank of Jamaica. Their transfers feed Jamaica remittances that have now topped US$3 billion in a fiscal year.

Money-transfer firms and banks that serve this corridor can read Jamaica remittances as steady demand, with recent months running above a year earlier. Investors in Jamaican assets can watch the monthly table for any change in that pattern.

Travellers and relatives may want to note that the government has invited the diaspora to Jamaica’s 65th Independence anniversary events on 5 to 8 August 2027. The theme is “Celebrate, Connect, Experience, Give Back”.

What Is Not Known

The minister did not say how his Jamaica remittances total of US$3.12 billion was built, and the Bank of Jamaica has not published a press release on it that we could find. Our match rests on adding the named country lines in the bank’s table, which leaves out a separate “other remittances” line of about US$401 million for the year.

With that line included the table’s own total for the year is US$3.52 billion. The sources reviewed do not explain what the extra line covers.

It is also not known which three months the US$93 million refers to, or how much of the extra money was sent for hurricane relief. The August 2026 row in the bank’s file carries a label dated 1 August, which we read as the full month because the file’s stated range runs to August 2026.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much did Jamaicans abroad send home in 2025/26?

Minister Alando Terrelonge said US$3.12 billion in the fiscal year 2025/26. Our sum of the named country lines in Bank of Jamaica data for April 2025 to March 2026 matches that figure.

How much of the money comes from the United States?

About 68% in the fiscal year, or US$2.125 billion, according to our calculation from the Bank of Jamaica table. The United Kingdom and Canada follow.

When was the record month for remittances?

December 2025, at about US$297 million, was the highest month in the Bank of Jamaica table, which starts in January 2012. The minister put it at US$296 million.

Where did the minister announce the figures?

He spoke on Friday 23 October 2026 at Temple University in Philadelphia, at the opening of the second Jamaica Diaspora Northeast USA Conference. More than 300 delegates attended.

Are remittances still rising in 2026?

Yes, on the Bank of Jamaica table, with January to August 2026 up 5.5% on the same months of 2025. July and August were US$290.0 million and US$280.8 million.

Sources: Bank of Jamaica, inbound remittances by corridor (table ES.RMT.01, data to August 2026); Caribbean National Weekly, 23 October 2026; South Florida Caribbean News, 23 October 2026; Jamaica Observer, 23 October 2026.

World.title: Costa Rica Used-Car Imports Fall 85% After Tax Loophole Closes
World.content:
Imports of used vehicles into Costa Rica fell 85% in September compared with the same month last year, the first full month under new customs rules that stop importers from declaring cars at a fraction of their market value. Finance Ministry figures show 631 used vehicles entered the country in September, down from 4,262 a year earlier and 3,769 in August.

At the same time, the average customs value of each imported used vehicle doubled, from $4,085 in September 2025 to $8,227 this September. The average tax collected on each used vehicle rose about 71%, from 1.19 million colones (about $2,600) to 2.04 million colones (about $4,470).

Total vehicle imports fell 47.7% year over year, to 5,019 units. New-vehicle imports dropped a more modest 17.7%, to 4,388 units, while the average customs value of a new vehicle rose 7.7% to $21,383. The shift follows an executive decree announced on Aug. 28 that changed how customs values vehicles. The invoice value an importer declares, including freight and insurance, is now compared with the Finance Ministry’s own fiscal value for an identical vehicle, and taxes are calculated on whichever figure is higher.

Vehicles that do not appear on the official list require technical documentation to establish their value. The gap dated to mid-September 2024, when the ministry repealed three decrees that set minimum taxable values by brand, model and year. From then on, the importer’s invoice became the sole basis for valuation.

In early September, the ministry said it had identified at least 30,000 vehicles that entered the country below market value, most of them nearly new 2024 and 2025 models, some with very low mileage. It estimated the resulting tax evasion at 20 billion colones (about $43.8 million). In one case that surfaced last month, a 2025 BMW X6 M was declared at $7,367, a model that can sell for more than $130,000 in the United States.

Vice Minister of Revenue Víctor Carvajal has described the declared values as artificially low and said some people built a business around the gap. He has traced the loophole to the law that reduced the marchamo, the annual vehicle property tax, and ruled out an administrative investigation.

The National Customs Service said no single cause explains the drop. It noted that importers tend to hold back when regulations change, and that the emissions certificate required by the Ministry of Public Works and Transport has been difficult to obtain, particularly for used vehicles, leaving many units unable to complete customs clearance.

Customs also said the decree is likely one factor behind the higher average values, but that the increase cannot be attributed to it entirely. The ministry added that a shift in the mix toward new or higher-value vehicles may have contributed. The decline was concentrated in used passenger cars, which fell from 3,640 units to 496. Used cargo vehicles dropped from 622 to 135. New passenger cars fell 22%, to 3,187 units, while new cargo vehicles held nearly flat at 1,201.

Carlos Aguilar, executive director of the vehicle and machinery importers’ association Aivema, said new-vehicle imports move in cycles and that September is historically one of the slowest months of the year, which places its figures within normal ranges. He said undervaluation had been a practice in the used segment rather than among new-car distributors, and that the association views the new measures favorably.

Lower volume pulled down overall revenue. The ministry collected 17.7 billion colones (about $38.8 million) in vehicle import taxes in September, 27.2% less than a year earlier, with new vehicles accounting for 16.4 billion colones of the total. The ministry said it expects the market to adjust as importers adapt to the new framework.

The ministry has also proposed legislation that would allow the tax administration to adjust the registered values of vehicles that entered under the old rules, which would raise the marchamo owed on affected cars. It has said most vehicle owners would see no change.

October figures will show whether September marks a lasting reset in the used-import market or a pause while importers adjust to the new valuation rules and the emissions certificate backlog. The changes come as other vehicle costs are also under review, including a proposal to end electric vehicle tax breaks.

World.title: Have you seen Aisha Arnold?

Have you seen Aisha Arnold?

By Zoila Palma: The family and friends of Belize City student Aisha Arnold, 16, is concerned about her whereabouts.
