World.title: YouTube, AI and neurodivergent representation: How Gen Z and Gen Alpha are redefining modern storytelling
World.content:
In an era of entertainment that's dominated by nostalgia, younger generations are redefining storytelling through YouTube, TikTok, and even artificial intelligence (AI), according to the 2026 Teens and Screens report.

 

Conducted by the Center for Scholars & Storytellers (CSS) at the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA), the report began five years ago as a way to analyse the media habits of more than 1,500 Americans aged 10-24.

Its latest findings highlight how much contemporary storytelling has diversified, with Gen Alpha and Gen Z finding just as much value in unconventional media formats like 30-second videos to feature-length films.

The majority of the survey's respondents (72.9%) chose YouTube as their favourite medium for storytelling, while nearly 4 in 5 said that short-form videos can tell a story too, with TikTok (64.2%) scoring highest among social media platforms.

TV shows (70.3%), movies (70.2%) and video games (68.5%) all followed closely behind, with respondents choosing the cinema as their favourite weekend activity for the third year in a row.

This mirrors recent findings across Europe, with 50% of cinemagoers in the UK under 35-years-old according to the Cinema Advertising Association. Meanwhile, CineEurope reports that 47% of young people now discover films through TikTok.

More 'relatable' characters

Stranger Things has been praised among Gen Z for its relatable characters and LGBTQ+ representation. Netflix

Despite younger audiences being a major target demographic for the entertainment industry, their actual experiences and desires are still frequently unheard or misunderstood.

A recurring theme is their desire to see more relatable stories, with 55% of those surveyed wanting to see more neurodivergent characters on screen — a number that increased among LGBTQIA+ youth.

Only 22.7% of respondents felt that current media portrayals of neurodivergence “ring true to real life” most of the time. One such portrayal that received huge backlash in 2021 was Sia's directorial debut Music, in which Maddie Ziegler, a neurotypical actress, played a nonverbal autistic woman.

The adolescents and young adults also said they wanted to see more “hopeful, uplifting stories with people beating the odds,” “friendships and social groups,” and “people with lives like mine.”

This continues the findings of previous reports that young people want less sex on screen and more platonic relationships, with 52% saying they believe that romantic relationships in media are more central to the lives of fictional characters than they are in real life.

“The call for greater neurodivergent and friendship representation is just some examples we found of the broader demand for more diverse and authentic portrayals,” said study co-author Stephanie Rivas-Lara.

Opinions on AI

From fake actors to social media slop, AI has rapidly taken over the media landscape and become a major source of contention among younger viewers.

Despite this, the survey's respondents seem more curious than worried about the technology, with 28.2% saying they were “fascinated" and 25.6% “excited". On the other hand, 22% said they felt "doomed" and 10.1% were "scared".

Opinions on AI were most positive among the youngest respondents, aged 10-13, with 44.2% describing programmes about AI as "fascinating".

The future of entertainment

'Backrooms', made by YouTube Kane Parsons, was one of 2026's most successful blockbusters. A24

While cinema attendance massively declined during the pandemic, there's been a steady increase in the years since as young people strive to escape their phone screens, find communities, and reconnect with the outside world.

Recent blockbuster hits like Backrooms and Obsession, which were directed by YouTube creators, also prove that younger audiences are craving more original stories that utilise internet formats and lore; reflecting the digital worlds they have grown up in.

“The gatekeepers have changed, and young people themselves are deciding what they want to watch and what they want to see more of in the content they choose,” said Yalda T. Uhls, founder and CEO of CSS and adjunct professor in UCLA’s psychology department.

“Industry leaders should ‘tune in’ to young people as well as the experts who have positive youth development and their well-being in mind,” Uhls added.

“This year’s report clearly illustrates that this is the key to creating quality content that wins over today’s youth.”

World.title: Booking an electric flight in Europe is only 10 years away, says influential Dutch researcher
World.content:
The Netherlands is pushing the world towards electric flight faster than most European countries.

 

One of the world’s first battery-powered passenger planes is being built by Dutch start-up Elysian Aircraft. Development is well underway: “There will be six engines. And we have folding wingtips, so that we fit into the current gates’ infrastructure of the airports, because the wings are very large,” explains co-founder Daniel Jacobson.

Cutting fossil fuel emissions is the most pressing challenge facing the world, and aviation is a big contributor. “By being able to transport 90 passengers for initially 800 kilometres and eventually 1,000 kilometres you can reduce emissions to zero, from half the world’s flights,” Jacobson says. “That is a very large amount of flight activity in the world. And you reduce total emissions from aerospace by 20 per cent.”

Development is well underway, confirms Elysian Aircraft co-founder Daniel Jacobson (at the right). Hans von der Brelie

Should the European Union be backing electric air travel? What can e-planes learn from EVs? When will ordinary passengers be able to fly in an electric plane?

Euronews Earth sat down with Maarten Steinbuch, a renowned Professor of Mechanical Engineering at Eindhoven University of Technology, to get his expert view of the future of electric flight.

Euronews Earth met with Maarten Steinbuch (at the left), a renowned Professor of Mechanical Engineering at Eindhoven University of Technology. Hans von der Brelie

We can’t leave it to the airlines to cut their own emissions

Aviation contributes six per cent to global heating, when CO2 as well as other emissions are taken into account. In wealthy countries, aviation is responsible for a much larger share, according to data seen by campaign group Stay Grounded.

The aviation industry is, of course, aware of its impact and has made promises to cut emissions. The International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO), the UN agency responsible for regulating international aviation, adopted the goal of “carbon neutral growth from 2020”. However, CO2 emissions from international aviation have increased since 2020, as the goal focuses on offsetting the sector’s CO2 emissions rather than committing to real emissions reductions.

Climate Action Tracker rates the ICAO’s goal of carbon neutral growth from 2020 levels as “Highly insufficient”.

The European Commission, Professor Steinbuch says, is focused on helping “current aviation” to “become as sustainable as possible”. But rather than helping current planes to reduce the emissions they create, the Commission should be supporting a pivot to zero emissions planes – electric ones. “There is not enough attention yet to have a revolution in airspace electrification. So, it’s more an evolution and not yet a revolution.”

“There is not enough attention yet to have a revolution in airspace electrification. So, it’s more an evolution and not yet a revolution”, says Maarten Steinbuch. Hans von der Brelie

Could electric planes become as common as EVs?

Electric vehicles have been adopted across Europe, faster than many people predicted. Sales grew year-on-year from 2020 to 2025, with one in four cars sold worldwide in 2025 being electric, according to the International Energy Agency. As a result, about five per cent of the global car stock is now electrified, displacing 1.2 million barrels of oil per day in 2025.

This shift did not happen by magic but because car companies were put under pressure through government policy. “I have seen, in the electrification of passenger cars, that being strict on dates when manufacturers of cars effectively should have a sufficient number of models of electric cars available really helped,” says Professor Steinbuch.

He believes that if similar requirements were made of aeroplane manufacturers, we could see real change. “We need legislation saying that part of a fleet could be electrified in this or that year. Push that also with legislation.”

The European Commission also needs to speed up how quickly new aeroplane designs are certified. Safety must be the “first, second and third” priority, of course, but “it could help if the European Commission would put a little bit more effort in, so that those processes could be accelerated and giving space for scale-ups to build up both on the infrastructure for electrification of airflights, but also for the manufacturing and the startups who make new planes.”

In the workshop of the Dutch start-up Elysian Aircraft: the wings will be fully packed with batteries. Hans von der Brelie

When will electric flights be available to us all?

Seeing the owners of low-cost airlines become influential millionaires, it can be difficult to imagine aviation losing its grip on the market.

But Professor Steinbuch says there are plenty of reasons to be optimistic that electric flights will be common in the not too distant future – and there’s one key component.

“It’s not a dream, it is very real and the most important part of development is the batteries. Batteries are the key thing. All over the world billions of euros and dollars are spent in development. Why? Because everybody knows that batteries are the Holy Grail for the transition both in mobility as well as in energy.”

Batteries are so crucial because they power electric planes, and how long they last determines how far they can fly. “If solid-state batteries with double the capacity – up to 500 watt-hours per kilogram – come onto the market, electric flying will attract the interest of far more people. And this point will come soon.”

Euronews Earth takes a ride in an electric 2-seater: Start-ups such as E-Flight Academy already started to train pilots in electrical airplanes. Hans von der Brelie

How soon? “I think in 2032 or so, within six years, we might see the first 500 km range airplanes for cargo and for passengers, at five seats, so that's a very small scale – but still it will be a start for specialised purposes.” Three years later, in 2035, “we could see nine-seaters, maybe 20-seaters, flying with a range of 500 kilometres. 80- or 90-seaters will be more close to 2040, even maybe beyond.”

World.title: Grocery prices across Europe: Where is food most expensive and why?
World.content:
Food takes a sizeable share of household budgets across Europe, but the cost of filling a shopping basket varies widely from country to country. In the EU, food and non-alcoholic beverages account for 13.6% of household spending, compared with 23.6% for housing and utility bills, according to Eurostat.

 

Which countries are the most expensive for groceries, and what drives these differences?

According to mid-2026 data from Numbeo, a crowdsourced cost-of-living database, the grocery index ranges from 57.2 in Moldova to 189.2 in Switzerland, with the EU average set at 100. This means groceries are 89.2% more expensive than the EU average in Switzerland, while they are 42.8% cheaper in Moldova.

To illustrate the gap, a basket costing €100 at average EU prices would cost €189.20 in Switzerland and €57.20 in Moldova, based on the index.

Numbeo’s index takes New York as the base at 100. Euronews Business converted the index to use the EU average as 100.

Which are the most expensive countries?

Three of the five most expensive countries are Nordic. Iceland (183.6) ranks second, followed by Norway (154.4), Luxembourg (134.9) and Denmark (128.4). The other Nordic countries are also above the EU average: Finland (119.7) and Sweden (116.6).

Among five of Europe’s major economies, France is the most expensive for groceries, at 27.5% above the EU average. Spain (89.7) is the only one below the average. The UK (111.9), Germany (111.6) and Italy (110.2) are above it, with similar price levels.

Austria (124.5), Ireland (122), Belgium (117.6) and the Netherlands (116.4) are also among the more expensive countries, all above the EU average.

Cheapest EU country: Groceries in Romania cost a third less

Within the EU, Romania (66.7) is the cheapest country for groceries, with prices 33.3% below the EU average.

More broadly, groceries are cheaper in Eastern European and Balkan countries, including EU candidates. For example, the index is 59.8 in North Macedonia, 67.9 in Bosnia and Herzegovina and 68.8 in Serbia.

Turkey (82.1) is more expensive than several EU members, although it remains below the EU average. Turkey also has the highest food inflation in Europe.

Lower prices do not mean greater affordability

Ilaria Benedetti, an associate professor at the University of Tuscia, pointed out that while food prices are lower than the EU average in some countries, households spend a larger share of their budget on food. For example, groceries are cheaper in Romania, but households spend 23.1% of their budgets on food and non-alcoholic drinks. This share is also above 20% in Bulgaria.

“Lower prices do not necessarily mean greater affordability,” Prof. Jeremiás Máté Balogh from Corvinus University told Euronews Business.

Pointing to differences in wages and purchasing power, he emphasised that groceries can be cheaper in absolute terms but less affordable relative to what people earn after tax.

An 18-item grocery basket costs €69.84 in the EU

Numbeo lists 19 items in its “Markets” category. Euronews Business collected the prices of these items in October 2026. Adding together the listed prices of 18 items, with each counted once rather than weighted, gives an average EU basket cost of €69.84.

Cigarettes are excluded from the Euronews calculation because prices vary substantially and the share of smokers differs across countries.

As with the index, the grocery basket is most expensive in Switzerland at €137.90, while Moldova is the cheapest at €41.10.

The basket also costs more than €100 in Norway (€116.10). Other expensive countries include Luxembourg (€99), Austria (€88.10) and Denmark (€87.70).

France is still the most expensive among the five major economies compared. The basket costs €87.40 in France, compared with just €63 in Spain. These groceries cost €80 in Italy, €75.20 in Germany and €69.10 in the UK.

The 18 grocery items can be bought for less than €50 in North Macedonia (€43.90), Kosovo (€45.50), Romania (€45.90), Georgia (€46.90), Poland (€49.60), Serbia (€49.70), Montenegro (€49.80) and Bosnia and Herzegovina (€49.80).

However, these rankings are based on nominal prices. When purchasing power is taken into account, the gap narrows. The rankings may also change slightly when the basket is weighted.

The role of energy prices and labour costs

“Labour costs have likely become one of the most persistent drivers of grocery prices across Europe, but energy costs remain an important factor,” Balogh said. He noted that higher energy, fuel, and transportation costs continue to affect agricultural production, food processing, and distribution.

Benedetti said that energy is the main driver of recent rises in food prices, particularly fuel this time. She added that, since the strikes on Iran at the end of February, the average price of diesel in the EU had risen from €1.59 per litre on 23 February to €2.24 on 28 September, the highest level since records began in 2005.

“Diesel moves the whole food chain, from tractors to the lorries that supply supermarkets,” she told Euronews Business.

She also pointed out that when inflation slows, prices do not necessarily fall. If inflation remains positive, they keep rising, only more slowly, from a higher level.

Why does bread cost more than three times as much in Denmark as in Bulgaria?

“The price of food in a shop is only partly the cost of the food itself,” Benedetti said.

“It also includes wages, energy, rents, transport and taxes, which are much higher in richer countries.”

She noted that a 500g loaf of fresh white bread costs €3.18 in Denmark and €1.02 in Bulgaria — more than three times as much, according to Numbeo. A dozen eggs, a more standardised product, costs €4.52 in Denmark and €2.69 in Estonia, less than twice as much.

Balogh explained that differences in grocery prices across European countries reflect a combination of factors, including wages, land and labour costs, retail market structure, taxation, exchange rates, logistics and transportation costs, agricultural productivity and consumer preferences.

World.title: Sun, sand and snorkelling: A week in the Maldives on two stunning resort islands
World.content:
Up until recently, when I pictured a trip to the Maldives, I only imagined villas over turquoise blue waters and barefoot luxury on sandy shores. In October, I had the chance to see beyond the picture-postcard image with a visit to two island retreats on the Indian Ocean archipelago.

 

My week-long stay began with a brief arrival to the bustling capital, Malé, before hopping in a speedboat to the first stop on my trip: OBLU Nature Helengeli by SENTIDO.

On the compact island of Helengeli, I stayed in a lagoon villa complete with a private pool that spills onto the vast Indian Ocean. A highlight of my stay was the open-air bathroom designed to bring the tropical outdoors indoors, while still maintaining privacy.

After three nights on Helengeli, I was whisked away on a speedboat to the island of Sangeli. Upon my arrival to the resort, OBLU Select Sangeli, I was given a traditional Maldivian “maruhabaa” welcome, with coconut leaf origami necklace placed around my neck as a “boduberu” drum procession played in the background.

My water villa also had a private infinity pool and direct access to the lagoon. The distinctive touch, however, was the room’s glass floor panel that offered a glimpse of the waters below.

From the comfort of my room, I could peer into the water and watch the occasional sea creature swim by.

House reef snorkelling and dolphin encounters

There’s always a first time for everything, and having never snorkelled before, I wasn’t quite sure what I’d find within the islands’ house reefs. Across both stays, access to the house reefs is a mere walk or swim away.

Donning my snorkel mask, flippers and trusty life jacket, I met the islands’ deep sea residents, including spotting sea turtles, eagle rays and stingrays and an array of reef fish, including a mellow puffer fish.

My sea encounters were not limited to daylight hours, either.

As the sky formed sunset-orange hues, I boarded a traditional wooden dhoni for a cruise along the atoll’s blue waters. Here, I saw a pod of spinner dolphins, with some putting on an acrobatic display of leaps and twirls above the water.

Fresh sea catches, coconuts and lots of tuna

If snorkelling was the highlight of my week, then eating my way through the islands came a very close second, especially with the variety of buffet and à la carte concepts to choose from.

I sampled the popular Maldivian breakfast dish, “mas huni”, simply meaning fish and coconut. Typically served alongside local flatbreads like a faratta or roshi, the protein-filled breakfast combines tuna chunks with finely grated coconut, alongside zesty lime and onions and topped with chilli flakes to taste.

Speaking of which, tuna lovers are certainly spoiled for choice at the resorts, with offerings from tuna dumplings to smoked and spiced chunks of tuna.

The kachori chat, where each bite was mixture of crunchy texture from the flaky casing to the spiced mixed vegetable filling, was the star of Raga Route's menu Fakhriya M. Suleiman/Euronews Travel

The archipelago’s palate is also heavily influenced by other south Asian cuisines, including flavours from India and Sri Lanka. My favourite sweet treat came from Raga Route in the form of a gulab jamun cheesecake, which was so tasty, my sweet tooth goaded me to order seconds.

My week ended with an Indian Ocean gala dinner at the Courtyard eatery on Sangeli. The gathering can be considered as a Maldivian "Malaafai", which are feasts shared among friends and families.

During the dinner, there were live cooking stations for guests to choose from samosa, papdi or aloo tiki chaat as well as quickly sample a morsel of panipuri. The buffet featured popular rice dishes, including biryani and a cart serving Indian faloodas.

Rest and relaxation

After snorkelling, swimming in my private pool and strolling in the sand, it was only right that a spa treatment (actually, two…) made it onto my itinerary.

On Helengeli, I sauntered to the ELE|NA Ayur facility and opted for the “relax and unwind” treatment, which focused on my back and included a mini foot massage. I was able to enjoy my massage in the outdoor treatment area, where the aroma of the applied hot coconut oil was accompanied by birdsong and the quiet ripple of koi fish in the nearby pond.

I also visited ELE|NA Ayur on Sangeli, but this time, the focus was my skin. The treatment was designed to detoxify, regulate excess oils and give me that sought-after island glow. Before my facial had even started, I was presented a tray with a turmeric, honey and brown sugar shot, along with a refreshing cold towel infused in fragrant lemongrass oil.

In the treatment room, a gentle vitamin C cleanser was applied, followed by a cucumber mist and a citrusy yoghurt-based exfoliant to finish.

The outdoor treatment area at ELE|NA Ayur spa on Helengeli Fakhriya M. Suleiman/Euronews Travel

What to know before you go and getting there

EU citizens, as with all foreign nationals travelling to the Maldives, must complete the free digital self traveller declaration, "IMUGA", at least 96 hours before arriving to the Indian Ocean archipelago. After approval, tourists are then granted a visa on arrival for a stay up to 30 days.

Guests staying at OBLU Nature Helengeli and OBLU Select Sangeli must also check in online via the apps prior to arrival.

When arriving at Velana International Airport, the main international airport in the Maldives, resort representatives guide you to the speedboat annex to continue the journey by sea, or, if catching a seaplane, there’s a dedicated terminal with a fleet of 11 seaplanes that fly to four islands.

Fakhriya M. Suleiman was hosted by OBLU Nature Helengeli by SENTIDO and OBLU Select Sangeli. Both resorts are part of the Colours of Oblu collection in the Atmosphere Core portfolio.

World.title: Azerbaijan hijab ban exposes strain in ‘brotherly’ ties with Turkey
World.content:
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, a staunch advocate of Muslim rights, has been notably silent on Azerbaijan’s recent hijab ban in schools. For years, Erdogan and Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev have shared a close alliance, but the ban is putting the Turkish president in a tight spot.

Advertising

School uniform rules introduced in September in predominantly Muslim Azerbaijan, which is a secular state, have been used to bar pupils wearing the hijab. Teachers have also reported being excluded. The new rules do not explicitly mention hijabs, but prohibit clothing deemed incompatible with school uniforms or secular education.

With Turkish social media awash with videos of Azerbaijani children wearing hijabs and pleading to be let into their schools, the ban has sparked outrage among Turkey’s religious conservatives.

Yet Erdogan, a vocal defender of Muslim rights both at home and on the world stage, has remained silent on the issue.

"He's unusually muted because Azerbaijan and Turkey, of course, had this extremely good relationship,“ said Turkish political analyst Sezin Oney. "If it were another country, he would have had a harsher reaction.”

‘We're fighting a daily battle': Iranian women dare to shed hijab in public

Baku's response

Erdogan, who is religiously conservative, rose to political prominence in the 1990s by challenging a similar ban in Turkish universities, and went on to become a global advocate of Muslim rights.

Oney predicts his silence on Azerbaijan will damage this reputation.

"[It's] a far cry from the days when Erdogan could stand up against the powerful of the world. That was the image he projected, and now he cannot even stand up to Aliyev."

Aliyev has publicly dismissed criticism of the hijab ban by one of the Turkish president’s advisors and Baku has issued international arrest warrants for several prominent Turkish Islamist and conservative figures, along with banning others from entering the country after similar criticism.

Azerbaijani officials accuse the critics of threatening its sovereignty and national security.

Shifting status

Aliyev and Erdogan have enjoyed close ties for more than two decades, built on economic and defence cooperation, with the mantra of ‘two states, one nation’.

“Erdogan and Turkey [still] see Azerbaijan as a little brother,” explains Tbilisi-based defence and security expert Eugene Kogan.

“I think that's not the perspective that comes from Baku because they say quite clearly that their relationship is no longer between a big brother and a little brother, and their relationship is now of equals.”

He added: “I think this phrase 'equal' is not fully accepted in Ankara. So that puts a strain on bilateral relations between the two countries."

Energy-rich Azerbaijan is growing in economic importance, in comparison with Turkey’s struggling economy. It is also among Turkey’s largest foreign investors.

Earlier this month, the two countries signed arms agreements worth more than $500 million. Azerbaijan’s state oil company SOCAR says it has invested around $19.5 billion in Turkey.

“SOCAR is the flagship of investments in Turkey – it's huge," said Turkish analyst Atilla Yesilada of Global Source Investments.

“Turkey has a chronic deficit in plastics and petrochemicals. In fact, there are plans to establish a huge petrochemical complex in the Adana or Antalya area with a cost of $10 billion. I don’t think domestic capital has that kind of funding. Eventually, if Turkey wants to cover its petrochemical deficit, it needs SOCAR to get involved."

Shipping attacks threaten Turkey's resolve to keep warships out of Black Sea

Relations with Israel

Azerbaijan’s deepening relationship with Israel, despite its Turkish ally’s condemnation of Israel’s war in Gaza and broader escalating tensions, is another source of friction with Ankara.

International media reported that Azerbaijan signed a $235 million arms deal with Israel’s Elbit Systems this month, although neither side has commented on the reports.

Azerbaijan also remains a key oil supplier to Israel, with oil piped through Turkey and shipped from the Turkish Ceyhan port. In 2024, Erdogan moved swiftly to suppress mounting protests against these exports – protests led largely by religious conservatives who form a crucial part of his political support.

However, Kogan believes Israel will not try to exploit any rift between Baku and Ankara. “The stability of relations between Ankara, Baku and Tel Aviv is very, very important for Tel Aviv,” Kogan said.

Turkey-Azerbaijan alliance strained by opposing stances on Israel

Baku last year hosted talks between Turkey and Israel aimed at defusing tensions over Syria.

'[Isreal] understands that it could come to war [with Turkey] and Baku can still act as a meeting point for both countries. I cannot really think of another meeting point between Ankara and Tel Aviv at the moment,” Kogan said.

With Turkey the main export route for Azerbaijan’s oil and gas, mutual dependency remains a powerful means to contain any tensions.

Gasimov suggests the current rift is part of a learning process.

“I wouldn’t read it as reshuffling or rebalancing, but rather as a new chapter that may have opened up now, if the two sides learn from it and are ready to accept these kinds of differences."

As Turkey wrestles with mounting financial and economic woes, Erdogan is expected to look for ways to smooth things over with his affluent neighbour. But the full impact on their ties of this dispute remains to be seen.

World.title: Will Guinea-Bissau remain trapped in political chaos?
World.content:
Elections scheduled for December 6 in Guinea-Bissau have been postponed indefinitely. No new date has been set, leaving the country's return to civilian rule uncertain.

The parliamentary and presidential elections scheduled for December 6, 2026, in Guinea-Bissau will not take place as planned. Aly Silva, spokesperson for transitional Prime Minister Ilidio Vieira Te, confirmed to DW that the vote had been postponed until further notice. No new date has been set. The government first intends to discuss the matter in cabinet before publicly announcing when the elections will be held. It remains unclear whether they will take place in 2027 or not until 2028.

The country's political crisis dates back to November 26, 2025. Three days earlier, voters in Guinea-Bissau had elected a new parliament and president. Before the official results could be announced, the military seized power and halted the electoral process. Both then-President Umaro Sissoco Embalo and his challenger, Fernando Dias da Costa, had claimed victory. The military leadership promised a return to constitutional order.

Guinea-Bissau's General Horta N'Tam (center) was sworn in as transitional leader and commander-in-chief on November 27, 2025 Image: Patrick Meinhardt/AFP

For lawyer and political analyst Cabi Sanha, the postponement comes as no surprise. Since the coup, little has been done to create the conditions for credible elections, he says.

"The postponement was foreseeable," Sanha told DW. December 6 had indeed been set as the new election date. "But nothing was done to ensure that these elections could actually take place."

Political freedoms under pressure

The transitional government has justified the postponement by citing the lack of organizational and political conditions necessary for elections. The deadline for submitting candidacies had already passed on October 6. Political parties and potential candidates had not submitted their applications. According to the prime minister, the parties had also failed to hold congresses to select their candidates.

Sanha sees this as more than an organizational problem. He points to restrictions on political activities and the lack of dialogue with key actors in the electoral process. Political parties and civil society have not been sufficiently involved, he says. Mediation efforts by the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) and Senegal have so far failed to produce a solution.

"Free, transparent and inclusive elections are only possible if the necessary conditions are established beforehand," the lawyer says.

He therefore also views the parties' failure to nominate candidates as a consequence of the political environment. "How are parties supposed to nominate candidates when political activities are restricted in the country? They cannot hold party congresses or organize rallies."

The funeral of human rights activist Vigario Balanta in Bissau, Guinea-Bissau. His body was found on March 31, bearing signs of torture, in a swamp outside the capital Image: DW

Leading opposition figures are also staying abroad. Domingos Simoes Pereira, head of the main opposition party, the African Party for the Independence of Guinea and Cape Verde (PAIGC), was allowed to travel to Portugal in July 2026 for medical treatment after being released from detention. He had previously been held in pretrial detention in connection with an investigation into an alleged coup attempt. His defense team denies the allegations and has criticized the proceedings as politically motivated.

The absence of key opposition figures and restrictions on political organizing are making it harder to conduct an electoral process intended to pave the way for a return to civilian government.

An election date without a timetable

What happens next remains unclear. Government spokesperson Aly Silva says the transitional government will first discuss the matter in cabinet. Only afterward will a new election date be announced publicly. So far, there is no concrete timetable.

It is therefore also unclear when political parties will be able to complete their internal selection procedures, nominate candidates and begin campaigning. For Sanha, this is another indication that there is still insufficient evidence of the political will needed to restore constitutional order.

"I do not believe that logistical problems are the main issue. Rather, there appears to be a lack of political will to move the electoral process forward," he says.

Dispute over the constitution

The political crisis has been compounded by a controversial constitutional reform. In a referendum on August 30, 2026, voters approved constitutional amendments that expand the president's powers and reduce the size of parliament from 102 to 65 seats. Critics question the legitimacy of the process because the reform was prepared under military rule and without a regularly elected parliament. The opposition had called for a boycott of the vote.

Fernando Vaz, spokesperson for the National Transitional Council, defends the changes. He says the process was not a comprehensive rewriting of the constitution but a targeted revision. The reform is intended to help overcome the country's political instability, he argues.

"The constitution must be one of the instruments that lead our country toward greater stability," Vaz told DW. The transitional period had provided an opportunity to amend provisions that, in the military leadership's view, were obstructing the country's political development.

Vaz also rejects criticism that the reform gives the president additional powers at the expense of the prime minister. "The president of the republic is the head of state, while the prime minister is the head of government," he emphasizes.

Critics see it differently. The new constitutional framework strengthens the presidency: the president is to appoint and dismiss the prime minister and the government and, under certain conditions, dissolve parliament. At the same time, the number of parliamentary seats is being reduced. It remains disputed whether the reform will genuinely contribute to stability or instead concentrate more power in the presidency.

Around 70 percent of valid votes in a constitutional referendum on August 30, 2026, were cast in favor of constitutional amendments Image: DW

Local elections are not enough

The transitional government has announced plans to hold local elections in 2027. Sanha broadly welcomes the proposal: Guinea-Bissau has never held such elections since independence. Nevertheless, he stresses that they must not replace the outstanding national elections.

"First, parliamentary and presidential elections must take place so that the country can return to constitutional order. Local elections can follow afterward," he says.

Local elections cannot compensate for the lack of democratic legitimacy at the national level. Political freedoms must also be restored so that parties can select their candidates and voters can genuinely choose between political alternatives.

A Transition With No Clear End

Guinea-Bissau has endured decades of political instability, marked by military coups, institutional crises and repeated interruptions of democratic processes. The latest coup continues this pattern.

The renewed postponement of the elections shows how far the country remains from a return to constitutional order. Setting a new election date alone will not be enough. Political activities must be permitted again, parties must be included in the process, and reliable conditions for elections must be established, lawyer Cabi Sanha told DW.

This article was originally published in German.

World.title: EU moves to loosen rules on pesticide use as experts sound the alarm
World.content:
The European Union wants to relax rules for pesticides, saying it will be easier for farmers to adopt more environmentally friendly options. But health and environmental experts say the risks are far too great.

As part of its drive to "streamline and simplify" EU laws, the European Commission has proposed sweeping changes for agriculture and food safety legislation. These include a move to ease rules controlling the use of pesticides and herbicides, which help fight pests and weeds.

Under current EU rules, which date back to 2011, primary pesticide components, or active substances, are only granted approval for limited periods of no more than 15 years.

The European Commission's proposed revamp of the system would make indefinite greenlighting — including of the controversial glyphosate, which has been linked to cancer and kills almost all plant life — the default. Safety reviews would only be done in exceptional cases, and regulatory authorities, not the industry, would bear responsibility.

The commission has said its goal is to cut costs, simplify work for authorities and help farmers stay competitive. Scientists and doctors, however, warn that concerns over human health and environmental impact from these toxic substances are being brushed aside.

Why does the EU want to deregulate pesticides?

The European Commission has said it's responding to complaints from farmers and the agriculture industry to clarify EU rules that govern pesticide use.

A joint statement released in May by 19 food associations, including CropLife Europe, which promotes pesticides, said complicated administrative procedures and a lengthy approvals process meant farmers were "left without any effective solutions to protect their crops against insects, weeds and diseases," putting food security and livelihoods at risk.

"The existing system of periodic renewal assessment of every active substance has become unsustainable," the commission's press service told DW, citing "chronic delays" and "bottlenecks" in the approval of new, more sustainable products.

In recent negotiations, EU member states said open-ended authorizations should be restricted to "low-risk active substances."

But their stance is still wanting to extend initial approval periods for other substances to up to 15 years, and a maximum of 25 years for renewals.

Herbert Dorfmann, a center-right Italian member of the European Parliament, said there is currently a yearslong delay in approving new pesticides, including more eco-friendly options, meaning farmers are forced to rely on older substances. Or, if these are banned, go without altogether.

The commission wants to "make the system more efficient and responsive," while guaranteeing that "the protection of human and animal health and the environment remain the highest priorities."

Dorfmann, who as co-rapporteur is responsible for interinstitutional negotiations on the issue, backs the commission's stance, saying the EU needs "to open up the system for innovation."

He aims to bring the parliament's proposal on the new pesticide rules to a vote among EU lawmakers before the end of the year.

How do pesticides affect human health, environment?

Ecologists and medical experts, however, have spoken out forcefully against the proposed changes, saying the potential implications for human health and the environment are being downplayed.

In September, more than 500 experts from across the EU signed an open letter calling on the European Parliament to suspend its consideration of the new regulations and conduct an independent investigation into health and environmental impacts.

On October 7, UN rights experts also backed the call for a full review into whether the proposed changes violated the EU's obligations under international human rights law, especially with regard to agricultural workers and children.

Pesticides can persist in the environment, contaminating water and degrading soils. They can also drive biodiversity loss and poison other animals higher up the food chain.

In January 2020, beekeepers in Berlin protested the continued authorization of glyphosate by leaving unsellable tainted honey at the entrance to Germany's Agriculture Ministry Image: Adam Berry/Getty Images

When it comes to humans, the European Environment Agency has said it was "not yet possible to estimate the burden of disease linked to current levels of exposure to all pesticides."

However, exposure to chemical pesticides, including banned substances that still persist in the environment, has been linked to various cancers, chronic respiratory disease, neurological disorders and developmental delays, as well as problems with fertility and behavior.

And exposure is widespread: A survey conducted between 2014 and 2021 found that 84% of urine samples from both children and adults in five European countries contained residue from two or more pesticides.

Martina Vijver, scientific director and ecotoxicology expert at Leiden University in the Netherlands, said experts were "deeply concerned" that the EU's current plan "will weaken rather than strengthen the level of protection for pesticide regulation."

Speaking at the European Parliament in September, she said regular reassessments were key to evaluating the safety of pesticides with new findings, pointing out that the perception of risk changes over time.

"The regulatory system must remain capable of correcting yesterday's decisions with tomorrow's knowledge," she said.

More than 50 substances banned since 2011

Salome Roynel, a policy officer at the Pesticide Action Network Europe, an NGO based in Brussels, said the harmful effects of pesticides aren't often fully understood until years later, when the product is up for reconsideration.

"New science emerges all the time," she told DW, highlighting how 56 active substances have been banned in the EU since 2011 as a result of periodic reviews.

That includes the insecticide chlorpyrifos, previously used in orchards and on vegetable and cereal crops, which has been tied to harmful effects on children's brain development.

Pesticides banned in Europe linked to bees deaths in Kenya To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Roynel said it was "obvious that there was some kind of alignment" between the changes proposed by the EU institutions and the demands of the pesticide lobby.

This echoes a new report by nonprofit research and campaign group Corporate Europe Observatory, which said Dorfmann and other lawmakers had "copy-pasted […] industry demands" into their regulatory proposals.

Dorfmann denied the lobby influence, telling DW he had met with "both sides, industry and environmental associations," in public debates on the issue.

"The main objective is not to keep old products in the market. The main objective is to bring new ones to the market," Dorfmann said.

Part of that plan, he added, would be to help more environmentally friendly "biocontrol" products and low-risk substances to bypass current administrative hurdles and get on the market faster.

Farmers need 'incentive' to switch to safer pesticides

It's an idea previously championed by Vijver, who agrees that the current system means more environmentally friendly pesticides are stuck in an administrative "traffic jam." She told DW that biocontrol products could go in a green "bus lane" to ease the way to approval at the European Food Safety Authority, while maintaining crucial safety reviews to filter out the more dangerous products.

Can we cut down on pesticide use with 'plant vaccines'? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Roynel also supports the plan to speed up approval for biocontrol substances, but said it needs to be part of a wider system change that includes financial support, monitoring and training to use these new products, as well as maintaining the restrictions on more harmful chemical pesticides ― not further deregulation.

"If farmers get easier access to synthetic pesticides tomorrow, they would have no incentive to switch to biocontrol," she said. "It's important to put [biocontrol pesticides] on the market and we fully support that, but… it will not be the silver bullet."

Edited by: Tamsin Walker

World.title: Germany news: Merz calls for unity at CSU party conference
World.content:
Skip next section No change to 'firewall' when it comes to AfD, says Merz

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz once again stood firm on any notion of ever working with Germany's far-right.

Merx restated his opposition to any change in the"firewall" policy of isolating the far-right Alternative ​for Germany party (AfD) at the CSU conference in Munich.

"Anyone who feels they have to ​vote for these people has no place ⁠in ​our Union. ​They have no ​place amongst ‌us," Merz said.

The AfD, has been topping national opinion ⁠polls although a Friday poll showed Merz's conservative bloc closing the gap.

Nevertheless, according to the poll, Merz's coalition would still fall short of a majority were an election to be held.

The poll, conducted for public broadcaster ZDF, asked voters which party they would support if a federal election were held this Sunday.

World.title: North Korean leader Kim Jong Un travels to Chinese border city via newly opened bridge
World.content:
North Korean leader Kim Jong Un travelled to China’s border city of Dandong via a newly opened bridge linking the two countries, where he met a senior Chinese official.

North Korean leader Kim Jong Un arrived in China via the newly opened bridge on Saturday. He arrived in the Chinese border city of Dandong via the New Yalu River Bridge linking the two countries.

China’s top political adviser Wang Huning met North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, Chinese state media reported.

Wang conveyed President Xi Jinping’s "greetings and best wishes to Kim," Xinhua reported.

China and North Korea pledged to "strengthen strategic communication and cooperation to safeguard their sovereignty, security and development interests," Chinese state media said.

The two countries also vowed to expand people-to-people exchanges and economic and trade cooperation through the opening of the New Yalu River Bridge.

The four-lane bridge was completed in 2014 but remained unused for 12 years due to a lack of connecting roads and customs facilities on the North Korean side.

It officially opened about a week ago, marking a step towards strengthening economic ties between the neighbouring countries.

China is North Korea’s largest trading partner and a key source of diplomatic, economic and political support for the isolated, nuclear-armed state, although relations between the two have not always been smooth.

Kim’s trip coincides with key dates in China

The trip coincides with the anniversary of China’s entry into the Korean War, known in China as the "War to Resist US Aggression and Aid Korea." It remains unclear whether Kim will attend commemorative events.

During the 1950-53 war, Chinese troops fought alongside North Korea against South Korea and US-led United Nations forces.

Kim’s visit also comes ahead of a key political meeting in Beijing on Monday, when Chinese President Xi Jinping and other senior officials gather for the fifth plenary session of the Communist Party’s powerful Central Committee.

Xi visited Pyongyang in June 2019, the first visit by a Chinese leader in 14 years (File image) Image: Ahn Young-joon/AP Photo/picture alliance

Bridge highlights North Korea's ties with China

The New Yalu River Bridge opened just over a month after North Korea and Russia inaugurated their first road bridge, which Pyongyang hailed as a sign of closer ties.

While North Korea’s trade with Russia largely involves military supplies, trade with China could provide goods needed to develop its civilian economy, analysts say.

Edited by: Zac Crellin

World.title: France protests: More violence feared amid renewed demonstrations
World.content:
France's Yellow Vest movement, one of the key groups behind recent protests against the high cost of living, on Saturday called for new demonstrations on October 31.

Organizers from the largely rural-based group said in Paris that they wanted fresh rallies and a sit-in outside parliament, as well as outside city halls nationwide, to be held in protest at what it called the "authoritarian drift" of President Emmanuel Macron.

Members of the group have also refused to comply with a police order to shift the route of a union-organized route to the edge of the capital, although the unions themselves have agreed to do so.



Next Saturday, "we will protest for the freedom to protest, and for all our freedoms," a coordinator from the group told journalists at Paris's Bastille square, which was where the march was due to set off originally.

After being central to protests from 2018 to 2020 against rising fuel prices, the Yellow Vest movement went into abeyance but has recently come to the fore once again amid the current wave of demonstrations sweeping France.

World.title: Taiwan: Typhoon Champi leaves 1 dead, over 500 injured
World.content:
After killing one person and causing major disruptions in Taiwan, Typhoon Champi is now headed towards China.

Typhoon Champi killed at least one person and left more than 500 people with injuries as it passed through Taiwan on Saturday.

Taiwan's fire department said the death toll remained at 1, after a man was swept ​away by waves from the island of Liuqiu. At least 527 others were injured during the heavy wind and torrential rain.

Several parts in Taiwan received heavy rain and strong winds that prompted authorities to cut off power, leaving thousands of people without power supply.

Some 280,000 households were knocked out of power, according to United Daily News, a local Taiwanese newspaper. By Saturday morning, the power supply was restored to 80% of the households.

Despite weakening, Champi is still packing strong winds near its center Image: I-Hwa Cheng/AFP

Champi also led to 259 flights cancellations, an improvement from Friday, ⁠when ​the number was almost 1,000, the Transport Ministry said.

Several trees were downed amid strong gusts In the capital Taipei.

Authorities in several districts of northern and central Taiwan, including Taipei, declared a second day of office and school closures on Saturday.

Champi headed to China

The typhoon continued to weaken as it moved north towards the Chinese coast though it was not expected to make landfall there.

Chinese authorities have sent a team to ​the eastern province of Zhejiang as Champi ⁠approached, warning of strong winds and heavy rain through Sunday.

Schools and offices were closed in several districts in Taiwan because of Champi Image: I-Hwa Cheng/AFP

It said it had readied 400 rescue workers and 600 pieces of equipment, ⁠while more than 41,000 firefighters were on ​emergency duty.

Typhoon Champi started out as a super typhoon and one of the strongest storms in the Pacific this year. While it is weakening, Champi is still packing ​gusts of around 78 km/h (126 mph) near its center, according to Taiwan's Central Weather Administration (CWA).

World.title: India news: Neha Bora refuses to sign peace bond, cites right to democratic dissent
World.content:
10/24/2026 October 24, 2026 Neha Bora refuses to sign police peace bond

Bora said AISA had not called the Central Park protest cited in the notice as grounds for the bond [FILE: October 16, 2026] Image: Adnan Abidi/REUTERS

Student leader Neha Bora said on Saturday they would not sign a peace bond, alleging that the evidence cited by police was factually incorrect.

The All India Students' Association (AISA) leader, who uses they/them pronouns, made the statement a day after the Delhi High Court dismissed their plea challenging a police notice directing them to execute a Rs 10,000 (€94.39) personal bond with surety to maintain peace.

AISA and India's youth-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), along with other organizations, are demanding the resignation of controversy-hit Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar after a newspaper investigation alleged impropriety during a large-scale voter-roll revision, which saw the deletion of more than 130 million names from draft electoral rolls nationwide.

"Our concern is that people may be deprived of one of their most fundamental democratic rights: the right to vote," Bora wrote in an oped in the Indian Express newspaper on Saturday.

Bora said AISA had not called the Central Park protest cited in the notice as grounds for the bond. They also questioned whether peaceful demonstrations against alleged voter deletions under the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) exercise could be considered a breach of peace.

"It is essential that peaceful protests and democratic demonstrations on the streets are not declared a breach of peace," they said, adding that they would challenge the interpretation and enforcement of such bonds in court.

Bora said neither they nor AISA would sign the bond, arguing that it violated the fundamental right to democratic dissent.

World.title: Hitler's Eagle's Nest retreat catches fire, police say
World.content:
Authorities have arrested a suspect as firemen try to put out the fire in Bavaria, near the Austrian border.

A fire broke out on Friday evening at the Kehlsteinhaus in Bavaria, more commonly known as the Eagle's Nest and used as a retreat by Adolf Hitler and Nazi officials.

The Kehlsteinhaus was engulfed in flames, a police statement read, adding that a suspect has been arrested and the incident was being criminally investigated.

What do we know so far about the Kehlsteinhaus fire?

A fire alarm went off at the Kehlsteinhaus on the Obersalzberg in Berchtesgaden at around 9:15 p.m. local time (1915 GMT) on Friday, the police said in a statement.

"The fire brigades, who were alerted immediately, could already see flames clearly visible at the Kehlsteinhaus as they approached," the police statement read.

Some 200 firefighters and emergency personnel were deployed to the site. Firefighters struggled to reach the Kehlsteinhaus, which sits at some 1,834 meters (6,017 feet) above sea level, with their engines.

Police added that the building and its immediate vicinity could only be entered while wearing respiratory protective equipment (RPE).

Police said they were unaware of any injuries as of yet.

The site once housed the Nazi leader's heavily fortified country residence [FILE: Jun 21, 2004] Image: Peter Kneffel/dpa/picture alliance

The site once housed Hitler's heavily fortified country residence, where he is believed to have partially written his book "Mein Kampf." It was built in 1938 as a guest house for Nazi officials.

It remains a symbol of the Nazi regime and is among only a few monuments of the Hitler era that survived the World War II bombing unscathed. Today, it is classified as a historical monument and is home to a popular restaurant.

World.title: Última hora de la actualidad política, en directo | Sánchez promete blindar el derecho al aborto en la Constitución si gobierna de nuevo
World.content:
Montero y Rufián arremeten contra el Frente Amplio: “Una izquierda que se presenta en la misma papeleta con el PSOE no va a arreglar los problemas”

La suma de Podemos y Esquerra Republicana de Catalunya (ERC) ha tenido su puesta de largo este sábado, en un acto en el distrito barcelonés de Nou Barris. Las cúpulas de ambos partidos han arropado a Irene Montero y a Gabriel Rufián en un mitin en que ambos han puesto en el foco de sus críticas a las derechas española y catalana, pero también a Frente Amplio. “Una izquierda que se presenta en la misma papeleta con el PSOE no va a arreglar los problemas”, ha asegurado Montero, en referencia al acuerdo que han alcanzado para ir juntos al Senado. “Yo quiero un Gobierno del PSOE sometido a las izquierdas soberanistas”, ha apostillado el republicano.

Ha habido pocas propuestas concretas, salvo la idea lanzada de Montero de querer subir el salario mínimo a los 1.800 euros y rebajar la jornada laboral a las 30 horas. Ambos han coincidido en la idea de expropiar a los fondos buitres, haciendo evidente que será la vivienda el tema central de la campaña.

Montero ha comenzado su intervención con un alegato contra las declaraciones de Alberto Núñez Feijóo en Cadena SER, el pasado viernes. “Feijóo, tu machismo mata”, ha asegurado la candidata morada para afear al líder popular su propuesta de eliminar el Ministerio de Igualdad y reabrir el debate sobre el aborto. La eurodiputada ha sido especialmente dura tras recordar que Feijóo aseguró que era “feminista” porque había sido criado por mujeres. “¿No te das cuenta? ¿No te preguntas donde estaban los hombres? Porque son ellas las que soportan en sus cuerpos, en sus enfermedades y en sus tristezas las tareas de sus cuidados”.

World.title: ¿Dónde y por qué se protesta en Europa? Las reivindicaciones de los jóvenes de cada país
World.content:
Estudiantes, sindicatos y vecinos han convocado más de 170 manifestaciones en poco más de un mes en todo el continente. Sus motivos a menudo coinciden

Media Europa vuelve a salir a la calle este sábado. Hay convocatorias desde Grecia hasta Bélgica, pasando por Albania, Francia, Portugal y España. Son las últimas de un otoño de movilizaciones: entre el 15 de septiembre y el 23 de octubre, 12 países europeos suman al menos 177 protestas o manifestaciones. La cifra es parecida a la media de 190 protestas mensuales entre septiembre y octubre de los otoños más intensos de la crisis del euro (2010, 2011 y 2012), según los registros de PolDem, un proyecto universitario que recopila protestas a partir de noticias de agencias. Francia, España, Italia, Portugal y Bélgica concentran la mayoría de las movilizaciones contabilizadas.

Las reivindicaciones cambian de un país a otro, pero tres se repiten de forma constante: la vivienda, la educación y el coste de la vida. Francia es ahora el centro de las concentraciones por la educación y el coste de la vida, y esas protestas se han extendido a Italia y Bélgica. En España, el foco es la vivienda: la primera gran manifestación del otoño se celebró el 26 de septiembre, tras el desahucio de Maricarmen, y reunió a al menos 25.000 personas en Madrid, según la Delegación del Gobierno (el Sindicato de Inquilinas contabilizó 300.000). Hasta esa fecha, fue la mayor protesta en una sola ciudad de este ciclo, y ha inspirado a manifestantes de Portugal e Italia. Al este del continente, los motivos son otros: la corrupción es el problema principal en Albania y en Serbia. En Alemania, las concentraciones son más pequeñas y se centran en la oposición al servicio militar y al rearme.

Images) Estudiantes se manifiestan contra la falta de recursos y personal en el sistema educativo, en la plaza de la República de París, el 4 de octubre de 2026. Veronique de Viguerie (Getty Images)

Los estudiantes han protagonizado buena parte de las protestas, pero se han ido sumando sindicatos, docentes y otros colectivos. Coinciden en el tiempo y comparten reivindicaciones, pero responden a conflictos nacionales distintos y no forman un movimiento coordinado. Que coincidan en otoño tiene una explicación en el calendario: “Los estudiantes vuelven a los centros, las redes organizativas se activan y los cambios en las tasas, las ayudas y las condiciones de estudio se vuelven inmediatamente tangibles”, explica Luka Lešić, de la Unión Europea de Estudiantes.

Los datos recopilados por EL PAÍS, a partir de agencias, medios y fuentes oficiales, incluyen las protestas contra medidas gubernamentales que reunieron al menos un centenar de personas y tuvieron cobertura en medios nacionales. Como se ve en el gráfico, los cinco países con más movilizaciones reúnen el 80% de las registradas.

La mayoría de las manifestaciones han sido pacíficas. Según los datos recopilados por este periódico, 49 protestas han terminado con detenidos y al menos 30 con agentes de la policía heridos. Ha habido episodios violentos en Italia, Albania y, sobre todo, Francia. Allí, la jornada del 17 de octubre reunió a 550.000 manifestantes en todo el país, según el Ministerio del Interior y terminó con más de 2.000 detenidos, casi 1.000 agentes heridos y destrozos importantes en varias ciudades, como el incendio del Ayuntamiento de Limoges. En Italia, el 18 de octubre, unos 2.000 jóvenes convocados por redes sociales, sin organización ni reivindicaciones políticas, irrumpieron en el centro de Milán para romper escaparates y saquear tiendas. La policía llevó a comisaría a 271, el 80% de ellos menores. Mientras, en Albania, más de 10 días de movilizaciones violentas han dejado el Tribunal Supremo, el Ministerio de Educación y otros edificios de la ciudad incendiados.

Manifestantes vandalizan un establecimiento durante unas protestas en Milán, Italia, el 18 de octubre de 2026. Andrea Carrubba (Anadolu/Getty Images)

A continuación, repasamos las causas y las razones de las reivindicaciones más transversales entre las protestas del continente.

Educación

En Francia, las protestas empezaron a mediados de septiembre con bloqueos de institutos y se extendieron en tres semanas a todo el país. El 1 de octubre hubo cientos de centros bloqueados. Los alumnos piden que se cubran las plazas de profesores vacantes —al comienzo del curso faltaba al menos uno en el 53% de los centros, según el sindicato docente SNES-FSU—, menos alumnos por clase y edificios en mejor estado. Este malestar social, en parte provocado por la necesidad de Francia de hacer recortes presupuestarios para reducir un elevado nivel de endeudamiento, ha cristalizado en el mayor movimiento de protesta en décadas.

La furia de los estudiantes franceses también encendió la ira de sus compañeros de la Bélgica francófona, que protestan desde octubre contra la subida de las tasas y los recortes presupuestarios, sobre todo en Bruselas y en Lieja. En prevención de posibles nuevos disturbios este fin de semana, Bruselas emitió una prohibición de circulación de patinetes y bicicletas eléctricas compartidas entre las diez de la mañana del viernes y las 22.00 del sábado en el centro de la ciudad.

En Italia salieron a la calle el 16 de octubre, entre otros motivos contra la norma que limita al 30% la presencia de determinadas categorías de alumnos extranjeros en las clases de primer curso. En Madrid, los profesores de la enseñanza pública están en huelga indefinida desde el 14 de octubre, y en Atenas más de 10.000 personas, según la policía, secundaron el día 21 una huelga de maestros.

Vivienda y coste de la vida

En España, a la acampada de Sol le siguió el 3 de octubre una jornada de marchas en medio centenar de ciudades, un día después de que el Congreso tumbara los dos decretos de vivienda del Gobierno. Los sindicatos mayoritarios convocaron una huelga general para el 11 de noviembre. En Portugal, las acampadas de Lisboa y Oporto pedían retirar un proyecto de ley que facilita los desahucios: la policía las ha desalojado el 20 de octubre.

El combustible movilizó a los transportistas del sur de Italia, que bloquean carreteras desde mediados de octubre, con el gasóleo a 2,30 euros el litro. En 2018, la subida de su impuesto ya llevó a la calle en Francia a los chalecos amarillos. En Alemania, los sindicatos reunieron el 26 de septiembre a 175.000 personas, según los convocantes, contra los recortes en pensiones y sanidad. La inflación se ha moderado desde el máximo de 2022, pero desde entonces los precios han subido un 23,6% en la UE, según Eurostat.

Corrupción

En Albania, la protesta empezó en mayo como un movimiento pacífico, la llamada revolución de los flamencos, contra la cesión de una reserva natural a empresarios vinculados con Jared Kushner, yerno de Donald Trump. Con el comienzo del curso, el 13 de octubre, se sumaron los estudiantes y las protestas se volvieron violentas: el 14 ardieron los ministerios de Educación y de Finanzas, y hasta el 19 hubo 310 heridos, según Europa Press. Piden la dimisión del primer ministro, Edi Rama, en el poder desde 2013, y acusan al Gobierno de proteger a grupos mafiosos. Ningún tribunal lo ha probado, aunque la Fiscalía investiga a la exviceprimera ministra, Belinda Balluku, por corrupción y blanqueo y el alcalde de Tirana, Erion Veliaj, permanece en prisión preventiva desde febrero de 2025, acusado de los mismos cargos.

Manifestantes hablan con agentes de policía durante una protesta antigubernamental de estudiantes en Tirana, Albania, el 20 de octubre de 2026. Louisa Gouliamaki (REUTERS)

En Serbia, el movimiento estudiantil ha madurado a lo lago de dos años en las calles, después de la muerte de 16 personas en el derrumbe de la estación de Novi Sad, en noviembre de 2024. Sus demostraciones forzaron al Gobierno de Aleksandar Vucic a adelantar las elecciones, convocadas para este domingo. El movimiento se presenta como Lista de Estudiantes y es la segunda fuerza, según la última encuesta de Ipsos. El jueves, unas 150.000 personas se concentraron en Belgrado, según recuentos independientes.

La respuesta de los gobiernos

En Francia, el Gobierno decretó toques de queda en París y otras ciudades, y también anunció más de 3.000 profesores suplentes y retiró la subida de algunas tasas universitarias. Para este sábado, el Ejecutivo solo ha autorizado las marchas sindicales y ha prohibido las concentraciones en Lyon y Marsella, con un despliegue policial un 20% mayor que el del 17 de octubre.

En Italia, el decreto de seguridad ya castigaba la participación violenta en una manifestación con hasta cinco años de prisión, y de cara a la jornada de hoy las autoridades han blindado el centro de Milán y las estaciones de la periferia desde las que llegaron los jóvenes.

La policía lleva a cabo detenciones y arrestos de los manifestantes tras las protestas contra el alto costo de la vida en Milán, Italia, el 18 de octubre de 2026. Andrea Carrubba (Anadolu/ Getty Images)

Las próximas citas llegan en noviembre: una jornada sindical en Francia el día 5, una jornada estudiantil en Alemania el 17, la huelga general del sindicato CGIL en Italia el 20 y, en Portugal, una manifestación de la CGTP ante el Parlamento portugués el 24. Además de la huelga general convocada en España para el 11 de noviembre.

Con información de Raquel Villaécija, desde París; Silvia Ayuso, desde Bruselas; Francisco Peregil, desde Tirana, e Íñigo Domínguez, desde Roma.
