World.title: Cox Plate as it happened: Stars align for Cosmic Crusader as trainer Andrea Leek makes history
World.content:
Andrea Leek almost had the perfect day. The only thing missing as she celebrated becoming the first woman to train the winner of the Cox Plate in 32 years, and the first at Flemington, was her husband by her side.

John Leek Jr was at a friend’s house, cheering from the couch as his wife’s horse Cosmic Crusader defied the firepower of the country’s biggest stables.

Jockey Willie Pike and trainer Andrea Leek were congratulated by owner Bob Peters (right) after Cosmic Crusader’s win. Getty Images

He was unable to walk through Flemington’s famous gates, having been rubbed out of racing and banned from all tracks for three years in August on a charge of attempting to stomach tube a horse.

He is also banned from staying in the family house at Nar Nar Goon North under the rules of racing because it is a training property.

“It’s devastating not having him here,” Leek said in the mounting yard after Cosmic Crusader and jockey William Pike had powered down the Flemington straight to edge out Chris Waller’s pair Birdman and Aeliana.

“He’s my biggest supporter, and he’s devastated he’s not able to be here.

“But he’ll still be in the background, and he’ll be celebrating with us tonight.”

The salute: William Pike after passing the finishing post. Getty Images

Leek, 53, took a moment away from the biggest win of her fledgling career to explain that her family were still working through the ramifications of her husband’s disqualifications.

“Look, he’s actually in one way happy that he’s been pushed into retirement,” she said of the 72-year-old former trainer.

“But not being able to be on the family farm is very hard, and not being able to have him at home, you know, being at home on my own is very, very difficult.

“So I think November 17, they (the Racing Victoria board) are looking at that and whether they can put in some safety parameters and he can be with his cows and dogs and just be in the house and not near any horses.

“We are really hoping that will prevail.”

Even in her husband’s absence, the historic Flemington victory belonged to Leek who joined Deirdre Stein (Rising Prince in 1985) and Moira Murdoch (Solvit, 1994) as the only female trainers to lift the Cox Plate.

Gai Waterhouse’s import Sir Delius ran sixth, leaving the champion still without a win in the race.

“I said before I feel like I’m an imposter,” Leek said of her name being etched into the record books. She can’t feel that way any longer.

While the former jumps jockey, and the first woman to ride the winner of the Great Eastern Steeple in 2004, might not have felt deserving of sharing the stage with the likes of Waller and Ciaron Maher, a victory in the $6 million Cox Plate changes everything.

One person who always believed in her undoubted potential was astute Western Australian owner Bob Peters.

The Perth billionaire chuckled when asked why he had shunned a well-worn path to the front doors of Waller and Maher in favour of entrusting Cosmic Crusader’s care to Leek.

Trainer Andrea Leek, with Mitchell Leek. Getty Images

“Oh, a lot of people told me I should do that when he (Cosmic Crusader) came over (from Perth),” Peters said.

“I said I’d probably gone a bit senile, but it’s worked out all right.”

Leek’s career boost came at the most unusual of times in the most unlikely of places.

She took a phone call from Peters during the depths of winter while watching the jumps racing at Terang.

“He said, ‘Now I’m thinking of sending you this horse. Are you prepared?’,” she recalled.

“And, you know, he gave me some guidelines that I had to do, and I said, ‘absolutely, I’m up for it’, and here we are, we’ve won the Cox Plate.”

Her appeal to a hands-on owner such as Peters was a lifetime working with horses and the rolling hills of her Nar Nar Goon North property, but the initial contact came through her husband.

“An owner I had earlier in my career, Jason, said to Bob, ‘there’s a guy, John Leek, and he trains things the way you like training so why don’t you have a look at his establishment’,” she said.

“Bob listened and said he’d send a horse, and then he sent a few. I was lucky enough six months ago when he rang me up and said ‘how about I give you a few horses’ and it has turned into this.”

Sharing the post-race jubilation was the punters’ pal, William Pike, known as The Wizard of the west to those who have clawed out of a luckless day by “backing Pikey in the last” at Ascot.

A long-time ally of Peters, he rode the perfect race.

He dropped Cosmic Crusader back to third last in a 14-horse field from the gates, stalking favourite Aeliana, as Land Legend set a hot pace and made his move as they turned for home in Flemington’s famous straight.

He powered over the top of Aeliana and Birdman in the last 50m, with Ceolwulf in fourth.

“I wanted him to be back because he (Cosmic Crusader) loves the thrill of the kill and getting past them. That’s what we do in trackwork,” Leek said.

“He’s always got a bunny to chase and that is what he loves. That is what he needed and he got it today.”

Overcome with the madness of the biggest win of his career, Pike stood up in the irons and screamed to the heavens.

“I had in my mind over the line, I’m not much of a saluter, I’m like ‘don’t salute, don’t salute’ and then the moment gets the better of you and you stand up and you salute and you carry on,” he said.

“It’s amazing, it’s infectious. (There’s a) big crowd, an iconic day – most likely the only ever Cox Plate to be run here – so it’s nice that we get to etch our name in there.”

All smiles: Jockey William Pike. Getty Images

Victory in the weight-for-age championship put to bed the disappointment Leek, Peters and Pike had felt after finishing fourth in last week’s Caulfield Cup.

“Maybe the Caulfield Cup was a slip in run. We were always hoping he was good enough for a Cox Plate, and he is,” Leek said.

“He’s an amazing horse. I said to Bob this morning that I think I had him a little bit flat for the Caulfield Cup and may have done too much on the Tuesday.

“He was better going into today. I knew going into today I had him cherry ripe. I was praying for rain but we didn’t get it. He was still too good.”

World.title: No October joy for Carlton stars on Cox Plate’s sojourn to Flemington
World.content:
SportRacingCox Plate No October joy for Carlton stars on Cox Plate’s sojourn to Flemington Andrew Wu and Danny Russell October 24, 2026 — 7:56pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Patrick Cripps has had his share of sporting heartbreak in August and September. He can now add October to the list. For a few fleeting moments, it looked as if Irish import Birdman was about to deliver one of Australian racing’s greatest prizes for the Carlton champion only for his Cox Plate dream to be dashed by a horse from his home state. As trainer Andrea Leek, who operates stables in Nar Nar Goon North, celebrated becoming the first woman in 32 years to win Australia’s weight-for-age championship with West Australian star Cosmic Crusader, the dual Brownlow winner and his Carlton crew were left to wonder what might have been. Trainer Andrea Leek poses with the trophy. Getty Images Blues champion Chris Judd let out a curse – his sense of frustration at coming so close shared throughout the Baggers Naggers syndicate, which also features former captains Marc Murphy and Sam Docherty, Sam Walsh and former Carlton midfielder Will Setterfield.



Birdman has taken the Blues brigade on a wild ride since their former line coach John Barker dropped the captain’s name as part of his spiel to get into prominent owner Ozzie Kheir’s exclusive racing circle two years ago. Kheir had initially bought Birdman with eyes on Melbourne Cup glory only for master Sydney trainer Chris Waller to change tack 12 months ago and focus on middle distances with the galloper. The salute: William Pike after passing the finishing post. Getty Images Unlike in football, where the pain of defeat is sharp, there were no heads hung in disappointment or walks of shame from the field. There is a prize for second in a Cox Plate, but the reasons to celebrate are deeper than an $800,000 cheque, of which Cripps and his football mates will take home only a micro-fraction.



“The whole thing about racing is bringing people together,” Cripps, who flew in from Perth on Friday for the race, said. “That’s what makes footy clubs special, and it’s what makes racing syndicates special – you bring people together. You make good memories together.” Jockey Ben Melham was given warm applause by Birdman’s ownership, of which the Baggers Naggers syndicate is one of many, as he returned to the mounting yard to deliver his race debrief. Then it was Kheir’s turn. He thanked his fellow owners for their “amazing support”.



Sam Walsh and Patrick Cripps. AFL Photos “It’s the hardest race to win, nearly in the world,” Kheir told them. Sent out an $11 chance by punters, Birdman looked the winner for a few strides after kicking strongly once clear at the 300-metre mark, only for Will Pike and Cosmic Crusader to collar him in the final 50 metres. “It was crazy,” Cripps said. “You don’t get many moments in life when you get a feeling like that. It’s pretty cool.” Cripps likened the thrilling finish to the race to that of a nailbiter in a big game at the MCG – with one major difference.



“You get the same buzz, the hard thing is in a race you don’t have control over the outcome,” Cripps said. “At least on the footy field, you can have some sort of control. If you ask anyone in racing, this is probably the grand final in racing. For us, it’s a privilege to be a part of it.” Barker, the manager of the syndicate, was a regular at Moonee Valley on Cox Plate day. His father recently became a life member of the Moonee Valley Racing Club. Related Article Spring racing carnival Cox Plate as it happened: Stars align for Cosmic Crusader as trainer Andrea Leek makes history “At the 150, I thought geezers, this can’t happen,” Barker, who played for Hawthorn, Brisbane and Fitzroy, said.



They are already eyeing another crack next year. “We’ve got a horse with a bit of talent, we’ve got a superstar trainer, so the future’s bright,” Barker said. “I’ll still be able to connect with these Carlton boys.“ Barker, Cripps, Judd, Murphy and Walsh are part of a smaller group in another syndicate, the Baggers Five, who recently acquired a share in Melbourne Cup hope James J Braddock. For them, redemption can come in November. Sports news, results and expert commentary.

World.title: ‘Everyone can do difficult things’: The surprise Sydney school offering Latin
World.content:
NationalNSWHSC ‘Everyone can do difficult things’: The surprise Sydney school offering Latin Christopher Harris October 24, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Andrew Gollan has had quite the career. After completing an arts degree in Latin and ancient Greek in the 1990s, he moved to America, became a US resident and worked in Silicon Valley as a software engineer. But he felt there was more to life than writing code. “I really wanted to do something which, I thought, was important,” he said. Year 12 Latin teacher from Caringbah High School Andrew Gollan. Sam Mooy After completing a master’s degree, where the language of instruction was Latin, he worked as a teacher across America before returning home to Australia. In 2019, he arrived at the Shire’s Caringbah High to relaunch the classical language at the school. Across NSW, Latin has had some difficult decades, falling from 1558 enrolments – about 8 per cent of all students in the first year of the HSC – in 1967 to 129 students this year.



It is a long, steep decline which some might describe as terminal, so it might seem strange that Caringbah High would revive the language. German had been on offer but struggled to attract students past year 8. The then-principal, who had his own fond memories of studying Latin, felt it might be a better fit. “That’s how he presented it to me at least,” Gollan says. Six years on, things are going well. Year 7 students entering high school do a medley of languages, a term each is spent on French, Japanese and Latin before choosing one. So far, Latin has enough students to fill two year 8 classes and a decent-sized year 9 class. “I lose a couple between year 9 and year 10,” says Gollan. The first cohort of year 7 students who commenced in 2021 sat the HSC Latin continuers exam this year. And six students who commenced the subject when in year 8 completed HSC exams last year. “It’s a big ask for a school like this to run classes that are this small, and to do it regularly enough so the kids know that they’ve got a decent pathway to the HSC and they’re not going to be, sort of, chopped off at the knees,” he says.



In NSW, it’s not just Latin in crisis but other languages too. In the 1960s, over a third of students learnt a language other than English. Now it is about 6 per cent. When the NSW curriculum was reviewed in 2020, it was recommended requiring every student to commence learning a second language in primary. But it was never adopted. Part of the problem is a lack of teachers – a French teacher at Newtown High pocketed a $20,000 sign-on bonus just for taking the job earlier this year. Year 12 Caringbah High School Latin students Henry He, Xander Ezzy and Sarah Napper after their HSC exam this week. Sam Mooy Students in public schools are aware of the challenges with running languages, including Caringbah High’s Sarah Napper, 18. She associates Latin with exclusive private and certain selective schools. By comparison, she says while her school is selective, it’s commonly perceived as a “mid-tier”. “I don’t think Latin should be exclusively taught in selective schools or these upper-tier private schools … I think everyone can do difficult things, and I think doing Latin has been really good for me,” she says.



While she enjoys the subject now, she says it was a steep learning curve. “It’s an analytical language, which basically means that instead of using many words like English to encode a meaning, it instead encodes meaning through changing the words itself,” she said. HSC enrolment data shows over the past 15 years, Latin has dropped from 176 students to 140 last year. But some schools have seen a small bounce in Latin enrolments, including some selective and certain private schools. Among them is all-boys school Shore, where eight students took the subject last year. Latin teacher Joanna Watkins likes to categorise students who choose the subject into three distinct groups. “The students with a maths brain enjoy the decoding of Latin,” she says.



There are the linguistic-inclined and then those with an interest in all aspects of ancient Roman culture. She’s also noticed something else. Related Article HSC ‘We are in crisis’: The HSC subject bleeding enrolments “More recently, we get kids who have been tutored in Latin before they come into year 7,” she said. She is unsure what exactly is driving that. “I can only guess that the parents are looking at schools which offer Latin,” she said. She linked the subject’s popularity with the school’s high performance in the subject, while students aspiring to study at universities overseas saw it as an advantage. “In the US, those universities tend to value Latin. Cambridge and Oxford have a strong tradition.”



Dr Robert Kowalski, who has taught Latin and Classical Greek at the University of Sydney and numerous private schools and now works as a tutor, said the demand was driven by parents. “I think they want to have the kids very well-educated. If you give the kids an opportunity, they will pick it up.” Related Article Editorial

Schools Language learning is the gift we must give our children The Herald's View Editorial Across Sydney, the biggest enrolment of students in Latin is Sydney Grammar. Its head of classical languages, Nathan Bottomley, said there were about six boys in his Latin class when he attended the school as a student in the 1980s. This year, there are almost 30. He said some believe it is useful when it comes to getting a high ATAR for university entry. “Sometimes they get the impression, which we try to dispel, that it scales very well.



“The kids who I teach are genuinely enthusiastic,” he said. But success comes with persistence and practice. “Students always want the trick. And the answer is always really boring – you just have to keep doing it. There’s something about being inquisitive in mastering a complex system, the pleasure of getting good at something.” The next biggest cohort of students in Latin is Sydney Girls followed by Meriden, which has also seen a bounce. Meriden principal Lisa Brown said it had strong enrolments in languages across the board and there was no special push to boost Latin enrolments. “You have to have an ability and a real interest in Latin to be able to persevere. It is not an easy subject, you can’t just have a go at it, there has to be a deep interest and an ability to work hard.”



St Joseph’s College in Hunters Hill normally has about five students enrolled in HSC Latin. Last year it was just one studying the subject. Director of teaching and learning Darren Frost said the school runs an “off-timetable” class in year 8. “The boys love it, compared to the other languages. It is a skill they can transfer, which is one of the big reasons we maintain it,” he said. When it comes to the HSC, he has noticed across the board a narrowing of the curriculum. “The breadth is so important for our society,” he said. “People are gaming the system, as opposed to what education is about, and the passion of learning is lost.”



Back at Caringbah High, Xander Ezzy, 18, knows there’s only a small community in Sydney where he can converse in Latin. But its power was connecting with people who lived thousands of years ago. “That was most enjoyable being able to connect it to a whole lifestyle that isn’t the lifestyle we have today,” he said. World.title: Inside the NBA’s luxury bubble, and why Joe Ingles was ready to leave
World.content:
SportBasketballNBA Inside the NBA’s luxury bubble, and why Joe Ingles was ready to leave Jon Pierik October 24, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

When Australian basketball great Joe Ingles was in the prime of his NBA career, the multimillion-dollar teams were flown across the US in chartered private jets. Having returned to the NBL after 12 seasons in America, he’s back to flying cattle class on Melbourne United’s road trips. The comedown in airline luxury from his days with the Utah Jazz, Milwaukee Bucks, Orlando Magic and Minnesota Timberwolves hasn’t fazed him, and that’s because he knows how relentless the NBA grind is on its athletes. Having his say: Joe Ingles is back playing in the NBL, but is also keeping a close eye on the new NBA season. Daniel Pockett Ingles is enjoying hanging out with Melbourne United teammates, coaches and staff in the Virgin club lounge, as he did on their trip to Perth before the 103-102 loss on Friday night. “We hang out in the lounge, grab a coffee, yeah, I mean, I got no complaints,” Ingles, 39, said.



Related Article NBA Ben Simmons was on the verge of an NBA comeback after 538 days. A serious injury has derailed it Never short of a quip, he added: “Will Larry [Kestelman, majority owner of the NBL] charter us a plane? Probably not. It’d be nice if he would, but no, I mean it’s cool, man.” The NBA can deliver a life of luxury. There are the eye-watering contracts that could soon even have the top players earning $US1 million ($1.4 million) per game, not to mention the endorsement riches on offer. Then there are the chartered flights, allowing players and staff to swiftly exit a city late at night and arrive at their next destination in the early hours of the morning. “The flying is cool, like it’s cool flying five nights a week and getting home at 4am,” Ingles said, sarcastically. “Is it a necessity? Yes, for the amount of games you play and the schedule. You, obviously, can’t sit in the Virgin lounge and wait until the next day and then fly into a city and play. Does it make it a f---load easier? Absolutely. You pull up to the airport, you walk on the plane, and you take off, kind of thing.



Related Article NBL ‘Have you not seen what I have made?’ Why Joe Ingles gave up $5.1 million to play in the NBL “Comfy seats, team nutritionists will have food on there. You can sleep if you want. You can play cards. There’s tables on there. It’s very luxurious in a way, I guess. But, obviously, in saying that, don’t get twisted looking from the outside looking in. The salaries, the big house, the chartered flights, whatever it is, it’s a brutal season and I think people take that for granted. “I did prior to being in the NBA. I used to sit there and think: ‘Well, of course, LeBron averages 30 a game. It’s LeBron.’ But when you see what it takes on the day to day, on your mind and your body, and the physicality of it, [Minnesota star] Ant Edwards is getting double-teamed every game four or five nights a week and is still putting up 30 points a game, it’s a true level of professionalism.” Ingles is enjoying life in the NBL, the competition which propelled him into NBA stardom, and a career which has netted him riches he never expected. But as the new NBA season got underway this week, there was a period of adjustment for the father of three who this season is also an ambassador for Prime Video, one of the league’s key broadcasters. “It was, obviously, a big part of my life for a long time, so it’s very different to be sitting on this end. But yeah, excited to sit back and watch it and watch how it plays out from here and watch the NBA Cup and watch the play-in tournament,” Ingles said.



“All these different things that I’ve I’ve been involved in for so long – it’ll be weird, but it’ll be nice to be on the other side.” Ingles’ primary focus remains on United, who on Sunday host the defending champions Sydney Kings at John Cain Arena, giving him a chance to catch up with great mate and fellow former NBA player Matthew Dellavedova, who is nursing a calf issue. View post on X United have had a stuttering start to a season, with new coach Jacob Chancefinding his way, while injuries, particularly to marksman Chris Goulding, have hurt. Ingles has delivered as the veteran play-making forward, who can nail a long jump shot – and can still trash talk with the best. Friday night’s loss to the Wildcats stung, leaving United at 3-5, wasting a huge game from hometown boy Luke Travers, who had 26 points, nine rebounds and five assists.



Import Josh Oduro was strong with 22 points, four rebounds and two blocks, point guard Cole Anthony had 19 points and three assists before fouling out late, while Ingles had 11 points, eight assists, six rebounds and three steals. “We’ve got a bunch of games left, and you want to be playing pretty well a bit later in the season,” Ingles said. Time to make a run: Joe Ingles and Melbourne United need to get busy if they are to make the NBL play-offs. Getty Images “But we, obviously, have to build towards that, too, so there’s no excuse from that point. We should be, and can, play better.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: ‘Give them a go’: Liberal candidate advises vote for One Nation in upper house
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsVictoriaVictorian election ‘Give them a go’: Liberal candidate advises vote for One Nation in upper house Kieran Rooney and Angus Delaney October 24, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. A Liberal candidate in a key battleground seat has been caught out encouraging people to vote for One Nation in the upper house while campaigning in the electorate that is considered vulnerable to Pauline Hanson’s party. Five weeks out from the state election, the incident is a fresh headache for Opposition Leader Jess Wilson as she asks voters to elect a Coalition government outright in the face of Labor attacks tying the conservative political movements together. Liberal candidate Simmone Cottom ran for the federal seat of Hawke in 2025 and is now running in Sunbury. Justin McManus The Liberal Party has also been forced to intervene after a sitting MP planned to appear as a guest speaker at a fundraiser for an independent candidate, despite her party having endorsed a candidate to run in the same seat. In a recording made last weekend, which has been obtained by The Age, the Liberal candidate for Sunbury Simmone Cottom was asked by a voter about her position on the possibility of a coalition with One Nation.



Simmone Cottom campaigning in Sunbury last weekend. Facebook “Both the leaders, [One Nation leader] Warren Pickering and Jess [Wilson] have said we want to try and win in our own right,” she replied. “A lot of people have asked me about preferences. That’s open until November 9 for people to nominate to be candidates and then our preferences will be done.” When pressed further, Cottom said: “I’m encouraging people to change the government. In the lower house, vote Liberals and in the upper house, vote One Nation.” The voter then asked: “So you’re advocating One Nation?”



Cottom replied: “Lower house, Liberals, and if you really want One Nation, give them a go in the upper house.” When the voter made it clear he was not interested in supporting Hanson’s party, Cottom focused more on her own party, reiterating that they wanted to “win in our own right”. “I personally don’t have [a relationship with One Nation] ... We believe that we can win and not need them.” In a statement to The Age on Saturday, Cottom said she regretted her comments. “I shouldn’t have said it,” she said. “It’s not our position. We want Victorians voting Liberal and Nationals in both houses.”



Wilson, who has faced repeated questions about how her party will deal with One Nation, has consistently told voters that the only way to remove the three-term Labor government is to vote for her Coalition MPs. As the major parties shift into campaign mode, The Age can also reveal that Liberal upper house MP Ann-Marie Hermans has been advertised as a guest speaker for a fundraiser for Caroline White – an independent candidate running in Clarinda – alongside Libertarian MP David Limbrick and Albert Park independent Adrian King. The fundraising event for Clarina independent Caroline White, where Liberal MP Ann-Marie Hermans was advertised as a guest speaker. White is running against John Paganis, the Liberal candidate for the seat held by Labor’s Meng Heang Tak. “If I was John Paganis, I’d be super annoyed and super confused,” another Liberal candidate said, speaking on the condition of anonymity to detail internal matters.



Hermans’ attendance was cancelled on Saturday after The Age contacted the party to ask if it was appropriate. “Ann-Marie will not be attending this event,” a Liberal Party spokesperson said. “She is supporting John Paganis, the Liberal candidate for Clarinda, and is focused on helping elect a Liberal and Nationals government on 28 November.” Liberal MP Ann-Marie Hermans will not be attending the fundraiser, a party spokesperson said. Justin McManus Hermans was contacted for comment.



White also ran for Clarinda in 2022 and preferenced the Liberal candidate, an arrangement the party matched. Both put Labor’s candidate last on their how-to-vote cards. Related Article Victorian election Deal or no deal? How the major parties are tackling the minority government risk Cottom, the Sunbury candidate, has run for parliament twice before – in the same seat at the 2022 state election, and in the federal seat of Hawke at last year’s federal election. In April 2025, members of the Plymouth Brethren Christian Church – formerly known as the Exclusive Brethren – were identified wearing Liberal T-shirts and assisting Cottom’s campaign at an early voting booth in Melton. Sunbury is currently held by Labor’s Josh Bull on a typically safe margin of 6.4 per cent, but it is considered in play as the government braces for a sizeable swing against them, particularly in such outer suburban electorates that are considered vulnerable amid the rise of One Nation.



The Age’s Resolve Political Monitor has One Nation with a primary vote of 23 per cent. If that is replicated in the upper house, Hanson’s party would be in a strong position to hold the balance of power, forcing whichever party that forms government to negotiate with them to pass legislation. Wilson has ruled out a formal coalition with One Nation, saying there would be “no deals”. But she has sidestepped questions about how she would deal with Hanson’s party in the event that she required the support of its MPs to form government. In turn, Labor strategists have built their campaign around the claim that Wilson will not be able to claim power without One Nation’s support, using every media release and press conference to warn of the possibility of a “Liberal-One Nation” government. The latest Resolve poll has the Coalition with a primary vote of 28 per cent and Labor on 25 per cent. These numbers would most likely deliver a change of government – given the Coalition is expected to be favoured by One Nation preferences – but it remains unclear whether Wilson could form a majority in her own right.



A primary vote under 30 per cent has traditionally been diabolical for a party seeking to govern in its own right, but the rise of One Nation has led to widespread uncertainty about the outcome of one of the nation’s first true three-cornered contests. The final result in many seats will come down to which party runs third and where its preferences flow. The May by-election in Nepean was the first Victorian example of how this phenomenon could play out. Liberal candidate Anthony Marsh was comfortably elected when One Nation’s Darren Hercus ran third, with 77.5 per cent of One Nation voters preferencing Marsh above independent Tracee Hutchison. World.title: By all means, pay tribute to musicians – just spare me the wigs
World.content:
CultureMusicThe Verdict By all means, pay tribute to musicians – just spare me the wigs Great songs deserve to be free, not squeezed into hand-me-down trousers. Michael Dwyer October 24, 2026 — 7:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

It looked like Jim Morrison was having a few for the road. He’d stepped offstage at the Borderline in London an hour or so earlier and slouched to the bar still in his blousy shirt, brown leather pants and trademark belt with its big silver medallions. Jim Morrison had been dead 22 years that night. This guy, having sung a set of Doors songs with a band that looked and sounded uncannily like the Doors, told me in a suspiciously affected mumble they were off to play Paris the next day. I told him to be careful and went home. There’s nothing wrong with musicians covering songs by other artists – but are tribute acts a bridge too far? You have to draw your own line with tribute acts. For me, with his excellent hair and accurate trousers and cultivated cool, this cat was on the wrong side of it. It’s the in-character vibe that makes me nervous when I see, for example, an ad for Starman: The David Bowie Show, with the guy prowling in his orange bouffant and sleek jumpsuit promising an “uncanny” conjuring of the real deal. And it’s not only because he’s hotter than I am.



OK, full disclosure. My band plays David Bowie songs too. Nobody plays David though, and we do it on ukuleles. Not a tribute act; an art project, I tell people – often as they eye the exit. I get that. You have to draw your own line with art projects. Great songs should be kept alive. A familiar title on a new album is usually where I drop the needle or point my mouse first. There’s the pleasure of recognition, followed by the fascinating question of what this particular person has found in it. Songs actually accumulate value that way. Lucinda Williams covered the music of The Beatles in her From Abbey Road album – while remaining true to herself. Paul Rovere That dub reggae version of Dark Side of the Moon? Fantastic. Hayseed Dixie playing AC/DC as bluegrass? Brilliant. A school choir singing Wichita Lineman? Shut up and give me a tissue. None of these require us to imagine the original artist has returned in a crap Halloween costume. Nor does every cover need a clever new arrangement. Sing it straight, by all means. Just let me hear what it means to you. Somewhere in the gap between your voice and the one in my memory, there’s space for something unexpected. The smaller that gap, the more I’ll just notice what’s missing.



Lucinda Williams singing the Beatles on her From Abbey Road album and Chrissie Hynde singing Dylan on Standing in the Doorway remain unmistakably themselves. That’s the attraction: two people in the song, the one who wrote it and the one who’s finding something of herself there. The impersonator, by contrast, is all about closing that distance. Every vowel, gesture and trouser line reassures us that we’re going somewhere we’ve been before. I do appreciate the dedication of the guy with Liam Gallagher’s haircut, anorak and top lip glued to the microphone. It’s just his ambition that leaves me cold. This prejudice becomes harder to defend at the cinema, where impersonating a famous singer is considered an Oscar-worthy artistic undertaking. Jeremy Allen White becomes Bruce Springsteen. Marisa Abela becomes Amy Winehouse. Jennifer Hudson becomes Aretha Franklin. Joaquin Phoenix even becomes Johnny Cash. We celebrate these musicians because they’re unique, then the vocal coach gets to work proving someone else can do it. Give me Angela Bassett miming to Tina Turner any day. At least I get to hear Tina Turner. Timothée Chalamet singing like Bob Dylan is a cute party trick that robs me of the only thing in the picture I care about: Bob Dylan.



Meanwhile on the street, ubiquitous tribute band posters are engaged in a shameless war of branding creep. Fleetwood Mac, the Eagles and Paul McCartney appear to be playing near me every other week, unless you’re stopped at the lights long enough to pull over, run across the road and read the fine print. Related Article The Verdict Murder on the dancefloor: Hollywood’s nightclub scenes are a crime “We went to an ’80s tribute fest at Port Beach,” a mate of mine texted from Perth last week. “Pretenders and Style Council were awesome ... Pat Benatar really went for it. Mellencamp had a cowboy hat and was still only four foot tall.” There’s a world of difference between singing somebody else’s songs and helping yourself to their name, logo and identity. “The Dire Straits Experience? I can assure you it’s not that,” Mark Knopfler grumbled last time we spoke. “I think they should do it on ice. Yeah,” he said, picturing the poster. “Sultans of Swing On Ice.” That sounded like an art project I could get behind. As long as nobody’s wearing sweatbands.

World.title: ‘You’re gonna have to kill me’: Alleged MP attacker in earlier police stand-off
World.content:
Updated PoliticsFederalHaines attack ‘You’re gonna have to kill me’: Alleged MP attacker in earlier police stand-off Shelby Brooks and Isabel McMillan Updated October 24, 2026 — 9:20pm ,first published 11:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. New vision has emerged showing the moments before two police officers arrested Wangaratta man Brendan Nugent four years before he allegedly mowed down independent MP Helen Haines. The vision, obtained by Nine News, shows now 43-year-old Brendan Nugent in a previous altercation with police. Loading Captured in 2022, Nugent is seen in the video speaking with two police officers while holding a wooden garden stake. “Now you’re gonna have to shoot me,” he tells officers in the video.



“You’re gonna have to kill me.” As he becomes increasingly agitated, the officers spray him with capsicum spray before Tasering him. Brendan Nugent in a stand-off with police in 2022. Nine News Nugent, who was 39 at the time of the video, was taken to hospital for assessment, but no charges were laid following the incident. It comes after Haines’ condition was downgraded from critical to serious but stable, five days after she was struck by a car in an alleged intentional attack outside her office in north-east Victoria.



The Indi MP had been in a critical condition since she was injured on Monday afternoon, which ultimately resulted in surgeons amputating both her legs. She remains in The Alfred hospital in Melbourne, which confirmed on Saturday morning that her condition had improved. Helen Haines lost both her legs in the alleged attack. Jason Robins Phil Haines, her husband of 40 years, said on Wednesday that the road to recovery for the MP and her family would be long and difficult. “Her heart is huge – she is a very compassionate, caring, loving person, incredibly supportive of all around her,” Phil Haines said in his address. Helen Haines’ husband, Phil Haines, with Governor-General Sam Mostyn at The Alfred on Wednesday. Justin McManus



“And her mind – she has the sharpest intellect. She has always had the most intense desire to learn, to read, to synthesise and to understand what’s going on. Floral tributes outside Helen Haines’ office in Wangaratta this week. Jason Robins “We are grateful and thankful that, at this stage, both her heart and her mind are in good shape.” Helen Haines, 65, was allegedly struck multiple times by a white Toyota LandCruiser on Monday outside her office in Wangaratta about 3.35pm. Her husband was joined on Wednesday by Governor-General Sam Mostyn as he described his wife as a “fighter”.



“But we know she is a fighter. She is a determined person to do her best, with our support and love, to recover,” Phil Haines said. “And that is what we hope for.” Related Article Haines attack Haines pursues a political experiment – that decent people can disagree. Has this attack changed that? Helen Haines was retrieving items from the boot of her car on Murphy Street when witnesses saw a LandCruiser perform a sharp U-turn and ram Haines against her own vehicle. The LandCruiser then reversed and rammed her again. Brendan Nugent, 43, has been charged with dangerous driving causing injury, intentionally causing injury and a Commonwealth offence of causing harm to a Commonwealth public official. He appeared in Wangaratta Magistrates’ Court on Wednesday. Police allege the incident was targeted. Nugent, who remains in custody, has since been charged with additional counts for cultivating cannabis and possessing cannabis.

World.title: AFLW round 11: Bruising win for Geelong, top spot the reward; Lions maul St Kilda
World.content:
Geelong have secured an AFLW qualifying final at “our house” with a 30-point win that also put a massive hole in Fremantle’s top-eight hopes.

There could be major injury ramifications out of Saturday’s physical clash at GMHBA Stadium, which the Cats won 9.10 (64) to 5.4 (34).

Rachel Kearns of the Cats collides with Emma O’Driscoll of the Dockers on Saturday. AFL Photos via Getty Images

A heavy collision early in the last quarter put Geelong’s Rachel Kearns out of the game, while Fremantle player Noa McNaughton needed help from two trainers when she also went off in the final term with an ankle injury.

Geelong forward Chantal Mason suffered an ugly cut to her face in a marking contest. Fremantle’s Aoife Healy, Aisling McCarthy and Kiara Bowers, plus Cats player Aishling Moloney all needed injury treatment during the game.

Fremantle started the clash in eighth spot and dropped to 10th. They will host seventh-placed Sydney in the last game of round 12 next Sunday, with the finals starting the following weekend.

The Cats led by 48 points early in the final term, after coach Mick Stinear urged in their three-quarter time huddle to finish the job at “our house”.

It was their fourth home win in a 10-game streak overall that has shot them to second on the ladder. Their only blemish was the 73-point loss in round one to two-time defending premiers North Melbourne, who will most likely again finish the regular season on top of the ladder.

Dynamic midfield duo Georgie Prespakis and Nina Morrison starred for the Cats, while Dockers defender Emma O’Driscoll capped her excellent game with a stunning contested mark in the final quarter.

AAP

World.title: Cox Plate as it happened: Stars align for Cosmic Crusader as trainer Andrea Leek makes history
World.content:
Andrea Leek almost had the perfect day. The only thing missing as she celebrated becoming the first woman to train the winner of the Cox Plate in 32 years, and the first at Flemington, was her husband by her side.

John Leek Jr was at a friend’s house, cheering from the couch as his wife’s horse Cosmic Crusader defied the firepower of the country’s biggest stables.

Jockey Willie Pike and trainer Andrea Leek were congratulated by owner Bob Peters (right) after Cosmic Crusader’s win. Getty Images

He was unable to walk through Flemington’s famous gates, having been rubbed out of racing and banned from all tracks for three years in August on a charge of attempting to stomach tube a horse.

He is also banned from staying in the family house at Nar Nar Goon North under the rules of racing because it is a training property.

“It’s devastating not having him here,” Leek said in the mounting yard after Cosmic Crusader and jockey William Pike had powered down the Flemington straight to edge out Chris Waller’s pair Birdman and Aeliana.

“He’s my biggest supporter, and he’s devastated he’s not able to be here.

“But he’ll still be in the background, and he’ll be celebrating with us tonight.”

The salute: William Pike after passing the finishing post. Getty Images

Leek, 53, took a moment away from the biggest win of her fledgling career to explain that her family were still working through the ramifications of her husband’s disqualifications.

“Look, he’s actually in one way happy that he’s been pushed into retirement,” she said of the 72-year-old former trainer.

“But not being able to be on the family farm is very hard, and not being able to have him at home, you know, being at home on my own is very, very difficult.

“So I think November 17, they (the Racing Victoria board) are looking at that and whether they can put in some safety parameters and he can be with his cows and dogs and just be in the house and not near any horses.

“We are really hoping that will prevail.”

Even in her husband’s absence, the historic Flemington victory belonged to Leek who joined Deirdre Stein (Rising Prince in 1985) and Moira Murdoch (Solvit, 1994) as the only female trainers to lift the Cox Plate.

Gai Waterhouse’s import Sir Delius ran sixth, leaving the champion still without a win in the race.

“I said before I feel like I’m an imposter,” Leek said of her name being etched into the record books. She can’t feel that way any longer.

While the former jumps jockey, and the first woman to ride the winner of the Great Eastern Steeple in 2004, might not have felt deserving of sharing the stage with the likes of Waller and Ciaron Maher, a victory in the $6 million Cox Plate changes everything.

One person who always believed in her undoubted potential was astute Western Australian owner Bob Peters.

The Perth billionaire chuckled when asked why he had shunned a well-worn path to the front doors of Waller and Maher in favour of entrusting Cosmic Crusader’s care to Leek.

Trainer Andrea Leek, with Mitchell Leek. Getty Images

“Oh, a lot of people told me I should do that when he (Cosmic Crusader) came over (from Perth),” Peters said.

“I said I’d probably gone a bit senile, but it’s worked out all right.”

Leek’s career boost came at the most unusual of times in the most unlikely of places.

She took a phone call from Peters during the depths of winter while watching the jumps racing at Terang.

“He said, ‘Now I’m thinking of sending you this horse. Are you prepared?’,” she recalled.

“And, you know, he gave me some guidelines that I had to do, and I said, ‘absolutely, I’m up for it’, and here we are, we’ve won the Cox Plate.”

Her appeal to a hands-on owner such as Peters was a lifetime working with horses and the rolling hills of her Nar Nar Goon North property, but the initial contact came through her husband.

“An owner I had earlier in my career, Jason, said to Bob, ‘there’s a guy, John Leek, and he trains things the way you like training so why don’t you have a look at his establishment’,” she said.

“Bob listened and said he’d send a horse, and then he sent a few. I was lucky enough six months ago when he rang me up and said ‘how about I give you a few horses’ and it has turned into this.”

Sharing the post-race jubilation was the punters’ pal, William Pike, known as The Wizard of the west to those who have clawed out of a luckless day by “backing Pikey in the last” at Ascot.

A long-time ally of Peters, he rode the perfect race.

He dropped Cosmic Crusader back to third last in a 14-horse field from the gates, stalking favourite Aeliana, as Land Legend set a hot pace and made his move as they turned for home in Flemington’s famous straight.

He powered over the top of Aeliana and Birdman in the last 50m, with Ceolwulf in fourth.

“I wanted him to be back because he (Cosmic Crusader) loves the thrill of the kill and getting past them. That’s what we do in trackwork,” Leek said.

“He’s always got a bunny to chase and that is what he loves. That is what he needed and he got it today.”

Overcome with the madness of the biggest win of his career, Pike stood up in the irons and screamed to the heavens.

“I had in my mind over the line, I’m not much of a saluter, I’m like ‘don’t salute, don’t salute’ and then the moment gets the better of you and you stand up and you salute and you carry on,” he said.

“It’s amazing, it’s infectious. (There’s a) big crowd, an iconic day – most likely the only ever Cox Plate to be run here – so it’s nice that we get to etch our name in there.”

All smiles: Jockey William Pike. Getty Images

Victory in the weight-for-age championship put to bed the disappointment Leek, Peters and Pike had felt after finishing fourth in last week’s Caulfield Cup.

“Maybe the Caulfield Cup was a slip in run. We were always hoping he was good enough for a Cox Plate, and he is,” Leek said.

“He’s an amazing horse. I said to Bob this morning that I think I had him a little bit flat for the Caulfield Cup and may have done too much on the Tuesday.

“He was better going into today. I knew going into today I had him cherry ripe. I was praying for rain but we didn’t get it. He was still too good.”

World.title: Models of behaviour start from the bottom up
World.content:
Russian to obey Russian oil is back on the market, new sanctions are sitting in a drawer, and Ukraine is under pressure. In the past, Moscow would have had to pay for such concessions with years of negotiations. This time, a few weeks in October and a single phone call were enough. Donald Trump is the best American president the Russians have ever had in the White House. Helena Kilingerova, Vermont

The enemy already here If Australia can spend $368 billion on nuclear submarines, surely we can find the money for 12 aerial tankers to defend us from an enemy already at our door (“ Parachute plan for growing fire threat ”, 23/10). Bushfires are getting more ferocious, and with longer, overlapping fire seasons here and overseas, we can no longer rely on leasing firefighting aircraft from abroad. A sovereign firefighting fleet and better early detection are essential. The Albanese government could make coal and gas corporations foot the bill (“Levy the polluters”, 23/10). Those who fuel the fires should help put them out. Sarah Brennan, Hawthorn

It starts with us Your correspondent (Letters, 23/10), rightly calls on politicians to lift the standard of parliamentary debate. “Common decency” should be the norm, he states; “personal attacks” should be avoided. I couldn’t agree more. My reaction to their closing thought is, however, more complicated. They argue that we “can’t be asking the public to ‘lower the temperature’ of debate when our elected representatives aren’t being seen to do the same. It starts from the top.” Respectfully, I beg to differ. I’m all for criticising politicians who build careers by stoking division, or who are too cowardly to call out the cynical tactics of their colleagues. But let’s remember that every one of them – including those who nakedly and unapologetically fan racial and ethnic hatred for their own tawdry benefit – are in parliament in the first place because we put them there. That’s what democracy literally means: “rule by the people”. We are responsible. All of us. It starts at the bottom. Nick Eckstein, Kangaroo Ground

To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au . Please include your home address and telephone number. No attachments, please include your letter in the body of the email. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published.

The right path

Columnist Waleed Aly draws attention to the worrying fact that violence begets violence, with the undeniable risk of political escalation (“After Haines attack, what happens is important”, 23/10). That’s exactly why I was particularly struck by the single hopeful aspect in reports of this appalling incident: the positive and peaceful intervention of bystanders. We should be forever grateful for the bravery and swift actions of those who prevented further damage.

The prime minister is right to call for us all to turn down the political heat; the shocking events in Wangaratta show that there can be non-violent ways of doing so.

Jenifer Nicholls, Windsor

Democracy, imperfect

People have long complained about parliamentary Question Time behaviour – when I was a child in the 1960s. Perhaps we need to look at this quaint procedure differently. Parliament is mostly tedious, procedural and long-winded albeit often about important matters. Question Time allows members to blow off a bit of steam asking and answering mostly predictable questions specially composed for political manoeuvring. Hubris is brought down to size, agendas exposed as folly and egos punctured. The great performers live on in our memory.

It’s the imperfectly human side of democracy.

Mark Freeman, Macleod

What a tawdry display

As has been pointed out by many letters contributors in recent days, I observed the appalling behaviour of many of our elected representatives. It wasn’t the members of minor parties or the independents, it was Labor and Coalition members. The Speaker of the House, was, I thought, extremely tolerant of the behaviour that would not have been accepted in any community forum or a classroom. Few were ejected.

The most disappointing aspect of this behaviour was that it was in front of the observation galleries filled with schoolchildren, but also notable Australians and overseas visitors who had been publicly acknowledged by the Speaker as being present and warmly welcomed.

So, knowing these people were there the two major parties obviously felt comfortable displaying their socially unacceptable behaviour. I was embarrassed. What a spectacle to be taken away and shared with the wider community and world.

Anthony Albanese is right to have been asking people to ″⁣dial it down″⁣ for quite a while now but obviously only when it applies to others.

Jenny Callaghan, Hawthorn

Ease up on the horn

As we seem to be undergoing a lack of respect throughout society, I suggest that we start by showing more tolerance on the roads. The prolonged horn blast for some inconvenience that would make the journey 10 seconds longer is not necessary. If this occurred between pedestrians on the footpath, a common response would be an apology and a smile.

The car horn should be only used to let people know that you are near or to let someone in from a side street. In Indonesia, there is a cacophony of beeps from motorcycles, but rarely in anger. Who knows, more tolerance on the roads might lead to more civility in society.

Geoff Goonan, Glen Iris

Focus on positives

While it’s been a brutal week, we need to look for the positives. It’s not enough to “turn the temperature down”, we need to have a discussion, at every level, about where Australians go from here. As outlined by “The Tipping Point” (24/10) it feels like we have reached a fork in the road and our actions will determine the future of our democracy. As mentioned in your article, “the warning signs have been accumulating” , online conspiracy theories, divisions created by war, anger in the community at rising costs of living, all these factors are leading us to a precipice.

I’m reminded of the quote, “The only thing necessary for the triumph of evil is for good men to do nothing”. Now is the time for grassroots action in every sector of our community. It starts with parents, teachers, neighbours, work colleagues, shopkeepers all having a conversation about what it means to be together on this planet.

Let’s focus on the positives.

Marisa Di Giacomo, Beaumaris

World.title: No October joy for Carlton stars on Cox Plate’s sojourn to Flemington
World.content:
SportRacingCox Plate No October joy for Carlton stars on Cox Plate’s sojourn to Flemington Andrew Wu and Danny Russell October 24, 2026 — 7:56pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Patrick Cripps has had his share of sporting heartbreak in August and September. He can now add October to the list. For a few fleeting moments, it looked as if Irish import Birdman was about to deliver one of Australian racing’s greatest prizes for the Carlton champion only for his Cox Plate dream to be dashed by a horse from his home state. As trainer Andrea Leek, who operates stables in Nar Nar Goon North, celebrated becoming the first woman in 32 years to win Australia’s weight-for-age championship with West Australian star Cosmic Crusader, the dual Brownlow winner and his Carlton crew were left to wonder what might have been. Trainer Andrea Leek poses with the trophy. Getty Images Blues champion Chris Judd let out a curse – his sense of frustration at coming so close shared throughout the Baggers Naggers syndicate, which also features former captains Marc Murphy and Sam Docherty, Sam Walsh and former Carlton midfielder Will Setterfield.



Birdman has taken the Blues brigade on a wild ride since their former line coach John Barker dropped the captain’s name as part of his spiel to get into prominent owner Ozzie Kheir’s exclusive racing circle two years ago. Kheir had initially bought Birdman with eyes on Melbourne Cup glory only for master Sydney trainer Chris Waller to change tack 12 months ago and focus on middle distances with the galloper. The salute: William Pike after passing the finishing post. Getty Images Unlike in football, where the pain of defeat is sharp, there were no heads hung in disappointment or walks of shame from the field. There is a prize for second in a Cox Plate, but the reasons to celebrate are deeper than an $800,000 cheque, of which Cripps and his football mates will take home only a micro-fraction.



“The whole thing about racing is bringing people together,” Cripps, who flew in from Perth on Friday for the race, said. “That’s what makes footy clubs special, and it’s what makes racing syndicates special – you bring people together. You make good memories together.” Jockey Ben Melham was given warm applause by Birdman’s ownership, of which the Baggers Naggers syndicate is one of many, as he returned to the mounting yard to deliver his race debrief. Then it was Kheir’s turn. He thanked his fellow owners for their “amazing support”.



Sam Walsh and Patrick Cripps. AFL Photos “It’s the hardest race to win, nearly in the world,” Kheir told them. Sent out an $11 chance by punters, Birdman looked the winner for a few strides after kicking strongly once clear at the 300-metre mark, only for Will Pike and Cosmic Crusader to collar him in the final 50 metres. “It was crazy,” Cripps said. “You don’t get many moments in life when you get a feeling like that. It’s pretty cool.” Cripps likened the thrilling finish to the race to that of a nailbiter in a big game at the MCG – with one major difference.



“You get the same buzz, the hard thing is in a race you don’t have control over the outcome,” Cripps said. “At least on the footy field, you can have some sort of control. If you ask anyone in racing, this is probably the grand final in racing. For us, it’s a privilege to be a part of it.” Barker, the manager of the syndicate, was a regular at Moonee Valley on Cox Plate day. His father recently became a life member of the Moonee Valley Racing Club. Related Article Spring racing carnival Cox Plate as it happened: Stars align for Cosmic Crusader as trainer Andrea Leek makes history “At the 150, I thought geezers, this can’t happen,” Barker, who played for Hawthorn, Brisbane and Fitzroy, said.



They are already eyeing another crack next year. “We’ve got a horse with a bit of talent, we’ve got a superstar trainer, so the future’s bright,” Barker said. “I’ll still be able to connect with these Carlton boys.“ Barker, Cripps, Judd, Murphy and Walsh are part of a smaller group in another syndicate, the Baggers Five, who recently acquired a share in Melbourne Cup hope James J Braddock. For them, redemption can come in November. Sports news, results and expert commentary.

World.title: ‘Everyone can do difficult things’: The surprise Sydney school offering Latin
World.content:
NationalNSWHSC ‘Everyone can do difficult things’: The surprise Sydney school offering Latin Christopher Harris October 24, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Andrew Gollan has had quite the career. After completing an arts degree in Latin and ancient Greek in the 1990s, he moved to America, became a US resident and worked in Silicon Valley as a software engineer. But he felt there was more to life than writing code. “I really wanted to do something which, I thought, was important,” he said. Year 12 Latin teacher from Caringbah High School Andrew Gollan. Sam Mooy After completing a master’s degree, where the language of instruction was Latin, he worked as a teacher across America before returning home to Australia. In 2019, he arrived at the Shire’s Caringbah High to relaunch the classical language at the school. Across NSW, Latin has had some difficult decades, falling from 1558 enrolments – about 8 per cent of all students in the first year of the HSC – in 1967 to 129 students this year.



It is a long, steep decline which some might describe as terminal, so it might seem strange that Caringbah High would revive the language. German had been on offer but struggled to attract students past year 8. The then-principal, who had his own fond memories of studying Latin, felt it might be a better fit. “That’s how he presented it to me at least,” Gollan says. Six years on, things are going well. Year 7 students entering high school do a medley of languages, a term each is spent on French, Japanese and Latin before choosing one. So far, Latin has enough students to fill two year 8 classes and a decent-sized year 9 class. “I lose a couple between year 9 and year 10,” says Gollan. The first cohort of year 7 students who commenced in 2021 sat the HSC Latin continuers exam this year. And six students who commenced the subject when in year 8 completed HSC exams last year. “It’s a big ask for a school like this to run classes that are this small, and to do it regularly enough so the kids know that they’ve got a decent pathway to the HSC and they’re not going to be, sort of, chopped off at the knees,” he says.



In NSW, it’s not just Latin in crisis but other languages too. In the 1960s, over a third of students learnt a language other than English. Now it is about 6 per cent. When the NSW curriculum was reviewed in 2020, it was recommended requiring every student to commence learning a second language in primary. But it was never adopted. Part of the problem is a lack of teachers – a French teacher at Newtown High pocketed a $20,000 sign-on bonus just for taking the job earlier this year. Year 12 Caringbah High School Latin students Henry He, Xander Ezzy and Sarah Napper after their HSC exam this week. Sam Mooy Students in public schools are aware of the challenges with running languages, including Caringbah High’s Sarah Napper, 18. She associates Latin with exclusive private and certain selective schools. By comparison, she says while her school is selective, it’s commonly perceived as a “mid-tier”. “I don’t think Latin should be exclusively taught in selective schools or these upper-tier private schools … I think everyone can do difficult things, and I think doing Latin has been really good for me,” she says.



While she enjoys the subject now, she says it was a steep learning curve. “It’s an analytical language, which basically means that instead of using many words like English to encode a meaning, it instead encodes meaning through changing the words itself,” she said. HSC enrolment data shows over the past 15 years, Latin has dropped from 176 students to 140 last year. But some schools have seen a small bounce in Latin enrolments, including some selective and certain private schools. Among them is all-boys school Shore, where eight students took the subject last year. Latin teacher Joanna Watkins likes to categorise students who choose the subject into three distinct groups. “The students with a maths brain enjoy the decoding of Latin,” she says.



There are the linguistic-inclined and then those with an interest in all aspects of ancient Roman culture. She’s also noticed something else. Related Article HSC ‘We are in crisis’: The HSC subject bleeding enrolments “More recently, we get kids who have been tutored in Latin before they come into year 7,” she said. She is unsure what exactly is driving that. “I can only guess that the parents are looking at schools which offer Latin,” she said. She linked the subject’s popularity with the school’s high performance in the subject, while students aspiring to study at universities overseas saw it as an advantage. “In the US, those universities tend to value Latin. Cambridge and Oxford have a strong tradition.”



Dr Robert Kowalski, who has taught Latin and Classical Greek at the University of Sydney and numerous private schools and now works as a tutor, said the demand was driven by parents. “I think they want to have the kids very well-educated. If you give the kids an opportunity, they will pick it up.” Related Article Editorial

Schools Language learning is the gift we must give our children The Herald's View Editorial Across Sydney, the biggest enrolment of students in Latin is Sydney Grammar. Its head of classical languages, Nathan Bottomley, said there were about six boys in his Latin class when he attended the school as a student in the 1980s. This year, there are almost 30. He said some believe it is useful when it comes to getting a high ATAR for university entry. “Sometimes they get the impression, which we try to dispel, that it scales very well.



“The kids who I teach are genuinely enthusiastic,” he said. But success comes with persistence and practice. “Students always want the trick. And the answer is always really boring – you just have to keep doing it. There’s something about being inquisitive in mastering a complex system, the pleasure of getting good at something.” The next biggest cohort of students in Latin is Sydney Girls followed by Meriden, which has also seen a bounce. Meriden principal Lisa Brown said it had strong enrolments in languages across the board and there was no special push to boost Latin enrolments. “You have to have an ability and a real interest in Latin to be able to persevere. It is not an easy subject, you can’t just have a go at it, there has to be a deep interest and an ability to work hard.”



St Joseph’s College in Hunters Hill normally has about five students enrolled in HSC Latin. Last year it was just one studying the subject. Director of teaching and learning Darren Frost said the school runs an “off-timetable” class in year 8. “The boys love it, compared to the other languages. It is a skill they can transfer, which is one of the big reasons we maintain it,” he said. When it comes to the HSC, he has noticed across the board a narrowing of the curriculum. “The breadth is so important for our society,” he said. “People are gaming the system, as opposed to what education is about, and the passion of learning is lost.”



Back at Caringbah High, Xander Ezzy, 18, knows there’s only a small community in Sydney where he can converse in Latin. But its power was connecting with people who lived thousands of years ago. “That was most enjoyable being able to connect it to a whole lifestyle that isn’t the lifestyle we have today,” he said. World.title: Inside the NBA’s luxury bubble, and why Joe Ingles was ready to leave
World.content:
SportBasketballNBA Inside the NBA’s luxury bubble, and why Joe Ingles was ready to leave Jon Pierik October 24, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

When Australian basketball great Joe Ingles was in the prime of his NBA career, the multimillion-dollar teams were flown across the US in chartered private jets. Having returned to the NBL after 12 seasons in America, he’s back to flying cattle class on Melbourne United’s road trips. The comedown in airline luxury from his days with the Utah Jazz, Milwaukee Bucks, Orlando Magic and Minnesota Timberwolves hasn’t fazed him, and that’s because he knows how relentless the NBA grind is on its athletes. Having his say: Joe Ingles is back playing in the NBL, but is also keeping a close eye on the new NBA season. Daniel Pockett Ingles is enjoying hanging out with Melbourne United teammates, coaches and staff in the Virgin club lounge, as he did on their trip to Perth before the 103-102 loss on Friday night. “We hang out in the lounge, grab a coffee, yeah, I mean, I got no complaints,” Ingles, 39, said.



Related Article NBA Ben Simmons was on the verge of an NBA comeback after 538 days. A serious injury has derailed it Never short of a quip, he added: “Will Larry [Kestelman, majority owner of the NBL] charter us a plane? Probably not. It’d be nice if he would, but no, I mean it’s cool, man.” The NBA can deliver a life of luxury. There are the eye-watering contracts that could soon even have the top players earning $US1 million ($1.4 million) per game, not to mention the endorsement riches on offer. Then there are the chartered flights, allowing players and staff to swiftly exit a city late at night and arrive at their next destination in the early hours of the morning. “The flying is cool, like it’s cool flying five nights a week and getting home at 4am,” Ingles said, sarcastically. “Is it a necessity? Yes, for the amount of games you play and the schedule. You, obviously, can’t sit in the Virgin lounge and wait until the next day and then fly into a city and play. Does it make it a f---load easier? Absolutely. You pull up to the airport, you walk on the plane, and you take off, kind of thing.



Related Article NBL ‘Have you not seen what I have made?’ Why Joe Ingles gave up $5.1 million to play in the NBL “Comfy seats, team nutritionists will have food on there. You can sleep if you want. You can play cards. There’s tables on there. It’s very luxurious in a way, I guess. But, obviously, in saying that, don’t get twisted looking from the outside looking in. The salaries, the big house, the chartered flights, whatever it is, it’s a brutal season and I think people take that for granted. “I did prior to being in the NBA. I used to sit there and think: ‘Well, of course, LeBron averages 30 a game. It’s LeBron.’ But when you see what it takes on the day to day, on your mind and your body, and the physicality of it, [Minnesota star] Ant Edwards is getting double-teamed every game four or five nights a week and is still putting up 30 points a game, it’s a true level of professionalism.” Ingles is enjoying life in the NBL, the competition which propelled him into NBA stardom, and a career which has netted him riches he never expected. But as the new NBA season got underway this week, there was a period of adjustment for the father of three who this season is also an ambassador for Prime Video, one of the league’s key broadcasters. “It was, obviously, a big part of my life for a long time, so it’s very different to be sitting on this end. But yeah, excited to sit back and watch it and watch how it plays out from here and watch the NBA Cup and watch the play-in tournament,” Ingles said.



“All these different things that I’ve I’ve been involved in for so long – it’ll be weird, but it’ll be nice to be on the other side.” Ingles’ primary focus remains on United, who on Sunday host the defending champions Sydney Kings at John Cain Arena, giving him a chance to catch up with great mate and fellow former NBA player Matthew Dellavedova, who is nursing a calf issue. View post on X United have had a stuttering start to a season, with new coach Jacob Chancefinding his way, while injuries, particularly to marksman Chris Goulding, have hurt. Ingles has delivered as the veteran play-making forward, who can nail a long jump shot – and can still trash talk with the best. Friday night’s loss to the Wildcats stung, leaving United at 3-5, wasting a huge game from hometown boy Luke Travers, who had 26 points, nine rebounds and five assists.



Import Josh Oduro was strong with 22 points, four rebounds and two blocks, point guard Cole Anthony had 19 points and three assists before fouling out late, while Ingles had 11 points, eight assists, six rebounds and three steals. “We’ve got a bunch of games left, and you want to be playing pretty well a bit later in the season,” Ingles said. Time to make a run: Joe Ingles and Melbourne United need to get busy if they are to make the NBL play-offs. Getty Images “But we, obviously, have to build towards that, too, so there’s no excuse from that point. We should be, and can, play better.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: ‘Give them a go’: Liberal candidate advises vote for One Nation in upper house
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsVictoriaVictorian election ‘Give them a go’: Liberal candidate advises vote for One Nation in upper house Kieran Rooney and Angus Delaney October 24, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

A Liberal candidate in a key battleground seat has been caught out encouraging people to vote for One Nation in the upper house while campaigning in the electorate that is considered vulnerable to Pauline Hanson’s party. Five weeks out from the state election, the incident is a fresh headache for Opposition Leader Jess Wilson as she asks voters to elect a Coalition government outright in the face of Labor attacks tying the conservative political movements together. Liberal candidate Simmone Cottom ran for the federal seat of Hawke in 2025 and is now running in Sunbury. Justin McManus The Liberal Party has also been forced to intervene after a sitting MP planned to appear as a guest speaker at a fundraiser for an independent candidate, despite her party having endorsed a candidate to run in the same seat. In a recording made last weekend, which has been obtained by The Age, the Liberal candidate for Sunbury Simmone Cottom was asked by a voter about her position on the possibility of a coalition with One Nation.



Simmone Cottom campaigning in Sunbury last weekend. Facebook “Both the leaders, [One Nation leader] Warren Pickering and Jess [Wilson] have said we want to try and win in our own right,” she replied. “A lot of people have asked me about preferences. That’s open until November 9 for people to nominate to be candidates and then our preferences will be done.” When pressed further, Cottom said: “I’m encouraging people to change the government. In the lower house, vote Liberals and in the upper house, vote One Nation.” The voter then asked: “So you’re advocating One Nation?”



Cottom replied: “Lower house, Liberals, and if you really want One Nation, give them a go in the upper house.” When the voter made it clear he was not interested in supporting Hanson’s party, Cottom focused more on her own party, reiterating that they wanted to “win in our own right”. “I personally don’t have [a relationship with One Nation] ... We believe that we can win and not need them.” In a statement to The Age on Saturday, Cottom said she regretted her comments. “I shouldn’t have said it,” she said. “It’s not our position. We want Victorians voting Liberal and Nationals in both houses.”



Wilson, who has faced repeated questions about how her party will deal with One Nation, has consistently told voters that the only way to remove the three-term Labor government is to vote for her Coalition MPs. As the major parties shift into campaign mode, The Age can also reveal that Liberal upper house MP Ann-Marie Hermans has been advertised as a guest speaker for a fundraiser for Caroline White – an independent candidate running in Clarinda – alongside Libertarian MP David Limbrick and Albert Park independent Adrian King. The fundraising event for Clarina independent Caroline White, where Liberal MP Ann-Marie Hermans was advertised as a guest speaker. White is running against John Paganis, the Liberal candidate for the seat held by Labor’s Meng Heang Tak. “If I was John Paganis, I’d be super annoyed and super confused,” another Liberal candidate said, speaking on the condition of anonymity to detail internal matters.



Hermans’ attendance was cancelled on Saturday after The Age contacted the party to ask if it was appropriate. “Ann-Marie will not be attending this event,” a Liberal Party spokesperson said. “She is supporting John Paganis, the Liberal candidate for Clarinda, and is focused on helping elect a Liberal and Nationals government on 28 November.” Liberal MP Ann-Marie Hermans will not be attending the fundraiser, a party spokesperson said. Justin McManus Hermans was contacted for comment.



White also ran for Clarinda in 2022 and preferenced the Liberal candidate, an arrangement the party matched. Both put Labor’s candidate last on their how-to-vote cards. Related Article Victorian election Deal or no deal? How the major parties are tackling the minority government risk Cottom, the Sunbury candidate, has run for parliament twice before – in the same seat at the 2022 state election, and in the federal seat of Hawke at last year’s federal election. In April 2025, members of the Plymouth Brethren Christian Church – formerly known as the Exclusive Brethren – were identified wearing Liberal T-shirts and assisting Cottom’s campaign at an early voting booth in Melton. Sunbury is currently held by Labor’s Josh Bull on a typically safe margin of 6.4 per cent, but it is considered in play as the government braces for a sizeable swing against them, particularly in such outer suburban electorates that are considered vulnerable amid the rise of One Nation.



The Age’s Resolve Political Monitor has One Nation with a primary vote of 23 per cent. If that is replicated in the upper house, Hanson’s party would be in a strong position to hold the balance of power, forcing whichever party that forms government to negotiate with them to pass legislation. Wilson has ruled out a formal coalition with One Nation, saying there would be “no deals”. But she has sidestepped questions about how she would deal with Hanson’s party in the event that she required the support of its MPs to form government. In turn, Labor strategists have built their campaign around the claim that Wilson will not be able to claim power without One Nation’s support, using every media release and press conference to warn of the possibility of a “Liberal-One Nation” government. The latest Resolve poll has the Coalition with a primary vote of 28 per cent and Labor on 25 per cent. These numbers would most likely deliver a change of government – given the Coalition is expected to be favoured by One Nation preferences – but it remains unclear whether Wilson could form a majority in her own right.



A primary vote under 30 per cent has traditionally been diabolical for a party seeking to govern in its own right, but the rise of One Nation has led to widespread uncertainty about the outcome of one of the nation’s first true three-cornered contests. The final result in many seats will come down to which party runs third and where its preferences flow. The May by-election in Nepean was the first Victorian example of how this phenomenon could play out. Liberal candidate Anthony Marsh was comfortably elected when One Nation’s Darren Hercus ran third, with 77.5 per cent of One Nation voters preferencing Marsh above independent Tracee Hutchison.
